F. BIBO Stability (Bounded-Input Bounded-Output)

A system is BIBO stable if every bounded input \(|x(t)| le M_x < \infty\) produces an output that remains strictly bounded for all time:

\[ |y(t)| le M_y < \infty \quad \text{for all } t, \text{ whenever } |x(t)| le M_x < \infty \]

For an LTI system with impulse response \(h(t)\), BIBO stability is mathematically equivalent to the impulse response being absolutely integrable (CT) or absolutely summable (DT):

\[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |h(t)|,dt < \infty \qquad \text{or} \qquad \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} |h[n]| < \infty \]

3. Step-by-Step Diagnostic Framework for System Properties

System EquationMemory?Causal?Linear?Time-Invariant?BIBO Stable?Invertible?
\(y(t) = x(2t)\)DynamicNo (future for \(t>0\))YesNo (Time-variant)YesYes: \(x(t) = y(t/2)\)
\(y(t) = x(t) + 5\)StaticYesNo (fails zero-input)YesYesYes: \(x(t) = y(t) - 5\)
\(y(t) = t x(t)\)StaticYesYesNo (coefficient \(t\))No (for \(x(t)=1\), \(y(t)=t o \infty\))Yes (for \(t \neq 0\))
\(y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^t x(\tau)d\tau\)DynamicYesYesYesNo (for \(x(t)=u(t)\), \(y(t)=t o \infty\))Yes: \(x(t) = \frac{dy}{dt}\)
\(y[n] = x^2[n]\)StaticYesNo (fails additivity)YesYesNo (sign ambiguous)

4. Worked Numerical Examples

Problem 1: Rigorous Linearity & Time-Invariance Proof

Analyze \(y(t) = x(t) \cos(\omega_c t)\) (an ideal balanced modulator / mixer).

1. Linearity: Let input x_3(t) = a x_1(t) + b x_2(t). y_3(t) = x_3(t) cos(ω_c t) = [a x_1(t) + b x_2(t)] cos(ω_c t) = a x_1(t) cos(ω_c t) + b x_2(t) cos(ω_c t) = a y_1(t) + b y_2(t). ===> Strictly LINEAR. 2. Time Invariance: Let input be delayed by t_0: x_d(t) = x(t - t_0). Output for delayed input: y(t, t_0) = x_d(t) cos(ω_c t) = x(t - t_0) cos(ω_c t). Now, delay the original output y(t) by t_0: y(t - t_0) = x(t - t_0) cos(ω_c (t - t_0)). Notice that y(t, t_0) ≠ y(t - t_0) because cos(ω_c t) ≠ cos(ω_c(t - t_0)). ===> Strictly TIME-VARIANT.

Problem 2: BIBO Stability Test of an Integrator vs. Decaying Exponential

Determine the stability of (a) an ideal integrator \(h(t) = u(t)\), (b) a first-order lowpass filter \(h(t) = e^{-3t}u(t)\).

(a) For h(t) = u(t): ∫_{-∞}^∞ |h(t)| dt = ∫₀^∞ 1 dt = [t]₀^∞ = ∞. Integral diverges to infinity ===> UNSTABLE (e.g. bounded step input u(t) gives unbounded ramp output t). (b) For h(t) = e^(-3t) u(t): ∫_{-∞}^∞ |h(t)| dt = ∫₀^∞ e^(-3t) dt = [-1/3 e^(-3t)]₀^∞ = 0 - (-1/3) = 1/3 < ∞. Integral is finite (1/3) ===> BIBO STABLE.
Common Mistake — The Affine Trap: Engineers frequently mistake the affine equation \(y(t) = m x(t) + c\) for a linear system because it graphs as a straight line. In linear systems theory, linearity strictly requires passing through the origin. When \(c \neq 0\), \(\mathcal{T}{0} = c \neq 0\). Doubling the input gives \(2 m x(t) + c \neq 2(m x(t) + c)\). It fails both additivity and homogeneity!
Placement Trap — The Time-Compression Causality Trap: In interviews at Intel, Analog Devices, and Texas Instruments, students are asked: "Is the time-compressor \(y(t) = x(2t)\) causal?" Many candidates say: "Yes, it only scales time by 2." This is wrong! Evaluate at \(t = 1\): \(y(1) = x(2)\). The output at present time \(t=1\) requires knowledge of the input at future time \(t=2\). Hence, any time-scaling system \(y(t) = x(at)\) with \(|a| > 1\) is non-causal for \(t > 0\).

Quick Revision Summary

  • Memoryless: Output at \(t\) depends only on input at \(t\). Purely resistive circuits are static.
  • Invertible: Distinct inputs produce distinct outputs. Zero-input produces zero-output.
  • Causal: Output at present instant depends only on present and past inputs. No future anticipation.
  • Linear: Satisfies superposition \(\mathcal{T}{a x_1 + b x_2} = a y_1 + b y_2\). \(\mathcal{T}{0} = 0\) is mandatory.
  • Time-Invariant: \(\mathcal{T}{x(t - t_0)} = y(t - t_0)\). Time scaling and time-dependent coefficients destroy time-invariance.
  • BIBO Stability: Every bounded input yields a bounded output. For LTI systems: \(\int |h(t)|dt < \infty\).

emt-coordinate-systems.title: Coordinate Systems for Electromagnetic Theory
emt-coordinate-systems.body:
In electromagnetic field theory, boundary conditions, charge distributions, and current geometries dictate the choice of spatial coordinate systems. Physical laws are coordinate-independent, yet solving Maxwell's equations analytically is only tractable when coordinate surfaces align with physical boundaries—such as planes in Cartesian coordinates, coaxial cylinders in cylindrical coordinates, or concentric spheres in spherical coordinates. Mastering the metric coefficients, differential elements (length, surface, volume), and point-and-vector transformation matrices is the foundational prerequisite for all electrostatic, magnetostatic, and wave propagation problems.

1. Prerequisite & Mathematical Concept Anchor

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Coordinate Systems for Electromagnetic Theory

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Coordinate Systems for Electromagnetic Theory.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Vector analysis in Euclidean 3-space \(\mathbb{R}^3\) relies on orthogonal curvilinear coordinates \((u_1, u_2, u_3)\). In an orthogonal system, the coordinate surfaces \(u_i = \text{constant}\) intersect at mutually perpendicular angles, meaning the unit base vectors satisfy \(\mathbf{a}_{u_i} \cdot \mathbf{a}_{u_j} = \delta_{ij}\) (Kronecker delta) and form a right-handed triad \(\mathbf{a}_{u_1} \times \mathbf{a}_{u_2} = \mathbf{a}_{u_3}\).

2. Cartesian Coordinate System \((x, y, z)\)

The Cartesian system uses three mutually orthogonal linear axes with metric scale factors \(h_1 = h_x = 1\), \(h_2 = h_y = 1\), and \(h_3 = h_z = 1\). Any position vector is: \[ \mathbf{r} = x\mathbf{a}_x + y\mathbf{a}_y + z\mathbf{a}_z \] The ranges of the coordinates are \(-\infty < x < \infty\), \(-\infty < y < \infty\), and \(-\infty < z < \infty\). The base vectors \(\mathbf{a}_x, \mathbf{a}_y, \mathbf{a}_z\) are globally constant in magnitude and direction throughout space, which implies \(\frac{\partial \mathbf{a}_x}{\partial x} = \mathbf{0}\), greatly simplifying spatial derivatives.

3. Cylindrical Coordinate System \((\rho, \phi, z)\)

Cylindrical coordinates represent a point by the radial distance \(\rho\) from the \(z\)-axis, the azimuthal angle \(\phi\) measured from the \(+x\)-axis in the \(xy\)-plane, and the axial height \(z\). The coordinate ranges are: \[ 0 le \rho < \infty, \quad 0 le \phi < 2\pi, \quad -\infty < z < \infty \] The scale factors are \(h_\rho = 1\), \(h_\phi = \rho\), and \(h_z = 1\). Crucially, the unit vectors \(\mathbf{a}_\rho\) and \(\mathbf{a}_\phi\) vary with position: \[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{a}_\rho}{\partial \phi} = \mathbf{a}_\phi, \quad \frac{\partial \mathbf{a}_\phi}{\partial \phi} = -\mathbf{a}_\rho \] The position vector in cylindrical coordinates is \(\mathbf{r} = \rho\mathbf{a}_\rho + z\mathbf{a}_z\) (note that \(\mathbf{a}_\phi\) does not appear explicitly because \(\mathbf{r}\) is in the meridian plane containing the point).

4. Spherical Coordinate System \((r, \theta, \phi)\)

Spherical coordinates describe a point by the radial distance \(r\) from the origin, the polar/colatitude angle \(\theta\) from the \(+z\)-axis, and the azimuthal angle \(\phi\) from the \(+x\)-axis in the \(xy\)-plane: \[ 0 le r < \infty, \quad 0 le \theta le \pi, \quad 0 le \phi < 2\pi \] The scale factors are \(h_r = 1\), \(h_\theta = r\), and \(h_\phi = r\sin\theta\). The position vector is simply: \[ \mathbf{r} = r\mathbf{a}_r \] All three unit vectors \(\mathbf{a}_r, \mathbf{a}_\theta, \mathbf{a}_\phi\) are functions of spatial position \((\theta, \phi)\).

5. Differential Elements: Length, Surface Area, and Volume

For general orthogonal coordinates with scale factors \(h_1, h_2, h_3\):

  • Differential Length Vector: \(d\mathbf{l} = h_1 du_1\mathbf{a}_1 + h_2 du_2\mathbf{a}_2 + h_3 du_3\mathbf{a}_3\)
  • Cartesian: \(d\mathbf{l} = dx\mathbf{a}_x + dy\mathbf{a}_y + dz\mathbf{a}_z\)
  • Cylindrical: \(d\mathbf{l} = d\rho\mathbf{a}_\rho + \rho d\phi\mathbf{a}_\phi + dz\mathbf{a}_z\)
  • Spherical: \(d\mathbf{l} = dr\mathbf{a}_r + r d\theta\mathbf{a}_\theta + r\sin\theta d\phi\mathbf{a}_\phi\)
Differential normal areas and volume elements follow directly:
  • Cartesian Volume: \(dv = dx, dy, dz\)
  • Cylindrical Volume: \(dv = \rho, d\rho, d\phi, dz\)
  • Spherical Volume: \(dv = r^2\sin\theta, dr, d\theta, d\phi\)

6. Point Conversion between Coordinate Systems

To transform the coordinates of a physical point \(P\):

  • Cartesian to Cylindrical: \(\rho = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\), \(\phi = \arctan(y/x)\), \(z = z\).
  • Cylindrical to Cartesian: \(x = \rho\cos\phi\), \(y = \rho\sin\phi\), \(z = z\).
  • Cartesian to Spherical: \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\), \(\theta = \arccos(z/r) = \arctan(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}/z)\), \(\phi = \arctan(y/x)\).
  • Spherical to Cartesian: \(x = r\sin\theta\cos\phi\), \(y = r\sin\theta\sin\phi\), \(z = r\cos\theta\).

7. Transformation of a Vector from Cartesian to Cylindrical

A vector \(\mathbf{A} = A_x\mathbf{a}_x + A_y\mathbf{a}_y + A_z\mathbf{a}_z\) is projected onto the cylindrical unit vectors via scalar products: \[ A_\rho = \mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{a}_\rho = A_x(\mathbf{a}_x \cdot \mathbf{a}_\rho) + A_y(\mathbf{a}_y \cdot \mathbf{a}_\rho) \] Evaluating direction cosines: \(\mathbf{a}_x \cdot \mathbf{a}_\rho = \cos\phi\), \(\mathbf{a}_y \cdot \mathbf{a}_\rho = \sin\phi\), \(\mathbf{a}_x \cdot \mathbf{a}_\phi = -\sin\phi\), \(\mathbf{a}_y \cdot \mathbf{a}_\phi = \cos\phi\). In matrix form: \[ \begin{bmatrix} A_\rho A_\phi A_z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\phi & \sin\phi & 0 -\sin\phi & \cos\phi & 0 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} A_x A_y A_z \end{bmatrix} \] The inverse transformation uses the orthogonal transpose matrix: \[ \begin{bmatrix} A_x A_y A_z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\phi & -\sin\phi & 0 \sin\phi & \cos\phi & 0 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} A_\rho A_\phi A_z \end{bmatrix} \]

8. Transformation of a Vector from Cartesian to Spherical

Projecting \(\mathbf{A}\) onto \(\mathbf{a}_r, \mathbf{a}_\theta, \mathbf{a}_\phi\): \[ \begin{bmatrix} A_r A_\theta A_\phi \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta\cos\phi & \sin\theta\sin\phi & \cos\theta \cos\theta\cos\phi & \cos\theta\sin\phi & -\sin\theta -\sin\phi & \cos\phi & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} A_x A_y A_z \end{bmatrix} \] Because the transformation matrix \(\mathbf{T}\) is orthogonal, \(\mathbf{T}^{-1} = \mathbf{T}^T\): \[ \begin{bmatrix} A_x A_y A_z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta\cos\phi & \cos\theta\cos\phi & -\sin\phi \sin\theta\sin\phi & \cos\theta\sin\phi & \cos\phi \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} A_r A_\theta A_\phi \end{bmatrix} \]

9. Worked Numerical Example: Vector Transformation and Invariance

Problem: Given point \(P(-2, 6, 3)\) and vector \(\mathbf{A} = y\mathbf{a}_x + (x+z)\mathbf{a}_y\), determine \(\mathbf{A}\) in cylindrical coordinates at point \(P\), and verify that its magnitude is invariant.

Solution:
1. Evaluate point \(P\) cylindrical variables: \[ \rho = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{40} \approx 6.325 \] \[ \phi = \arctan(6 / -2) = 180^\circ - 71.565^\circ = 108.435^\circ \] \[ \cos\phi = \frac{-2}{\sqrt{40}} = -0.3162, \quad \sin\phi = \frac{6}{\sqrt{40}} = 0.9487 \]
2. Evaluate Cartesian components at \(P\): \[ A_x = y = 6, \quad A_y = x + z = -2 + 3 = 1, \quad A_z = 0 \] Magnitude in Cartesian: \(|\mathbf{A}| = \sqrt{6^2 + 1^2 + 0^2} = \sqrt{37} \approx 6.0828\).
3. Compute cylindrical components: \[ A_\rho = A_x\cos\phi + A_y\sin\phi = 6(-0.3162) + 1(0.9487) = -1.8974 + 0.9487 = -0.9487 \] \[ A_\phi = -A_x\sin\phi + A_y\cos\phi = -6(0.9487) + 1(-0.3162) = -5.6922 - 0.3162 = -6.0084 \] \[ A_z = 0 \] \[ \mathbf{A} = -0.9487\mathbf{a}_\rho - 6.0084\mathbf{a}_\phi \] Magnitude in Cylindrical: \(|\mathbf{A}| = \sqrt{(-0.9487)^2 + (-6.0084)^2} = \sqrt{0.9000 + 36.1009} = \sqrt{37.0009} \approx 6.0828\). The magnitude is exactly invariant under orthogonal coordinate transformation.

Exam Pitfall & Angle Traps:
  • Quadrant Disregard: When computing \(\phi = \arctan(y/x)\), simply typing \(\arctan(y/x)\) on a calculator yields values in \([-90^\circ, 90^\circ]\). For points with \(x < 0\), you must add \(\pi\) (\(180^\circ\)) to place \(\phi\) in the correct quadrant (II or III).
  • Polar vs. Azimuthal Mixing: In spherical coordinates, \(\theta\) is measured from the \(+z\)-axis (\(0 le \theta le \pi\)), while \(\phi\) is measured in the \(xy\)-plane (\(0 le \phi < 2\pi\)). Swapping \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) leads to incorrect differential surface integrals.
  • Treating Curvilinear Unit Vectors as Constants: Never pull \(\mathbf{a}_\rho, \mathbf{a}_\phi, \mathbf{a}_r, \mathbf{a}_\theta\) outside of spatial integrals or derivatives. For example, \(\int_0^{2\pi} \mathbf{a}_\rho d\phi = \mathbf{0}\), not \(2\pi\mathbf{a}_\rho\).

10. Real-World Engineering Applications

  • Power Transmission & Underground Cables: Coaxial high-voltage AC/DC cables possess cylindrical symmetry. Using cylindrical coordinates reduces the Laplace equation \( abla^2 V = 0\) to \(\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{d}{d\rho}\left(\rho\frac{dV}{d\rho}\right) = 0\), yielding direct logarithmic potential and radial electric field distributions.
  • Satellite Radar & Antenna Radiation: Antenna radiation patterns, radar cross-sections (RCS), and satellite telemetry naturally decouple in spherical coordinates, where the far-field Poynting vector is purely radial: \(\mathbf{S} = \frac{|\mathbf{E}|^2}{2\eta}\mathbf{a}_r\).
  • Planar Microstrip & PCB Trace Design: Stripline and microstrip waveguides on multilayer printed circuit boards conform to planar Cartesian boundaries for automated finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) meshing.

11. Computational Simulation & Grid Meshing

In computational electromagnetics (CEM) codes such as CST Microwave Studio, ANSYS HFSS, and COMSOL Multiphysics:

  • Structured Cartesian Grids: FDTD grids divide space into Yee cells of size \(\Delta x \times \Delta y \times \Delta z\).
  • Body-Fitted Curvilinear Grids: Cylindrical and spherical geometries avoid "staircasing" numerical reflection artifacts by formulating metric tensors \(g_{ij} = \sum_{k} \frac{\partial x_k}{\partial u_i}\frac{\partial x_k}{\partial u_j}\).

Fundamental Transformation and Metric Summary

  • Cartesian Scale Factors: \(h_x = 1, h_y = 1, h_z = 1\); \(dv = dx,dy,dz\)
  • Cylindrical Scale Factors: \(h_\rho = 1, h_\phi = \rho, h_z = 1\); \(dv = \rho,d\rho,d\phi,dz\)
  • Spherical Scale Factors: \(h_r = 1, h_\theta = r, h_\phi = r\sin\theta\); \(dv = r^2\sin\theta,dr,d\theta,d\phi\)
  • Cylindrical \( o\) Cartesian Vector: \(A_x = A_\rho\cos\phi - A_\phi\sin\phi\); \(A_y = A_\rho\sin\phi + A_\phi\cos\phi\); \(A_z = A_z\)
  • Spherical \( o\) Cartesian Vector: \(A_x = A_r\sin\theta\cos\phi + A_\theta\cos\theta\cos\phi - A_\phi\sin\phi\)
  • Vector Invariance: \(\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{A} = A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2 = A_\rho^2 + A_\phi^2 + A_z^2 = A_r^2 + A_\theta^2 + A_\phi^2\)

12. Step-by-Step Analytical Derivation: Surface Integration of Sphere

To demonstrate differential element integration, consider the total surface area of a sphere of radius \(R\): \[ S = \int_{\phi=0}^{2\pi} \int_{\theta=0}^{\pi} dS_r = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^\pi (R, d\theta)(R\sin\theta, d\phi) = R^2 \int_0^{2\pi} d\phi \int_0^\pi \sin\theta, d\theta \] Evaluating the integrals: \[ \int_0^{2\pi} d\phi = 2\pi, \quad \int_0^\pi \sin\theta, d\theta = [-\cos\theta]_0^\pi = -(-1 - 1) = 2 \] \[ S = R^2 (2\pi)(2) = 4\pi R^2 \] Similarly, integrating volume: \[ V = \int_0^R r^2 dr \int_0^\pi \sin\theta, d\theta \int_0^{2\pi} d\phi = \left(\frac{R^3}{3}\right)(2)(2\pi) = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \]

13. GATE / IES Exam Tips & Shortcuts

  • When evaluating \(\int \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{l}\) around a circle of radius \(a\) in the \(z=0\) plane, use \(d\mathbf{l} = a, d\phi,\mathbf{a}_\phi\). The integral selects only the \(A_\phi\) component!
  • To find normal unit vectors to coordinate surfaces: \(\mathbf{a}_n = \pm \frac{ abla f}{| abla f|}\). For a cylinder \(\rho = c\), \(\mathbf{a}_n = \mathbf{a}_\rho\); for a sphere \(r = c\), \(\mathbf{a}_n = \mathbf{a}_r\).
  • If an electric field is purely radial in cylindrical coordinates \(\mathbf{E} = E_\rho(\rho)\mathbf{a}_\rho\), in Cartesian coordinates its components are \(E_x = E_\rho\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\) and \(E_y = E_\rho\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\).

14. Special Cases & Asymptotic Coordinates

As \(r o \infty\), spherical waves locally approximate planar waves over any finite aperture \(\Delta S\). The local spherical wave surface with curvature \(1/R\) asymptotically approaches a planar wavefront with normal vector \(\mathbf{k} = k\mathbf{a}_r\), where \(\mathbf{a}_r\) acts identically to the Cartesian propagation vector \(\mathbf{a}_z\).

15. Cross-Topic Bridges & Forward Look

Coordinate transformation and differential volumes directly underpin Gauss's Law (\(oint \mathbf{D} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = Q_{\text{encl}}\)), Ampere's Law (\(oint \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = I_{\text{encl}}\)), and the separation-of-variables solutions to Laplace's equation \( abla^2 V = 0\) across coaxial cables, spherical capacitors, and circular waveguides in Modules II, III, and V.

emt-vector-calculus.title: Gradient, Divergence, Curl, and the Two Integral Theorems
emt-vector-calculus.body:
Vector calculus constitutes the operational language of classical electrodynamics. Electric and magnetic fields are spatial vector fields whose fundamental sources (charges and currents) and spatial variations are mathematically governed by differential operators: the gradient (\( abla V\)) which converts scalar potentials into force fields, the divergence (\( abla \cdot \mathbf{D}\)) which maps net field expansion to enclosed sources, and the curl (\( abla \times \mathbf{H}\)) which characterizes field circulation driven by vortex sources. Gauss's Divergence Theorem and Stokes' Theorem form the exact mathematical bridges that link local differential equations to macroscopic integral formulations.

1. Prerequisite & Mathematical Concept Anchor

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Gradient, Divergence, Curl, and the Two Integral Theorems

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Gradient, Divergence, Curl, and the Two Integral Theorems.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

The Del symbolic operator \( abla\) in three dimensions operates on scalar fields \(V(x,y,z)\) and vector fields \(\mathbf{A}(x,y,z)\). In Cartesian coordinates, the vector differential operator is: \[ abla = \mathbf{a}_x\frac{\partial}{\partial x} + \mathbf{a}_y\frac{\partial}{\partial y} + \mathbf{a}_z\frac{\partial}{\partial z} \] Because basis vectors in curvilinear coordinates rotate with spatial position, \( abla\) cannot simply be written with partial derivatives of components; it must incorporate metric scale factors \(h_1, h_2, h_3\).

2. Gradient of a Scalar Field \( abla V\) & Physical Interpretation

The gradient of a scalar field \(V\) represents the maximum rate of spatial change of \(V\) per unit distance, and points in the direction of maximum spatial increase: \[ dV = abla V \cdot d\mathbf{l} = | abla V|, dl \cos\alpha \] Thus, \(dV/dl\) is maximized when \(\alpha = 0\), proving that \( abla V\) is orthogonal to equipotential surfaces \(V(x,y,z) = \text{constant}\). In electrostatics, the electric field is the negative gradient of electric potential: \[ \mathbf{E} = - abla V \] The negative sign signifies that electric flux lines naturally point from regions of higher potential toward regions of lower potential.

3. Divergence of a Vector Field \( abla \cdot \mathbf{A}\) & Physical Meaning

The divergence of a vector field \(\mathbf{A}\) at point \(P\) is defined as the net outward flux of \(\mathbf{A}\) per unit volume as the volume shrinks to zero: \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{A} = lim_{\Delta v o 0} \frac{oint_S \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}{\Delta v} \] Physical Interpretation:

  • \( abla \cdot \mathbf{A} > 0\): Point \(P\) is a source (net positive field lines diverge outward, e.g., positive electric charge \( abla \cdot \mathbf{D} = ho_v\)).
  • \( abla \cdot \mathbf{A} < 0\): Point \(P\) is a sink (field lines converge inward, e.g., negative charge).
  • \( abla \cdot \mathbf{A} = 0\): The field is solenoidal; lines of flux neither start nor terminate, e.g., magnetic fields \( abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\).

4. Curl of a Vector Field \( abla \times \mathbf{A}\) & Circulation

The curl of a vector field \(\mathbf{A}\) at point \(P\) is an axial vector representing the maximum line integral (circulation) of \(\mathbf{A}\) per unit area as the enclosing contour shrinks to zero: \[ ( abla \times \mathbf{A})_n = lim_{\Delta S o 0} \frac{oint_L \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{l}}{\Delta S} \] Physical Interpretation:

  • \( abla \times \mathbf{A} e \mathbf{0}\): The field possesses rotational vorticity or circulation around an axis, driven by vortex sources (e.g., Ampere's law \( abla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J}\)).
  • \( abla \times \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{0}\): The field is irrotational or conservative (e.g., electrostatic field \( abla \times \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{0}\)). Any irrotational field can be expressed as the gradient of a scalar potential: \(\mathbf{A} = - abla V\).

5. Curvilinear Formulations for Del Operators

Using metric scale factors \((h_1, h_2, h_3)\):

  • Cylindrical \((\rho, \phi, z)\): \((1, \rho, 1)\) \[ abla V = \frac{\partial V}{\partial \rho}\mathbf{a}_\rho + \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial V}{\partial \phi}\mathbf{a}_\phi + \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\mathbf{a}_z \] \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{A} = \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}(\rho A_\rho) + \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial A_\phi}{\partial \phi} + \frac{\partial A_z}{\partial z} \] \[ abla \times \mathbf{A} = \frac{1}{\rho}\begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{a}_\rho & \rho\mathbf{a}_\phi & \mathbf{a}_z \frac{\partial}{\partial \rho} & \frac{\partial}{\partial \phi} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} A_\rho & \rho A_\phi & A_z \end{vmatrix} \]
  • Spherical \((r, \theta, \phi)\): \((1, r, r\sin\theta)\) \[ abla V = \frac{\partial V}{\partial r}\mathbf{a}_r + \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial V}{\partial \theta}\mathbf{a}_\theta + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial V}{\partial \phi}\mathbf{a}_\phi \] \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{A} = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(r^2 A_r) + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}(\sin\theta A_\theta) + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial A_\phi}{\partial \phi} \] \[ abla \times \mathbf{A} = \frac{1}{r^2\sin\theta}\begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{a}_r & r\mathbf{a}_\theta & r\sin\theta\mathbf{a}_\phi \frac{\partial}{\partial r} & \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} & \frac{\partial}{\partial \phi} A_r & r A_\theta & r\sin\theta A_\phi \end{vmatrix} \]

6. The Laplacian Operator \( abla^2\)

The scalar Laplacian is the divergence of the gradient: \( abla^2 V = abla \cdot ( abla V)\).

  • Cartesian: \( abla^2 V = \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial z^2}\)
  • Cylindrical: \( abla^2 V = \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}\left(\rho\frac{\partial V}{\partial \rho}\right) + \frac{1}{\rho^2}\frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial \phi^2} + \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial z^2}\)
  • Spherical: \( abla^2 V = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^2\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial V}{\partial \theta}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial \phi^2}\)
The vector Laplacian satisfies: \( abla^2 \mathbf{A} = abla( abla \cdot \mathbf{A}) - abla \times ( abla \times \mathbf{A})\).

7. Fundamental Vector Null Identities

Two mathematical identities hold identically for any smooth field:

  1. The Curl of any Gradient is Identically Zero: \[ abla \times ( abla V) = \mathbf{0} \] Consequence: Any irrotational vector field (\( abla \times \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{0}\)) can be written as \(\mathbf{E} = - abla V\).
  2. The Divergence of any Curl is Identically Zero: \[ abla \cdot ( abla \times \mathbf{A}) = 0 \] Consequence: Any solenoidal vector field (\( abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\)) can be written as the curl of a magnetic vector potential: \(\mathbf{B} = abla \times \mathbf{A}\).

8. Simulation Examples & Physical Field Visualizations

In numerical electromagnetic field solvers (such as MATLAB PDE Toolbox or Python FEniCS):

  • Fluid Paddle-Wheel Simulation for Curl: Place an infinitesimal paddle wheel in a vector velocity field \(\mathbf{v}\). If the paddle rotates about its axis, the field has non-zero curl at that point: \(\mathbf{\omega} = \frac{1}{2} abla \times \mathbf{v}\). In electrostatic fields, the paddle never rotates.
  • Expanding Bubble Simulation for Divergence: Enclose a volume with a virtual permeable elastic membrane. If more fluid mass emerges than enters, \( abla \cdot \mathbf{J} < 0\) indicates fluid depletion or negative source rate. For point charges, field vectors diverge radially outward like spikes on a hedgehog.
  • Topographical Contour Simulation for Gradient: A 2D electric potential surface \(V(x,y)\) plotted as elevation contours: the gradient vectors \( abla V\) are always strictly orthogonal to the contour lines, pointing straight uphill along the steepest incline.

9. Gauss-Ostrogradsky Divergence Theorem

The Divergence Theorem states that the total outward flux of a vector field \(\mathbf{A}\) through a closed surface \(S\) is equal to the volume integral of the divergence of \(\mathbf{A}\) over the enclosed volume \(v\): \[ oint_S \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_v ( abla \cdot \mathbf{A}), dv \] Significance: Converts complex closed-surface flux integrals into straightforward volume integrals, and proves that Gauss's Law in integral form (\(oint \mathbf{D} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = Q_{\text{encl}}\)) is mathematically identical to differential form (\( abla \cdot \mathbf{D} = ho_v\)).

10. Stokes' Circulation Theorem

Stokes' Theorem states that the circulation of a vector field \(\mathbf{A}\) around a closed contour \(L\) equals the surface integral of the curl of \(\mathbf{A}\) over any open surface \(S\) bounded by \(L\): \[ oint_L \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \int_S ( abla \times \mathbf{A}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} \] Significance: Directly links Ampere's Circuital Law (\(oint \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = I_{\text{encl}}\)) to its differential form (\( abla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J}\)), and Faraday's Law of induction.

11. Worked Numerical Example: Verification of Divergence Theorem

Problem: Given vector field \(\mathbf{F} = x\mathbf{a}_x + y\mathbf{a}_y + z\mathbf{a}_z\), evaluate \(oint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\) over a sphere of radius \(R = 2\text{ m}\) centered at the origin: (a) using surface integration, and (b) using the Divergence Theorem.

Solution:
Method A (Surface Integral): On the spherical surface, \(r = R = 2\). The differential surface normal is \(d\mathbf{S} = R^2\sin\theta, d\theta, d\phi,\mathbf{a}_r\). Note that in spherical coordinates, \(\mathbf{F} = x\mathbf{a}_x + y\mathbf{a}_y + z\mathbf{a}_z = r\mathbf{a}_r\). At \(r = 2\), \(\mathbf{F} = 2\mathbf{a}_r\). \[ oint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^\pi (2\mathbf{a}_r) \cdot (2^2\sin\theta, d\theta, d\phi,\mathbf{a}_r) = 8 \int_0^{2\pi} d\phi \int_0^\pi \sin\theta, d\theta = 8(2\pi)(2) = 32\pi \]
Method B (Divergence Theorem): Compute \( abla \cdot \mathbf{F}\) in Cartesian coordinates: \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial z} = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 \] Apply volume integral: \[ \int_v ( abla \cdot \mathbf{F}), dv = \int_v 3, dv = 3 \times \text{Volume of sphere} = 3 \left(\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3\right) = 4\pi (2^3) = 32\pi \] Both methods yield exactly \(32\pi \approx 100.53\), verifying the Divergence Theorem.

12. Worked Numerical Example: Verification of Stokes' Theorem

Problem: Given \(\mathbf{A} = y\mathbf{a}_x - x\mathbf{a}_y\), verify Stokes' Theorem for a circular contour of radius \(\rho = 3\) on the \(z = 0\) plane, oriented counter-clockwise.

Solution:
1. Line Integral: Along the circular path, \(x = 3\cos\phi\), \(y = 3\sin\phi\), \(z = 0\). \(d\mathbf{l} = \rho, d\phi,\mathbf{a}_\phi = 3, d\phi,\mathbf{a}_\phi\). In cylindrical coordinates, \(\mathbf{A} = y\mathbf{a}_x - x\mathbf{a}_y = (3\sin\phi)\mathbf{a}_x - (3\cos\phi)\mathbf{a}_y\). Projecting onto \(\mathbf{a}_\phi = -\sin\phi\mathbf{a}_x + \cos\phi\mathbf{a}_y\): \[ A_\phi = \mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{a}_\phi = -3\sin^2\phi - 3\cos^2\phi = -3 \] \[ oint_L \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \int_0^{2\pi} (-3)(3, d\phi) = -9(2\pi) = -18\pi \]
2. Surface Integral of Curl: \[ abla \times \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{a}_z \left(\frac{\partial(-x)}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial(y)}{\partial y}\right) = \mathbf{a}_z(-1 - 1) = -2\mathbf{a}_z \] The surface is the circular disk of radius 3 in the \(z=0\) plane with normal \(d\mathbf{S} = \rho, d\rho, d\phi,\mathbf{a}_z\). \[ \int_S ( abla \times \mathbf{A}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_0^{2\pi} d\phi \int_0^3 (-2\mathbf{a}_z) \cdot (\mathbf{a}_z \rho, d\rho) = -2(2\pi)\left[\frac{\rho^2}{2}\right]_0^3 = -4\pi(4.5) = -18\pi \] Both results match identically (\(-18\pi\)), confirming Stokes' theorem.

Exam Pitfalls & Integral Traps:
  • Closed vs. Open Surfaces: The Divergence Theorem applies only to closed surfaces bounding a finite volume. Stokes' Theorem applies to an open surface bounded by a closed contour. Applying Divergence Theorem to an open hemisphere without adding the base cap is a severe exam error.
  • Right-Hand Orientation in Stokes' Theorem: The contour direction \(d\mathbf{l}\) and surface normal \(d\mathbf{S}\) are strictly tied by the right-hand rule: fingers curl along the contour, thumb points in the direction of \(+d\mathbf{S}\).
  • Forgetting \(\rho\) in Cylindrical Divergence: \( abla \cdot \mathbf{A} e \frac{\partial A_\rho}{\partial \rho} + dots\); the factor of \(\rho\) must be multiplied before differentiation: \(\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}(\rho A_\rho)\).

Fundamental Vector Calculus Equations

  • Gradient: \(dV = abla V \cdot d\mathbf{l}\); \(\mathbf{E} = - abla V\)
  • Divergence Theorem: \(oint_S \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_v ( abla \cdot \mathbf{A}), dv\)
  • Stokes' Theorem: \(oint_L \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \int_S ( abla \times \mathbf{A}) \cdot d\mathbf{S}\)
  • Null Identities: \( abla \times ( abla V) = \mathbf{0}\) (irrotational); \( abla \cdot ( abla \times \mathbf{A}) = 0\) (solenoidal)
  • Vector Laplacian: \( abla^2 \mathbf{A} = abla( abla \cdot \mathbf{A}) - abla \times ( abla \times \mathbf{A})\)
  • Helmholtz's Theorem: Any vector field is uniquely determined by its divergence (sources) and its curl (vortices) plus boundary conditions.

13. Real-World Engineering Applications

  • Electric Machine Core Design: Magnetic fields inside transformer laminations and motor air gaps are governed by \( abla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J}\) and \( abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\). Eddy current losses are minimized by laminating cores parallel to flux lines to block curl paths.
  • High-Voltage Insulator Optimization: In power substations, dielectric breakdown occurs where electric potential gradient \(| abla V|\) exceeds the dielectric strength of air (\(\approx 30\text{ kV/cm}\)). Insulator sheds are geometrically contoured to equalize equipotential spacing.
  • Electromagnetic Wave Radiation: In antenna design, the wave equation \( abla^2 \mathbf{E} - \mu\epsilon\frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2} = \mathbf{0}\) is derived directly from the vector curl curl identity.

14. GATE / IES Exam Tips & Shortcuts

  • If a question asks for \(oint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\) over a closed surface and \(\mathbf{F}\) can be written as \( abla \times \mathbf{G}\), the answer is immediately zero because \( abla \cdot ( abla \times \mathbf{G}) equiv 0\).
  • If asked whether a vector field can represent an electrostatic field, test \( abla \times \mathbf{E}\). If \( abla \times \mathbf{E} e \mathbf{0}\), it cannot be electrostatic!
  • If \( abla \cdot \mathbf{B} e 0\), it implies magnetic monopoles, violating Maxwell's second equation.

15. Cross-Topic Bridges & Forward Look

The divergence and curl operators directly produce all four of Maxwell's equations in Module III, Poisson's and Laplace's boundary equations in Module II, and the Helmholtz wave equations in Module IV.

📐 Vector Calculus Operators in Orthogonal Coordinate Systems

$$\text{Cartesian Gradient: } abla V = \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} \hat{a}_x + \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \hat{a}_y + \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} \hat{a}_z$$ $$\text{Cartesian Divergence: } abla \cdot \vec{A} = \frac{\partial A_x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial A_y}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial A_z}{\partial z}$$ $$\text{Cartesian Curl: } abla \times \vec{A} = \left(\frac{\partial A_z}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial A_y}{\partial z}\right)\hat{a}_x + \left(\frac{\partial A_x}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial A_z}{\partial x}\right)\hat{a}_y + \left(\frac{\partial A_y}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial A_x}{\partial y}\right)\hat{a}_z$$

emt-coulombs-law-fields.title: Coulomb's Law, Electric Field Intensity, and Continuous Charge Distributions
emt-coulombs-law-fields.body:
Electrostatics deals with spatial electric fields produced by static charges at rest. Formulated experimentally by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785, the electrostatic force between point charges is the fundamental empirical law from which electric field intensity, field superposition, and continuous charge distributions are developed. Continuous spatial charge distributions—volume charges in dielectric media, surface charge layers on conductors, and line charges along thin conductors—form the physical framework for analyzing electric flux density \(\mathbf{D}\), permittivity, and high-voltage electrical insulation.

1. Prerequisite & Mathematical Concept Anchor

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Coulomb's Law, Electric Field Intensity, and Continuous Charge Distributions

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Coulomb's Law, Electric Field Intensity, and Continuous Charge Distributions.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Electrostatic analysis requires mastering vector addition, the principle of linear superposition, and spatial integration over curves, surfaces, and volumes. The fundamental position vector from source charge at \(\mathbf{r}'(x', y', z')\) to observation field point at \(\mathbf{r}(x, y, z)\) is the separation vector: \[ \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}', \quad R = |\mathbf{R}| = \sqrt{(x-x')^2 + (y-y')^2 + (z-z')^2} \] The unit vector directed from source to field point is \(\mathbf{a}_R = \frac{\mathbf{R}}{R} = \frac{\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'}{|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|}\).

2. Coulomb's Law & Electric Field Intensity

Coulomb's Law states that the electrostatic force between two stationary point charges \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) separated by distance \(R\) in a linear, isotropic, homogeneous medium with permittivity \(\epsilon = \epsilon_0\epsilon_r\) is: \[ \mathbf{F}_{12} = \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4\pi\epsilon R^2}\mathbf{a}_{12} \] where \(\epsilon_0 \approx 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m} \approx \frac{1}{36\pi \times 10^9}\text{ F/m}\) is the vacuum permittivity.
The Electric Field Intensity \(\mathbf{E}\) at an observation point is the force experienced per unit positive test charge \(q_t\) as \(q_t o 0\): \[ \mathbf{E} = lim_{q_t o 0} \frac{\mathbf{F}}{q_t} = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon R^2}\mathbf{a}_R \quad [\text{V/m or N/C}] \] For an assembly of \(N\) discrete point charges \(Q_k\) located at \(\mathbf{r}_k\), the total field is obtained by the superposition principle: \[ \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{k=1}^N \frac{Q_k (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_k)}{4\pi\epsilon |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_k|^3} \]

3. Electric Field Due to Line Charge Distribution

When charge is distributed along a line with linear charge density \( ho_L\text{ (C/m)}\), the differential charge element is \(dQ = ho_L dl'\). The total electric field is: \[ \mathbf{E} = \int_L \frac{ ho_L dl'}{4\pi\epsilon R^2}\mathbf{a}_R \] Infinite Straight Line Charge along the \(z\)-axis: By symmetry, the axial (\(E_z\)) and azimuthal (\(E_\phi\)) components cancel identically, leaving only a radial field: \[ \mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_L}{2\pi\epsilon \rho}\mathbf{a}_\rho \] where \(\rho\) is the perpendicular distance from the line charge. Notice the \(1/\rho\) spatial decay rate, which is slower than the \(1/R^2\) decay of a point charge.

4. Finite Line Charge Formulation

For a straight line charge of uniform density \( ho_L\) extending along the \(z\)-axis from \(z = A\) to \(z = B\), observing at point \(P(\rho, \phi, 0)\): \[ E_\rho = \frac{ ho_L}{4\pi\epsilon \rho}(\sinalpha_2 - \sinalpha_1), \quad E_z = -\frac{ ho_L}{4\pi\epsilon \rho}(\cosalpha_2 - \cosalpha_1) \] where \(alpha_1\) and \(alpha_2\) are the subtended angles from the observation normal to the endpoints of the wire. As the line becomes infinitely long (\(alpha_1 o -\pi/2, alpha_2 o +\pi/2\)), \(E_z o 0\) and \(E_\rho = \frac{ ho_L}{2\pi\epsilon \rho}\).

5. Electric Field Due to Surface Charge Distribution

For a surface charge with density \( ho_S\text{ (C/m}^2)\), \(dQ = ho_S dS'\): \[ \mathbf{E} = \int_S \frac{ ho_S dS'}{4\pi\epsilon R^2}\mathbf{a}_R \] Infinite Uniform Plane Sheet of Charge in the \(z = 0\) Plane: Dividing the plane into concentric rings of radius \(r'\) and integrating: \[ \mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_S}{2\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_n \] where \(\mathbf{a}_n\) is the unit normal vector directed away from the charged sheet into the half-space of the observation point: \[ \mathbf{a}_n = \begin{cases} +\mathbf{a}_z, & z > 0 -\mathbf{a}_z, & z < 0 \end{cases} \] Fundamental Consequence: The electric field of an infinite sheet of charge is completely independent of distance from the sheet!

6. Two Parallel Oppositely Charged Infinite Sheets

Consider sheet 1 at \(z = d\) with \(+ ho_S\) and sheet 2 at \(z = 0\) with \(- ho_S\):

  • For \(z > d\): \(\mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_S}{2\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_z - \frac{ ho_S}{2\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_z = \mathbf{0}\)
  • For \(z < 0\): \(\mathbf{E} = -\frac{ ho_S}{2\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_z + \frac{ ho_S}{2\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_z = \mathbf{0}\)
  • Between the plates (\(0 < z < d\)): \(\mathbf{E} = -\frac{ ho_S}{2\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_z - \frac{ ho_S}{2\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_z = -\frac{ ho_S}{\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_z\)
This uniform electric field \(\mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_S}{\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_n\) is the operational foundation of parallel-plate capacitors.

7. Electric Flux and Electric Flux Density \(\mathbf{D}\)

Michael Faraday introduced the concept of electric flux \(\Psi\) (measured in Coulombs) originating from positive charges and terminating on negative charges. Faraday proved that one Coulomb of charge emits exactly one Coulomb of electric flux: \[ \Psi = Q \] The Electric Flux Density (or electric displacement) \(\mathbf{D}\) is the vector flux per unit surface area: \[ \Psi = \int_S \mathbf{D} \cdot d\mathbf{S} \] In a linear, isotropic medium: \[ \mathbf{D} = \epsilon \mathbf{E} = \epsilon_0\epsilon_r \mathbf{E} \quad [\text{C/m}^2] \] Crucially, \(\mathbf{D}\) depends only on the charge configuration and geometry, and is independent of the dielectric medium permittivity \(\epsilon\), whereas \(\mathbf{E}\) decreases inversely with relative permittivity \(\epsilon_r\).

8. Volume Charge Distribution

For a continuous 3D volume charge density \( ho_v\text{ (C/m}^3)\), the differential charge is \(dQ = ho_v dv'\): \[ \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{v'} \frac{ ho_v(\mathbf{r}')(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}')}{4\pi\epsilon |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|^3}, dv' \] \[ \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{v'} \frac{ ho_v(\mathbf{r}')(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}')}{4\pi |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|^3}, dv' \]

9. Worked Numerical Example: Line Charge Electric Field and Flux Density

Problem: An infinitely long line charge with uniform density \( ho_L = 25\text{ nC/m}\) lies along the line \(x = 2, z = 1\) in free space. Find the electric field intensity \(\mathbf{E}\) and flux density \(\mathbf{D}\) at point \(P(4, 5, 1)\).

Solution:
1. Identify the shortest perpendicular vector \(\mathbf{R}\) from the line to the observation point: Since the line is parallel to the \(y\)-axis (\(x=2, z=1\)), the point on the line closest to \(P(4, 5, 1)\) is \(P'(2, 5, 1)\). \[ \mathbf{R} = (4-2)\mathbf{a}_x + (5-5)\mathbf{a}_y + (1-1)\mathbf{a}_z = 2\mathbf{a}_x \] Perpendicular distance: \(\rho = |\mathbf{R}| = 2\text{ m}\). Unit vector: \(\mathbf{a}_\rho = \mathbf{a}_x\).
2. Compute \(\mathbf{E}\): \[ \mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_L}{2\pi\epsilon_0 \rho}\mathbf{a}_\rho = \frac{25 \times 10^{-9}}{2\pi \times (8.854 \times 10^{-12}) \times 2}\mathbf{a}_x = \frac{25 \times 10^{-9}}{1.1126 \times 10^{-10}}\mathbf{a}_x = 224.7\mathbf{a}_x\text{ V/m} \] Using the constant \(\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2\): \[ \mathbf{E} = 2 \times (9 \times 10^9) \times \frac{25 \times 10^{-9}}{2}\mathbf{a}_x = 225\mathbf{a}_x\text{ V/m} \]
3. Compute \(\mathbf{D}\): \[ \mathbf{D} = \epsilon_0 \mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_L}{2\pi \rho}\mathbf{a}_\rho = \frac{25 \times 10^{-9}}{2\pi \times 2}\mathbf{a}_x = \frac{25 \times 10^{-9}}{12.566}\mathbf{a}_x = 1.989 \times 10^{-9}\mathbf{a}_x\text{ C/m}^2 = 1.99\mathbf{a}_x\text{ nC/m}^2 \]

Exam Pitfalls & Charge Distribution Traps:
  • Shortest Perpendicular Distance in Line Charge: Never use the origin-to-point distance for \(\rho\). \(\rho\) is strictly the perpendicular distance from the line charge axis to the observation point.
  • Sign of Normal Vector in Surface Charge: For an infinite sheet at \(z = z_0\), \(\mathbf{a}_n = +\mathbf{a}_z\) for \(z > z_0\), but \(\mathbf{a}_n = -\mathbf{a}_z\) for \(z < z_0\). Forgetting to reverse \(\mathbf{a}_n\) when crossing the sheet produces catastrophic sign errors.
  • Mixing Units of \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{D}\): \(\mathbf{E}\) is in \(\text{V/m}\) (\(\text{N/C}\)); \(\mathbf{D}\) is in \(\text{C/m}^2\). They differ dimensionally by permittivity \(\epsilon\text{ (F/m)}\).

Coulomb's Law and Field Intensity Formulas

  • Point Charge: \(\mathbf{E} = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon R^2}\mathbf{a}_R\); \(\mathbf{D} = \frac{Q}{4\pi R^2}\mathbf{a}_R\)
  • Infinite Line Charge: \(\mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_L}{2\pi\epsilon \rho}\mathbf{a}_\rho\); \(\mathbf{D} = \frac{ ho_L}{2\pi \rho}\mathbf{a}_\rho\)
  • Infinite Surface Sheet: \(\mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_S}{2\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_n\); \(\mathbf{D} = \frac{ ho_S}{2}\mathbf{a}_n\)
  • Parallel Plate Capacitor: \(\mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_S}{\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_n\); \(\mathbf{D} = ho_S \mathbf{a}_n\)
  • Constitutive Relation: \(\mathbf{D} = \epsilon_0 \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P} = \epsilon_0\epsilon_r \mathbf{E}\)

10. Real-World Engineering Applications

  • Electrostatic Precipitators (ESP): Industrial coal plants utilize high-voltage corona discharge wires (\(-50\text{ to }-100\text{ kV}\)) creating high radial fields \(\mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_L}{2\pi\epsilon \rho}\mathbf{a}_\rho\) that ionize flue gas, charge airborne fly ash particles, and collect them onto grounded collector plates with >99% efficiency.
  • Xerography & Laser Printers: A photoconductive drum is electrostatically charged uniformly with surface charge density \( ho_S\) using a corona wire (corotron). Laser light selectively discharges image pixels, allowing toner particles to adhere electrostatically.
  • Overhead Power Line Electric Field Safety: Extra-High-Voltage (EHV 400 kV / 765 kV) transmission conductors create ground-level electric fields calculated using image line charges to verify that field levels beneath the span remain below occupational health thresholds (\(< 5\text{ to }10\text{ kV/m}\)).

11. Laboratory & Diagnostic Methods

Electric fields are experimentally measured using vibrating-vane field mills and non-contact capacitive probes (Kelvin probes). In dielectric oil testing, breakdown voltage is measured between spherical electrodes separated by \(2.5\text{ mm}\) per IEC 60156 standards to verify insulating oil withstand strength (\(> 30\text{ kV}\)).

12. Computational Boundary Element Method (BEM)

The integral formulation \(\mathbf{E} = \int \frac{ ho_S dS'}{4\pi\epsilon R^2}\mathbf{a}_R\) forms the core of the Method of Moments (MoM) and Boundary Element Method (BEM). Charge densities on metallic conductors are discretized into planar patches, reducing the integral equation into an invertible dense linear system \([Z][I] = [V]\).

13. Special Cases: Finite Strip and Ring of Charge

For a circular ring of radius \(a\) carrying total charge \(Q\) in the \(z = 0\) plane, the field on the \(z\)-axis is: \[ \mathbf{E} = \frac{Q z}{4\pi\epsilon (a^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}\mathbf{a}_z \] Notice that at the center \(z = 0\), \(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{0}\) by circular symmetry. For \(z gg a\), the field asymptotically becomes \(\mathbf{E} \approx \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon z^2}\mathbf{a}_z\), behaving exactly like a point charge.

14. GATE / IES Exam Tips & Shortcuts

  • The spatial decay exponents: Point charge \(propto 1/R^2\); Line charge \(propto 1/R\); Sheet of charge \(propto R^0\) (constant); Electric Dipole \(propto 1/R^3\). Remembering this sequence solves multiple-choice questions instantly!
  • When finding the field from multiple infinite sheets, write the step functions for \(\mathbf{a}_n\) for each sheet and sum region-by-region.
  • For any closed surface in a uniform field \(\mathbf{E}\), the net outward flux is always identically zero: \(oint \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\).

15. Cross-Topic Bridges & Forward Look

The concept of electric flux density \(\mathbf{D}\) and continuous charge integration bridges directly into Gauss's Law in the next lesson, where geometric symmetry enables determining \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{D}\) without tedious Coulomb vector integration.

emt-gauss-law-potential.title: Gauss's Law, Electric Potential, Conservative Fields, and Equipotential Surfaces
emt-gauss-law-potential.body:
Gauss's Law is the first of Maxwell's four fundamental electromagnetic field equations, encapsulating the deep physical truth that electric charges act as the sole divergent sources and sinks of electrostatic flux. Complementing Gauss's flux law is the conservative nature of electrostatic fields: because electrostatic forces do zero net work around any closed contour, the vector field \(\mathbf{E}\) can be completely described by a single scalar potential function \(V\). Electric potential, potential gradient, and equipotential surfaces provide the ultimate analytical framework for electrostatic energy storage, insulation grading, and high-voltage circuit design.

1. Prerequisite & Mathematical Concept Anchor

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Gauss's Law, Electric Potential, Conservative Fields, and Equipotential Surfaces

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Gauss's Law, Electric Potential, Conservative Fields, and Equipotential Surfaces.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Gauss's Law requires an understanding of closed surface integrals and spatial symmetry. Electric potential requires line integration of conservative vector fields. If a vector field satisfies \(oint_L \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = 0\), the line integral between two points \(A\) and \(B\) is path-independent: \[ V_{AB} = V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} \] The negative sign represents the external work required to move a positive unit test charge against the electric field.

2. Gauss's Law: Integral and Differential Forms

Integral Form: The net outward electric flux \(\Psi\) passing through any closed Gaussian surface \(S\) is equal to the total net charge enclosed within that surface: \[ oint_S \mathbf{D} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = Q_{\text{encl}} = \int_v ho_v, dv \] Applying the Divergence Theorem to the left-hand side: \[ oint_S \mathbf{D} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_v ( abla \cdot \mathbf{D}), dv = \int_v ho_v, dv \] Since this equality holds for an arbitrary volume \(v\), the integrands must be identical at every point in space: \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{D} = ho_v \quad \text{(Maxwell's First Equation)} \] In a linear, homogeneous, and isotropic medium where \(\mathbf{D} = \epsilon\mathbf{E}\): \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_v}{\epsilon} \]

3. Classical Applications of Gauss's Law

To apply Gauss's Law analytically, a symmetric Gaussian surface is chosen such that \(\mathbf{D}\) is everywhere either strictly normal to the surface (with constant magnitude) or strictly tangential (\(\mathbf{D} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\)):

  • Point Charge \(Q\): Concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius \(r\). \[ D_r (4\pi r^2) = Q implies \mathbf{D} = \frac{Q}{4\pi r^2}\mathbf{a}_r, \quad \mathbf{E} = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon r^2}\mathbf{a}_r \]
  • Uniformly Charged Solid Sphere of Radius \(a\) (total charge \(Q\)):
    • Outside (\(r ge a\)): \(D_r (4\pi r^2) = Q implies \mathbf{E} = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon r^2}\mathbf{a}_r\)
    • Inside (\(r < a\)): \(Q_{\text{encl}} = ho_v \left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right) = Q\left(\frac{r^3}{a^3}\right)\). \[ D_r (4\pi r^2) = Q\frac{r^3}{a^3} implies \mathbf{E} = \frac{Q r}{4\pi\epsilon a^3}\mathbf{a}_r = \frac{ ho_v r}{3\epsilon}\mathbf{a}_r \]
    The field grows linearly with \(r\) from 0 at the center to a peak at \(r = a\), then decays as \(1/r^2\).
  • Infinite Coaxial Cable (inner radius \(a\), outer radius \(b\)): For \(a < \rho < b\), choose a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius \(\rho\) and length \(L\): \[ D_\rho (2\pi\rho L) = ho_L L implies \mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_L}{2\pi\epsilon \rho}\mathbf{a}_\rho \]

4. Conservative Property of Electrostatic Fields

Because electrostatic Coulomb forces are central and obey inverse-square laws, moving a charge in a complete closed loop returns it to its initial state with zero net energy change: \[ oint_L \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = 0 \] Applying Stokes' Theorem: \[ oint_L \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \int_S ( abla \times \mathbf{E}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0 implies abla \times \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{0} \] Thus, all electrostatic fields are strictly conservative and irrotational.

5. Electric Potential and Potential Reference

The electric potential \(V\) at a point \(\mathbf{r}\) relative to a reference zero at infinity is: \[ V(\mathbf{r}) = -\int_\infty^\mathbf{r} \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} \]

  • Potential of a Point Charge \(Q\) at Origin: \[ V(r) = -\int_\infty^r \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon r'^2}, dr' = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon r} \]
  • Potential of an Assembly of \(N\) Point Charges: \[ V(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{k=1}^N \frac{Q_k}{4\pi\epsilon |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_k|} \]
  • Potential of Continuous Volume Charge: \[ V(\mathbf{r}) = \int_v \frac{ ho_v(\mathbf{r}'), dv'}{4\pi\epsilon |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|} \]

6. Potential Gradient & Relationship to Electric Field

From the differential work definition, the change in potential \(dV\) along an arbitrary displacement \(d\mathbf{l}\) is: \[ dV = - \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} \] By the directional derivative definition of the gradient: \[ dV = abla V \cdot d\mathbf{l} \] Equating these two expressions for an arbitrary \(d\mathbf{l}\) yields: \[ \mathbf{E} = - abla V \] The electric field vector at any point is identically equal to the negative gradient of the electric potential.

7. Equipotential Surfaces

An equipotential surface is a geometric locus of spatial points having identical potential: \(V(x, y, z) = C\). Fundamental Properties:

  1. Along an equipotential surface, \(dV = 0\), which means \(d\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{E} = 0\). Therefore, electric field lines are everywhere strictly perpendicular to equipotential surfaces.
  2. No work is done in moving any electric charge along an equipotential surface.
  3. The surface of any ideal electrical conductor in static equilibrium is an equipotential surface.
  4. Equipotential surfaces never intersect each other (as potential is a single-valued function of position).

8. Potential of a Uniformly Charged Solid Sphere

Consider a solid dielectric sphere of radius \(a\) with uniform charge density \( ho_v\) (total charge \(Q\)):

  • Outside (\(r ge a\)): \(V(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon r}\)
  • On the surface (\(r = a\)): \(V_a = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon a}\)
  • Inside (\(r < a\)): \[ V(r) = V_a - \int_a^r E_r, dr' = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon a} - \int_a^r \frac{Q r'}{4\pi\epsilon a^3}, dr' = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon a} - \frac{Q}{8\pi\epsilon a^3}(r^2 - a^2) \] \[ V(r) = \frac{Q}{8\pi\epsilon a}\left(3 - \frac{r^2}{a^2}\right) \]
At the origin (\(r = 0\)), the potential is \(V(0) = \frac{3}{2}\frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon a} = 1.5 V_a\).

9. Worked Numerical Example: Potential Gradient and Electric Field

Problem: In a region of free space, the electric potential is given by \(V(x, y, z) = 2x^2 y - 5z\text{ volts}\). Find: (a) The electric field intensity \(\mathbf{E}\) at point \(P(-4, 3, 6)\), (b) The magnitude of \(\mathbf{E}\) at \(P\), and (c) The volume charge density \( ho_v\) at \(P\).

Solution:
1. Determine \(\mathbf{E} = - abla V\): \[ \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} = 4xy, \quad \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} = 2x^2, \quad \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} = -5 \] \[ \mathbf{E} = -\left(4xy\mathbf{a}_x + 2x^2\mathbf{a}_y - 5\mathbf{a}_z\right) = -4xy\mathbf{a}_x - 2x^2\mathbf{a}_y + 5\mathbf{a}_z\text{ V/m} \]
2. Evaluate \(\mathbf{E}\) at point \(P(-4, 3, 6)\): \[ E_x = -4(-4)(3) = +48\text{ V/m} \] \[ E_y = -2(-4)^2 = -2(16) = -32\text{ V/m} \] \[ E_z = +5\text{ V/m} \] \[ \mathbf{E}_P = 48\mathbf{a}_x - 32\mathbf{a}_y + 5\mathbf{a}_z\text{ V/m} \] Magnitude: \[ |\mathbf{E}_P| = \sqrt{48^2 + (-32)^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{2304 + 1024 + 25} = \sqrt{3353} \approx 57.905\text{ V/m} \]
3. Determine \( ho_v\) using Maxwell's first equation: \[ ho_v = abla \cdot \mathbf{D} = \epsilon_0( abla \cdot \mathbf{E}) \] \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{E} = \frac{\partial(-4xy)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial(-2x^2)}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial(5)}{\partial z} = -4y + 0 + 0 = -4y \] At point \(P\), \(y = 3\): \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{E} = -4(3) = -12\text{ V/m}^2 \] \[ ho_v = \epsilon_0 (-12) = -12 \times (8.854 \times 10^{-12}) = -1.062 \times 10^{-10}\text{ C/m}^3 = -106.2\text{ pC/m}^3 \]

Exam Pitfalls & Potential Traps:
  • Forgetting the Negative Sign: \(\mathbf{E} = - abla V\). Dropping the minus sign reverses the field direction and inverts boundary charge calculations.
  • Potential Difference Direction: \(V_{AB} = V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l}\). Be cautious: some older Indian textbooks write \(V_{AB} = V_A - V_B\); always check the defined subscript convention on university exam sheets.
  • Equipotential Work Myth: Work is only zero when moving between points at the same potential. Moving between two different equipotential surfaces requires work \(W = q(V_B - V_A)\) regardless of path taken.

Gauss's Law and Potential Formulation

  • Gauss's Law (Integral): \(oint_S \mathbf{D} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = Q_{\text{encl}}\)
  • Gauss's Law (Point Form): \( abla \cdot \mathbf{D} = ho_v\)
  • Conservative Condition: \(oint_L \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = 0 iff abla \times \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{0}\)
  • Potential from Field: \(V = -\int \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l}\)
  • Field from Potential: \(\mathbf{E} = - abla V\)
  • Electrostatic Energy Density: \(w_E = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{E} = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon |\mathbf{E}|^2\text{ [J/m}^3\text{]}\)
  • Total Stored Energy: \(W_E = \frac{1}{2}\int_v \epsilon |\mathbf{E}|^2, dv = \frac{1}{2}QV = \frac{1}{2}CV^2\)

10. Real-World Engineering Applications

  • High-Voltage Cable Grading: In high-voltage underground cables, dielectric breakdown begins at the inner conductor surface where \(E_{\max} = \frac{V_0}{a\ln(b/a)}\). Capacitance grading (using layers of dielectrics with decreasing permittivity \(\epsilon_{r1} > \epsilon_{r2} > \epsilon_{r3}\)) equalizes peak electric fields across the insulation.
  • Faraday Cages & Lightning Protection: Because electric charge resides solely on the outer conductor surface (\(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{0}\) inside), metallic aircraft fuselages and Faraday cages provide absolute electrostatic shielding for sensitive avionics and occupants during direct lightning strikes.
  • Gas-Insulated Switchgear (GIS): GIS substations utilize pressurized Sulfur Hexafluoride (\(\text{SF}_6\)) gas enclosed in grounded cylindrical aluminum housings. Field distributions are computed using Gauss's Law to keep maximum surface gradient below the ionization threshold of \(\text{SF}_6\) (\(\approx 8.9\text{ kV/mm}\)).

11. Field Mapping by Curvilinear Squares

In irregular two-dimensional geometries lacking analytical symmetry, graphical field plotting maps equipotential lines (\(V = \text{const}\)) and flux stream lines (\(\Psi = \text{const}\)) into orthogonal curvilinear squares where \(\Delta l \approx \Delta n\). Total capacitance is then evaluated directly as \(C = \epsilon \frac{N_f}{N_p}\), where \(N_f\) is the number of flux tubes and \(N_p\) is the number of potential increments.

12. Method of Images for Electrostatic Boundaries

When a point charge \(+q\) is placed at distance \(d\) above an infinite, grounded conducting plane (\(V=0\) at \(z=0\)), the boundary condition is satisfied by replacing the conductor with a fictitious image charge \(-q\) at \(z = -d\). By the uniqueness theorem, the field in the upper half-space \(z > 0\) is identical to that of the two-charge system.

13. Special Cases: Dipole and Quadrupole Potentials

While a single monopole charge produces potential \(V propto 1/r\), an electric dipole produces \(V propto \frac{\cos\theta}{r^2}\), and an electric quadrupole produces \(V propto \frac{3\cos^2\theta - 1}{r^3}\). As spatial order increases, potential decays more rapidly with distance due to destructive field cancellation.

14. GATE / IES Exam Tips & Shortcuts

  • If asked for the work done in moving a charge between two points in an electrostatic field, ignore the path completely! Simply compute \(W = q(V_B - V_A)\).
  • For a spherical shell of radius \(R\) with uniform surface charge \(Q\): the electric field inside (\(r < R\)) is identically 0, but the potential inside is constant and non-zero: \(V(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon R}\).
  • The optimum ratio of outer-to-inner radius of a coaxial cable to minimize maximum electric field for a given applied voltage is \(b/a = e \approx 2.718\).

15. Cross-Topic Bridges & Forward Look

Combining \(\mathbf{E} = - abla V\) with Gauss's Law \( abla \cdot \mathbf{D} = ho_v\) leads directly to Poisson's equation \( abla^2 V = - ho_v/\epsilon\) and Laplace's equation \( abla^2 V = 0\), which are formulated and solved for boundary-value problems in the following lesson.

⚡ Gauss's Law Derivation for Uniformly Charged Spherical Shell

For a thin spherical shell of radius \(R\) carrying total surface charge \(Q\):

$$\text{Gauss's Law Integral Form: } \Psi = oint_S \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{S} = Q_{\text{enclosed}}$$ $$\text{Region 1 (Outside } r ge R\text{): } D_r (4 \pi r^2) = Q implies E_r = \frac{Q}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2}$$ $$\text{Region 2 (Inside } r < R\text{): } Q_{\text{enclosed}} = 0 implies E_r = 0$$

emt-dipole-capacitance-poisson.title: Electric Dipoles, Transmission Line/Coaxial Capacitance, and Poisson's & Laplace's Equations
emt-dipole-capacitance-poisson.body:
The electrostatic dipole—a pair of equal and opposite point charges separated by an infinitesimal distance—forms the microscopic physical basis for dielectric polarization and radio frequency antennas. In practical power transmission and high-frequency electronics, conductors separated by dielectric media form capacitance structures whose charge-voltage relationships dictate line charging currents, characteristic impedance, and capacitive cross-talk. When charge distributions are unknown and only conductor voltages are specified, Poisson's and Laplace's second-order partial differential equations govern the unique potential field throughout space.

1. Prerequisite & Mathematical Concept Anchor

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Electric Dipoles, Transmission Line/Coaxial Capacitance, and Poisson's & Laplace's Equations

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Electric Dipoles, Transmission Line/Coaxial Capacitance, and Poisson's & Laplace's Equations.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Boundary-value problems in electrostatics require solving the scalar Laplace equation \( abla^2 V = 0\) subject to Dirichlet (\(V\) specified on boundary) or Neumann (\(\frac{\partial V}{\partial n}\) specified on boundary) conditions. The Uniqueness Theorem guarantees that any solution to Laplace's equation that satisfies all prescribed boundary conditions is the one and only physically correct solution.

2. The Electric Dipole: Potential and Electric Field

An electric dipole consists of two point charges \(+q\) and \(-q\) separated by distance \(d\) aligned along the \(z\)-axis, centered at the origin. The Electric Dipole Moment vector is defined as: \[ \mathbf{p} = q\mathbf{d} = q d\mathbf{a}_z \quad [\text{C}\cdot\text{m}] \] In the far field (\(r gg d\)), the distance from the charges to the observation point approximates as \(r_1 \approx r - \frac{d}{2}\cos\theta\) and \(r_2 \approx r + \frac{d}{2}\cos\theta\).
Electric Potential: \[ V(r, \theta) = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon}\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right) \approx \frac{q d\cos\theta}{4\pi\epsilon r^2} = \frac{\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{a}_r}{4\pi\epsilon r^2} \] Electric Field Intensity: Taking \(\mathbf{E} = - abla V\) in spherical coordinates: \[ E_r = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial r} = \frac{2p\cos\theta}{4\pi\epsilon r^3}, \quad E_\theta = -\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial V}{\partial \theta} = \frac{p\sin\theta}{4\pi\epsilon r^3}, \quad E_\phi = 0 \] \[ \mathbf{E}(r, \theta) = \frac{p}{4\pi\epsilon r^3}\left(2\cos\theta\mathbf{a}_r + \sin\theta\mathbf{a}_\theta\right) \] Notice that the dipole electric field decays as \(1/r^3\), one order faster than a monopole point charge (\(1/r^2\)).

3. Torque and Energy of a Dipole in an External Field

When an electric dipole with moment \(\mathbf{p}\) is placed in a uniform external electric field \(\mathbf{E}_{\text{ext}}\):

  • Net translational force: \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = q\mathbf{E} + (-q)\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{0}\)
  • Net mechanical torque: \[ \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{E}_{\text{ext}} \quad [\text{N}\cdot\text{m}] \] The torque acts to align the dipole moment parallel with the applied field.
  • Potential energy stored in dipole orientation: \[ U = -\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\text{ext}} \quad [\text{J}] \] Minimum energy occurs when \(\mathbf{p}\) is fully aligned with \(\mathbf{E}\) (\(\theta = 0\)).

4. Capacitance: General Definition

Capacitance \(C\) is the ratio of the magnitude of charge \(Q\) on either conductor of a two-conductor system to the potential difference \(V\) between them: \[ C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{oint_S \epsilon \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}{-\int_-^+ \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l}} \quad [\text{Farads, F}] \] Capacitance depends solely on the physical geometry (dimensions, shapes, spacing) and the permittivity \(\epsilon\) of the separating dielectric, and is completely independent of charge \(Q\) or voltage \(V\).

5. Capacitance of a Coaxial Cable

Consider a coaxial cable with inner conductor of radius \(a\) and outer conductor of inner radius \(b\), filled with a dielectric of permittivity \(\epsilon\):

  1. Assume linear charge density \(+ ho_L\) on inner conductor and \(- ho_L\) on outer conductor.
  2. From Gauss's Law, the radial field in the dielectric (\(a < \rho < b\)) is: \[ \mathbf{E} = \frac{ ho_L}{2\pi\epsilon \rho}\mathbf{a}_\rho \]
  3. Compute potential difference between conductors: \[ V_{ab} = -\int_b^a E_\rho, d\rho = -\int_b^a \frac{ ho_L}{2\pi\epsilon \rho}, d\rho = \frac{ ho_L}{2\pi\epsilon}\ln\left(\frac{b}{a}\right) \]
  4. Determine capacitance per unit length (\(C' = ho_L / V_{ab}\)): \[ C' = \frac{2\pi\epsilon}{\ln(b/a)} \quad [\text{F/m}] \] For a cable of length \(L\): \(C = \frac{2\pi\epsilon L}{\ln(b/a)}\).

6. Capacitance of a Two-Wire Transmission Line

Consider two parallel infinite circular conductors of radius \(r\) separated by center-to-center distance \(D\) (where \(D > 2r\)) in a medium of permittivity \(\epsilon\): Using the method of image line charges and calculating the potential between the conductor surfaces: \[ V = \frac{ ho_L}{\pi\epsilon}\ln\left(\frac{D - r}{r}\right) \approx \frac{ ho_L}{\pi\epsilon}\ln\left(\frac{D}{r}\right) \quad (\text{for } D gg r) \] The exact expression using hyperbolic functions is: \[ C' = \frac{\pi\epsilon}{operatorname{arcosh}(D / 2r)} \approx \frac{\pi\epsilon}{\ln(D/r)} \quad [\text{F/m}] \] For an overhead single-phase power line operating above ground, mutual and ground capacitance are calculated using Carson's earth return formulas.

7. Poisson's and Laplace's Equations

Starting from Maxwell's first equation in a linear, homogeneous medium: \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{D} = ho_v implies abla \cdot (\epsilon \mathbf{E}) = ho_v \] Substitute \(\mathbf{E} = - abla V\): \[ abla \cdot (-\epsilon abla V) = ho_v implies abla^2 V = -\frac{ ho_v}{\epsilon} \quad \text{(Poisson's Equation)} \] In charge-free regions where \( ho_v = 0\) (such as dielectric insulation between conductors): \[ abla^2 V = 0 \quad \text{(Laplace's Equation)} \]

8. Uniqueness Theorem in Electrostatics

The Uniqueness Theorem states that if a solution to Poisson's (or Laplace's) equation satisfies all prescribed boundary conditions on the bounding surfaces of a volume, then that solution is unique. Proof outline: Suppose two solutions \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) exist. Define difference potential \(V_d = V_1 - V_2\). Then \( abla^2 V_d = 0\) and \(V_d = 0\) on all boundaries. By Green's first identity: \(\int_v | abla V_d|^2 dv = 0\), which requires \( abla V_d = \mathbf{0}\) everywhere, proving \(V_1 equiv V_2\).

9. Worked Numerical Example: Coaxial Cable Design & Maximum Stress

Problem: A coaxial cable with inner radius \(a = 5\text{ mm}\) and outer radius \(b = 20\text{ mm}\) is filled with polyethylene (\(\epsilon_r = 2.25\)). An operating voltage of \(V_0 = 30\text{ kV}\) is applied between conductors. Calculate: (a) The capacitance per kilometer of the cable, (b) The maximum electric field stress in the insulation, and (c) The total electrostatic energy stored per kilometer.

Solution:
1. Capacitance per unit length: \[ \epsilon = \epsilon_0\epsilon_r = (8.854 \times 10^{-12}) \times 2.25 = 1.992 \times 10^{-11}\text{ F/m} \] \[ \ln(b/a) = \ln(20/5) = \ln(4) \approx 1.3863 \] \[ C' = \frac{2\pi\epsilon}{\ln(b/a)} = \frac{2\pi \times (1.992 \times 10^{-11})}{1.3863} = \frac{1.2516 \times 10^{-10}}{1.3863} = 9.028 \times 10^{-11}\text{ F/m} = 90.28\text{ pF/m} \] Per kilometer (\(L = 1000\text{ m}\)): \[ C_{\text{km}} = 90.28 \times 10^{-12} \times 1000 = 90.28\text{ nF/km} \]
2. Maximum electric field stress: The field is highest at the inner conductor surface \(\rho = a\): \[ E_{\max} = E(\rho = a) = \frac{V_0}{a\ln(b/a)} = \frac{30 \times 10^3}{(5 \times 10^{-3}) \times 1.3863} = \frac{30 \times 10^3}{6.9315 \times 10^{-3}} = 4.328 \times 10^6\text{ V/m} = 4.33\text{ kV/mm} \] (This is well below the dielectric breakdown strength of polyethylene, \(\approx 20\text{ kV/mm}\)).
3. Stored energy per kilometer: \[ W_E = \frac{1}{2} C_{\text{km}} V_0^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times (90.28 \times 10^{-9}\text{ F}) \times (30 \times 10^3\text{ V})^2 \] \[ W_E = 0.5 \times (90.28 \times 10^{-9}) \times (9 \times 10^8) = 0.5 \times 81.252 = 40.63\text{ Joules/km} \]

Exam Pitfalls & Capacitance Traps:
  • Two-Wire Line vs. Coaxial Line Factor of 2: Coaxial line capacitance has \(2\pi\epsilon / \ln(b/a)\); a two-wire line has \(\pi\epsilon / \ln(D/r)\). The two-wire line formula has \(\pi\), NOT \(2\pi\), because the two wires are in series with respect to the neutral plane.
  • Dipole Field Dependence: A dipole field decays as \(1/r^3\), NOT \(1/r^2\). Forgetting the extra power of \(r\) is the most common exam trap in dipole questions.
  • Laplace vs. Poisson Domain Check: Never apply Laplace's equation (\( abla^2 V = 0\)) inside an electron cloud, semiconductor space-charge depletion region, or plasma sheath where volume charge \( ho_v e 0\). Poisson's equation must be used there.

Dipole, Capacitance, and Boundary Equations

  • Dipole Moment: \(\mathbf{p} = q\mathbf{d}\); Potential: \(V = \frac{p\cos\theta}{4\pi\epsilon r^2}\)
  • Dipole Field: \(\mathbf{E} = \frac{p}{4\pi\epsilon r^3}(2\cos\theta\mathbf{a}_r + \sin\theta\mathbf{a}_\theta)\)
  • Dipole Torque & Energy: \(\mathbf{T} = \mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{E}\); \(U = -\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{E}\)
  • Parallel-Plate: \(C = \frac{\epsilon A}{d}\)
  • Coaxial Cable: \(C = \frac{2\pi\epsilon L}{\ln(b/a)}\); \(E(\rho) = \frac{V_0}{\rho\ln(b/a)}\)
  • Two-Wire Line: \(C = \frac{\pi\epsilon L}{\ln(D/r)}\) (\(D gg r\))
  • Spherical Capacitor: \(C = \frac{4\pi\epsilon}{\frac{1}{a} - \frac{1}{b}} = \frac{4\pi\epsilon ab}{b - a}\)
  • Poisson's Equation: \( abla^2 V = -\frac{ ho_v}{\epsilon}\)
  • Laplace's Equation: \( abla^2 V = 0\)

10. Real-World Engineering Applications

  • Subsea HVDC Power Transmission Cables: High-Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) subsea interconnectors (such as the 500 kV Western Link in the UK) require rigorous coaxial capacitance analysis to evaluate charging transient energy, capacitive discharge hazards during maintenance, and sheath overvoltage protection.
  • MOSFET Channel Potential Modeling: In semiconductor device physics, the channel inversion layer and depletion region widths are solved using 1D Poisson's equation: \(\frac{d^2 V}{dx^2} = -\frac{q N_A}{\epsilon_{si}}\).
  • Microstrip Characteristic Impedance: Printed circuit board (PCB) traces are analyzed using Laplace's equation solvers (such as Wheeler's formulas or 2D boundary element solvers) to match \(50 \Omega\) transmission line impedance for high-speed DDR memory and PCIe channels.

11. 1D Analytical Solutions to Laplace's Equation

When potential depends on only one coordinate:

  • Cartesian \(V(x)\): \(\frac{d^2 V}{dx^2} = 0 implies V(x) = A x + B\) (Linear potential, uniform field \(E = -A\)).
  • Cylindrical \(V(\rho)\): \(\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{d}{d\rho}\left(\rho\frac{dV}{d\rho}\right) = 0 implies V(\rho) = A\ln\rho + B\) (Logarithmic potential, \(E propto 1/\rho\)).
  • Spherical \(V(r)\): \(\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{d}{dr}\left(r^2\frac{dV}{dr}\right) = 0 implies V(r) = -\frac{A}{r} + B\) (Hyperbolic potential, \(E propto 1/r^2\)).

12. Method of Separation of Variables for 2D Laplace Problems

For a rectangular boundary \(V(x, y)\) with \( abla^2 V = \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial y^2} = 0\): Assume product solution \(V(x, y) = X(x)Y(y)\). Dividing by \(XY\): \[ \frac{1}{X}\frac{d^2 X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y}\frac{d^2 Y}{dy^2} = 0 implies \frac{d^2 X}{dx^2} = -k^2 X, \quad \frac{d^2 Y}{dy^2} = +k^2 Y \] This yields Fourier series solutions \(V(x, y) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty C_n \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{a}\right)\sinh\left(\frac{n\pi y}{a}\right)\).

13. Dielectric Boundary Conditions

At an interface between two dielectric media 1 and 2:

  • Tangential \(\mathbf{E}\) is continuous: \(E_{1t} = E_{2t}\) (or \(D_{1t}/\epsilon_1 = D_{2t}/\epsilon_2\)).
  • Normal \(\mathbf{D}\) is discontinuous by free surface charge density: \(D_{1n} - D_{2n} = ho_S\). If free surface charge is absent (\( ho_S = 0\)), normal \(\mathbf{D}\) is continuous: \(D_{1n} = D_{2n} implies \epsilon_1 E_{1n} = \epsilon_2 E_{2n}\).
  • Refraction law of field lines: \(\frac{\tan\theta_1}{\tan\theta_2} = \frac{\epsilon_{r1}}{\epsilon_{r2}}\).

14. GATE / IES Exam Tips & Shortcuts

  • For any concentric spherical capacitor with radii \(a\) and \(b\), if \(b o \infty\), the capacitance of an isolated conducting sphere of radius \(a\) is \(C = 4\pi\epsilon a\). For Earth (\(R \approx 6400\text{ km}\)), \(C_{\text{Earth}} \approx 711 \mu\text{F}\).
  • In dielectric boundary refraction, when electric field enters a higher permittivity medium (\(\epsilon_2 > \epsilon_1\)), the field lines bend AWAY from the normal (\(\theta_2 > \theta_1\)).
  • A dipole oriented at \(90^\circ\) (\(\theta = \pi/2\)) to the \(z\)-axis has zero potential everywhere along the \(xy\)-plane (\(V = 0\)), making the plane a zero-potential equipotential.

15. Cross-Topic Bridges & Forward Look

Poisson's and Laplace's boundary value solutions transition directly into steady magnetic fields (Module III), where the magnetic vector potential \(\mathbf{A}\) satisfies the vector Poisson equation \( abla^2 \mathbf{A} = -\mu\mathbf{J}\).

emt-biot-savart-ampere.title: Biot-Savart Law, Magnetic Field Intensity of Current Loops, and Ampere's Circuital Law
emt-biot-savart-ampere.body:
Magnetostatics investigates constant magnetic fields produced by steady, time-invariant electric currents (direct current \(\partial \mathbf{J}/\partial t = \mathbf{0}\)). Discovered experimentally by Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart in 1820, the Biot-Savart Law provides the fundamental differential building block linking current elements to magnetic field intensity \(\mathbf{H}\) and magnetic flux density \(\mathbf{B}\). For highly symmetric geometries, Ampère's Circuital Law provides a powerful line-integral technique directly analogous to Gauss's Law in electrostatics. Introducing the magnetic vector potential \(\mathbf{A}\) enforces the physical truth that magnetic monopoles do not exist (\( abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\)).

1. Prerequisite & Mathematical Concept Anchor

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Biot-Savart Law, Magnetic Field Intensity of Current Loops, and Ampere's Circuital Law

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Biot-Savart Law, Magnetic Field Intensity of Current Loops, and Ampere's Circuital Law.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Magnetostatics builds on cross-product algebra and line integration of vector fields. A steady current element \(I d\mathbf{l}\) produces a magnetic field that is perpendicular to both the current direction and the radial distance vector. In SI units:

  • Magnetic Field Intensity \(\mathbf{H}\) is measured in \(\text{Amperes per meter (A/m)}\).
  • Magnetic Flux Density \(\mathbf{B}\) is measured in \(\text{Tesla (T) or Weber per square meter (Wb/m}^2\text{)}\).
