  • Constitutive relation: \(\mathbf{B} = \mu \mathbf{H} = \mu_0\mu_r \mathbf{H}\), where \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ H/m}\).

2. The Biot-Savart Law

The Biot-Savart Law states that the differential magnetic field intensity \(d\mathbf{H}\) produced at an observation point \(P\) by a differential current element \(I d\mathbf{l}'\) located at source point \(\mathbf{r}'\) is: \[ d\mathbf{H} = \frac{I d\mathbf{l}' \times \mathbf{a}_R}{4\pi R^2} = \frac{I d\mathbf{l}' \times (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}')}{4\pi |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|^3} \quad [\text{A/m}] \] where \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'\) is the displacement vector from source to field point. For continuous current configurations:

  • Surface current \(\mathbf{K}\text{ (A/m)}\): \(\mathbf{H} = \int_S \frac{\mathbf{K} \times \mathbf{a}_R}{4\pi R^2}, dS'\)
  • Volume current \(\mathbf{J}\text{ (A/m}^2\text{)}\): \(\mathbf{H} = \int_v \frac{\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{a}_R}{4\pi R^2}, dv'\)

3. Magnetic Field of Finite and Infinite Straight Current-Carrying Wires

Consider a straight wire carrying steady current \(I\) along the \(z\)-axis from \(z = A\) to \(z = B\). Observing at distance \(\rho\) from the wire: \[ \mathbf{H} = \frac{I}{4\pi\rho}(\cosalpha_1 - \cosalpha_2)\mathbf{a}_\phi \] where \(alpha_1\) and \(alpha_2\) are the angles subtended by the wire endpoints with the positive \(z\)-axis.
Infinitely Long Straight Wire: As \(A o -\infty\) (\(alpha_1 o 0\)) and \(B o +\infty\) (\(alpha_2 o \pi\)): \[ \cos(0) - \cos(\pi) = 1 - (-1) = 2 \] \[ \mathbf{H} = \frac{I}{2\pi\rho}\mathbf{a}_\phi \quad [\text{A/m}] \] \[ \mathbf{B} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi\rho}\mathbf{a}_\phi \quad [\text{T}] \] The magnetic field lines form concentric circles centered on the wire, obeying the right-hand thumb rule.
Semi-Infinite Wire (starting at \(z = 0\) to \(z = \infty\)): \[ \mathbf{H} = \frac{I}{4\pi\rho}\mathbf{a}_\phi \]

4. Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Current Loop

Consider a circular loop of radius \(a\) in the \(xy\)-plane carrying steady current \(I\). We observe at point \(P(0, 0, h)\) on the \(z\)-axis: By symmetry, components of \(d\mathbf{H}\) perpendicular to the \(z\)-axis (\(d\mathbf{H}_\rho\)) cancel across diametrically opposite elements. Only the axial component \(d H_z = d H \sin\alpha = d H \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + h^2}}\) survives: \[ H_z = \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{I (a, d\phi')}{4\pi (a^2 + h^2)} \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + h^2}} = \frac{I a^2 (2\pi)}{4\pi (a^2 + h^2)^{3/2}} \] \[ \mathbf{H}(0, 0, h) = \frac{I a^2}{2(a^2 + h^2)^{3/2}}\mathbf{a}_z \quad [\text{A/m}] \] Special Cases:

  • At the center of the loop (\(h = 0\)): \(\mathbf{H} = \frac{I}{2a}\mathbf{a}_z\). For an \(N\)-turn compact coil: \(\mathbf{H} = \frac{N I}{2a}\mathbf{a}_z\).
  • Far-field along axis (\(h gg a\)): \(\mathbf{H} \approx \frac{I a^2}{2 h^3}\mathbf{a}_z = \frac{m}{2\pi h^3}\mathbf{a}_z\), where \(m = I(\pi a^2)\) is the magnetic dipole moment.

5. Magnetic Field of a Rectangular Current Loop

For a rectangular loop with sides \(2a\) (along \(x\)) and \(2b\) (along \(y\)) carrying current \(I\), the magnetic field at the center of the loop (\(z = 0\)) is obtained by summing the contributions of the four straight segments: \[ H_z = \frac{2 I}{\pi}\left(\frac{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}{a b}\right)\mathbf{a}_z \] For a square loop of side \(L\) (\(2a = 2b = L\)): \[ H_z = \frac{2\sqrt{2} I}{\pi L}\mathbf{a}_z \] On the axis at distance \(h\) above the center of a square loop of side \(L\): \[ H_z = \frac{2 I L^2}{\pi (L^2 + 4h^2)\sqrt{L^2 + 2h^2}} \]

6. Ampère's Circuital Law

Ampère's Circuital Law states that the line integral of magnetic field intensity \(\mathbf{H}\) around any closed path (Amperian loop) \(L\) is equal to the net direct current \(I_{\text{encl}}\) enclosed by that path: \[ oint_L \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = I_{\text{encl}} = \int_S \mathbf{J} \cdot d\mathbf{S} \] Applying Stokes' Theorem to the left-hand side: \[ oint_L \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \int_S ( abla \times \mathbf{H}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_S \mathbf{J} \cdot d\mathbf{S} \] Since this holds for an arbitrary surface \(S\), the point form (Maxwell's curl equation for static fields) is: \[ abla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J} \]

7. Classical Applications of Ampère's Circuital Law

  • Long Solid Cylindrical Conductor of Radius \(a\) carrying uniform current \(I\): \[ J_z = \frac{I}{\pi a^2} \]
    • Outside (\(\rho ge a\)): \(oint \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = H_\phi (2\pi\rho) = I implies \mathbf{H} = \frac{I}{2\pi\rho}\mathbf{a}_\phi\)
    • Inside (\(\rho < a\)): \(I_{\text{encl}} = J_z (\pi\rho^2) = I \frac{\rho^2}{a^2}\). \[ H_\phi (2\pi\rho) = I \frac{\rho^2}{a^2} implies \mathbf{H} = \frac{I\rho}{2\pi a^2}\mathbf{a}_\phi \]
    The field rises linearly with \(\rho\) inside the conductor from 0 at the axis, peaks at the surface \(\rho = a\), and falls as \(1/\rho\) outside.
  • Infinitely Long Solenoid ( \(n\) turns per meter carrying \(I\) ): \[ \mathbf{H} = n I \mathbf{a}_z \quad \text{(inside)}, \quad \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{(outside)} \]
  • Toroid of Mean Radius \(r_0\) and \(N\) Turns: \[ \mathbf{H} = \frac{N I}{2\pi\rho}\mathbf{a}_\phi \quad \text{(inside core)}, \quad \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{(outside)} \]

8. Non-Existence of Magnetic Monopoles & Magnetic Vector Potential \(\mathbf{A}\)

Because magnetic flux lines are continuous closed loops with neither beginning nor end, the net magnetic flux leaving any closed surface is identically zero: \[ oint_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0 iff abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0 \quad \text{(Gauss's Law for Magnetism)} \] Because the divergence of any curl is identically zero (\( abla \cdot ( abla \times \mathbf{A}) equiv 0\)), \(\mathbf{B}\) can always be expressed as the curl of a Magnetic Vector Potential \(\mathbf{A}\): \[ \mathbf{B} = abla \times \mathbf{A} \quad [\text{Wb/m or T}\cdot\text{m}] \] Using the Coulomb gauge condition \( abla \cdot \mathbf{A} = 0\) in steady currents: \[ abla \times ( abla \times \mathbf{A}) = abla( abla \cdot \mathbf{A}) - abla^2 \mathbf{A} = - abla^2 \mathbf{A} = \mu \mathbf{J} \] \[ abla^2 \mathbf{A} = -\mu \mathbf{J} \quad \text{(Vector Poisson's Equation)} \] Its integral solution is directly analogous to electrostatic scalar potential: \[ \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}) = \int_v \frac{\mu \mathbf{J}(\mathbf{r}'), dv'}{4\pi |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|} \] Total magnetic flux \(\Phi\) through an open surface \(S\) bounded by contour \(L\) is: \[ \Phi = \int_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_S ( abla \times \mathbf{A}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = oint_L \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{l} \]

9. Worked Numerical Example: Coaxial Cable Magnetic Field & Flux

Problem: A coaxial cable has an inner solid conductor of radius \(a = 2\text{ mm}\), an outer cylindrical conductor with inner radius \(b = 6\text{ mm}\) and outer radius \(c = 8\text{ mm}\). A DC current \(I = 10\text{ A}\) flows in the \(+z\) direction in the inner conductor and returns in the \(-z\) direction uniformly distributed in the outer conductor. Calculate \(\mathbf{H}\) at: (a) \(\rho = 1\text{ mm}\), (b) \(\rho = 4\text{ mm}\), (c) \(\rho = 7\text{ mm}\), and (d) \(\rho = 10\text{ mm}\).

Solution:
1. Region 1 (\(\rho < a = 2\text{ mm}\)): \[ H_\phi = \frac{I\rho}{2\pi a^2} = \frac{10 \times (1 \times 10^{-3})}{2\pi \times (2 \times 10^{-3})^2} = \frac{0.010}{2\pi \times 4 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{0.010}{2.5133 \times 10^{-5}} = 397.9\text{ A/m} \] \[ \mathbf{H} = 397.9\mathbf{a}_\phi\text{ A/m} \]
2. Region 2 (\(a < \rho < b = 4\text{ mm}\)): The enclosed current is the full inner current \(I = 10\text{ A}\): \[ H_\phi = \frac{I}{2\pi\rho} = \frac{10}{2\pi \times (4 \times 10^{-3})} = \frac{10}{0.025133} = 397.9\text{ A/m} \] \[ \mathbf{H} = 397.9\mathbf{a}_\phi\text{ A/m} \]
3. Region 3 (\(b < \rho < c = 7\text{ mm}\)): The return current is distributed in the ring between \(b\) and \(c\). Enclosed fraction of outer current: \[ I_{\text{outer, encl}} = -10 \times \frac{\rho^2 - b^2}{c^2 - b^2} = -10 \times \frac{7^2 - 6^2}{8^2 - 6^2} = -10 \times \frac{49 - 36}{64 - 36} = -10 \times \frac{13}{28} = -4.643\text{ A} \] Total enclosed current: \[ I_{\text{encl}} = 10 - 4.643 = 5.357\text{ A} \] \[ H_\phi = \frac{I_{\text{encl}}}{2\pi\rho} = \frac{5.357}{2\pi \times (7 \times 10^{-3})} = \frac{5.357}{0.04398} = 121.8\text{ A/m} \] \[ \mathbf{H} = 121.8\mathbf{a}_\phi\text{ A/m} \]
4. Region 4 (\(\rho > c = 10\text{ mm}\)): The total enclosed current is \(I_{\text{inner}} + I_{\text{outer}} = +10\text{ A} - 10\text{ A} = 0\). \[ H_\phi = 0 implies \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{0} \] The coaxial cable produces zero external magnetic field outside its outer conductor.

Exam Pitfalls & Magnetostatic Traps:
  • Ampère's Law Applicability: Ampère's Circuital Law (\(oint \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = I_{\text{encl}}\)) is always mathematically true for steady currents, but it can only be used to calculate \(\mathbf{H}\) if the field has sufficient geometric symmetry (infinite cylinder, infinite plane sheet, infinite solenoid, toroid). For a finite wire or loop, you MUST use the Biot-Savart Law!
  • Solenoid End-Field Drop: The magnetic field inside an infinitely long solenoid is \(B = \mu_0 n I\). At the exact physical end of a semi-infinite solenoid, the field drops to exactly half: \(B_{\text{end}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 n I\).
  • Vector Potential Direction: \(\mathbf{A}\) always points in the same direction as the source current density \(\mathbf{J}\). If \(\mathbf{J} = J_z \mathbf{a}_z\), then \(\mathbf{A} = A_z \mathbf{a}_z\).

Magnetostatics Formulas and Constants

  • Biot-Savart Law: \(d\mathbf{H} = \frac{I d\mathbf{l} \times \mathbf{a}_R}{4\pi R^2}\)
  • Infinite Straight Wire: \(\mathbf{H} = \frac{I}{2\pi\rho}\mathbf{a}_\phi\); \(\mathbf{B} = \frac{\mu I}{2\pi\rho}\mathbf{a}_\phi\)
  • Circular Loop on Axis: \(H_z = \frac{I a^2}{2(a^2 + h^2)^{3/2}}\); Center: \(H_z = \frac{I}{2a}\)
  • Square Loop Center: \(H = \frac{2\sqrt{2} I}{\pi L}\)
  • Ampère's Law: \(oint \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = I_{\text{encl}} iff abla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J}\)
  • Solenoid: \(H = n I\); Toroid: \(H = \frac{N I}{2\pi r}\)
  • Gauss's Law for \(\mathbf{B}\): \( abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0 iff \mathbf{B} = abla \times \mathbf{A}\)
  • Vector Poisson: \( abla^2 \mathbf{A} = -\mu \mathbf{J}\); Flux: \(\Phi = oint_L \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{l}\)
  • Magnetic Energy Density: \(w_M = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{2}\mu |\mathbf{H}|^2\text{ [J/m}^3\text{]}\)

10. Real-World Engineering Applications

  • Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Superconducting Coils: MRI scanners utilize niobium-titanium (NbTi) superconducting solenoids carrying thousands of amperes at \(4.2\text{ K}\) to create ultra-uniform magnetic fields of 1.5 T to 3 T, governed by Helmholtz coil configurations optimizing \(\partial^2 B_z / \partial z^2 = 0\).
  • DC Busbar Short-Circuit Mechanical Forces: High-current busbars in generating stations experience severe electromagnetic forces during fault conditions (\(F/L = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}\)), requiring robust mechanical bracing designed to withstand kilonewton peak loads.
  • Hall-Effect Current Sensors: Isolated DC/AC current transducers in electric vehicles and solar inverters place a Hall sensor in an air gap of a magnetic toroid core, measuring \(oint \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l}\) without physical electrical contact.

11. Self and Mutual Inductance Formulation

Magnetic flux linkage is defined as \(\lambda = N\Phi\).

  • Self-inductance \(L = \frac{\lambda}{I} = \frac{N\Phi}{I}\). For a long solenoid of length \(l\), cross-section \(S\), and \(N\) turns: \(L = \frac{\mu N^2 S}{l}\).
  • Coaxial cable inductance per unit length: \(L_{\text{ext}} = \frac{\mu}{2\pi}\ln(b/a)\text{ H/m}\). Internal inductance due to flux inside the solid conductor: \(L_{\text{int}} = \frac{\mu_0}{8\pi}\text{ H/m}\) (constant, independent of radius).

12. Magnetic Dipole Moment and Force on Moving Charges

A planar current loop of area \(S\) and current \(I\) has magnetic dipole moment \(\mathbf{m} = I S \mathbf{a}_n\). When placed in a magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\), it experiences mechanical torque \(\mathbf{T} = \mathbf{m} \times \mathbf{B}\) and magnetic potential energy \(U = -\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{B}\). A moving point charge \(q\) with velocity \(\mathbf{u}\) experiences the Lorentz force \(\mathbf{F} = q(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{B})\).

13. Magnetic Scalar Potential \(V_m\)

In current-free regions where \(\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{0}\), \( abla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{0}\). Under this condition, \(\mathbf{H}\) can be expressed as the negative gradient of a magnetic scalar potential: \(\mathbf{H} = - abla V_m\). Combining with \( abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\) yields Laplace's equation for magnetic potential: \( abla^2 V_m = 0\).

14. GATE / IES Exam Tips & Shortcuts

  • The internal inductance of any solid round non-magnetic wire carrying uniform low-frequency current is always \(\frac{\mu_0}{8\pi} = \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}{8\pi} = 0.5 \times 10^{-7}\text{ H/m} = 0.05 \mu\text{H/m}\), regardless of its radius!
  • For two long parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction: they attract each other. In opposite directions: they repel each other.
  • Magnetic forces do no work on moving charges because the magnetic force \(\mathbf{F}_m = q(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{B})\) is always strictly perpendicular to velocity \(\mathbf{u}\) (\(\mathbf{F}_m \cdot d\mathbf{l} = 0\)).

15. Cross-Topic Bridges & Forward Look

When currents and fields become time-varying, Ampère's static law (\( abla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J}\)) violates the continuity equation for charge. Maxwell solved this dilemma by introducing displacement current, completing the electrodynamic revolution formulated in the next lesson.

emt-maxwell-boundary-conditions.title: Electromagnetic Boundary Conditions, Displacement Current, and Maxwell's Equations
emt-maxwell-boundary-conditions.body:
In 1864, James Clerk Maxwell synthesized electricity, magnetism, and optics into a unified theory of electromagnetism. By resolving an algebraic inconsistency in Ampère's Circuital Law through the introduction of displacement current (\(\partial \mathbf{D}/\partial t\)), Maxwell proved that time-varying electric fields generate magnetic fields, and conversely, time-varying magnetic fields induce electric fields (Faraday's Law). Together with boundary conditions at media interfaces and the continuity equation of charge, Maxwell's four equations govern the generation, radiation, and propagation of all electromagnetic phenomena from power line transients to millimeter-wave radio waves.

1. Prerequisite & Mathematical Concept Anchor

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Electromagnetic Boundary Conditions, Displacement Current, and Maxwell's Equations

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Electromagnetic Boundary Conditions, Displacement Current, and Maxwell's Equations.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Time-varying electrodynamics bridges static field theory through partial time derivatives. For sinusoidal time-harmonic fields with angular frequency \(\omega\), time differentiation transforms to algebraic multiplication by \(j\omega\) in the frequency (phasor) domain: \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} longleftrightarrow j\omega \] Electromagnetic interfaces require applying closed surface and contour integrations across shrinking pillboxes and rectangles straddling the interface.

2. The Continuity Equation for Electric Charge

The principle of conservation of electric charge dictates that the net electric current flowing out of any closed surface must equal the time rate of decrease of charge enclosed within the volume: \[ I_{\text{out}} = oint_S \mathbf{J} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = -\frac{dQ_{\text{encl}}}{dt} = -\frac{d}{dt}\int_v ho_v, dv = -\int_v \frac{\partial ho_v}{\partial t}, dv \] Applying the Divergence Theorem to the left-hand side: \[ \int_v ( abla \cdot \mathbf{J}), dv = -\int_v \frac{\partial ho_v}{\partial t}, dv \] Since this holds for an arbitrary volume, the differential Continuity Equation is: \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{J} = -\frac{\partial ho_v}{\partial t} \] In steady DC conditions where \(\partial ho_v/\partial t = 0\), \( abla \cdot \mathbf{J} = 0\), which is Kirchhoff's Current Law in field form.

3. Maxwell's Displacement Current & Modified Ampère's Law

Consider the divergence of Ampère's static law: \( abla \cdot ( abla \times \mathbf{H}) = abla \cdot \mathbf{J}\). Because the divergence of any curl is identically zero, this requires \( abla \cdot \mathbf{J} = 0\). However, by the continuity equation, \( abla \cdot \mathbf{J} = -\partial ho_v/\partial t\). This is an explicit mathematical contradiction for time-varying fields!
To resolve this contradiction, Maxwell substituted Gauss's Law (\( ho_v = abla \cdot \mathbf{D}\)): \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{J} = -\frac{\partial}{\partial t}( abla \cdot \mathbf{D}) = - abla \cdot \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\right) implies abla \cdot \left(\mathbf{J} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\right) = 0 \] Maxwell recognized that the total current density consists of two distinct components: \[ \mathbf{J}_{\text{total}} = \mathbf{J}_c + \mathbf{J}_d \] where:

  • \(\mathbf{J}_c = \sigma \mathbf{E}\) is the Conduction Current Density (physical drift of charge carriers in conductors).
  • \(\mathbf{J}_d = \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t} = \epsilon \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}\) is the Displacement Current Density (rate of change of electric flux density).
This yields the celebrated Maxwell-Ampère Equation: \[ abla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t} \] In integral form: \[ oint_L \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \int_S \mathbf{J} \cdot d\mathbf{S} + \int_S \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = I_c + I_d \]

4. Physical Verification: AC Capacitor Circuit

Consider a parallel-plate capacitor with plate area \(A\) and separation \(d\) driven by AC voltage \(V(t) = V_0 \sin(\omega t)\): In the connecting wire, conduction current flows: \[ I_c = C\frac{dV}{dt} = \left(\frac{\epsilon A}{d}\right) \omega V_0 \cos(\omega t) \] Between the plates, no electrons cross the dielectric gap (\(J_c = 0\)). However, an electric field exists: \(E(t) = V(t)/d\), so \(D(t) = \epsilon E(t) = \frac{\epsilon V_0 \sin(\omega t)}{d}\). The displacement current passing through the dielectric is: \[ I_d = \int_A \frac{\partial D}{\partial t}, dA = A \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac{\epsilon V_0 \sin(\omega t)}{d}\right) = \left(\frac{\epsilon A}{d}\right) \omega V_0 \cos(\omega t) \] Therefore: \[ I_d equiv I_c \] Displacement current maintains complete circuit continuity across insulating dielectric gaps, proving Ampère's Law is valid through any open surface spanning the capacitor.

5. Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction

Michael Faraday discovered that a time-varying magnetic flux induces an electromotive force (EMF) around a closed circuit: \[ \text{EMF} = oint_L \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt} = -\frac{d}{dt}\int_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S} \] The negative sign expresses Lenz's Law: the induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the original change in flux. Applying Stokes' Theorem: \[ \int_S ( abla \times \mathbf{E}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = -\int_S \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} \cdot d\mathbf{S} \] For stationary contours, the point form is: \[ abla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} \quad \text{(Maxwell's Third Equation)} \] Crucial Insight: In time-varying fields, \( abla \times \mathbf{E} e \mathbf{0}\)! The electric field is no longer conservative; voltage between two points becomes path-dependent.

6. Summary of Maxwell's Equations

The four fundamental equations of classical electrodynamics are summarized below:
Equation Differential Form Integral Form Physical Law
I \( abla \cdot \mathbf{D} = ho_v\) \(oint_S \mathbf{D} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = Q_{\text{encl}}\) Gauss's Law for Electric Fields
II \( abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\) \(oint_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\) Gauss's Law for Magnetic Fields (No Monopoles)
III \( abla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}\) \(oint_L \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = -\frac{d}{dt}\int_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\) Faraday's Law of Induction
IV \( abla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\) \(oint_L \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \int_S \left(\mathbf{J} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\right) \cdot d\mathbf{S}\) Ampère-Maxwell Circuital Law
Constitutive relations: \(\mathbf{D} = \epsilon\mathbf{E}\), \(\mathbf{B} = \mu\mathbf{H}\), \(\mathbf{J} = \sigma\mathbf{E}\).

7. Boundary Conditions for Electric and Magnetic Fields

At an interface between two distinct physical media with properties \((\epsilon_1, \mu_1, \sigma_1)\) and \((\epsilon_2, \mu_2, \sigma_2)\), Maxwell's equations impose strict boundary matching conditions:

  1. Tangential Electric Field Condition: From \(oint_L \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = 0\) as rectangle height \(\Delta h o 0\): \[ E_{1t} = E_{2t} iff \mathbf{a}_{n21} \times (\mathbf{E}_1 - \mathbf{E}_2) = \mathbf{0} \] The tangential component of electric field intensity is always strictly continuous across any interface.
  2. Normal Electric Flux Density Condition: From \(oint_S \mathbf{D} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = Q_{\text{encl}}\) across a pillbox as height \(\Delta h o 0\): \[ D_{1n} - D_{2n} = ho_S iff \mathbf{a}_{n21} \cdot (\mathbf{D}_1 - \mathbf{D}_2) = ho_S \] The normal component of \(\mathbf{D}\) is discontinuous by the free surface charge density \( ho_S\). If the interface has no free charge (\( ho_S = 0\), dielectric-dielectric boundary): \(D_{1n} = D_{2n} implies \epsilon_1 E_{1n} = \epsilon_2 E_{2n}\).
  3. Normal Magnetic Flux Density Condition: From \(oint_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\): \[ B_{1n} = B_{2n} iff \mathbf{a}_{n21} \cdot (\mathbf{B}_1 - \mathbf{B}_2) = 0 \] The normal component of magnetic flux density is always strictly continuous across any material interface.
  4. Tangential Magnetic Field Condition: From \(oint_L \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = I_{\text{encl}}\): \[ H_{1t} - H_{2t} = K iff \mathbf{a}_{n21} \times (\mathbf{H}_1 - \mathbf{H}_2) = \mathbf{K} \] where \(\mathbf{K}\) is the surface current density on the interface. If both media have finite conductivity (\(\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{0}\)): \(H_{1t} = H_{2t} implies \frac{B_{1t}}{\mu_1} = \frac{B_{2t}}{\mu_2}\).

8. Perfect Conductor (PEC) Boundary Conditions

Inside a perfect electric conductor (\(\sigma o \infty\)), static and high-frequency fields vanish identically: \(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{0}\) and \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{0}\). Therefore, on the exterior surface of a PEC: \[ E_t = 0, \quad D_n = ho_S, \quad B_n = 0, \quad H_t = K \] Electric field lines must meet a conducting surface strictly perpendicularly; magnetic field lines must be strictly parallel to the surface.

9. Worked Numerical Example: Displacement Current in Teflon Dielectric

Problem: In a lossy dielectric material with \(\epsilon_r = 2.1\), \(\mu_r = 1\), and \(\sigma = 10^{-4}\text{ S/m}\), the electric field is \(\mathbf{E} = 200\sin(10^9 t - \beta z)\mathbf{a}_x\text{ V/m}\). Determine: (a) The conduction current density \(\mathbf{J}_c\), (b) The displacement current density \(\mathbf{J}_d\), (c) The ratio of the peak magnitudes \(|J_c| / |J_d|\), and (d) The loss tangent \(\tan\delta\).

Solution:
1. Conduction Current Density \(\mathbf{J}_c\): \[ \mathbf{J}_c = \sigma \mathbf{E} = 10^{-4} \times 200\sin(10^9 t - \beta z)\mathbf{a}_x = 0.02\sin(10^9 t - \beta z)\mathbf{a}_x\text{ A/m}^2 = 20\sin(10^9 t - \beta z)\mathbf{a}_x\text{ mA/m}^2 \] Peak magnitude: \(J_{c0} = 0.02\text{ A/m}^2\).
2. Displacement Current Density \(\mathbf{J}_d\): \[ \epsilon = \epsilon_0\epsilon_r = (8.854 \times 10^{-12}) \times 2.1 = 1.8593 \times 10^{-11}\text{ F/m} \] \[ \mathbf{J}_d = \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t} = \epsilon \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} = (1.8593 \times 10^{-11}) \times 200 \times (10^9) \cos(10^9 t - \beta z)\mathbf{a}_x \] \[ \mathbf{J}_d = 3.719\cos(10^9 t - \beta z)\mathbf{a}_x\text{ A/m}^2 \] Peak magnitude: \(J_{d0} = 3.719\text{ A/m}^2\).
3. Ratio of peak magnitudes: \[ \frac{J_{c0}}{J_{d0}} = \frac{0.02}{3.719} \approx 0.005378 \approx 5.38 \times 10^{-3} \]
4. Loss Tangent: \[ \tan\delta = \frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon} = \frac{J_{c0}}{J_{d0}} \approx 0.00538 \] Since \(\tan\delta ll 1\), the material behaves as an excellent low-loss dielectric at this frequency (\(f = 10^9 / 2\pi \approx 159\text{ MHz}\)).

Exam Pitfalls & Maxwell Traps:
  • Displacement Current Has No Physical Charges: Displacement current is NOT a flow of physical charge carriers; it is the time rate of change of the electric flux density \(\partial \mathbf{D}/\partial t\). It produces a magnetic field identically to a physical conduction current.
  • Tangential vs. Normal Continuity: Remember: E is continuous tangentially; B is continuous normally. Swapping them is an instant mark-loser in university exams!
  • Phase Difference Between \(\mathbf{J}_c\) and \(\mathbf{J}_d\): Because \(\mathbf{J}_c propto \sin(\omega t)\) and \(\mathbf{J}_d propto \cos(\omega t)\), displacement current leads conduction current by exactly \(90^\circ\) in time phase.

Maxwell's Equations & Boundary Conditions Summary

  • Continuity: \( abla \cdot \mathbf{J} = -\frac{\partial ho_v}{\partial t}\)
  • Maxwell-Ampère: \( abla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\); \(\mathbf{J}_d = \epsilon\frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}\)
  • Faraday's Law: \( abla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}\)
  • Dielectric Interface: \(E_{1t} = E_{2t}\); \(D_{1n} - D_{2n} = ho_S\); \(B_{1n} = B_{2n}\); \(H_{1t} - H_{2t} = K\)
  • Refraction at Interface (\( ho_S = 0\)): \(\frac{\tan\theta_1}{\tan\theta_2} = \frac{\epsilon_{r1}}{\epsilon_{r2}}\)
  • Magnetic Refraction (\(K = 0\)): \(\frac{\tan\theta_1}{\tan\theta_2} = \frac{\mu_{r1}}{\mu_{r2}}\)
  • Loss Tangent: \(\tan\delta = \frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon} = \frac{|\mathbf{J}_c|}{|\mathbf{J}_d|}\)

10. Real-World Engineering Applications

  • Microwave Heating & Dielectric Loss: In industrial microwave drying and domestic microwave ovens (\(2.45\text{ GHz}\)), dielectric materials with high loss tangent \(\tan\delta\) (such as liquid water) absorb displacement current energy, converting electromagnetic energy into volumetric thermal heat: \(P_v = \omega\epsilon_0\epsilon''_r |\mathbf{E}|^2\).
  • Transformer Core Lamination Insulation: Transformer sheets are coated with thin varnish insulation. Because \(B_n = B_{1n} = B_{2n}\), magnetic flux passes freely through laminations, while the varnish boundaries enforce \(E_t\) continuity, quenching eddy currents.
  • Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) Enclosures: Metallic shielded enclosures protect microprocessors from external RF interference by enforcing \(E_t = 0\) on PEC boundaries, reflecting incoming RF waves back into space.

11. Phasor Form of Maxwell's Equations

For sinusoidal steady-state time-harmonic fields of the form \(e^{j\omega t}\): \[ abla \cdot ilde{\mathbf{D}} = ilde{\rho}_v \] \[ abla \cdot ilde{\mathbf{B}} = 0 \] \[ abla \times ilde{\mathbf{E}} = -j\omega ilde{\mathbf{B}} = -j\omega\mu ilde{\mathbf{H}} \] \[ abla \times ilde{\mathbf{H}} = ilde{\mathbf{J}} + j\omega ilde{\mathbf{D}} = (\sigma + j\omega\epsilon) ilde{\mathbf{E}} \] Here, \(\sigma + j\omega\epsilon = j\omega\epsilon_c\) defines the complex permittivity \(\epsilon_c = \epsilon - j\frac{\sigma}{\omega}\).

12. Potentials in Time-Varying Fields: Retarded Potentials

Because \( abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\), \(\mathbf{B} = abla \times \mathbf{A}\) still holds. Substituting into Faraday's Law: \[ abla \times \left(\mathbf{E} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{A}}{\partial t}\right) = \mathbf{0} implies \mathbf{E} = - abla V - \frac{\partial \mathbf{A}}{\partial t} \] Under the Lorenz gauge condition \( abla \cdot \mathbf{A} = -\mu\epsilon\frac{\partial V}{\partial t}\), both potentials decouple into inhomogeneous wave equations: \[ abla^2 V - \mu\epsilon\frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial t^2} = -\frac{ ho_v}{\epsilon}, \quad abla^2 \mathbf{A} - \mu\epsilon\frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{A}}{\partial t^2} = -\mu\mathbf{J} \] Because signals travel at finite speed \(u = 1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}\), the potentials depend on the delayed (retarded) time \(t' = t - R/u\).

13. Magnetic Monopole Hypotheses & Duality Principle

If hypothetical magnetic charges with density \( ho_{vm}\) and magnetic current \(\mathbf{J}_m\) existed, Maxwell's equations would become completely symmetric: \( abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = ho_{vm}\) and \( abla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} - \mathbf{J}_m\). The Duality Principle allows solving new electromagnetic antenna problems by mapping \(\mathbf{E} o \mathbf{H}\), \(\mathbf{H} o -\mathbf{E}\), \(\epsilon o \mu\), \(\mu o \epsilon\).

14. GATE / IES Exam Tips & Shortcuts

  • If asked for the ratio of conduction current to displacement current in a good conductor (\(\sigma gg \omega\epsilon\)), the ratio is \(gg 1\). In a good dielectric (\(\omega\epsilon gg \sigma\)), the ratio is \(ll 1\).
  • At the boundary of a perfect conductor, \(\mathbf{E}\) is purely normal (\(E_t = 0, D_n = ho_S\)) and \(\mathbf{H}\) is purely tangential (\(B_n = 0, H_t = K\)).
  • Displacement current was Maxwell's greatest intellectual contribution; it enabled the theoretical prediction of electromagnetic waves propagating at the speed of light.

15. Cross-Topic Bridges & Forward Look

Taking the curl of Maxwell's curl equations in source-free space leads directly to the electromagnetic wave equation in Module IV, proving that oscillating electric and magnetic fields self-sustain and propagate through vacuum at \(c \approx 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

emt-uniform-plane-waves.title: Wave Equations, Uniform Plane Waves, and Propagation in Lossless, Lossy, and Conducting Media
emt-uniform-plane-waves.body:
The greatest triumph of Maxwell's field theory was the theoretical prediction that coupled electric and magnetic fields propagate through space as electromagnetic waves at the speed of light. In a source-free region, taking the curl of Maxwell's curl equations decouples the field vectors into second-order vector wave equations (Helmholtz equations). A Uniform Plane Wave (UPW)—where electric and magnetic field vectors are mutually perpendicular, transverse to the direction of propagation (TEM wave), and spatially uniform across planes of constant phase—serves as the universal prototype for optical beams, radio links, and radar propagation across free space, dielectrics, and good conductors.

1. Prerequisite & Mathematical Concept Anchor

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Wave Equations, Uniform Plane Waves, and Propagation in Lossless, Lossy, and Conducting Media

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Wave Equations, Uniform Plane Waves, and Propagation in Lossless, Lossy, and Conducting Media.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Wave propagation analysis requires mastering the vector identity: \[ abla \times ( abla \times \mathbf{A}) = abla( abla \cdot \mathbf{A}) - abla^2 \mathbf{A} \] In the frequency domain with harmonic time dependence \(e^{j\omega t}\), temporal derivatives become algebraic: \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t} o j\omega\) and \(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2} o -\omega^2\).

2. Derivation of Wave Equations from Maxwell's Equations

Consider a linear, isotropic, homogeneous, and source-free medium (\( ho_v = 0, \mathbf{J} = \mathbf{0}\)) with permittivity \(\epsilon\), permeability \(\mu\), and conductivity \(\sigma\):

  1. Start with Faraday's Law: \[ abla \times \mathbf{E} = -\mu \frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial t} \]
  2. Take the curl of both sides: \[ abla \times ( abla \times \mathbf{E}) = -\mu \frac{\partial}{\partial t}( abla \times \mathbf{H}) \]
  3. Substitute the vector identity \( abla \times ( abla \times \mathbf{E}) = abla( abla \cdot \mathbf{E}) - abla^2 \mathbf{E}\). Since \( ho_v = 0\), \( abla \cdot \mathbf{E} = 0\), so the left side is \(- abla^2 \mathbf{E}\).
  4. Substitute Maxwell-Ampère's Law \( abla \times \mathbf{H} = \sigma \mathbf{E} + \epsilon \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}\) on the right side: \[ - abla^2 \mathbf{E} = -\mu \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\sigma \mathbf{E} + \epsilon \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}\right) \] \[ abla^2 \mathbf{E} - \mu\sigma \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} - \mu\epsilon \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2} = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{(General Wave Equation for E)} \]
  5. Following an identical procedure for \(\mathbf{H}\): \[ abla^2 \mathbf{H} - \mu\sigma \frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial t} - \mu\epsilon \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{H}}{\partial t^2} = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{(General Wave Equation for H)} \]
In a lossless medium (\(\sigma = 0\)): \[ abla^2 \mathbf{E} - \mu\epsilon \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2} = \mathbf{0} \] Comparing with the classical wave equation \( abla^2 \psi - \frac{1}{u^2}\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial t^2} = 0\), the wave propagation velocity is: \[ u = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}} \] In free space (\(\mu = \mu_0, \epsilon = \epsilon_0\)): \[ c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4\pi \times 10^{-7})(8.854 \times 10^{-12})}} \approx 2.9979 \times 10^8\text{ m/s} \approx 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s} \]

3. Wave Equations in Phasor Form (Vector Helmholtz Equations)

Assuming time-harmonic variation \(e^{j\omega t}\): \[ abla^2 ilde{\mathbf{E}} - j\omega\mu\sigma ilde{\mathbf{E}} + \omega^2\mu\epsilon ilde{\mathbf{E}} = \mathbf{0} \] \[ abla^2 ilde{\mathbf{E}} - \gamma^2 ilde{\mathbf{E}} = \mathbf{0}, \quad abla^2 ilde{\mathbf{H}} - \gamma^2 ilde{\mathbf{H}} = \mathbf{0} \] where \(\gamma\) is the complex Propagation Constant: \[ \gamma = \alpha + j\beta = \sqrt{j\omega\mu(\sigma + j\omega\epsilon)} \]

  • \(\alpha\) = Attenuation Constant in Nepers per meter (\(\text{Np/m}\))
  • \(\beta\) = Phase Constant in Radians per meter (\(\text{rad/m}\))

4. Uniform Plane Waves (UPW) & TEM Wave Structure

A plane wave is a uniform plane wave if the wavefronts (surfaces of constant phase) are infinite parallel planes, and the field magnitudes \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) are constant everywhere over those planes. Consider a wave propagating in the \(+z\) direction with electric field linearly polarized along the \(x\)-axis: \[ ilde{\mathbf{E}}(z) = E_x(z)\mathbf{a}_x = E_0 e^{-\gamma z}\mathbf{a}_x = E_0 e^{-\alpha z} e^{-j\beta z}\mathbf{a}_x \] From Faraday's Law: \[ ilde{\mathbf{H}} = \frac{1}{-j\omega\mu} abla \times ilde{\mathbf{E}} = \frac{1}{-j\omega\mu}\left(\mathbf{a}_y \frac{\partial E_x}{\partial z}\right) = \frac{-\gamma E_0 e^{-\gamma z}}{-j\omega\mu}\mathbf{a}_y = \frac{E_0}{\eta} e^{-\gamma z}\mathbf{a}_y \] where \(\eta\) is the Intrinsic Impedance of the medium: \[ \eta = \frac{E_x}{H_y} = \sqrt{\frac{j\omega\mu}{\sigma + j\omega\epsilon}} \quad [\Omega] \] Key Properties of Transverse Electromagnetic (TEM) Waves:

  1. \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) are transverse to the direction of propagation (\(E_z = 0, H_z = 0\)).
  2. \(\mathbf{E} perp \mathbf{H}\) everywhere (\(\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{H} = 0\)).
  3. The direction of wave propagation is given by \(\mathbf{a}_k = \mathbf{a}_E \times \mathbf{a}_H\).
  4. \(|\mathbf{E}| / |\mathbf{H}| = |\eta|\).

5. Wave Propagation in Free Space

In vacuum: \(\sigma = 0, \epsilon = \epsilon_0, \mu = \mu_0\). \[ \alpha = 0 \quad (\text{No attenuation}) \] \[ \beta = \omega\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0} = \frac{\omega}{c} = \frac{2\pi f}{c} = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \] \[ \eta_0 = \sqrt{\frac{\mu_0}{\epsilon_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}}} \approx 120\pi \approx 376.73 \Omega \approx 377 \Omega \] The instantaneous time-domain electric and magnetic fields are: \[ \mathbf{E}(z, t) = E_0 \cos(\omega t - \beta z)\mathbf{a}_x \quad [\text{V/m}] \] \[ \mathbf{H}(z, t) = \frac{E_0}{\eta_0} \cos(\omega t - \beta z)\mathbf{a}_y \quad [\text{A/m}] \] \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) are strictly in-phase in free space.

6. Propagation in Lossless Dielectrics

For a perfect dielectric: \(\sigma = 0, \epsilon = \epsilon_0\epsilon_r, \mu = \mu_0\mu_r\). \[ \alpha = 0 \] \[ \beta = \omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon} = \frac{\omega}{c}\sqrt{\mu_r\epsilon_r} \] \[ u_p = \frac{\omega}{\beta} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu_r\epsilon_r}} = \frac{c}{n} \] where \(n = \sqrt{\epsilon_r}\) is the optical refractive index (for non-magnetic media \(\mu_r = 1\)). \[ \eta = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\epsilon}} = \frac{\eta_0}{\sqrt{\epsilon_r}}\sqrt{\mu_r} \quad [\Omega] \] Wavelength in the dielectric: \(\lambda = \frac{u_p}{f} = \frac{\lambda_0}{\sqrt{\epsilon_r}}\).

7. Propagation in Lossy Dielectrics

For general media where conductivity \(\sigma e 0\): The loss tangent characterizes the dissipation: \[ \tan\theta = \frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon} \] The exact propagation parameters are: \[ \alpha = \omega\sqrt{\frac{\mu\epsilon}{2}}\left[\sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon}\right)^2} - 1\right]^{1/2} \quad [\text{Np/m}] \] \[ \beta = \omega\sqrt{\frac{\mu\epsilon}{2}}\left[\sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon}\right)^2} + 1\right]^{1/2} \quad [\text{rad/m}] \] \[ \eta = \sqrt{\frac{j\omega\mu}{\sigma + j\omega\epsilon}} = |\eta|e^{j\theta_\eta}, \quad \theta_\eta = \frac{1}{2}\arctan\left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon}\right) \] Because \(\theta_\eta > 0\), the magnetic field lags the electric field by phase angle \(\theta_\eta\) in time.
Low-Loss Dielectric Approximation (\(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon} ll 1\)): Using binomial expansion: \[ \alpha \approx \frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\epsilon}} = \frac{\sigma}{2}\eta, \quad \beta \approx \omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}, \quad \eta \approx \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\epsilon}}\left(1 + j\frac{\sigma}{2\omega\epsilon}\right) \] Crucially, for low-loss dielectrics, attenuation \(\alpha\) is independent of frequency!

8. Wave Propagation in Good Conductors

A material is classified as a good conductor if conduction current dwarfs displacement current: \[ \frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon} gg 1 \] For copper (\(\sigma \approx 5.8 \times 10^7\text{ S/m}\)), this holds up to optical frequencies (\(10^{15}\text{ Hz}\)). Under this condition, \(j\omega\mu(\sigma + j\omega\epsilon) \approx j\omega\mu\sigma\): \[ \gamma = \sqrt{j\omega\mu\sigma} = \sqrt{\omega\mu\sigma} e^{j\pi/4} = \sqrt{\frac{\omega\mu\sigma}{2}} + j\sqrt{\frac{\omega\mu\sigma}{2}} \] Therefore: \[ \alpha = \beta = \sqrt{\frac{\omega\mu\sigma}{2}} = \sqrt{\pi f \mu \sigma} \] The intrinsic impedance is: \[ \eta = \sqrt{\frac{j\omega\mu}{\sigma}} = \sqrt{\frac{\omega\mu}{\sigma}}e^{j45^\circ} = (1 + j)\sqrt{\frac{\pi f\mu}{\sigma}} = (1 + j)\frac{1}{\sigma\delta} \] In a good conductor, the magnetic field lags the electric field by exactly \(45^\circ\)!

9. Skin Effect and Skin Depth \(\delta\)

The wave amplitude inside a conductor attenuates exponentially as \(e^{-\alpha z}\). The Skin Depth \(\delta\) (depth of penetration) is defined as the spatial distance over which the field amplitude decays to \(1/e\) (\(\approx 36.8%\)) of its surface value: \[ \delta = \frac{1}{\alpha} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\omega\mu\sigma}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f \mu \sigma}} \quad [\text{m}] \] At a depth of \(5\delta\), the field decays to \(e^{-5} \approx 0.0067\) (\(< 1%\)), meaning RF currents flow exclusively in an ultra-thin surface layer.
High-Frequency Surface Resistance: The effective AC resistance per unit square (surface resistivity) of a conductor of thickness \(gg \delta\) is: \[ R_s = \frac{1}{\sigma\delta} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi f \mu}{\sigma}} \quad [\Omega/square] \] Because \(R_s propto \sqrt{f}\), AC wire resistance increases with the square root of frequency.

10. Worked Numerical Example: Skin Depth and Attenuation in Copper

Problem: A uniform plane wave at \(f = 100\text{ MHz}\) penetrates a copper block (\(\sigma = 5.8 \times 10^7\text{ S/m}, \mu_r = 1, \epsilon_r = 1\)). Calculate: (a) Skin depth \(\delta\), (b) Propagation constant \(\gamma\), (c) Surface resistance \(R_s\), and (d) Distance \(d\) where field amplitude drops to \(10%\) of surface value.

Solution:
1. Check good conductor criterion: \[ \omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 10^8 = 6.283 \times 10^8\text{ rad/s} \] \[ \frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon_0} = \frac{5.8 \times 10^7}{(6.283 \times 10^8) \times (8.854 \times 10^{-12})} = \frac{5.8 \times 10^7}{5.563 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 1.04 \times 10^{10} gg 1 \quad (\text{Superb conductor}) \]
2. Calculate skin depth \(\delta\): \[ \delta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f \mu_0 \sigma}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi \times (10^8) \times (4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times (5.8 \times 10^7)}} \] \[ \delta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi^2 \times 10 \times 5.8 \times 10^7}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{39.478 \times 5.8 \times 10^8}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2.2897 \times 10^{10}}} = \frac{1}{1.5132 \times 10^5} \] \[ \delta \approx 6.608 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m} \approx 6.61 \mu\text{m} \]
3. Propagation constant \(\gamma = \alpha + j\beta\): \[ \alpha = \beta = \frac{1}{\delta} = \frac{1}{6.608 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.513 \times 10^5 \] \[ \gamma = (1.513 \times 10^5) + j(1.513 \times 10^5)\text{ m}^{-1} \] Attenuation is \(1.513 \times 10^5\text{ Np/m}\).
4. Surface resistance \(R_s\): \[ R_s = \frac{1}{\sigma\delta} = \frac{1}{(5.8 \times 10^7) \times (6.608 \times 10^{-6})} = \frac{1}{383.26} = 2.609 \times 10^{-3} \Omega = 2.61\text{ m}\Omega/square \]
5. Distance for \(10%\) amplitude: \[ e^{-\alpha d} = 0.10 implies -\alpha d = \ln(0.10) = -2.3026 \] \[ d = \frac{2.3026}{\alpha} = 2.3026 \delta = 2.3026 \times (6.61 \mu\text{m}) = 15.22 \mu\text{m} \]

Exam Pitfalls & Wave Traps:
  • Phase Angle in Good Conductor: In a good conductor, \(\mathbf{H}\) lags \(\mathbf{E}\) by exactly \(45^\circ\) (\(\pi/4\)). Never assume they are in phase as in lossless dielectrics!
  • Skin Depth Frequency Dependency: \(\delta propto 1/\sqrt{f}\). Doubling the frequency reduces the skin depth by a factor of \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414\), concentrating current closer to the surface.
  • TEM Wave in Waveguides: A hollow, single-conductor rectangular or circular metallic waveguide CANNOT support a TEM wave! TEM waves require at least two separate conductors (like a coaxial line or twin-lead) or an unbounded medium.

Uniform Plane Wave Formulas and Relations

  • Helmholtz Equation: \( abla^2 \mathbf{E} - \gamma^2 \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{0}\); \(\gamma = \alpha + j\beta = \sqrt{j\omega\mu(\sigma + j\omega\epsilon)}\)
  • Free Space: \(\alpha = 0\); \(\beta = \omega/c\); \(u_p = c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\); \(\eta_0 \approx 120\pi \approx 377 \Omega\)
  • Lossless Dielectric: \(\alpha = 0\); \(\beta = \omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}\); \(u_p = 1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}\); \(\eta = \sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}\)
  • Good Conductor: \(\alpha = \beta = \sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}\); \(\delta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}}\); \(\eta = (1+j)\sqrt{\frac{\pi f\mu}{\sigma}}\); Phase lag: \(45^\circ\)
  • Surface Resistance: \(R_s = \frac{1}{\sigma\delta} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi f\mu}{\sigma}}\)
  • TEM Orthogonality: \(\mathbf{a}_k = \mathbf{a}_E \times \mathbf{a}_H\); \(\mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{\eta}\mathbf{a}_k \times \mathbf{E}\)

11. Real-World Engineering Applications

  • Submarine ELF Radio Communication: Seawater has high conductivity (\(\sigma \approx 4\text{ S/m}\)), attenuating standard RF signals within centimeters. Navies use Extremely Low Frequency (ELF, \(30\text{ to }300\text{ Hz}\)) transmitters because at \(45\text{ Hz}\), skin depth in seawater expands to \(\delta \approx 37.5\text{ m}\), allowing messages to reach submerged submarines.
  • Induction Heating: High-frequency AC currents (\(10\text{ to }400\text{ kHz}\)) passed through induction work-coils produce intense eddy currents confined to the skin depth \(\delta\) of metallic workpieces, enabling rapid surface hardening of gear teeth without heating inner cores.
  • RF Shielding & Silver Plating: In high-Q microwave resonators and radar waveguides, components are electroplated with a thin layer (\(\approx 10 \mu\text{m}\)) of silver or gold to provide a low-resistance skin-depth conduction layer.

12. Electromagnetic Wave Polarization

The polarization of a plane wave describes the time locus of the tip of the \(\mathbf{E}\) vector at a fixed point in space:

  • Linear Polarization: \(E_x\) and \(E_y\) are in-phase (or \(180^\circ\) out of phase). The field vector traces a straight line.
  • Circular Polarization (CP): \(E_x\) and \(E_y\) have equal amplitudes (\(E_{0x} = E_{0y}\)) and a \(\pm 90^\circ\) phase difference (\(\delta = \pm \pi/2\)). Left-Hand (LHCP) or Right-Hand (RHCP). Used in satellite communications to eliminate Faraday rotation misalignment.
  • Elliptical Polarization: Arbitrary amplitudes and phase difference.

13. High-Conductivity vs. Poor-Conductivity Transition

The boundary between a lossy dielectric and a good conductor is defined by \(\sigma / (\omega\epsilon) = 1\), corresponding to the relaxation frequency \(f_{\text{relax}} = \frac{\sigma}{2\pi\epsilon}\). For typical soil (\(\sigma \approx 10^{-2}\text{ S/m}, \epsilon_r = 10\)), \(f_{\text{relax}} \approx 18\text{ MHz}\). Below 18 MHz, soil behaves as a conductor; above 18 MHz, it behaves as a lossy dielectric.

14. GATE / IES Exam Tips & Shortcuts

  • If the direction of propagation is \(+z\) and \(\mathbf{E}\) points in \(+\mathbf{a}_x\), then \(\mathbf{H}\) MUST point in \(+\mathbf{a}_y\) because \(\mathbf{a}_x \times \mathbf{a}_y = \mathbf{a}_z\). If propagation is in \(-z\), then \(\mathbf{H}\) points in \(-\mathbf{a}_y\).
  • To find the medium type from given parameters: evaluate \(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon}\). If \(< 0.01\), use low-loss formulas; if \(> 100\), use good-conductor formulas.
  • Nepers to Decibels conversion: \(1\text{ Np} = 20log_{10}(e) \approx 8.686\text{ dB}\).

15. Cross-Topic Bridges & Forward Look

Energy transported by propagating uniform plane waves is rigorously quantified by the Poynting vector, while wave reflections at media boundaries link directly to transmission line impedance transformations in Module V.

emt-poynting-wave-parameters.title: Phase and Group Velocity, Intrinsic Impedance, Propagation Constants, and Poynting Theorem
emt-poynting-wave-parameters.body:
Energy transmission is the ultimate physical purpose of electromagnetic waves—from gigawatt electrical power corridors and microwave telemetry to fiber-optic global backbones. The rate and direction of electromagnetic energy flow are governed by John Henry Poynting's 1884 theorem, which formulates the conservation of energy directly from Maxwell's equations. In dispersive physical media, the speed of individual phase fronts (phase velocity \(u_p\)) diverges from the propagation speed of the information envelope (group velocity \(u_g\)). Mastering the complex Poynting vector, dispersion relations, and intrinsic impedance is essential for antenna radiation, wireless link budgets, and microwave communications.

1. Prerequisite & Mathematical Concept Anchor

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Phase and Group Velocity, Intrinsic Impedance, Propagation Constants, and Poynting Theorem

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Phase and Group Velocity, Intrinsic Impedance, Propagation Constants, and Poynting Theorem.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Poynting's Theorem requires taking the divergence of the cross product of field vectors using the vector identity: \[ abla \cdot (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{H}) = \mathbf{H} \cdot ( abla \times \mathbf{E}) - \mathbf{E} \cdot ( abla \times \mathbf{H}) \] Phasor power calculations in electrodynamics parallel AC circuit analysis: instantaneous power oscillates at twice the source frequency (\(2\omega\)), while time-average power is computed via half the real part of the product with the complex conjugate.

2. Derivation of Poynting's Theorem

  1. Start from the two Maxwell curl equations: \[ abla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = -\mu \frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial t} \] \[ abla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t} = \mathbf{J} + \epsilon \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} \]
  2. Dot multiply the first equation by \(\mathbf{H}\) and the second by \(\mathbf{E}\): \[ \mathbf{H} \cdot ( abla \times \mathbf{E}) = -\mu \mathbf{H} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac{1}{2}\mu |\mathbf{H}|^2\right) \] \[ \mathbf{E} \cdot ( abla \times \mathbf{H}) = \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{J} + \epsilon \mathbf{E} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} = \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{J} + \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac{1}{2}\epsilon |\mathbf{E}|^2\right) \]
  3. Subtract the second equation from the first and apply the vector identity: \[ abla \cdot (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{H}) = -\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{J} - \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac{1}{2}\epsilon |\mathbf{E}|^2 + \frac{1}{2}\mu |\mathbf{H}|^2\right) \]
  4. Integrate over a volume \(v\) bounded by closed surface \(S\) and apply the Divergence Theorem: \[ oint_S (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{H}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = -\int_v \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{J}, dv - \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_v \left(\frac{1}{2}\epsilon |\mathbf{E}|^2 + \frac{1}{2}\mu |\mathbf{H}|^2\right), dv \]
Rearranging into the standard conservation-of-energy statement: \[ -oint_S \mathbf{S} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_v \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{J}, dv + \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_v (w_E + w_M), dv \]

3. Physical Interpretation of Poynting's Theorem

The integral balance equation states that:
\(\left[\begin{array}{c}\text{Total electromagnetic power} \text{flowing INWARD through surface } S\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{c}\text{Ohmic power dissipated as heat} \text{(Joule loss) inside volume } v\end{array}\right] + \left[\begin{array}{c}\text{Time rate of increase of stored} \text{electric and magnetic energy in } v\end{array}\right]\)

  • \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{H}\): Poynting Vector (Power density in \(\text{Watts per square meter, W/m}^2\)).
  • \(\int_v \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{J}, dv = \int_v \sigma |\mathbf{E}|^2, dv\): Total Ohmic power loss (Watts).
  • \(w_E = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon |\mathbf{E}|^2\): Stored electrostatic energy density (\(\text{J/m}^3\)).
  • \(w_M = \frac{1}{2}\mu |\mathbf{H}|^2\): Stored magnetostatic energy density (\(\text{J/m}^3\)).

4. Time-Average Poynting Vector for Harmonic Fields

For sinusoidal time-harmonic electromagnetic waves, the instantaneous Poynting vector fluctuates at \(2\omega\). In communication engineering and power radiation, we require the time-average power flow \(\mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}}\): \[ \mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}} = langle \mathbf{S}(t) angle = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T \mathbf{S}(t), dt = \frac{1}{2}operatorname{Re}\left( ilde{\mathbf{E}} \times ilde{\mathbf{H}}^*\right) \quad [\text{W/m}^2] \] where \( ilde{\mathbf{H}}^*\) is the complex conjugate of the magnetic phasor.
For a uniform plane wave propagating in the \(+z\) direction in a lossy medium with \( ilde{\mathbf{E}} = E_0 e^{-\alpha z}e^{-j\beta z}\mathbf{a}_x\) and \( ilde{\mathbf{H}} = \frac{E_0}{|\eta|}e^{-\alpha z}e^{-j\beta z}e^{-j\theta_\eta}\mathbf{a}_y\): \[ ilde{\mathbf{E}} \times ilde{\mathbf{H}}^* = \frac{|E_0|^2}{|\eta|}e^{-2\alpha z}e^{j\theta_\eta}\mathbf{a}_z \] \[ \mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{|E_0|^2}{|\eta|}e^{-2\alpha z}\cos\theta_\eta \mathbf{a}_z \quad [\text{W/m}^2] \] In a lossless medium (\(\alpha = 0, \theta_\eta = 0, \eta = \text{real}\)): \[ \mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{|E_0|^2}{\eta}\mathbf{a}_z = \frac{1}{2}\eta |H_0|^2\mathbf{a}_z \] Notice that the power density attenuates as \(e^{-2\alpha z}\)—twice as fast as the electric field amplitude (\(e^{-\alpha z}\)).

5. Phase Velocity \(u_p\)

The phase velocity is the speed at which a point of constant phase on the wave cycle travels through space: \[ \phi(z, t) = \omega t - \beta z = \text{constant} implies \frac{d\phi}{dt} = \omega - \beta \frac{dz}{dt} = 0 \] \[ u_p = \frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\omega}{\beta} \quad [\text{m/s}] \] In a non-dispersive medium where \(\beta = \omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}\) is strictly linear with frequency: \[ u_p = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}} = \text{constant} \] However, in waveguiding structures or plasmas, \(\beta(\omega)\) is non-linear, making \(u_p\) depend on frequency, and \(u_p\) can exceed the speed of light in vacuum (\(u_p > c\)) without violating special relativity because pure phase carries no physical information.

6. Group Velocity \(u_g\) & Dispersion

When an information-carrying modulated signal (wave packet) composed of multiple spectral frequencies propagates through a dispersive medium, the overall envelope (modulation profile) travels at the group velocity: \[ u_g = \frac{d\omega}{d\beta} = \left(\frac{d\beta}{d\omega}\right)^{-1} \quad [\text{m/s}] \] Relating phase and group velocity: Since \(\beta = \omega / u_p\), differentiating gives: \[ \frac{d\beta}{d\omega} = \frac{1}{u_p} - \frac{\omega}{u_p^2}\frac{du_p}{d\omega} implies u_g = \frac{u_p}{1 - \frac{\omega}{u_p}\frac{du_p}{d\omega}} = u_p - \lambda \frac{du_p}{d\lambda} \] Classification of Dispersion:

  • Normal Dispersion: \(\frac{du_p}{d\lambda} > 0 implies u_g < u_p\). Higher frequencies travel slower.
  • Anomalous Dispersion: \(\frac{du_p}{d\lambda} < 0 implies u_g > u_p\). Occurs near absorption bands.
  • Non-Dispersive Medium (Free Space): \(\frac{du_p}{d\lambda} = 0 implies u_g = u_p = c\). All frequency components travel at identical speeds; pulses propagate without distortion.
In hollow metallic waveguides, the fundamental product relation is: \[ u_p \cdot u_g = c^2 \] Since \(u_p > c\), the information velocity is strictly bounded: \(u_g < c\).

7. Intrinsic Impedance across Media

The intrinsic impedance represents the ratio of the transverse electric field to transverse magnetic field:

  • Vacuum: \(\eta_0 = \sqrt{\frac{\mu_0}{\epsilon_0}} \approx 377 \Omega\) (purely real, \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) in phase).
  • Lossless Dielectric: \(\eta = \frac{\eta_0}{\sqrt{\epsilon_r}}\) (purely real).
  • Good Conductor: \(\eta = \sqrt{\frac{\omega\mu}{\sigma}}\angle 45^\circ\) (complex, \(\mathbf{H}\) lags \(\mathbf{E}\) by \(45^\circ\)).
  • Plasma / Ionosphere: \(\eta = \frac{\eta_0}{\sqrt{1 - (\omega_p/\omega)^2}}\), where \(\omega_p\) is the plasma cut-off frequency. For \(\omega < \omega_p\), \(\eta\) becomes purely imaginary (total reflection, zero real power transmission).

8. Poynting Vector in a DC Circuit: Energy Flow Mechanism

A common misconception is that electrical energy flows inside the conducting wires of a DC circuit. Poynting's theorem reveals the true field mechanism: Consider a cylindrical resistor of radius \(a\), length \(L\), and conductivity \(\sigma\) carrying DC current \(I\):

  • Current produces an internal electric field along the axis: \(\mathbf{E} = \frac{I}{\sigma \pi a^2}\mathbf{a}_z\).
  • Current produces an azimuthal magnetic field at the surface: \(\mathbf{H} = \frac{I}{2\pi a}\mathbf{a}_\phi\).
  • The Poynting vector at the outer surface is directed radially inward into the resistor: \[ \mathbf{S} = \mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{H} = \left(\frac{I}{\sigma \pi a^2}\mathbf{a}_z\right) \times \left(\frac{I}{2\pi a}\mathbf{a}_\phi\right) = -\frac{I^2}{2\pi^2 \sigma a^3}\mathbf{a}_\rho \]
  • Integrating \(\mathbf{S}\) over the outer surface area \(2\pi a L\): \[ P_{\text{in}} = \int_S (-\mathbf{S}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \left(\frac{I^2}{2\pi^2 \sigma a^3}\right)(2\pi a L) = I^2 \left(\frac{L}{\sigma \pi a^2}\right) = I^2 R \]
Electromagnetic energy leaves the battery through the surrounding space and enters the resistor through its cylindrical boundary, where it is converted into heat!

9. Worked Numerical Example: Time-Average Poynting Vector in Lossy Earth

Problem: In a lossy soil medium with \(\epsilon_r = 9\), \(\mu_r = 1\), and \(\sigma = 0.02\text{ S/m}\), a uniform plane wave at \(f = 100\text{ MHz}\) has an electric field at the surface (\(z = 0\)) given by \(\mathbf{E}(0, t) = 50\cos(\omega t)\mathbf{a}_x\text{ V/m}\). Determine: (a) Attenuation constant \(\alpha\) and phase constant \(\beta\), (b) Intrinsic impedance \(\eta\), (c) Time-average power density \(\mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}}\) at the surface \(z = 0\), and (d) Time-average power density at depth \(z = 1\text{ meter}\).

Solution:
1. Evaluate loss tangent: \[ \omega = 2\pi \times 10^8 \approx 6.283 \times 10^8\text{ rad/s} \] \[ \epsilon = 9\epsilon_0 = 9 \times (8.854 \times 10^{-12}) = 7.9686 \times 10^{-11}\text{ F/m} \] \[ \tan\theta = \frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon} = \frac{0.02}{(6.283 \times 10^8) \times (7.9686 \times 10^{-11})} = \frac{0.02}{0.05007} \approx 0.3995 \] Since \(\tan\theta\) is neither \(ll 1\) nor \(gg 1\), use general formulas: \[ \sqrt{1 + (\tan\theta)^2} = \sqrt{1 + 0.3995^2} = \sqrt{1.1596} \approx 1.0768 \]
2. Compute \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\): \[ \omega\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon} = \frac{\omega}{c}\sqrt{\epsilon_r} = \frac{2\pi \times 10^8}{3 \times 10^8}\sqrt{9} = 2\pi = 6.283\text{ rad/m} \] \[ \alpha = 6.283 \left[\frac{1.0768 - 1}{2}\right]^{1/2} = 6.283 \sqrt{0.0384} = 6.283 \times 0.1960 \approx 1.231\text{ Np/m} \] \[ \beta = 6.283 \left[\frac{1.0768 + 1}{2}\right]^{1/2} = 6.283 \sqrt{1.0384} = 6.283 \times 1.0190 \approx 6.402\text{ rad/m} \]
3. Compute intrinsic impedance \(\eta\): \[ |\eta| = \frac{\sqrt{\mu_0/\epsilon}}{[1 + (\sigma/\omega\epsilon)^2]^{1/4}} = \frac{377 / 3}{(1.1596)^{1/4}} = \frac{125.67}{1.0377} \approx 121.1 \Omega \] \[ \theta_\eta = \frac{1}{2}\arctan(0.3995) = \frac{1}{2}(21.78^\circ) \approx 10.89^\circ \] \[ \eta = 121.1\angle 10.89^\circ \Omega \]
4. Power density at surface \(z = 0\): \[ S_{\text{avg}}(0) = \frac{1}{2}\frac{|E_0|^2}{|\eta|}\cos\theta_\eta = \frac{1}{2} \frac{50^2}{121.1} \cos(10.89^\circ) = \frac{2500}{242.2} \times 0.9820 = 10.322 \times 0.9820 \approx 10.14\text{ W/m}^2 \] \[ \mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}}(0) = 10.14\mathbf{a}_z\text{ W/m}^2 \]
5. Power density at depth \(z = 1\text{ meter}\): \[ S_{\text{avg}}(1) = S_{\text{avg}}(0) e^{-2\alpha(1)} = 10.14 \times e^{-2(1.231)} = 10.14 \times e^{-2.462} = 10.14 \times 0.08526 \approx 0.865\text{ W/m}^2 \] \[ \mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}}(1) = 0.865\mathbf{a}_z\text{ W/m}^2 \] Over \(91.5%\) of the wave power is absorbed by the lossy earth within the first meter!

Exam Pitfalls & Poynting Traps:
  • Forgetting the Factor of 1/2 in \(\mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}}\): When using peak amplitudes \(E_0\) and \(H_0\), \(\mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}operatorname{Re}( ilde{\mathbf{E}} \times ilde{\mathbf{H}}^*)\). If RMS values are used, the factor of 1/2 is omitted: \(\mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}} = operatorname{Re}(\mathbf{E}_{\text{rms}} \times \mathbf{H}_{\text{rms}}^*)\).
  • Power Attenuation Rate is \(2\alpha\): Field amplitude attenuates as \(e^{-\alpha z}\), but power density attenuates as \(e^{-2\alpha z}\). Squaring the field doubles the attenuation exponent!
  • Phase Velocity Exceeding \(c\): Finding \(u_p > c\) in a waveguide or plasma is completely physical and does not violate physics, provided \(u_g < c\). Never write that \(u_p > c\) is impossible!

Poynting Theorem and Wave Velocities Summary

  • Poynting Vector: \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{H}\text{ [W/m}^2\text{]}\)
  • Time-Average Power: \(\mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}operatorname{Re}( ilde{\mathbf{E}} \times ilde{\mathbf{H}}^*)\)
  • Power in Lossless Medium: \(S_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{|E_0|^2}{\eta} = \frac{1}{2}\eta |H_0|^2\)
  • Poynting Conservation: \(-oint_S \mathbf{S} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_v \mathbf{J} \cdot \mathbf{E}, dv + \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_v (w_E + w_M), dv\)
  • Phase Velocity: \(u_p = \frac{\omega}{\beta}\); Group Velocity: \(u_g = \frac{d\omega}{d\beta}\)
  • Waveguide Velocity Relation: \(u_p \cdot u_g = c^2\)
  • Energy Attenuation: \(P(z) = P_0 e^{-2\alpha z}\)

10. Real-World Engineering Applications

  • Solar Radiation & Solar Cell Sizing: At the edge of Earth's atmosphere, the sun's Poynting vector magnitude (solar constant) is \(S_{\text{avg}} \approx 1361\text{ W/m}^2\). At ground level on a clear day, \(S_{\text{avg}} \approx 1000\text{ W/m}^2\), directly determining photovoltaic panel area requirements.
  • Radiation Pressure & Solar Sails: When an electromagnetic wave strikes a surface, it exerts radiation pressure \(P_{\text{rad}} = \frac{langle S angle}{c}\) (for total absorption) or \(P_{\text{rad}} = \frac{2langle S angle}{c}\) (for total reflection). Interplanetary spacecraft utilize deployable reflective aluminized Mylar sails to achieve fuel-free propulsion driven by solar radiation pressure.
  • Specific Absorption Rate (SAR) in Mobile Phones: Cellular mobile safety standards (FCC/ICNIRP) regulate RF energy absorption in human tissue, quantifying SAR in Watts per kilogram: \(\text{SAR} = \frac{\sigma |\mathbf{E}|^2}{2 ho_{\text{mass}}}\).

11. Total Power Radiated by an Antenna

To compute the total power \(P_{\text{rad}}\) radiated by an antenna into space, the time-average Poynting vector is integrated over an imaginary enclosing sphere in the far field (\(r o \infty\)): \[ P_{\text{rad}} = oint_S \mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_0^{2\pi} d\phi \int_0^\pi S_r(r, \theta, \phi) r^2\sin\theta, d\theta \] For an isotropic radiator, \(S_r = \frac{P_{\text{rad}}}{4\pi r^2}\). For an infinitesimal Hertzian dipole: \(P_{\text{rad}} = 40\pi^2 I_0^2 (dl/\lambda)^2\).

12. Complex Poynting Vector & Reactive Power

The generalized complex Poynting vector is: \[ \mathbf{S}_c = \frac{1}{2} ilde{\mathbf{E}} \times ilde{\mathbf{H}}^* = \mathbf{P} + j\mathbf{Q} \] Taking its divergence: \[ abla \cdot \mathbf{S}_c = -\frac{1}{2}\sigma | ilde{\mathbf{E}}|^2 - 2j\omega\left(\frac{1}{4}\mu | ilde{\mathbf{H}}|^2 - \frac{1}{4}\epsilon | ilde{\mathbf{E}}|^2\right) \] The real part represents real time-average dissipated power, while the imaginary part represents net reactive power oscillating between magnetic and electric energy reservoirs.

13. Dispersion in Optical Fibers

In silica optical fibers, chromatic dispersion arises from material dispersion (\(dn/d\lambda e 0\)) and waveguide dispersion. High data rates cause optical pulses to broaden temporally as \(\Delta \tau = D \cdot L \cdot \Delta \lambda\) (where \(D\) is the dispersion parameter in \(\text{ps}/(\text{nm}\cdot\text{km})\)), causing inter-symbol interference (ISI) that requires dispersion-compensating fibers (DCF).

14. GATE / IES Exam Tips & Shortcuts

  • If an electric field is given as \(\mathbf{E} = E_0\cos(\omega t - \beta z)\mathbf{a}_x\), the time-average power is simply \(\frac{E_0^2}{2\eta}\mathbf{a}_z\). You do not need to integrate over time from scratch!
  • To find the direction of power flow, compute \(\mathbf{a}_E \times \mathbf{a}_H\). If \(\mathbf{E} = E_y\mathbf{a}_y\) and \(\mathbf{H} = H_x\mathbf{a}_x\), then \(\mathbf{S} propto \mathbf{a}_y \times \mathbf{a}_x = -\mathbf{a}_z\) (the wave propagates in \(-z\)).
  • For reflection at a perfect conductor, \(\mathbf{S}_{\text{avg}} = \mathbf{0}\) because the incident and reflected waves form a standing wave where \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) are in spatial and temporal quadrature (\(90^\circ\) phase difference).

15. Cross-Topic Bridges & Forward Look

Poynting power flow along guided structures transitions into guided wave propagation on transmission lines in Module V, where voltage and current waves represent integrated electric and magnetic fields.

emt-transmission-lines.title: Transmission Line Parameters, Wave Equations, Propagation Constants, and Characteristic Impedance
emt-transmission-lines.body:
When the physical length of an electrical interconnect becomes comparable to or exceeds approximately \(\lambda/10\) of the operating electrical signal wavelength, conventional lumped-element circuit theory (Kirchhoff's Voltage and Current Laws) breaks down due to finite propagation delays. Under these high-frequency conditions, distributed-parameter transmission line theory bridges circuit theory and Maxwell's field equations. A transmission line—whether an overhead power line, coaxial cable, or microstrip trace—is characterized by distributed resistance \(R'\), inductance \(L'\), conductance \(G'\), and capacitance \(C'\) per unit length. The resulting Telegrapher's Equations yield forward and backward traveling voltage and current waves governed by characteristic impedance \(Z_0\) and propagation constant \(\gamma\).

1. Prerequisite & Mathematical Concept Anchor

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Transmission Line Parameters, Wave Equations, Propagation Constants, and Characteristic Impedance

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Transmission Line Parameters, Wave Equations, Propagation Constants, and Characteristic Impedance.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Lumped vs. Distributed Criterion: If line length \(l < 0.01\lambda\), lumped analysis suffices. If \(0.01\lambda le l le 0.1\lambda\), lumped approximations with lumped parasitics may be used. If \(l > 0.1\lambda\), distributed wave analysis is mandatory. For example, for \(50\text{ Hz}\) power lines, \(\lambda = c/f = 3 \times 10^8 / 50 = 6000\text{ km}\); lines longer than \(60\text{ km}\) exhibit distributed wave phenomena. For a \(3\text{ GHz}\) CPU clock on a PCB, \(\lambda = 10\text{ cm}\); traces longer than \(1\text{ cm}\) behave as distributed transmission lines.

2. Distributed Transmission Line Parameters

A two-conductor transmission line is modeled as a cascade of infinitesimal sections of length \(\Delta z\), each containing:

  • \(R'\): Series resistance per unit length (\(\Omega/\text{m}\)), representing conductor Ohmic and skin-effect losses in both conductors.
  • \(L'\): Series inductance per unit length (\(\text{H/m}\)), representing total self-inductance (internal plus external magnetic flux linkage).
  • \(G'\): Shunt conductance per unit length (\(\text{S/m}\)), representing dielectric leakage conduction through the insulating medium separating the conductors.
  • \(C'\): Shunt capacitance per unit length (\(\text{F/m}\)), representing electrostatic charge storage between the conductors.
These four parameters are completely determined by line geometry and materials: For coaxial line: \(L' = \frac{\mu}{2\pi}\ln(b/a)\), \(C' = \frac{2\pi\epsilon}{\ln(b/a)}\), \(G' = \frac{2\pi\sigma}{\ln(b/a)}\). Notice that for all TEM transmission lines in a homogeneous medium: \[ L' C' = \mu\epsilon = \frac{1}{u^2}, \quad \frac{G'}{C'} = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon} \]

3. Derivation of Telegrapher's Equations

Consider an incremental line section between \(z\) and \(z + \Delta z\): Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law to the loop: \[ v(z, t) - R'\Delta z, i(z, t) - L'\Delta z \frac{\partial i(z, t)}{\partial t} - v(z + \Delta z, t) = 0 \] Dividing by \(\Delta z\) and taking the limit \(\Delta z o 0\): \[ -\frac{\partial v(z, t)}{\partial z} = R' i(z, t) + L' \frac{\partial i(z, t)}{\partial t} \quad \text{(First Telegrapher Equation)} \] Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law to the node: \[ i(z, t) - G'\Delta z, v(z + \Delta z, t) - C'\Delta z \frac{\partial v(z + \Delta z, t)}{\partial t} - i(z + \Delta z, t) = 0 \] Dividing by \(\Delta z\) as \(\Delta z o 0\): \[ -\frac{\partial i(z, t)}{\partial z} = G' v(z, t) + C' \frac{\partial v(z, t)}{\partial t} \quad \text{(Second Telegrapher Equation)} \]

4. Time-Harmonic (Phasor) Wave Equations

Assuming sinusoidal steady state (\(\frac{\partial}{\partial t} o j\omega\)): \[ -\frac{d V(z)}{dz} = (R' + j\omega L') I(z) = Z' I(z) \] \[ -\frac{d I(z)}{dz} = (G' + j\omega C') V(z) = Y' V(z) \] where \(Z' = R' + j\omega L'\) is the series impedance per unit length and \(Y' = G' + j\omega C'\) is the shunt admittance per unit length. Differentiating the voltage equation with respect to \(z\) and substituting the current derivative: \[ -\frac{d^2 V(z)}{dz^2} = Z' \frac{d I(z)}{dz} = Z' (-Y' V(z)) \] \[ \frac{d^2 V(z)}{dz^2} - \gamma^2 V(z) = 0 \] Similarly for current: \[ \frac{d^2 I(z)}{dz^2} - \gamma^2 I(z) = 0 \] where \(\gamma\) is the complex Propagation Constant of the line: \[ \gamma = \alpha + j\beta = \sqrt{Z' Y'} = \sqrt{(R' + j\omega L')(G' + j\omega C')} \]

5. Wave Solutions and Characteristic Impedance \(Z_0\)

The general solutions to the second-order ordinary differential equations are: \[ V(z) = V_0^+ e^{-\gamma z} + V_0^- e^{+\gamma z} \] \[ I(z) = I_0^+ e^{-\gamma z} + I_0^- e^{+\gamma z} \] where the \(e^{-\gamma z} = e^{-\alpha z}e^{-j\beta z}\) term represents a forward-traveling wave propagating in \(+z\), and the \(e^{+\gamma z}\) term represents a backward-traveling (reflected) wave propagating in \(-z\).
Substituting \(V(z)\) back into the first Telegrapher equation: \[ -\frac{dV}{dz} = \gamma V_0^+ e^{-\gamma z} - \gamma V_0^- e^{+\gamma z} = Z' I(z) \] \[ I(z) = \frac{\gamma}{Z'} V_0^+ e^{-\gamma z} - \frac{\gamma}{Z'} V_0^- e^{+\gamma z} \] The ratio of forward voltage to forward current is defined as the Characteristic Impedance \(Z_0\): \[ Z_0 = \frac{V_0^+}{I_0^+} = \frac{Z'}{\gamma} = \frac{R' + j\omega L'}{\sqrt{(R' + j\omega L')(G' + j\omega C')}} = \sqrt{\frac{R' + j\omega L'}{G' + j\omega C'}} \quad [\Omega] \] For the reflected wave, the current is reversed in direction: \(I_0^- / V_0^- = -1/Z_0\). Thus: \[ I(z) = \frac{V_0^+}{Z_0} e^{-\gamma z} - \frac{V_0^-}{Z_0} e^{+\gamma z} \]

6. Lossless Transmission Lines

For an ideal lossless line (\(R' = 0, G' = 0\)): \[ \gamma = \sqrt{(j\omega L')(j\omega C')} = j\omega\sqrt{L'C'} \] \[ \alpha = 0 \quad (\text{Zero attenuation}) \] \[ \beta = \omega\sqrt{L'C'} \quad [\text{rad/m}] \] \[ Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{L'}{C'}} \quad [\Omega] \quad (\text{Purely real and resistive}) \] Velocity of propagation: \[ u_p = \frac{\omega}{\beta} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L'C'}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu_r\epsilon_r}} \] Wavelength on the line: \[ \lambda = \frac{u_p}{f} = \frac{2\pi}{\beta} \] Notice that for a lossless line, \(Z_0\) and \(u_p\) are completely independent of frequency!

7. Distortionless Transmission Line (Heaviside Condition)

Oliver Heaviside proved that signal distortion occurs when attenuation \(\alpha\) varies with frequency or when phase velocity \(u_p = \omega/\beta\) varies with frequency. A line is distortionless if \(\alpha\) is independent of frequency and \(\beta\) is strictly proportional to frequency. Evaluating \(\gamma\): \[ \gamma = \sqrt{R' G'}\left(1 + j\omega\frac{L'}{R'}\right)^{1/2}\left(1 + j\omega\frac{C'}{G'}\right)^{1/2} \] If the time constants of the series and shunt branches are equal: \[ \frac{L'}{R'} = \frac{C'}{G'} iff R'C' = L'G' \quad \text{(Heaviside Distortionless Condition)} \] Then: \[ \gamma = \sqrt{R'G'}\left(1 + j\omega\frac{L'}{R'}\right) = \sqrt{R'G'} + j\omega L'\sqrt{\frac{G'}{R'}} = \sqrt{R'G'} + j\omega\sqrt{L'C'} \] Therefore: \[ \alpha = \sqrt{R'G'} \quad (\text{Constant with frequency!}) \] \[ \beta = \omega\sqrt{L'C'} implies u_p = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L'C'}} \quad (\text{Constant with frequency!}) \] \[ Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R'}{G'}} = \sqrt{\frac{L'}{C'}} \quad (\text{Purely resistive!}) \] In practical telephone lines, \(R'C' gg L'G'\). Pupin coils (lumped loading inductors added periodically) were historically used to increase \(L'\) to approach the Heaviside condition, drastically improving voice intelligibility over transcontinental lines.

8. Low-Loss Transmission Lines

When losses are very small but non-zero (\(R' ll \omega L'\) and \(G' ll \omega C'\)): Using binomial expansion: \[ \alpha \approx \frac{1}{2}\left(R'\sqrt{\frac{C'}{L'}} + G'\sqrt{\frac{L'}{C'}}\right) = \frac{R'}{2Z_0} + \frac{G' Z_0}{2} \quad [\text{Np/m}] \] \[ \beta \approx \omega\sqrt{L'C'}, \quad Z_0 \approx \sqrt{\frac{L'}{C'}} \]

9. Worked Numerical Example: High-Frequency Coaxial Line Parameters

Problem: A lossless coaxial cable has capacitance \(C' = 100\text{ pF/m}\) and characteristic impedance \(Z_0 = 50 \Omega\). The cable operates at \(f = 300\text{ MHz}\). Calculate: (a) Inductance per meter \(L'\), (b) Propagation velocity \(u_p\) and relative permittivity \(\epsilon_r\) of the dielectric (\(\mu_r = 1\)), (c) Phase constant \(\beta\) and wavelength \(\lambda\), and (d) Phase shift between two points separated by \(25\text{ cm}\).

Solution:
1. Determine inductance \(L'\): \[ Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{L'}{C'}} implies Z_0^2 = \frac{L'}{C'} \] \[ L' = Z_0^2 C' = (50)^2 \times (100 \times 10^{-12}) = 2500 \times 10^{-10} = 2.5 \times 10^{-7}\text{ H/m} = 0.25 \mu\text{H/m} = 250\text{ nH/m} \]
2. Velocity of propagation \(u_p\) and \(\epsilon_r\): \[ u_p = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L'C'}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2.5 \times 10^{-7}) \times (100 \times 10^{-12})}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-17}}} = \frac{1}{5 \times 10^{-9}} = 2 \times 10^8\text{ m/s} \] Since \(u_p = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\epsilon_r}}\): \[ \sqrt{\epsilon_r} = \frac{c}{u_p} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{2 \times 10^8} = 1.5 implies \epsilon_r = (1.5)^2 = 2.25 \quad (\text{Polyethylene}) \]
3. Phase constant \(\beta\) and wavelength \(\lambda\): \[ \lambda = \frac{u_p}{f} = \frac{2 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{300 \times 10^6\text{ Hz}} = \frac{2}{3}\text{ m} \approx 0.6667\text{ m} = 66.67\text{ cm} \] \[ \beta = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} = \frac{2\pi}{2/3} = 3\pi \approx 9.425\text{ rad/m} \] Alternatively: \(\beta = \omega\sqrt{L'C'} = \frac{2\pi \times (3 \times 10^8)}{2 \times 10^8} = 3\pi\text{ rad/m}\).
4. Phase shift over \(d = 25\text{ cm} = 0.25\text{ m}\): \[ \Delta\theta = \beta d = (3\pi\text{ rad/m}) \times (0.25\text{ m}) = 0.75\pi\text{ radians} = 135^\circ \]

Exam Pitfalls & Transmission Line Traps:
  • \(Z_0\) is NOT Input Impedance: The characteristic impedance \(Z_0\) is a property of the line alone; it is the input impedance of an infinite line. The actual input impedance \(Z_{\text{in}}\) of a finite line depends heavily on load impedance \(Z_L\) and line length \(l\).
  • Distortionless Condition Confusion: The Heaviside condition is \(R'/L' = G'/C'\) or \(R'C' = L'G'\). Do NOT write \(R'L' = G'C'\)! Check units: \(R'/L'\) has units of \(\text{s}^{-1}\), matching \(G'/C'\).
  • Velocity Never Exceeds \(c\): For any physical transmission line with standard dielectrics (\(\epsilon_r ge 1\)), \(u_p = c/\sqrt{\epsilon_r} le c\). If your calculated velocity exceeds \(3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\), your calculation is inverted!

Transmission Line Wave Parameters Summary

  • Telegrapher's Equations: \(-\frac{\partial v}{\partial z} = R' i + L'\frac{\partial i}{\partial t}\); \(-\frac{\partial i}{\partial z} = G' v + C'\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}\)
  • Propagation Constant: \(\gamma = \alpha + j\beta = \sqrt{(R' + j\omega L')(G' + j\omega C')}\)
  • Characteristic Impedance: \(Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R' + j\omega L'}{G' + j\omega C'}}\)
  • Lossless Line: \(\alpha = 0\); \(\beta = \omega\sqrt{L'C'}\); \(Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{L'}{C'}}\); \(u_p = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L'C'}}\)
  • Heaviside Condition: \(R'C' = L'G' implies \alpha = \sqrt{R'G'}\), \(\beta = \omega\sqrt{L'C'}\), \(Z_0 = \sqrt{L'/C'}\)
  • TEM Relations: \(L'C' = \mu\epsilon\); \(G'/C' = \sigma/\epsilon\)
  • Low-Loss Attenuation: \(\alpha \approx \frac{R'}{2Z_0} + \frac{G'Z_0}{2}\)

10. Real-World Engineering Applications

  • Overhead EHV Transmission Line Surge Impedance: Overhead 400 kV lines have characteristic impedance (surge impedance) \(Z_0 \approx 250\text{ to }400 \Omega\). The Surge Impedance Loading (SIL) \(P_{\text{SIL}} = V^2 / Z_0\) defines the optimal power transfer at which reactive power generated by line capacitance balances reactive power consumed by line inductance.
  • High-Speed Digital PCB Interconnects: In PCIe Gen 5 (\(32\text{ GT/s}\)) and DDR5 computer buses, trace geometry (trace width, copper thickness, dielectric core height) is strictly controlled to maintain differential impedance at \(85 \Omega\) or single-ended at \(50 \Omega \pm 10%\) to eliminate signal reflections that corrupt binary bits.
