This circuit is the simplest three-phase converter and it introduces the two ideas that carry over to every polyphase converter: the device with the most positive anode conducts, and the natural commutation point is no longer the supply zero crossing.

◆ Circuit and operation

Three SCRs, one per phase, with their cathodes commoned to form the positive output terminal; the load returns to the supply neutral. Only one device conducts at a time — whichever phase is most positive and has been triggered.

The crucial subtlety: with an uncontrolled diode version, phase A takes over from phase C at the instant where v_A becomes more positive than v_C, which is 30° after the zero crossing of v_A. That instant is the natural commutation point, and the firing angle α is measured from there, not from the phase voltage zero. Getting this reference wrong is the single most common error in three-phase rectifier problems.

Each device conducts for 120° in a cycle, giving three pulses per cycle (150 Hz ripple on a 50 Hz supply).

◆ Output voltage

For a resistive load with α ≤ 30°, conduction is continuous and:

V_dc = (3√3·V_mp / 2π)·cos α = 0.827·V_mp·cos α
SymbolMeaningUnit
V_mpPeak of the phase (line-to-neutral) voltageV
αFiring angle measured from the natural commutation point (30° after the phase voltage zero)degrees

For α > 30° with a resistive load, the output voltage would try to go negative, but a resistive load cannot carry negative current, so conduction becomes discontinuous and a different expression applies:

V_dc = (3V_mp/2π)·[1 + cos(α + 30°)] (R load, α > 30°)

◆ Worked example (verified)

A 400 V (line-to-line), 50 Hz supply feeds a three-phase half-wave controlled rectifier with a resistive load.

Phase voltage = 400/√3 = 231.0 V rms, so V_mp = √2 × 231.0 = 326.60 V.
At α = 0: V_dc = (3√3 × 326.60)/(2π) = 1696.9/6.2832 = 270.09 V.
At α = 30°: V_dc = 270.09 × cos 30° = 233.90 V — the boundary of continuous conduction.

◆ Comparison with single-phase

1-ph half-wave1-ph full bridge3-ph half-wave
Pulses per cycle123
Ripple frequency (50 Hz supply)50 Hz100 Hz150 Hz
Ripple magnitudeVery largeLargeModerate
Device conduction angleπ − α180° per pair120°
Transformer DC componentYesNoYes

More pulses means higher ripple frequency, which means a smaller and cheaper output filter for the same smoothing. That single sentence explains the whole industry preference for polyphase converters.

Common mistake: measuring α from the phase voltage zero crossing. In every polyphase converter, α is measured from the natural commutation point — the crossover with the preceding phase, 30° after the zero for a three-phase half-wave circuit. Using the wrong reference shifts every answer by 30°.
Placement trap: "Three-phase is better than single-phase, so why is the three-phase half-wave circuit still rarely used?" Because it shares the half-wave circuit's fatal flaw: each secondary winding carries current in one direction only for 120° per cycle, so there is a DC component in the supply transformer, which drives the core towards saturation and forces the transformer to be oversized. It also needs a neutral connection. The three-phase full bridge removes both objections — every winding carries symmetrical bidirectional current, there is no DC component, and no neutral is required — which is why it, not this circuit, is the industrial standard.

◆ Quick revision

  • Most positive triggered phase conducts; 120° conduction per device; 3 pulses per cycle
  • α measured from the natural commutation point, 30° after the phase voltage zero
  • V_dc = 0.827·V_mp·cos α for α ≤ 30° (R load, continuous)
  • α > 30° with R load ⇒ discontinuous ⇒ V_dc = (3V_mp/2π)[1 + cos(α + 30°)]
  • Needs a neutral and injects a DC component into the transformer ⇒ rarely used industrially

psa-stability-types.title: Power System Stability: Types, the Power-Angle Curve and the Steady-State Limit
psa-stability-types.body:
Prerequisite: The load flow problem — the power-angle relationship here is the same P = (V₁V₂/X)sin δ that underpins load-flow decoupling.

◆ Why this matters

A load flow tells you whether an operating point exists. Stability tells you whether the system will stay there after a disturbance. Every large blackout in the historical record is a stability failure, not a load-flow failure, and the classification below is asked in essentially every core power interview.

◆ Definition

Power system stability is the ability of a system, for a given initial operating condition, to regain a state of operating equilibrium after being subjected to a disturbance, with most system variables bounded so that the system remains essentially intact.

◆ The three classical types

TypeDisturbanceTimescaleWhat decides it
Steady-state stabilityVery small and gradual (slow load change)SlowWhether the operating point is on the rising part of the power-angle curve; governor and excitation action neglected or slow
Dynamic stabilitySmallSeconds to tens of secondsThe response of automatic controls — AVR, exciter, governor, PSS. Small-signal oscillations must damp out
Transient stabilityLarge and sudden (fault, line trip, large load rejection)First swing, about 1 secondWhether the machine's rotor angle swings back rather than running away; studied with the swing equation and the equal area criterion

The distinction that matters: steady-state and dynamic stability permit linearised analysis around an operating point; transient stability does not, because the disturbance is large and the sin δ non-linearity dominates.

◆ The power-angle curve

For a synchronous machine of internal EMF E connected through a reactance X to an infinite bus of voltage V, with resistance neglected:

P_e = (E·V / X)·sin δ = P_max·sin δ, where P_max = E·V/X
SymbolMeaningUnit
EInternal EMF behind the transient/synchronous reactancepu
VInfinite bus voltagepu
XTotal reactance between them (machine + transformer + line)pu
δRotor (power) angle — the angle by which E leads Velectrical degrees or rad

◆ Why δ = 90° is the steady-state limit

The mechanical input power P_m is a horizontal line that cuts the sine curve at two points: δ₀ on the rising side and δ_max = 180° − δ₀ on the falling side. Only one of them is stable, and the reason is the sign of the slope:

  • At δ₀ (rising side, dP/dδ > 0): a small increase in δ increases P_e above P_m, which decelerates the rotor and pushes δ back down. Self-correcting — stable.
  • At δ_max (falling side, dP/dδ < 0): a small increase in δ decreases P_e below P_m, so the rotor accelerates further and δ runs away. Self-reinforcing — unstable.

The quantity dP/dδ = P_max·cos δ is called the synchronising power coefficient. Stability requires it to be positive, which means δ < 90°. So:

Steady-state stability limit: P_max = E·V/X, reached at δ = 90°, where dP/dδ = 0

In practice machines are never operated near 90°; typical steady-state angles are 30–45°, leaving margin for disturbances.

◆ Worked example (verified)

A generator with E = 1.2 pu supplies an infinite bus at V = 1.0 pu through a total reactance of X = 0.6 pu, delivering P = 0.8 pu.

P_max = (1.2 × 1.0)/0.6 = 2.0 pu — this is the steady-state stability limit.
Operating angle: sin δ₀ = 0.8/2.0 = 0.4, so δ₀ = 23.58°.
Synchronising coefficient: dP/dδ = 2.0 × cos 23.58° = 1.833 pu per radian.
The unstable intersection is at δ = 180° − 23.58° = 156.42°.

◆ How the limit is raised

Since P_max = EV/X, there are only two levers, and both are used:

  • Reduce X: add parallel circuits, use bundled conductors, install series capacitors, use lower-reactance transformers.
  • Raise E: a fast, high-ceiling excitation system holds internal EMF up during a disturbance.
Common mistake: confusing the rotor angle δ with the power factor angle φ. They are different quantities — δ is the angle between the internal EMF E and the terminal/bus voltage V, while φ is between terminal voltage and current. A machine can be at δ = 30° with almost any power factor depending on its excitation.
Placement trap: "Is the operating point at δ = 120° stable?" The tempting answer is no, and it is right for steady-state stability because dP/dδ is negative there. But a sharper answer notes that during a transient swing the rotor angle routinely passes beyond 90° and still recovers, provided it turns around before δ_max — that is exactly what the equal area criterion computes. So "δ > 90° is unstable" is a statement about steady-state equilibrium points, not about instantaneous angles during a swing, and conflating the two is the actual trap.

◆ Quick revision

  • Steady-state (small, slow), dynamic (small, controls matter), transient (large, first swing)
  • P_e = P_max sin δ with P_max = EV/X
  • Two intersections with P_m: δ₀ stable (dP/dδ > 0), 180° − δ₀ unstable
  • Synchronising coefficient dP/dδ = P_max cos δ; limit at δ = 90°
  • Raise the limit by reducing X or raising E

psa-swing-equation.title: Mechanics of Angular Motion and the Swing Equation
psa-swing-equation.body:
Prerequisite: Power-angle curve and the steady-state limit.

◆ Why this matters

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Mechanics of Angular Motion and the Swing Equation

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Mechanics of Angular Motion and the Swing Equation.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

The swing equation is the equation of motion of a synchronous machine's rotor. Everything in transient stability — critical clearing time, the equal area criterion, every time-domain simulation a utility runs — is either the swing equation or a consequence of it.

◆ Derivation from Newton's law for rotation

A rotor is a mass on a shaft, so Newton's second law for rotation applies: net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.

J·(d²θ_m/dt²) = T_m − T_e

Multiplying by angular velocity converts torque to power, and expressing the inertia in the per-unit form used throughout power systems gives the standard swing equation:

(2H/ω_s)·(d²δ/dt²) = P_m − P_e = P_a

and equivalently, with M = 2H/ω_s called the inertia constant in the power form:

M·(d²δ/dt²) = P_a, M = 2H/ω_s = H/(π·f)
SymbolMeaningUnit
HInertia constant — stored kinetic energy at synchronous speed per unit of machine ratingMJ/MVA (= seconds)
δRotor angle relative to a synchronously rotating referenceelectrical rad or degrees
P_m, P_eMechanical input and electrical output powerpu
P_aAccelerating power, P_m − P_epu
ω_sSynchronous angular speed, 2πf electrical rad/srad/s

◆ What H physically means

H = (stored kinetic energy in MJ at synchronous speed) / (machine rating in MVA). Its unit works out to seconds, and the interpretation is direct and worth quoting: H is the time in seconds the machine could supply its rated output purely from its stored rotational kinetic energy. Typical values are 2–6 s for thermal units and 2–4 s for hydro units.

A high-H machine accelerates slowly when a fault removes its electrical load, so it is inherently more stable. This is precisely why the growth of inverter-based generation — which has no rotating mass and therefore contributes no inherent inertia — has made system inertia an operational concern, and why synthetic inertia from wind and battery plants is now a live topic.

◆ Useful working forms

When δ is in electrical degrees:

d²δ/dt² = (180·f/H)·P_a [elec deg/s²]

When δ is in electrical radians:

d²δ/dt² = (π·f/H)·P_a [elec rad/s²]

◆ Worked example (verified)

A 50 MVA, 50 Hz generator has H = 5 MJ/MVA and is delivering 0.8 pu when a three-phase fault at its terminals reduces P_e to zero.

Accelerating power P_a = 0.8 − 0 = 0.8 pu.
In degrees: d²δ/dt² = (180 × 50/5) × 0.8 = 1800 × 0.8 = 1440 elec deg/s².
In radians: d²δ/dt² = (π × 50/5) × 0.8 = 31.416 × 0.8 = 25.13 elec rad/s².
Inertia constant M = H/(πf) = 5/(π × 50) = 0.03183 pu·s²/elec rad.
Stored kinetic energy = H × rating = 5 × 50 = 250 MJ.

Since P_e = 0 the acceleration is constant, so δ(t) = δ₀ + ½(1440)t². Starting from δ₀ = 23.58°, after 0.2 s the angle has already advanced by ½ × 1440 × 0.04 = 28.8° to 52.4°. That is how fast a fault moves the rotor, and why protection clearing times are specified in cycles.

◆ Solving the swing equation

The swing equation is non-linear (P_e contains sin δ) and has no general closed-form solution, so it is integrated numerically.

MethodIdeaAccuracyNote
Point-by-point (step-by-step)Assume P_a constant over each small interval Δt and use the average accelerating power of the interval to update speed and angleFirst order; needs small ΔtThe classic hand-calculation method; Δt is typically 0.05 s or less
Modified EulerPredictor-corrector: estimate the derivative at the end of the step and average itSecond orderA simple improvement on point-by-point
Runge-Kutta (RK4)Four weighted derivative evaluations per stepFourth orderStandard in production software; allows larger Δt for the same accuracy

A subtlety that examiners like: when a discontinuity occurs — the instant a fault is applied or cleared — P_e jumps. The point-by-point method handles this by using the average of the accelerating power just before and just after the discontinuity for that one interval, rather than either value alone.

Common mistake: mixing mechanical and electrical angles. For a machine with P poles, δ_electrical = (P/2)·δ_mechanical. The swing equation as written above uses electrical angle throughout — substituting a mechanical angle silently scales the answer by the pole-pair number.
Placement trap: "Two identical generators, but one has twice the inertia constant H. Which is more transiently stable, and why?" The high-H machine, and the reason must be stated through the swing equation rather than asserted: acceleration is inversely proportional to H, so for the same accelerating power the high-H rotor gains angle more slowly, meaning the protection has more time to clear the fault before the critical clearing angle is reached. Its critical clearing time is longer, but note the critical clearing angle is unchanged — the angle depends only on the power-angle curves, not on inertia. Separating those two is what the question is actually testing.

◆ Quick revision

  • (2H/ω_s)(d²δ/dt²) = P_m − P_e; M = 2H/ω_s = H/(πf)
  • H in MJ/MVA = seconds the machine could supply rated output from stored KE; typically 2–6 s
  • d²δ/dt² = (180f/H)P_a in deg/s², or (πf/H)P_a in rad/s²
  • Solved numerically: point-by-point, modified Euler, RK4; average P_a across a discontinuity
  • Higher H ⇒ longer critical clearing time, but the same critical clearing angle

psa-equal-area.title: The Equal Area Criterion and Methods of Improving Stability Limits
psa-equal-area.body:
Prerequisite: The swing equation.

◆ Why this matters

The equal area criterion answers the central transient-stability question — will the machine stay in synchronism? — without integrating the swing equation at all. It is a graphical energy argument, it is examined constantly, and it gives the critical clearing angle in one line of algebra.

◆ The idea

Multiply the swing equation by 2(dδ/dt) and integrate. The result says the rotor returns to zero relative speed when:

∫[δ₀ to δ₁] (P_m − P_e) dδ = 0

In words: the accelerating area A₁ (where P_m > P_e, the rotor gains kinetic energy) must be exactly cancelled by an available decelerating area A₂ (where P_e > P_m, the rotor gives it back).

A₁ = A₂ ⇒ the machine is (first-swing) stable

If the maximum available decelerating area is smaller than the accelerating area, the rotor arrives at δ_max still turning faster than synchronous speed, passes it, and from there P_e < P_m so it accelerates without limit — loss of synchronism.

Drawn to scale for the worked example (P_max = 2.0 pu, P_m = 0.8 pu). During the fault P_e = 0, so the accelerating area A₁ is the rectangle P_m × (δ_c − δ₀) = 0.8 × (1.5599 − 0.4115) = 0.9187 pu·rad. After clearing, the decelerating area is A₂ = P_max(cos δ_c − cos δ_max) − P_m(δ_max − δ_c) = 2.0 × (0.01091 + 0.91652) − 0.8 × (2.7301 − 1.5599) = 0.9187 pu·rad. The two are equal — that equality is exactly what defines the critical clearing angle δ_c = 89.375°. Clear the fault later and A₁ grows past what A₂ can absorb.

◆ Critical clearing angle — fault at the machine terminals

For the classic case of a sudden three-phase fault at the generator terminals (so P_e = 0 during the fault) which is cleared without changing the network (the same power-angle curve applies before and after):

cos δ_c = (P_m/P_max)·(δ_max − δ₀) + cos δ_max, with δ_max = π − δ₀

and the corresponding critical clearing time, valid only because P_e = 0 makes the acceleration constant:

t_c = √[ 2H(δ_c − δ₀) / (π·f·P_m) ] (δ in electrical radians)

◆ Worked example (verified)

The generator from the previous lessons: P_max = 2.0 pu, P_m = 0.8 pu, H = 5 MJ/MVA, f = 50 Hz. A three-phase fault at its terminals drives P_e to zero. Find δ_c and t_c.

δ₀ = arcsin(0.8/2.0) = arcsin 0.4 = 23.578° = 0.4115 rad.
δ_max = 180° − 23.578° = 156.422° = 2.7301 rad.
cos δ_c = (0.8/2.0)(2.7301 − 0.4115) + cos(156.422°) = 0.4 × 2.3186 − 0.91652 = 0.92744 − 0.91652 = 0.01091.
δ_c = arccos(0.01091) = 89.375° = 1.5599 rad.
t_c = √[2 × 5 × (1.5599 − 0.4115)/(π × 50 × 0.8)] = √[11.483/125.66] = √0.09138 = 0.302 s.

So the fault must be cleared within about 302 ms, or roughly 15 cycles on a 50 Hz system. Modern transmission protection clears in 3–5 cycles, which is why this machine would survive comfortably — and why the margin shrinks alarmingly if breaker failure delays clearing to backup times of 300–500 ms.

◆ What the criterion cannot do

Being able to state the limitations is what separates understanding from memorisation:

  • It applies only to a single machine against an infinite bus (or two machines reducible to one). It cannot be used for a genuine multi-machine system.
  • It assesses only the first swing. A system can survive the first swing and then lose synchronism on a later swing through growing oscillations — a case only time-domain simulation reveals.
  • It assumes constant P_m (no governor action, reasonable over one second) and constant E behind transient reactance (no AVR or flux decay).
  • It neglects damping and resistance, which makes it slightly conservative — real machines have some damping that helps.

◆ Methods of improving stability limits

CategoryMethodMechanism
Reduce transfer reactanceParallel lines, bundled conductors, series capacitors, lower-reactance transformersRaises P_max = EV/X, which enlarges the available decelerating area A₂
Faster fault clearingHigh-speed breakers, single-pole auto-reclosing, fast protectionReduces the accelerating area A₁ directly — the most effective single measure
ExcitationFast, high-ceiling AVR; power system stabiliser (PSS)Holds E up during the disturbance and damps subsequent oscillations
Machine designHigher inertia constant H; damper windingsSlows the rotor's angular acceleration; damper bars oppose the swing
Fast valving / brakingTurbine fast valving, braking resistorsReduces P_m or adds artificial load to cut the accelerating power
OperationLower initial loading, HVDC links, FACTS devices (SVC, STATCOM, UPFC)Increases the margin between P_m and P_max; FACTS control voltage and effective reactance dynamically
Common mistake: using δ_max = π − δ₀ when the network changes on clearing. That relation holds only when the pre-fault and post-fault power-angle curves are identical. If clearing the fault also trips a line, the post-fault curve has a lower P_max, so δ_max must be recomputed from the post-fault curve as π − arcsin(P_m/P_max,post) — and the available area A₂ shrinks accordingly.
Placement trap: "How would you improve the transient stability of an existing line without building anything new?" The strong answer separates capital projects from operational ones. Reducing clearing time (retuning protection, enabling high-speed auto-reclose) and reducing the initial loading are available immediately and both act directly on A₁. Adding series compensation or a parallel circuit raises P_max but is a capital project. Naming faster clearing as the highest-leverage measure, because it attacks the accelerating area directly rather than enlarging the decelerating area, is what the question is looking for.

◆ Quick revision

  • A₁ = A₂ ⇒ first-swing stable; energy gained must be given back before δ_max
  • cos δ_c = (P_m/P_max)(δ_max − δ₀) + cos δ_max, with δ_max = π − δ₀ only if the network is unchanged
  • t_c = √[2H(δ_c − δ₀)/(πfP_m)], valid only when P_e = 0 during the fault
  • Limited to one machine vs infinite bus, first swing only, no damping
  • Best improvements: faster clearing (cuts A₁), lower X and fast excitation (raise A₂)

psa-pmu-wams.title: Phasor Measurement Units and Wide Area Monitoring Systems
psa-pmu-wams.body:
Prerequisite: The equal area criterion — WAMS exists largely to observe, in real time, the angular behaviour that stability theory predicts.

◆ Why this matters

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Phasor Measurement Units and Wide Area Monitoring Systems

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Phasor Measurement Units and Wide Area Monitoring Systems.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Everything earlier in this module is offline analysis: you assume a disturbance, compute whether the machine survives. A phasor measurement unit measures the rotor-angle story as it actually happens, across an entire grid, many times per second. This is the most modern topic in the syllabus and a natural place for an interviewer to check whether you follow the industry rather than only the textbook.

◆ What a PMU is

A PMU measures voltage and current waveforms at a substation and computes their synchrophasors — magnitude and phase angle referred to a common absolute time reference, normally GPS-disciplined UTC.

The phase angle is the point. Two substations hundreds of kilometres apart can each report a voltage angle, and because both are stamped against the same absolute time, the difference between them is meaningful. That angular difference is a direct measure of the power transfer and stress across the corridor between them — the δ of the power-angle curve, measured rather than inferred.

PropertyConventional SCADA / RTUPMU / WAMS
Reporting rateOne scan every 2–10 s25, 50 or 60 samples per second (and higher)
Time referenceLocal, not synchronised across sitesGPS-disciplined UTC, typically better than 1 µs
Phase angleNot directly measuredDirectly measured
State determinationEstimated non-linearly from P, Q, |V| measurementsMeasured directly — linear state estimation becomes possible
Suitable forSteady-state monitoring and controlDynamics: oscillations, angular separation, islanding

The rate difference is the decisive one. An inter-area oscillation at 0.2–0.8 Hz is completely invisible to a measurement taken every few seconds, and is clearly resolved at 50 samples per second.

◆ Standards and architecture

Synchrophasor measurement and reporting are defined by the IEEE C37.118 standards (measurement and data transfer), with IEC 61850-90-5 covering transmission over substation communication networks.

A typical WAMS is layered: PMUs in substations → phasor data concentrators (PDCs) that time-align streams from many PMUs → regional/central PDC → applications, visualisation and archiving. Time alignment at the PDC is essential; unaligned streams would make the angle differences meaningless.

◆ What WAMS is used for

  • Angular separation monitoring: a growing angle difference across a corridor is a direct, early indicator of stress, used to trigger operator alarms before limits are breached.
  • Oscillation detection and damping assessment: identifying poorly damped inter-area modes and verifying that PSS tuning actually works on the real system.
  • Linear state estimation: with enough PMU coverage the estimation problem becomes linear and far faster and more robust than the conventional non-linear estimator.
  • Post-event analysis: reconstructing the exact sequence of a disturbance. The 2003 North American blackout investigation was a landmark case for this, and it drove much of the subsequent PMU deployment.
  • Model validation: comparing the recorded response with simulation output to correct generator and load models — a persistent industry problem.
  • Islanding detection and controlled separation, and adaptive protection schemes.
  • Renewables integration: tracking declining system inertia and the dynamics of inverter-dominated areas.

◆ The Indian context

India operates one of the larger synchrophasor deployments globally, developed through the Unified Real Time Dynamic State Measurement initiative under POSOCO/Grid-India and the regional load despatch centres, covering the national grid after the progressive integration of the regional grids into a single synchronous system. This is a reasonable thing to mention in an interview for a utility or a transmission company — though treat any specific PMU count or project milestone as something to verify against the current official source rather than quote from memory.

◆ Limitations

PMUs are not a solved problem. They depend on GPS, which makes timing spoofing and signal loss a genuine cybersecurity and reliability concern. They generate very large data volumes that need real-time communication bandwidth and storage. Full observability requires careful optimal PMU placement, since instrumenting every bus is uneconomic. And the measurement is only as good as the instrument transformers feeding it — a CT or VT error propagates straight into the reported phasor.

Common mistake: describing a PMU as "a faster SCADA RTU". The reporting rate matters, but the defining feature is time synchronisation to an absolute reference, which is what makes angles from different substations comparable at all. A fast but unsynchronised measurement would still not yield a usable angle difference.
Placement trap: "You have PMU data showing the angle difference across a corridor rising steadily. What does it tell you, and what would you do?" The angle difference is a direct proxy for stress on that corridor: a rising δ means transfer is climbing towards the limit, and from the power-angle curve the synchronising coefficient dP/dδ = P_max cos δ is falling, so the corridor is becoming progressively less able to resist a disturbance. Actions are redispatch to reduce the transfer, bring reactive support online to raise voltage and hence P_max, or in the limit initiate a pre-planned scheme. The part that distinguishes a strong answer is connecting the measured quantity back to the theory — this is the same δ from the power-angle curve, now observed live rather than computed offline.

◆ Quick revision

  • PMU measures synchrophasors — magnitude and angle against GPS-disciplined UTC
  • Defining feature is absolute time synchronisation, not just speed (25–60+ samples/s vs SCADA's seconds)
  • IEEE C37.118; architecture PMU → PDC → central PDC → applications
  • Uses: angular separation, oscillation detection, linear state estimation, post-event analysis, model validation, islanding
  • Limits: GPS dependence and spoofing, data volume, optimal placement, instrument transformer accuracy

ac-alt-construction.title: Construction, Armature Windings and Principle of Operation of Alternators
ac-alt-construction.body:
◆ Why this matters

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Construction, Armature Windings and Principle of Operation of Alternators

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Construction, Armature Windings and Principle of Operation of Alternators.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Almost every unit of grid electricity is produced by a three-phase synchronous generator, called an alternator. Everything later in this course — voltage regulation, parallel operation, synchronous motors — rests on how it is built and how its EMF is produced.

Prerequisites: Faraday's law of induction and three-phase supply. EMF equation of a transformer uses the same flux-and-frequency idea.

◆ Principle of operation

A DC-excited rotor creates alternate N and S poles. The prime mover turns the rotor at synchronous speed, so the rotor flux sweeps past the stationary armature conductors and, by Faraday's law, induces an EMF in them. Three identical phase windings are placed 120° electrical apart in space, so the three induced EMFs are equal in magnitude and 120° apart in time — a balanced three-phase system.

N_s = 120·f / P (rpm) f = P·N_s / 120 (Hz)
SymbolMeaningUnit
PNumber of poles (not pole pairs)—
fFrequency of the generated EMFHz
N_sSynchronous speed of the rotorrpm

Worked example. At 50 Hz a 4-pole machine turns at 120 × 50 / 4 = 1500 rpm and a 24-pole machine at 120 × 50 / 24 = 250 rpm. At 60 Hz a 12-pole machine runs at 120 × 60 / 12 = 600 rpm.

◆ Construction

  • Stator (armature): a laminated silicon-steel core with slots on its inner surface carrying the three-phase winding. Laminations cut eddy-current loss.
  • Rotor (field): carries the DC field winding, supplied from an exciter through slip rings, or from a brushless exciter on the same shaft.
  • Damper (amortisseur) windings: short-circuited bars in the pole faces of salient-pole machines that damp rotor oscillations ("hunting").

Why the armature is stationary and the field rotates: the output is at high voltage and high current, so taking it from a fixed armature avoids passing large power through slip rings; the slip rings only carry the small DC field current at low voltage. A fixed armature is also easier to insulate and to cool, and the lighter rotor can be built for higher speed.

◆ Two rotor types

Salient-poleCylindrical (non-salient) rotor
SpeedLow (hydro, diesel sets)High — 3000 or 1500 rpm at 50 Hz
PolesMany2 or 4
ShapeLarge diameter, short axial lengthSmall diameter, long axial length
Air gapNon-uniformUniform
Prime moverWater turbine, diesel engineSteam or gas turbine

◆ Types of armature winding

  • Single-layer (one coil side per slot) versus double-layer (two coil sides per slot). Double-layer is the norm because it allows short-pitching and easier end-connections.
  • Full-pitch (coil span = one pole pitch = 180° electrical) versus short-pitch (chorded) — used to improve the waveform.
  • Concentrated (all coil sides of a phase per pole in one slot) versus distributed (spread over several slots per pole per phase).
  • Lap and wave connections; integral-slot and fractional-slot windings.
Slots per pole per phase m = S / (3P) Slot angle γ = 180°·P / S (electrical degrees)

Worked example. A 4-pole, 36-slot, three-phase armature has S/P = 9 slots per pole, m = 36/(3×4) = 3 slots per pole per phase, and slot angle γ = 180 × 4 / 36 = 20° electrical. (Check: 36 slots span 4 × 180° = 720° electrical, and 720/36 = 20°.) At 50 Hz it must turn at 1500 rpm.

Common mistake: putting the number of pole pairs into N_s = 120f/P. With P as pairs the formula becomes 60f/p. Using 120 with pairs gives half the true speed.
Placement trap: "Why does a hydro-generator have so many poles while a turbo-alternator has two?" Because f = PN/120 is fixed at 50 Hz: a slow water turbine (say 250 rpm) needs 24 poles, whereas a fast steam turbine (3000 rpm) needs only 2. A cylindrical rotor is also the only shape that survives the centrifugal stresses at 3000 rpm.

◆ Quick revision

  • N_s = 120f/P; 50 Hz: 2-pole 3000, 4-pole 1500, 24-pole 250 rpm
  • Stationary armature, rotating field — output without slip rings
  • Salient: slow, many poles, hydro. Cylindrical: fast, 2/4 poles, turbo
  • m = S/(3P), γ = 180P/S

ac-alt-emf.title: EMF Equation of an Alternator: Pitch and Distribution Factors
ac-alt-emf.body:
◆ Why this matters

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: EMF Equation of an Alternator: Pitch and Distribution Factors

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for EMF Equation of an Alternator: Pitch and Distribution Factors.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

The EMF equation links the terminal voltage of an alternator to its flux, frequency and winding. It is the starting point for every numerical on alternators, and the two winding factors in it are a favourite examination topic.

Prerequisite: Construction, armature windings and principle of operation.

◆ Derivation

Let Φ be the flux per pole and P the number of poles. In one revolution a conductor cuts total flux ΦP in time 60/N seconds, so the average EMF per conductor is ΦPN/60. Since f = PN/120 this equals 2fΦ. A turn has two conductors, so the average EMF per turn is 4fΦ. With a sinusoidal flux distribution the form factor is 1.11, so the RMS EMF per turn is 1.11 × 4fΦ = 4.44 fΦ. With T_ph turns in series per phase:

E_ph = 4.44 · K_p · K_d · f · Φ · T_ph (K_w = K_p·K_d)
SymbolMeaningUnit
E_phRMS generated EMF per phaseV
ΦFlux per poleWb
T_phSeries turns per phase = Z_ph / 2 (Z_ph = conductors per phase)—
K_pPitch (coil-span) factor—
K_dDistribution (breadth) factor—

◆ Why winding factors appear

Pitch factor. If the coil span is short of a full pole pitch by α electrical degrees, the two coil-side EMFs are no longer in phase, so their sum is smaller than the arithmetic sum:

K_p = cos(α/2) α = 180° − (coil span in electrical degrees)

Distribution factor. The EMFs of the m coils of one phase group are displaced by the slot angle γ, so their phasor sum is smaller than their arithmetic sum:

K_d = sin(mγ/2) / ( m · sin(γ/2) )

Both factors are ≤ 1. They cost a little EMF and buy a much better waveform (see the next lesson).

◆ Worked example 1 (verified)

A 4-pole, 36-slot, 3-phase, 50 Hz alternator has 4 conductors per slot and coil span 8 slots. Flux per pole is 0.05 Wb. Find the EMF per phase and the line EMF for a star connection.

Z = 36 × 4 = 144; Z_ph = 48; T_ph = 24. Full pitch = 9 slots, so the coil is short by 1 slot = 20° electrical: K_p = cos 10° = 0.9848. m = 3 and γ = 20°: K_d = sin 30° / (3 sin 10°) = 0.5/0.5209 = 0.9598. E_ph = 4.44 × 0.9848 × 0.9598 × 50 × 0.05 × 24 = 251.8 V. Star: E_L = √3 × 251.8 = 436.1 V. A concentrated full-pitch winding would give 266.4 V; the winding factors have cost 5.5 % of the EMF.

◆ Worked example 2 (verified): finding the flux

An 8-pole alternator runs at 750 rpm, so f = 8 × 750/120 = 50 Hz. It is star-connected and must generate 3300 V between lines. With K_p = 0.95, K_d = 0.955 and 100 turns per phase, the phase EMF is 3300/√3 = 1905.3 V, K_w = 0.95 × 0.955 = 0.9073, and

Φ = E_ph / (4.44 · K_w · f · T_ph) = 1905.3 / (4.44 × 0.9073 × 50 × 100) = 0.0946 Wb
Common mistake: using conductors per phase instead of turns per phase. One turn has two conductors, so putting Z_ph into the formula doubles the answer. The second frequent error is forgetting √3 when converting between star line and phase EMF.
Placement trap: "Short-pitching lowers the EMF — so why do manufacturers do it?" Because the small loss of fundamental EMF is repaid by removing or greatly reducing troublesome harmonics, and by shortening the end connections and saving copper.

◆ Quick revision

  • E_ph = 4.44 K_p K_d f Φ T_ph, with T_ph = Z_ph/2
  • K_p = cos(α/2); K_d = sin(mγ/2)/(m sin(γ/2))
  • Star: E_L = √3 E_ph; delta: E_L = E_ph

ac-alt-harmonics.title: Harmonics in Alternator EMF: Causes and Suppression
ac-alt-harmonics.body:
◆ Why this matters

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Harmonics in Alternator EMF: Causes and Suppression

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Harmonics in Alternator EMF: Causes and Suppression.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

The ideal alternator EMF is a pure sinusoid. Real machines produce a distorted wave, and harmonics heat the machine, waste power and interfere with communication circuits. Most of the design choices in the previous lesson exist to suppress them.

Prerequisite: EMF equation, pitch and distribution factors.

◆ Causes

  • Non-sinusoidal flux distribution in the air gap — pole-face shape, magnetic saturation and the flux-density profile rarely give a perfect sine.
  • Slotting — the armature teeth make the air-gap reluctance vary periodically, producing tooth (slot) harmonics.
  • Armature reaction under load distorts the flux distribution further.

The nth harmonic has frequency n·f. Because the waveform under N and S poles is symmetrical (half-wave symmetry), only odd harmonics (3rd, 5th, 7th …) occur; even harmonics are absent.

◆ Effects

  • Extra iron and copper loss, so more heating and lower efficiency
  • Interference (noise) in nearby telephone and communication lines
  • Possible resonance with line capacitance and torque pulsations in connected motors
  • Circulating currents if the armature is delta-connected (below)

◆ Suppression

K_pn = cos(nα/2) K_dn = sin(n·mγ/2) / ( m · sin(n·γ/2) )
  1. Short-pitched coils. The nth harmonic is eliminated when K_pn = 0, i.e. nα/2 = 90°, so α = 180°/n. For the 5th harmonic α = 36° (coil span 4/5 pole pitch); for the 7th α = 25.7°.
  2. Distributed windings — K_dn is generally much smaller for high orders than for the fundamental.
  3. Skewing the slots (or poles) by about one slot pitch to remove slot harmonics.
  4. Fractional-slot windings and shaped pole faces (wider air gap at the pole tips) to improve the flux waveform.
  5. Star connection — triplen harmonics (3rd, 9th …) are absent from the line voltage.

Why triplens vanish in a star. The 3rd-harmonic EMFs of the three phases are 3 × 120° = 360° apart, so they are in phase and cancel in the difference between two phases. In a closed delta, however, they add around the loop and drive a circulating third-harmonic current even at no load — extra loss and heating — which is why delta armatures are avoided.

◆ Worked example 1 (verified)

Compare pitch factors for a coil short-pitched by 30° electrical (span 5/6 of a pole pitch).

Fundamental: K_p1 = cos 15° = 0.9659. 5th harmonic: K_p5 = cos 75° = 0.2588. 7th: K_p7 = cos 105° = −0.2588 (magnitude 0.2588). So the 5th and 7th are cut to 0.2588/0.9659 = 26.8 % of their full-pitch relative size, for a fundamental loss of only 3.4 %.

Distribution with m = 3, γ = 20°: K_d1 = 0.9598, K_d3 = 0.6667, K_d5 = 0.2176, K_d7 = 0.1774 (magnitude) — the higher the order, the stronger the suppression.

◆ Worked example 2 (verified)

A star-connected alternator has per-phase EMF components: 231 V fundamental, 23.1 V third harmonic and 11.55 V fifth harmonic. Phase RMS = √(231² + 23.1² + 11.55²) = 232.4 V. The 3rd harmonic cancels in the line voltage, so E_L = √3 × √(231² + 11.55²) = 400.6 V, only slightly above the 400.1 V of the fundamental alone.

Common mistake: writing the pitch factor for the nth harmonic as cos(α/2) with the fundamental angle. The harmonic sees an electrical angle n times larger, so use cos(nα/2).
Placement trap: "Which harmonic should you eliminate first by short-pitching?" The 3rd is not chosen because star connection already removes it from the line voltage; short-pitching is aimed at the 5th and 7th, which do appear in the line.

◆ Quick revision

  • Only odd harmonics; nth has frequency nf
  • K_pn = cos(nα/2); eliminate nth by α = 180°/n
  • Star removes triplens from line voltage; delta circulates them
  • Distribution, skewing, fractional slots, pole shaping also help

ac-alt-armature-reaction.title: Armature Reaction and the Equivalent Circuit of an Alternator
ac-alt-armature-reaction.body:
◆ Why this matters

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Armature Reaction and the Equivalent Circuit of an Alternator

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Circuit network topology, nodal voltage distribution, and loop equations for Armature Reaction and the Equivalent Circuit of an Alternator.
  • Component Roles: Independent voltage source Vs drives network current; passive impedances R1, R2 determine branch voltage drops.
  • Working Mechanism: Kirchhoff's Laws (KCL ΣI = 0, KVL ΣV = 0): Solves simultaneous linear nodal equations for node potentials.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Current enters Node A from main supply loop and splits across parallel load branches.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Linear current-voltage operating point adhering to superposition and Thevenin/Norton equivalence.
  • Key Governing Formula: Nodal Equation: (Va - Vs)/Z1 + Va/Z2 + (Va - Vb)/Z3 = 0.
  • Engineering Meaning: Core foundation for linear circuit analysis, power system load flow, and analog network modeling.
  • Common Trap: Incorrect reference node assignment or sign convention errors during KVL loop summation.

When an alternator delivers current, the armature's own magnetic field interacts with the field of the rotor. This effect — armature reaction — explains why terminal voltage changes with load and leads directly to the equivalent circuit used for every regulation calculation.

Prerequisites: EMF equation and phasor impedance. The same idea for DC machines is in armature reaction and commutation.

◆ Armature reaction

Three-phase armature currents set up a rotating magnetic field that turns at synchronous speed — the same speed as the rotor — so it stays fixed relative to the poles. Its effect depends on the power factor of the load, i.e. the phase angle between the armature current I and the generated EMF E_f:

LoadArmature mmf relative to fieldEffect
Unity power factor90° to the main field axisCross-magnetising — distorts the flux under the poles, little change in its total
Zero p.f. laggingDirectly opposes the fieldDemagnetising — weakens the flux, terminal voltage falls
Zero p.f. leadingDirectly aids the fieldMagnetising — strengthens the flux, terminal voltage rises
Practical lagging loadBoth componentsMainly demagnetising plus some cross-magnetising

◆ Equivalent circuit (per phase)

The armature-reaction flux induces an EMF in the winding that is proportional to I and lags it by 90°, exactly like a voltage drop across a reactance. It is therefore represented by a fictitious armature-reaction reactance X_a. Adding the true leakage reactance X_l and the armature resistance R_a gives the per-phase circuit: the source E_f in series with R_a and X_s, delivering terminal voltage V.

X_s = X_a + X_l Z_s = R_a + jX_s E_f = V + I·(R_a + jX_s)
SymbolMeaningUnit
E_fGenerated (excitation) EMF per phase — depends on field current and speedV
VTerminal voltage per phaseV
X_sSynchronous reactanceΩ
R_aArmature resistance per phase (usually much smaller than X_s)Ω

Assumptions: a linear (unsaturated) magnetic circuit and a uniform air gap, so the effects of armature reaction and leakage can simply be added. This model fits a cylindrical-rotor machine; salient-pole machines need Blondel's two-reaction theory.

◆ Worked example (verified)

A three-phase star-connected alternator delivers 100 A at 0.8 lagging power factor with terminal voltage 400 V line, so V = 400/√3 = 231 V per phase. R_a = 0.1 Ω and X_s = 1 Ω (about 0.43 per unit on a 231 V / 100 A base). Find E_f.

Take V = 231∠0°. I = 100∠−36.87° = 80 − j60 A. I·(R_a + jX_s) = (80 − j60)(0.1 + j1) = 68 + j74 V. E_f = 231 + 68 + j74 = 299 + j74 V, so |E_f| = 308.0 V at an angle of 13.9° ahead of V. The angle is called the power (load) angle δ. The no-load line voltage the field would produce is therefore √3 × 308 = 533 V — a large rise compared with the 400 V on load.

Common mistake: treating X_s as the leakage reactance alone. X_s includes the (much larger) fictitious armature-reaction reactance; using X_l alone predicts almost no voltage drop.
Placement trap: "Can the terminal voltage of an alternator rise when the load is added?" Yes. With a strongly leading (capacitive) load the armature reaction is magnetising, so the terminal voltage can rise above its no-load value — the same reason an unloaded long line can push an alternator toward self-excitation.

◆ Quick revision

  • Lagging load: demagnetising. Unity: cross-magnetising. Leading: magnetising
  • X_s = X_a + X_l; Z_s = R_a + jX_s
  • E_f = V + I(R_a + jX_s), per phase
  • Valid for unsaturated cylindrical rotor

ac-alt-phasor-load.title: Phasor Diagrams and Load Characteristics of an Alternator
ac-alt-phasor-load.body:
◆ Why this matters

The phasor diagram shows at a glance how excitation, load current and terminal voltage are related, and it is the quickest way to compute voltage regulation. The load characteristics tell you how the terminal voltage will behave when the load changes — the practical question for a power-plant operator.

Prerequisite: Armature reaction and the equivalent circuit.

◆ Phasor diagram

Using V as the reference: E_f = V + I·R_a + jI·X_s. The drop I·R_a is parallel to I and the reactive drop jI·X_s leads I by 90°. The angle between E_f and V is the power (load) angle δ. The diagram below is drawn for the worked example of the previous lesson (0.8 lagging).

Resolving along and perpendicular to V gives the magnitude directly. With φ the load power-factor angle:

E_f = √[ (V cos φ + I R_a)² + (V sin φ ± I X_s)² ] (+ for lagging, − for leading)

◆ Load characteristics

The external (load) characteristic plots terminal voltage V against load current I at constant field current, constant speed and constant power factor.

Power factorBehaviour of V as I increasesReason
LaggingFalls steeplyDemagnetising reaction and the reactive drop both reduce V
UnityFalls moderatelyMainly the R_a drop and cross-magnetising effect
LeadingRisesMagnetising reaction strengthens the flux

◆ Voltage regulation

Regulation is how much the terminal voltage changes between no load and full load, with the excitation and speed held at their full-load values. At no load V = E_f, so:

% regulation = (E_f − V) / V × 100

◆ Worked example (verified)

Same alternator: V = 231 V per phase, I = 100 A, R_a = 0.1 Ω, X_s = 1 Ω.

LoadE_fRegulation
0.8 lagging (φ = 36.87°)√[(184.8+10)² + (138.6+100)²] = 308.0 V+33.3 %
Unity√[(231+10)² + 100²] = 260.9 V+12.95 %
0.8 leading√[(184.8+10)² + (138.6−100)²] = 198.6 V−14.0 %

The leading case has negative regulation: the terminal voltage is higher on load than at no load. (These values are large because X_s is a big fraction of the 2.31 Ω base impedance.)

Common mistake: using the wrong sign in the reactive term. For lagging loads the reactive drop adds (V sin φ + I X_s); for leading loads it subtracts (V sin φ − I X_s). Also, regulation is divided by V (the rated terminal voltage), not by E_f.
Placement trap: "Is regulation the difference between full-load and no-load voltage?" Only if the excitation is the same in both cases. The definition assumes E_f is the no-load EMF produced by the excitation that gave rated V on full load; readjusting the field current between the two measurements gives a different, meaningless number.

◆ Quick revision

  • E_f = V + I(R_a + jX_s); angle between E_f and V is δ
  • E_f = √[(V cosφ + IR_a)² + (V sinφ ± IX_s)²]
  • Lagging: V falls steeply; unity: falls; leading: rises
  • % reg = (E_f − V)/V × 100, negative for strongly leading loads

ac-alt-regulation-emf-mmf.title: Voltage Regulation of Alternators: The EMF Method and the MMF Method
ac-alt-regulation-emf-mmf.body:
◆ Why this matters

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Voltage Regulation of Alternators: The EMF Method and the MMF Method

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Voltage Regulation of Alternators: The EMF Method and the MMF Method.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

The equivalent-circuit calculation E_f = V + I(R_a + jX_s) from the previous module assumes a fixed, given X_s. In a real machine, X_s is not really constant — it is the sum of a true leakage reactance and a fictitious armature-reaction reactance that stands in for a magnetic circuit which actually saturates at high excitation. The EMF and MMF methods are the two classical ways of getting a usable synchronous-reactance value out of two simple tests (open-circuit and short-circuit), and — crucially — they do not agree with each other once saturation matters, which is exactly the point of studying both.

Prerequisite: Armature reaction and the equivalent circuit.

◆ The two tests behind both methods

TestProcedureResult
Open-circuit test (OCC)Alternator run at synchronous speed, armature terminals open, field current I_f raised in stepsOpen-circuit voltage E_o vs I_f — the OCC, a curve that bends over (saturates) at higher I_f
Short-circuit test (SCC)Armature terminals short-circuited through ammeters, I_f raised until rated armature current flowsShort-circuit current I_sc vs I_f — very nearly a straight line, because the iron carries almost no flux (the mmf is almost entirely balancing armature reaction and leakage, not driving flux through iron)

◆ EMF method (Behn-Eschenburg method)

Find the synchronous impedance Z_s directly as a ratio of open-circuit voltage to short-circuit current, both measured at the same field current I_f:

\(Z_s = \frac{E_o|_{I_f}}{I_{sc}|_{I_f}}\);     \(X_s = \sqrt{Z_s^2 - R_a^2}\);     \(\vec{E}_f = \vec{V} + \vec{I}(R_a + jX_s)\)

The catch: whichever I_f is used to form this ratio, one single value of Z_s is then applied at all load currents, including the (usually higher) internal EMF that full load actually requires — a region of the OCC that is more saturated, hence a real machine's effective reactance there is actually lower. The EMF method therefore uses an unsaturated-style E_o value against a linear SCC and treats the machine as if it never saturates, which overestimates X_s and overestimates the regulation — often very badly at low power factor. It is called the pessimistic method for exactly this reason.

◆ MMF method (Rotating-Ampere-Turn / Mixed-mmf method)

Instead of collapsing everything into one impedance, the MMF method works with the field currents needed on the OCC and SCC directly, as physical mmf quantities that can be added as phasors, and only converts back to a voltage as the very last step — which is why it can use the real, saturated part of the OCC properly:

F_O = field current that produces rated V on the OCC
F_AR = field current that circulates rated I on the SCC (represents the mmf needed to overcome armature reaction and leakage together)
F_R = √(F_O² + F_AR² + 2·F_O·F_AR·sinφ)  (lagging pf; use −2F_O F_AR sinφ for leading)
E_f = OCC value corresponding to F_R (read off the actual, saturated OCC curve)

Because the final step looks up E_f on the real OCC curve — saturation and all — instead of assuming a fixed reactance, the MMF method is markedly more realistic at high excitation, and is the optimistic method: it is closer to reality than EMF, but it tends to understate regulation.

◆ Worked example (verified) — same machine, both methods

A 3-phase, star-connected alternator (per-phase values) has R_a = 0.2 Ω and supplies rated current I = 100 A at V = 230 V, 0.8 lagging pf. Its OCC, from test data, is:

I_f (A)123456
E_o (V)100190260310345370

The SCC shows that I_f = 3 A on the OCC scale circulates the rated 100 A on short circuit, and the OCC shows I_f = 2.5 A gives the rated 230 V. Find the regulation by both methods.

EMF method: Z_s = E_o(I_f=3A)/I = 260/100 = 2.6 Ω. X_s = √(2.6² − 0.2²) = 2.592 Ω. With V = 230∠0° and I = 100∠−36.87°: E_f = V + I(R_a+jX_s) evaluates to |E_f| = 446.6 V, giving regulation = (446.6−230)/230×100 = +94.2 %.
MMF method: F_O = 2.5 A, F_AR = 3 A, φ = 36.87° (sinφ = 0.6). F_R = √(2.5² + 3² + 2×2.5×3×0.6) = √24.25 = 4.924 A. Reading the OCC at I_f = 4.924 A (interpolating between the 4 A/310 V and 5 A/345 V rows): E_f = 310 + (0.924)(345−310) = 342.4 V, giving regulation = (342.4−230)/230×100 = +48.9 %.

The two methods disagree by a factor of nearly 2 on the same machine, same operating point — purely because the EMF method's single fixed X_s, taken from the same test data, silently assumes the machine behaves at full load exactly as unsaturated as it did at the point the ratio was formed. This is precisely why the EMF method is described as pessimistic (over-states regulation) and the MMF method as the more trustworthy of the two simple test-based methods — though, as the next lesson develops, even the MMF method has a known weakness (it does not correctly separate leakage reactance from armature reaction), which is what the Potier and ASA methods refine further.

Common mistake: reading E_o for the EMF method's Z_s at the field current for rated voltage (2.5 A) rather than the field current used for the short-circuit test (3 A). Z_s must be formed from E_o and I_sc measured at the same I_f, because that is the only point where the ratio has a defined physical meaning as "volts per amp of short-circuit current."
Placement trap: "If EMF and MMF methods disagree, one of the test measurements must be wrong." Not necessarily — the two methods make different, and different-severity, approximations about saturation from the very same correct test data. A large gap between them, as in this example, is itself diagnostic: it tells you the machine is operating well into the saturated region of its OCC at the excitation needed for full load, which the EMF method's fixed-reactance model cannot represent.

◆ Quick revision

  • EMF method: one Z_s from E_o/I_sc at matched I_f, then E_f = V+I(R_a+jX_s) — simple but pessimistic (overestimates regulation)
  • MMF method: combine F_O and F_AR as phasors to get F_R, then read E_f off the real OCC at F_R — more realistic, uses actual saturation
  • sinφ term adds for lagging pf, subtracts for leading pf, in both the phasor-voltage and phasor-mmf combinations
  • Large EMF-vs-MMF disagreement signals heavy saturation at the full-load excitation point

ac-alt-potier-asa.title: Voltage Regulation of Alternators: The Potier (ZPF) Method and the ASA Method
ac-alt-potier-asa.body:
◆ Why this matters

The EMF and MMF methods of the previous lesson both fail for the same underlying reason: they cannot tell the two very different things inside the synchronous reactance apart. Armature leakage reactance X_L is a genuine voltage drop (I·X_L, in phase-quadrature with the current) that exists whatever the iron is doing. Armature reaction is a magnetomotive-force effect: the armature current's mmf opposes or aids the field mmf and must be balanced by extra field current. The EMF method treats everything as a voltage; the MMF method treats everything as an mmf. Neither is right, and neither can allow properly for saturation. The Potier (zero-power-factor, ZPF) method separates the two using one extra test. The ASA method keeps the MMF method's simplicity but adds an explicit correction for saturation.

Prerequisites: the EMF and MMF methods and armature reaction.

◆ The zero-power-factor (ZPF) test

The alternator is run at rated speed and loaded with a (nearly) purely inductive load, so the current lags the terminal voltage by almost exactly 90°. The excitation is raised until rated armature current flows at rated terminal voltage; that field current is one point of the ZPF curve (point B below). A second point comes free from the short-circuit test: the field current that circulates rated current on short circuit is the ZPF point at zero terminal voltage (point A). Two points are enough because, under the method's assumptions, the rest of the curve is simply the open-circuit curve moved.

Why zero power factor makes the separation possible: with the current 90° behind the voltage, the armature-reaction mmf is directly opposed to the field mmf, and the leakage drop I·X_L is directly in line with the voltages. Everything then adds arithmetically on one axis, so the ZPF curve is the OCC displaced to the right by F_AR (the field current that balances armature reaction) and down by I·X_L (the leakage drop):

ZPF(I_f) = OCC(I_f − F_AR) − I·X_L

Drawn to scale for the worked example below. The ZPF curve (teal) is the tabulated OCC (amber) moved 2.2 A right and 80 V down, so it starts at A (3 A, 0 V) and passes through B (6.2 A, 230 V). Triangle BDE is the Potier triangle. The OCC is the tabulated points joined by straight lines; a real curve would be smooth.

◆ Constructing the Potier triangle

  1. Plot the OCC and draw the air-gap line (the straight-line extension of its initial, unsaturated part).
  2. Mark B on the ZPF at rated voltage, and note A: the field current O–A that gives rated current on short circuit.
  3. From B draw BH parallel to the field-current axis, towards lower field current, with length equal to OA.
  4. Through H draw HD parallel to the air-gap line until it meets the OCC at D.
  5. Drop the vertical DE from D onto BH.
DE = I·X_L  ⇒  X_L = DE / I (the Potier reactance)
BE = F_AR (field current that balances armature reaction)

The Potier reactance is larger than the true armature leakage reactance because it also includes the effect of the rotor's field leakage flux, but it is the value the method uses. Note that BE is smaller than OA. The short-circuit field current OA has to cover the leakage drop as well as armature reaction, and the difference is exactly the field current needed to overcome I·X_L on the air-gap line: OA − BE = I·X_L / (air-gap-line slope). This is the error hidden inside the MMF method, which uses all of OA as its armature-reaction mmf.

◆ Regulation by the Potier method

  1. Find the air-gap EMF (the EMF behind the leakage reactance): E_r = V + I(R_a + jX_L), as a phasor sum at the load power factor. Let ψ be the angle between the current and E_r.
  2. Read F_fr, the field current for E_r, from the real OCC.
  3. Combine F_fr with F_AR as mmf phasors. F_AR acts opposite to the current, so for a lagging load it adds to the field requirement:
F_f = √(F_fr² + F_AR² + 2·F_fr·F_AR·sinψ)  (ψ counts as positive for a lagging current and negative for a leading one, which lowers F_f)
  1. Read E_0 from the OCC at F_f. Regulation = (E_0 − V)/V × 100 %.

◆ The ASA method (a saturation-corrected MMF method)

The American Standards Association (ASA) method keeps the MMF method's layout but deals with saturation explicitly. It needs the Potier reactance (from the ZPF test) only to find the saturation correction. Textbooks present it in slightly different forms; this lesson follows the common one below.

  1. Take F_1 as the field current for rated V on the air-gap line (the unsaturated value) and F_SC as the field current for rated current on short circuit. Combine them as in the MMF method: F_R = √(F_1² + F_SC² + 2F_1F_SC sinφ), with φ the load power-factor angle.
  2. Compute E_1 = |V + I(R_a + jX_L)| (the same air-gap EMF as in the Potier method) and find the saturation increment ΔF: the horizontal gap between the OCC and the air-gap line at the height E_1.
  3. Total excitation F = F_R + ΔF. Read E_0 from the OCC at F, then regulation as before.
ΔF = OCC⁻¹(E_1) − AGL⁻¹(E_1)
F = √(F_1² + F_SC² + 2F_1F_SC sinφ) + ΔF
E_0 = OCC(F)

The MMF method effectively assumes an unsaturated (straight-line) magnetic circuit when it combines mmfs; ΔF puts back the extra field current that partial saturation demands.

◆ How the four methods compare

MethodTests neededTreats leakage and armature reaction asSaturationUsual character
EMFOCC, SCCone lumped emf (X_s)ignoredPessimistic: overstates regulation
MMFOCC, SCCone lumped mmf (all of the SC field current)only through the final OCC lookupOptimistic: tends to understate regulation
Potier (ZPF)OCC, SCC, ZPFseparated: I·X_L as emf, F_AR as mmfOCC lookup at E_rBetween the two; generally the more reliable test-based method
ASAOCC, SCC, ZPFMMF-style mmf sum plus a correctionexplicit increment ΔFClose to Potier; also quoted for salient-pole machines, though the rigorous salient-pole treatment is the two-reaction theory (a later row)

Direct loading (actually loading the machine to rated output) would be the reference, but for large machines a full-power load and prime mover are impractical, which is why these test-based predictions exist at all.

◆ Worked example (verified) — the same machine, now by Potier and ASA

Use the alternator of the previous lesson: per phase, R_a = 0.2 Ω, V = 230 V, I = 100 A at 0.8 lagging, and the OCC below (points joined by straight lines; the air-gap line is 100 V per field ampere). The short-circuit test needs I_f = 3 A for rated current. The new ZPF test gives rated voltage at rated current for I_f = 6.2 A. (The ZPF point is chosen so the triangle works out cleanly; it is illustrative test data, not a measurement.)

I_f (A)123456
E_o (V)100190260310345370

Step 1: the Potier triangle. OA = 3 A, so H sits 3 A to the left of B: at I_f = 6.2 − 3 = 3.2 A on the 230 V line. The line through H parallel to the air-gap line is V = 230 + 100(I_f − 3.2); it meets the OCC at D, which lands exactly on the 4 A row (V = 310 V). Then DE = 310 − 230 = 80 V, so X_L = 80/100 = 0.8 Ω, and BE = 6.2 − 4.0 = 2.2 A = F_AR. (Compare the 3 A that the MMF method used: 3 − 2.2 = 0.8 A is the field current spent on the leakage drop.)

Step 2: Potier regulation. I = 100∠−36.87° = 80 − j60 A. I(R_a + jX_L) = (80 − j60)(0.2 + j0.8) = 64 + j52 V. So E_r = 230 + 64 + j52 = 294 + j52, |E_r| = 298.56 V at 10.03°, and ψ = 36.87° + 10.03° = 46.90° (sinψ = 0.7302). From the OCC (3 A = 260 V, 4 A = 310 V): F_fr = 3 + 38.56/50 = 3.771 A. Then F_f = √(3.771² + 2.2² + 2×3.771×2.2×0.7302) = √31.18 = 5.584 A. On the OCC (5 A = 345 V, 6 A = 370 V): E_0 = 345 + 0.584×25 = 359.6 V. Regulation = (359.6 − 230)/230 = +56.3 %.

Step 3: ASA regulation. F_1 = 230/100 = 2.3 A on the air-gap line, F_SC = 3 A, sinφ = 0.6: F_R = √(2.3² + 3² + 2×2.3×3×0.6) = √22.57 = 4.751 A. For E_1 = 298.56 V the OCC needs 3.771 A while the air-gap line needs 2.986 A, so ΔF = 0.786 A. Total F = 5.536 A, and E_0 = 345 + 0.536×25 = 358.4 V. Regulation = +55.8 %.

Method (same machine, 0.8 lag)Regulation
EMF+94.2 %
MMF (previous lesson, F_O = 2.5 A)+48.9 %
Potier+56.3 %
ASA+55.8 %

The ordering is the one the textbooks describe: EMF highest, MMF lowest, Potier and ASA in between and close to each other. Two honest caveats. First, no direct-loading result exists for this constructed machine, so the table shows the methods' tendencies, not which one is "right". Second, the previous lesson took F_O = 2.5 A as given; reading its OCC table by linear interpolation gives 2.571 A, which would make the MMF figure +49.8 %. The ordering is unchanged.

Common mistake: using the whole short-circuit field current (3 A) as F_AR in the Potier method. The Potier triangle side BE (2.2 A here) is the armature-reaction current; the 0.8 A difference is the leakage drop already accounted for as I·X_L in E_r. Using 3 A double-counts the leakage effect and overstates the field requirement.
Placement trap: "Why can't X_L be found from the open-circuit and short-circuit tests alone?" Because both tests give only the combined effect. In the short-circuit test the current is almost purely reactive, but the field current supplies leakage drop and armature reaction together and the two cannot be separated. The ZPF test at rated voltage adds a second, differently-saturated operating point, and the displacement of that point from the OCC gives two equations for the two unknowns: the vertical shift is I·X_L, the horizontal shift is F_AR.

◆ Quick revision

  • ZPF curve = OCC shifted right by F_AR and down by I·X_L; two points (A from the SCC, B from the ZPF test) fix it
  • Potier triangle: BH = OA, HD parallel to the air-gap line, DE vertical; DE = I·X_L, BE = F_AR (BE < OA)
  • Potier: E_r = V + I(R_a + jX_L), F_fr from OCC, F_f = √(F_fr² + F_AR² + 2F_frF_AR sinψ), E_0 from OCC
  • ASA: F_1 from the air-gap line, F_SC from the SCC, mmf sum at φ, plus the saturation increment ΔF taken at E_1
  • Typical ranking: EMF (pessimistic) > Potier ≈ ASA > MMF (optimistic)

ac-alt-blondel-two-reaction.title: Blondel's Two-Reaction Theory: Salient-Pole Alternators and Their Phasor Diagram
ac-alt-blondel-two-reaction.body:
◆ Why this matters

Every alternator method so far — the equivalent circuit, EMF, MMF, Potier and ASA — quietly assumed one thing: that the armature current's magnetic effect is the same whichever way it points relative to the field poles. That is nearly true of a cylindrical-rotor machine, whose air gap is uniform all round. It is false for a salient-pole machine, the type used for low-speed hydro and diesel-driven sets. The poles stick out, so the air gap is short in front of a pole and very long between poles. The same armature mmf produces a lot of flux when it acts along the pole axis and much less when it acts across it. One synchronous reactance cannot describe both. Blondel's two-reaction theory keeps the idea of a reactance but uses two of them, one for each axis.

Prerequisites: the phasor diagram of an alternator and the EMF and MMF methods. The earlier lesson on the Potier and ASA methods pointed here for the rigorous salient-pole treatment.

◆ The two axes

AxisWhere it liesAir gap and reluctanceWhat acts on it
Direct axis (d)Through the centre of a poleShort gap, low reluctanceThe field flux; the magnetising or demagnetising part of armature reaction
Quadrature axis (q)Midway between poles, 90° electrical from the d-axisLong gap, high reluctanceThe cross-magnetising part of armature reaction

The field flux lies on the d-axis, and the EMF it induces lags that flux by 90°, so the excitation EMF E_f lies on the q-axis. Everything in the method follows from that one placement.

◆ Splitting the armature current

Blondel's idea is to treat the armature current as the sum of two components, each producing its own armature-reaction mmf on its own axis, and to let the two reactions act independently:

  • I_q is the part of I in phase with E_f (along the q-axis). Its mmf lies on the q-axis, across the poles: cross-magnetising.
  • I_d is the part of I 90° from E_f (along the d-axis). Its mmf lies on the d-axis: demagnetising if the current lags E_f, magnetising if it leads.
I_d = I sin ψ    I_q = I cos ψ    (ψ = angle between I and E_f, positive when I lags E_f)

Note that ψ is not the power-factor angle φ. φ is the angle between I and the terminal voltage V; ψ is the angle between I and the excitation EMF E_f. They differ by the load angle δ.

◆ Two reactances, X_d and X_q

X_d = X_ad + X_l    X_q = X_aq + X_l    with X_aq < X_ad, so X_q < X_d

X_ad and X_aq are the armature-reaction reactances on the two axes and X_l is the armature leakage reactance, which is the same on both. Because the quadrature path crosses the long inter-pole gap, a given mmf makes much less flux there, so X_aq is smaller than X_ad. X_q is commonly quoted as roughly 0.6 to 0.7 of X_d for salient-pole machines. That is a rule of thumb; real values are measured (the slip test, which is the next syllabus row). In a cylindrical-rotor machine the gap is uniform, so X_d and X_q are nearly equal and both collapse to the single synchronous reactance X_s of the earlier lessons.

◆ The phasor equation and its diagram

With the current split, the alternator's terminal equation becomes one voltage drop per axis (for a lagging load, phasors):

E_f = V + I·R_a + j·I_d·X_d + j·I_q·X_q

The difficulty is that the axes are set by E_f, and E_f is the unknown, so ψ (and hence I_d and I_q) cannot be found straight from the power factor. The way out is a small trick. If the whole current is passed through X_q, the resulting phasor

E′ = V + I(R_a + jX_q)

differs from E_f only by j·I_d·(X_d − X_q), which lies along the q-axis. So E′ lies on the same line as E_f. Drawing E′ therefore fixes the position of the q-axis, the load angle δ and the angle ψ, after which I can be split and E_f found by simple extension.

Drawn to scale for the worked example below (voltages and currents both at 1.35 px per unit). The teal path is V → I·R_a → j·I·X_q, ending at E′ on the q-axis. The red extension of length I_d(X_d − X_q) carries E′ on to E_f. The dashed grey arrows I_q (along the q-axis, hidden under E′) and I_d (along the negative d-axis) are the two components of I.

◆ Construction, step by step

  1. Draw V as the reference. Draw I at the power-factor angle φ (behind V for a lagging load).
  2. Add I·R_a parallel to I, then j·I·X_q perpendicular to I (90° ahead of it). The end point is E′.
  3. The line from the origin through E′ is the q-axis. The d-axis is perpendicular to it. Read δ (angle from V to E′) and ψ (angle from I to E′).
  4. Resolve I: I_d = I sin ψ (along the d-axis) and I_q = I cos ψ (along the q-axis).
  5. Extend E′ along the q-axis by I_d(X_d − X_q) to reach E_f. Regulation = (E_f − V)/V × 100 %.
tan δ = (I·X_q·cos φ − I·R_a·sin φ) / (V + I·R_a·cos φ + I·X_q·sin φ)  (lagging; φ counts as negative for a leading load)
ψ = φ + δ (lagging)    ψ = δ − φ (leading)
E_f = |E′| + I_d(X_d − X_q) = V cos δ + I_q·R_a + I_d·X_d

For a leading load ψ comes out smaller, and can become negative. Then I_d is negative (magnetising), and the term I_d(X_d − X_q) subtracts from |E′|.

◆ Worked example (verified) — a salient-pole machine, 0.8 lagging

Per phase: V = 231 V, I = 100 A at 0.8 lagging (φ = 36.87°), R_a = 0.1 Ω, X_d = 1.0 Ω, X_q = 0.6 Ω. This is the same voltage, current and resistance as the cylindrical machine of the earlier phasor lesson, but with the reactance split into two.

Step 1: E′. I = 100∠−36.87° = 80 − j60 A. I(R_a + jX_q) = (80 − j60)(0.1 + j0.6) = (8 + 36) + j(48 − 6) = 44 + j42 V. So E′ = 231 + 44 + j42 = 275 + j42 V, giving |E′| = 278.19 V and load angle δ = tan⁻¹(42/275) = 8.68°.

Step 2: split the current. ψ = φ + δ = 36.87° + 8.68° = 45.55°. I_d = 100 sin 45.55° = 71.39 A and I_q = 100 cos 45.55° = 70.02 A.

Step 3: extend to E_f. E_f = 278.19 + 71.39 × (1.0 − 0.6) = 278.19 + 28.56 = 306.74 V. Regulation = (306.74 − 231)/231 = +32.8 %.

Cross-check with the second form: V cos δ + I_q R_a + I_d X_d = 228.35 + 7.00 + 71.39 = 306.74 V. The two forms agree.

◆ The same machine at other power factors

Load (I = 100 A)E_fδψI_dRegulationCylindrical, X_s = 1 Ω
0.8 lagging306.7 V8.68°45.55°+71.4 A+32.8 %+33.3 %, δ = 13.9°
Unity258.0 V13.98°13.98°+24.2 A+11.7 %+12.95 %, δ = 22.5°
0.8 leading195.1 V14.90°−21.97°−37.4 A−15.5 %−14.0 %, δ = 25.7°

Two things stand out for this machine. The regulation of the salient-pole model is within about 1.5 percentage points of the single-reactance model, so for a regulation estimate alone the shortcut does little harm. But the load angle is about 37 to 42 % smaller, because the reactance that matters for the angle is the small X_q. The load angle is what stability and power output depend on, which is where salience really shows up. (These are comparisons for one constructed machine, not a general law.)

◆ Salient pole against cylindrical rotor

Cylindrical rotorSalient pole
Air gapUniformShort at the pole, long between poles
ReactancesOne, X_s (X_d ≈ X_q)Two, X_d and X_q with X_q < X_d
Armature current in the modelUsed wholeSplit into I_d and I_q
Phasor constructionDirect: E_f = V + I(R_a + jX_s)Via E′, then extension by I_d(X_d − X_q)
Typical useHigh-speed steam and gas turbine setsLow-speed hydro and diesel sets

If X_d = X_q the extension term I_d(X_d − X_q) is zero, E′ becomes E_f, and the salient-pole construction reduces exactly to the cylindrical one. That is a useful sanity check on any answer.

What comes next in the syllabus: the following row shows how X_d and X_q are actually measured (the slip test) and derives the power a salient-pole machine develops, including the extra "reluctance" power that exists only because X_d ≠ X_q. This lesson covers the theory and the phasor diagram only.

Common mistake: forgetting that I_d is negative for a leading load. E_f = |E′| + I sin ψ (X_d − X_q) with a negative ψ reduces E_f below |E′|. Taking I_d as positive for a leading load gives an E_f that is too large, and can even change the sign of the regulation.
Placement trap: "Why can't you split the current into I_d and I_q straight from the power factor?" Because the split is defined relative to E_f, not V, and E_f is exactly what you are trying to find. The angle you need is ψ = φ + δ, which depends on the load angle δ, which depends on E_f. Drawing E′ = V + I(R_a + jX_q) first breaks the circle: it lies on the q-axis, so it gives δ and ψ before E_f is known. Using φ in place of ψ is the classic wrong answer.

◆ Quick revision

  • Salient pole: short gap on the d-axis (through the pole), long gap on the q-axis (between poles); so X_q < X_d
  • E_f lies on the q-axis; I_q is in phase with E_f, I_d is 90° from it; ψ (not φ) is the angle between I and E_f
  • X_d = X_ad + X_l, X_q = X_aq + X_l; X_q is commonly ≈ 0.6–0.7 X_d (rule of thumb)
  • E′ = V + I(R_a + jX_q) lies on the q-axis: it gives δ and ψ; then E_f = |E′| + I_d(X_d − X_q)
  • Leading load: ψ smaller or negative, I_d negative, so the extension subtracts
  • Salient regulation is close to the cylindrical estimate; the load angle is not

ac-alt-slip-test-power.title: Slip Test, Regulation of a Salient-Pole Alternator and the Power It Develops
ac-alt-slip-test-power.body:
◆ Why this matters

The previous lesson gave the rigorous way to handle a salient-pole alternator, Blondel's two-reaction theory, but it needs two numbers as inputs: X_d and X_q. The open-circuit and short-circuit tests cannot supply them. They give a single synchronous impedance, and that lumps the two axes together. The slip test is the standard way to measure X_d and X_q directly, and once you have them you can do two things: find the voltage regulation with the Blondel construction, and work out the power the machine develops. That power has a second component, the reluctance power, which a cylindrical-rotor machine does not have at all. This lesson covers the slip test, the regulation it leads to, and the power expression.

Prerequisites: Blondel's two-reaction theory (the d- and q-axes, X_d, X_q and the E′ construction), the phasor diagram of an alternator, and, for the power-angle idea, the power-angle curve from power system stability.

◆ The slip test: the idea

A rotating armature field crosses a salient-pole rotor at synchronous speed. If the rotor is turned at almost the same speed, the armature field creeps past the poles slowly. Over one slow cycle its mmf lines up with the pole axis (the d-axis), then with the gap between poles (the q-axis), then the d-axis again. The reactance the supply sees swings between X_d and X_q, and so the current swings too. Read the extremes of current and voltage and you have both reactances.

  • The rotor is driven (by a prime mover or a small motor) at a speed a little below or above synchronous, so the slip is very small.
  • The field winding is left open-circuited and unexcited.
