  • A balanced, reduced-voltage three-phase supply at rated frequency is applied to the armature, with the phase sequence that makes the armature field rotate in the same direction as the rotor.
  • The armature voltage and current are read together. The ammeter pointer swings between a minimum and a maximum, twice for every slip cycle.
Armature mmf lies onFlux pathReactance seenArmature currentTerminal voltage
d-axis (pole centre)Short air gap, low reluctanceX_d (the larger)Minimum, I_minMaximum, V_max
q-axis (between poles)Long air gap, high reluctanceX_q (the smaller)Maximum, I_maxMinimum, V_min
X_d = V_max / I_min     X_q = V_min / I_max     (per phase; for a star connection V = V_L/√3 and I = I_L)

The voltage swings only a little, because the supply is stiff: when the current is at its maximum the drop in the supply impedance is slightly larger, so the terminal voltage is slightly lower. The large swing is in the current, so the accuracy of the test rests mainly on reading I_min and I_max well.

◆ Why each condition is needed

ConditionReason
Field open-circuitedAny field current, whether supplied or induced in a closed winding by the armature field, adds its own mmf. Then V/I would no longer be a pure X_d or X_q. The armature field does induce a voltage in the open winding, so its terminals must be treated as live.
Very small slipThe armature mmf then moves so slowly relative to the poles that every instant is close to a steady state and the meters can be read. It is also what lets the current settle on X_d at one extreme and X_q at the other.
Reduced voltageKeeps the current within the machine's rating and the iron unsaturated. The reactances found are therefore unsaturated values.
Phase sequence matches the rotor directionIf the armature field rotated the other way, the relative speed would be nearly twice synchronous speed instead of a slow creep, and there would be no slow swing to read. Reverse two supply leads and repeat.

Strictly the ratios V_max/I_min and V_min/I_max are impedances Z_d and Z_q. Armature resistance is small next to reactance, so they are used as X_d and X_q. R_a is measured separately with a DC test.

◆ From the slip test to voltage regulation

The syllabus title says regulation of a salient-pole alternator by slip test. The method is: (1) slip test gives X_d and X_q; (2) a DC test gives R_a; (3) the Blondel construction of the previous lesson gives E_f at the load in question; (4) regulation = (E_f − V)/V × 100 %.

◆ Worked example (verified) — slip test to regulation

A 3-phase, star-connected alternator is rated 400 V, 50 A. A slip test gives, in line values, V_max = 100 V, V_min = 96 V, I_min = 14.5 A and I_max = 22.0 A. The DC test gives R_a = 0.25 Ω per phase. Find the regulation at full load, 0.8 lagging.

Step 1: reactances. X_d = (100/√3)/14.5 = 57.735/14.5 = 3.98 Ω and X_q = (96/√3)/22.0 = 55.426/22.0 = 2.52 Ω, so X_q/X_d = 0.633. (On the rated base Z_base = V_ph/I = 4.619 Ω these are 0.862 pu and 0.546 pu.) The rest of the example uses the two-decimal values.

Step 2: E′. V = 400/√3 = 230.94 V per phase. I = 50∠−36.87° = 40 − j30 A. I(R_a + jX_q) = (40 − j30)(0.25 + j2.52) = (10 + 75.6) + j(100.8 − 7.5) = 85.6 + j93.3 V. So E′ = 230.94 + 85.6 + j93.3 = 316.54 + j93.30 V, giving |E′| = 330.00 V and δ = tan⁻¹(93.30/316.54) = 16.42°.

Step 3: split the current. ψ = φ + δ = 36.87° + 16.42° = 53.29°. I_d = 50 sin ψ = 40.085 A and I_q = 50 cos ψ = 29.886 A.

Step 4: E_f. E_f = |E′| + I_d(X_d − X_q) = 330.004 + 40.085 × (3.98 − 2.52) = 330.004 + 58.524 = 388.53 V per phase (working to three decimals so the sum is exact). Regulation = (388.53 − 230.94)/230.94 = +68.2 %.

Cross-check: V cos δ + I_q R_a + I_d X_d = 221.52 + 7.47 + 159.54 = 388.53 V. The two forms agree.

What if salience were ignored and X_d used as a single synchronous reactance? The same load would give E_f = 390.97 V (+69.3 %), which is close, but the load angle would come out as 22.83° instead of 16.42°, an overestimate of about 39 %. As in the previous lesson, salience matters most for the angle. (This is one constructed machine, not a general law. Its reactances are large, which is why the regulation is high.)

◆ Power developed by a salient-pole machine

Take a generator on an infinite bus with terminal voltage V per phase, R_a neglected, and E_f on the q-axis leading V by the load angle δ. Resolving V along the two axes gives V_d = V sin δ and V_q = V cos δ, and the two axis equations are

V sin δ = I_q X_q    E_f − V cos δ = I_d X_d    ⇒   I_q = V sin δ / X_q    I_d = (E_f − V cos δ) / X_d

The component of I in phase with V is I_q cos δ + I_d sin δ, so the power per phase is P = V(I_q cos δ + I_d sin δ). Substituting the two currents and using 2 sin δ cos δ = sin 2δ:

P = (E_f V / X_d) sin δ + (V² / 2)(1/X_q − 1/X_d) sin 2δ    (per phase, R_a neglected; total = 3P with phase values)
Excitation powerReluctance power
Expression(E_f V / X_d) sin δ(V²/2)(1/X_q − 1/X_d) sin 2δ
Needs field current?Yes, proportional to E_fNo. Independent of E_f
Why it existsField flux linking the armatureOnly because X_d ≠ X_q: the rotor tries to line its poles up with the armature field
Peaks atδ = 90°δ = 45°, with value V²(X_d − X_q)/(2X_dX_q)
Beyond δ = 90°Falls, stays positive up to 180°Negative
Cylindrical rotor (X_d = X_q)The whole power, E_f V sin δ / X_sZero

With R_a neglected, the power developed by the armature equals the power delivered, and the torque is T = (3P)/ω_s with ω_s = 2πN_s/60. In per-unit the formula gives the total power directly.

Because the second term is negative beyond 90° and X_q < X_d, the sum reaches its maximum before 90°. Setting dP/dδ = 0, that is (E_f V/X_d) cos δ + V²(1/X_q − 1/X_d) cos 2δ = 0, and writing cos 2δ = 2cos²δ − 1 gives a quadratic in cos δ. The larger the excitation compared with V, the closer the peak moves to 90°.

◆ Worked example (verified) — the two power components

A salient-pole alternator with X_d = 1.0 pu and X_q = 0.6 pu is on an infinite bus with V = 1.0 pu, and its excitation emf is E_f = 1.5 pu (R_a neglected). Then E_f V/X_d = 1.5 and (V²/2)(1/X_q − 1/X_d) = 0.5 × (1.6667 − 1) = 0.3333, so P = 1.5 sin δ + 0.3333 sin 2δ.

δP_exc (pu)P_rel (pu)P total (pu)
0°0.00000.00000.0000
30°0.75000.28871.0387
45°1.06070.33331.3940
60°1.29900.28871.5877
70.06°1.41010.21371.6238
90°1.50000.00001.5000
120°1.2990−0.28871.0104

The total is largest at δ = 70.06°, where P_max = 1.624 pu. A cylindrical-rotor machine with X_s = X_d and the same E_f would give only the first term, peaking at 1.500 pu at 90°. The reluctance term therefore adds 8.3 % to the maximum power and moves the peak to a smaller angle. Note also that at δ = 90° the reluctance term is exactly zero.

Drawn to scale from P = 1.5 sin δ + 0.3333 sin 2δ (X_d = 1.0, X_q = 0.6, V = 1.0, E_f = 1.5 pu, R_a neglected). The dashed curve alone is what a cylindrical rotor with X_s = X_d would give. Adding the dotted reluctance curve lifts the total above it between 0° and 90° and pulls it below it beyond 90°.

◆ Salient pole against cylindrical rotor: the power expression

Cylindrical rotorSalient pole
P (per phase, R_a neglected)(E_f V / X_s) sin δ(E_f V / X_d) sin δ + (V²/2)(1/X_q − 1/X_d) sin 2δ
Maximum power atδ = 90°δ < 90° (depends on E_f/V)
Power with zero excitationZeroReluctance power only, peak V²(X_d − X_q)/(2X_dX_q) at 45°
Sanity checkPut X_q = X_d: the second term vanishes and the salient-pole formula becomes the cylindrical one

What comes next in the syllabus: the following rows cover the load test, parallel operation, and synchronising power and torque. The last of these uses the slope of the power-angle curve derived here. This lesson covers the slip test, the regulation it gives, and P(δ) only.

Common mistake: writing sin δ instead of sin 2δ in the reluctance term, or swapping X_d and X_q inside (1/X_q − 1/X_d), which flips the sign of the whole term. A quick check: X_q < X_d makes (1/X_q − 1/X_d) positive, so the reluctance power is positive for 0 < δ < 90°. In the slip test the mistake is the same kind of swap: the minimum current gives X_d and the maximum current gives X_q.
Placement trap: "Can a salient-pole synchronous machine develop torque with its field switched off?" Yes. With E_f = 0 the excitation term is zero, but the reluctance term (V²/2)(1/X_q − 1/X_d) sin 2δ is not, because it depends on X_d ≠ X_q and not on the field. It peaks at δ = 45°. A cylindrical-rotor machine, where X_d = X_q, develops nothing without excitation. This is the operating principle of the reluctance motor. The machine draws its magnetising current from the bus while it does this.

◆ Quick revision

  • Slip test: rotor at very small slip, field open, reduced balanced armature voltage, phase sequence matching the rotor direction
  • X_d = V_max/I_min (armature mmf on the pole axis: low reluctance, high reactance, small current); X_q = V_min/I_max
  • Slip-test reactances are unsaturated values; R_a comes from a DC test; then use the Blondel E′ construction for regulation
  • P = (E_f V/X_d) sin δ + (V²/2)(1/X_q − 1/X_d) sin 2δ per phase
  • Reluctance power: independent of excitation, peaks at 45°, negative beyond 90°, exists because X_d ≠ X_q
  • Maximum total power occurs before 90° for a salient-pole machine; a cylindrical machine peaks at 90°

ac-alt-synchronising-power-torque.title: Synchronising Power and Synchronising Torque of an Alternator
ac-alt-synchronising-power-torque.body:
◆ Why this matters

An alternator that is connected to a bus and running in step with it is always being disturbed a little: the prime-mover input changes, the network is switched, the load moves. Each disturbance pushes the rotor slightly ahead of, or behind, its steady-state position. Whether the machine then comes back into step or drifts away depends on one thing: how fast the electrical power it delivers changes when the load angle changes. That rate is the synchronising power, and its torque form is the synchronising torque. It tells you how stiff the electrical link between rotor and bus is. The previous lesson gave the power-angle equation P(δ); this lesson takes its slope, for both rotor types, and converts it into the units an examiner asks for: per electrical or mechanical degree, in watts or newton-metres.

Prerequisites: the power developed by a salient-pole machine (the P(δ) expressions used here), the power-angle curve and the synchronising coefficient in stability studies (the same idea for a machine behind a reactance), and the phasor diagram of an alternator (finding E_f and δ from the load).

◆ The idea: a small displacement and the restoring power

Take an alternator on an infinite bus (constant voltage V, constant frequency) with the mechanical input held steady at Pm, so it runs at load angle δ₀ where P(δ₀) = Pm. Now suppose a disturbance moves the rotor forward by a small angle Δδ.

  • The electrical output becomes P(δ₀ + Δδ) ≈ Pm + (dP/dδ)Δδ. The mechanical input has not changed.
  • If dP/dδ > 0 the output is now larger than the input, so the rotor slows and Δδ shrinks. If the rotor is pushed back, the output falls below the input, the rotor speeds up, and the angle closes again. The machine is pulled back to δ₀.
  • If dP/dδ < 0 the same push makes the output smaller, the rotor speeds up further, and the angle runs away. There is no restoring action.
P_syn = dP/dδ (evaluated at the operating angle δ₀)    ΔP ≈ P_syn · Δδ    (Δδ in electrical radians; small displacements only)

The unit is watts (or per unit) per electrical radian. Stable steady-state operation needs P_syn > 0. The word "synchronising" is exact: it is the power that pulls the rotor back into synchronism with the bus.

◆ The equations

Cylindrical rotor. P = (E_fV/X_s) sin δ per phase, so differentiating with E_f, V and X_s constant gives

P_syn = (E_f V / X_s) cos δ    (per phase; total = 3 × this with phase values)

Salient-pole rotor. Differentiating P = (E_fV/X_d) sin δ + (V²/2)(1/X_q − 1/X_d) sin 2δ from the previous lesson, and using d(sin 2δ)/dδ = 2 cos 2δ:

P_syn = (E_f V / X_d) cos δ + V² (1/X_q − 1/X_d) cos 2δ    (per phase; R_a neglected)
Cylindrical rotorSalient-pole rotor
P_syn(E_fV/X_s) cos δ(E_fV/X_d) cos δ + V²(1/X_q − 1/X_d) cos 2δ
Largest atδ = 0 (no load), value E_fV/X_sδ = 0 (no load), value E_fV/X_d + V²(1/X_q − 1/X_d)
Falls to zero atδ = 90°, the maximum-power angleThe maximum-power angle, which is below 90°
Beyond that angleNegative: no restoring actionNegative: no restoring action
Sanity checkPut X_q = X_d: the cos 2δ term vanishes and the salient formula becomes the cylindrical one

Two facts follow directly. First, P_syn is zero exactly where P is at its maximum, because that is where the slope of the power-angle curve is zero. Second, P_syn is greatest at no load and shrinks as the load angle grows, so a heavily loaded machine has the weakest restoring action.

◆ P_syn in terms of the power delivered

For a cylindrical rotor, P = (E_fV/X_s) sin δ and P_syn = (E_fV/X_s) cos δ, so dividing one by the other gives

P_syn = P cot δ    (cylindrical rotor: P = power at the operating angle, same units)

This shows the effect of excitation at a fixed load. Raising E_f while the machine still delivers the same real power lowers δ, so cot δ rises and the machine becomes stiffer. Take V = 1.0 pu, X_s = 1.0 pu and P = 0.8 pu:

E_f (pu)Load angle δP_syn (pu per rad)
1.241.81°0.8944
1.532.23°1.2689
1.826.39°1.6125

Each row satisfies P_syn = 0.8 cot δ. A lightly excited machine at the same load runs at a larger angle and has a weaker restoring power, which is why a machine with weak excitation carrying heavy load is the one most easily thrown out of step.

◆ From synchronising power to synchronising torque

The torque is the power divided by the synchronous mechanical speed. For a machine with p poles and supply frequency f:

Ns = 120f/p (rpm)    ωsm = 2πNs/60 (mechanical rad/s)    T = Ptotal/ωsm    Tsyn = dT/dδ = 3Psyn/ωsm

Here Psyn is the per-phase value and the 3 accounts for the three phases. With δ in electrical radians, Tsyn is in newton-metres per electrical radian. The syllabus and most textbook questions ask for the rotor displacement in mechanical degrees, and the two angles are linked by

electrical angle = (p/2) × mechanical angle

A 4-pole machine turns 2 electrical degrees for every mechanical degree, so a mechanical displacement of 1° is an electrical displacement of 2°. The conversions below apply to P_syn (total, three-phase) and to T_syn alike.

Quantity wantedMultiply the value per electrical radian by
Per electrical degreeπ/180 = 0.017453
Per mechanical radianp/2
Per mechanical degree(p/2)(π/180)
Torque (N·m) instead of power (W)Divide by ωsm

◆ Worked example (verified) — the slope of the salient-pole curve

Use the machine of the previous lesson: X_d = 1.0 pu, X_q = 0.6 pu, V = 1.0 pu, E_f = 1.5 pu, R_a neglected. Then E_fV/X_d = 1.5 and V²(1/X_q − 1/X_d) = 1.6667 − 1 = 0.6667, so P_syn = 1.5 cos δ + 0.6667 cos 2δ. For comparison, a cylindrical machine with X_s = X_d and the same E_f has P_syn = 1.5 cos δ. The P column repeats the total power of the previous lesson.

δP (pu)P_syn, salient (pu/rad)P_syn, cylindrical (pu/rad)
0°0.00002.16671.5000
30°1.03871.63241.2990
45°1.39401.06071.0607
60°1.58770.41670.7500
70.06°1.62380.00000.5116
90°1.5000−0.66670.0000
120°1.0104−1.0833−0.7500

Read the table against the P column. While P_syn is positive, P is still rising with δ. P_syn passes through zero at δ = 70.06°, exactly where P reaches its maximum of 1.6238 pu, and it is negative beyond. The cylindrical machine keeps a positive P_syn until 90°, so the reluctance term makes this machine reach its limit earlier. At small angles it does the opposite: at δ = 30° the salient machine has P_syn = 1.5 cos 30° + 0.6667 cos 60° = 1.2990 + 0.3333 = 1.6324 pu per radian against 1.2990 for the cylindrical one.

Per electrical degree that is 1.6324 × π/180 = 0.02849 pu. A 5° (electrical) push forward therefore changes the output by about 0.02849 × 5 = 0.142 pu. The exact change is P(35°) − P(30°) = 1.1736 − 1.0387 = 0.135 pu. The linear estimate is a little high because the slope is already falling across that 5°, which is why the estimate holds for small disturbances only.

Drawn to scale from P_syn = 1.5 cos δ + 0.6667 cos 2δ (solid) and P_syn = 1.5 cos δ (dashed), the two slopes of the power-angle curves in the previous lesson (X_d = 1.0, X_q = 0.6, V = 1.0, E_f = 1.5 pu, R_a neglected). The solid curve crosses zero at 70.06°, where P is a maximum; the dashed curve crosses at 90°.

◆ Worked example (verified) — a real machine, in watts and newton-metres

A 3-phase, star-connected, 4-pole, 50 Hz alternator is rated 5 MVA, 11 kV. Its synchronous reactance is 12 Ω per phase, R_a is negligible, and it delivers full load at 0.8 power factor lagging to an infinite bus. Find the synchronising power per electrical degree and per mechanical degree, and the synchronising torque per mechanical degree.

Step 1: phase quantities. V = 11000/√3 = 6350.85 V. I = 5×10⁶/(√3 × 11000) = 262.43 A, at 0.8 lagging: I = 262.43∠−36.87° = 209.94 − j157.46 A.

Step 2: E_f and δ. jX_sI = j12(209.94 − j157.46) = 1889.5 + j2519.3 V. E_f = 6350.85 + 1889.5 + j2519.3 = 8240.4 + j2519.3 V, so |E_f| = 8616.9 V per phase (14.93 kV line) and δ = tan⁻¹(2519.3/8240.4) = 17.00°. Check: P = 3(E_fV/X_s) sin δ = 3 × 4.5604×10⁶ × 0.2924 = 4.000 MW = 5 MVA × 0.8, as it must be with R_a neglected.

Step 3: synchronising power. Per phase, E_fV/X_s = 8616.9 × 6350.85/12 = 4.5604×10⁶ W. Total P_syn = 3 × 4.5604×10⁶ × cos 17.00° = 13.083 MW per electrical radian. Cross-check: P cot δ = 4.000 × cot 17.00° = 4.000 × 3.2708 = 13.083 MW per radian.

Step 4: change the angle. Per electrical degree: 13.0833 × π/180 = 0.228347 MW = 228.35 kW. For a 4-pole machine one mechanical degree is two electrical degrees, so per mechanical degree: 228.347 × 2 = 456.69 kW.

Step 5: torque. Ns = 120 × 50/4 = 1500 rpm and ωsm = 2π × 1500/60 = 157.08 rad/s. Tsyn = 13.0833×10⁶/157.08 = 83,291 N·m per electrical radian, so per mechanical degree Tsyn = 83,291 × 2 × π/180 = 2907.4 N·m. For scale, the full-load torque is 4.000×10⁶/157.08 = 25,465 N·m, so one mechanical degree of displacement brings a restoring torque of about 11.4 % of full-load torque.

Cross-check: 456.69 kW ÷ 157.08 rad/s = 2907.4 N·m. The power and torque routes agree.

◆ What this lesson does not cover

This lesson covers P_syn and T_syn as the slope of the power-angle curve, for both rotor types. It does not cover how the rotor oscillates after a disturbance (hunting, and its dependence on the rotor inertia), the load test on an alternator, the conditions for and the sharing of load in parallel operation, or the methods of synchronising a machine to the bus. The load test and parallel operation (the row before this one) are in their own lesson, "Load Test and Parallel Operation of Alternators"; the methods of synchronisation (the row after it) are in their own lesson, Methods of Synchronisation.

Common mistake: forgetting that the disturbance is measured in mechanical degrees while the formula works in electrical ones. In the example above, quoting 228.35 kW per degree as the answer for a mechanical degree is wrong by the factor p/2 = 2. A second, smaller slip is using sin δ where cos δ belongs: sin δ gives the power itself, cos δ gives its slope. Also remember the factor 3 when working with phase values.
Placement trap: "A cylindrical-rotor alternator is stable up to δ = 90°, so is it safe to run it at 85°?" Formally P_syn is still positive at 85°, but P_syn = (E_fV/X_s) cos 85° is only 8.7 % of its no-load value, so a small disturbance produces almost no restoring power, and a slightly larger one takes the rotor past 90°. Steady-state stability at a point and a healthy margin at that point are different things. This is why machines are run at modest load angles. The limit is also earlier than 90° for a salient-pole machine, as the table above shows.

◆ Quick revision

  • P_syn = dP/dδ, in W (or pu) per electrical radian; stable steady-state operation needs P_syn > 0
  • Cylindrical: P_syn = (E_fV/X_s) cos δ = P cot δ. Salient: P_syn = (E_fV/X_d) cos δ + V²(1/X_q − 1/X_d) cos 2δ
  • Greatest at no load, zero at the maximum-power angle (90° cylindrical, below 90° salient), negative beyond
  • At the same real power, higher excitation gives a smaller δ and a larger P_syn
  • T_syn = 3P_syn/ωsm (per electrical radian), with ωsm = 2πNs/60 and Ns = 120f/p
  • Electrical angle = (p/2) × mechanical angle: multiply by p/2 for mechanical radians and by π/180 for degrees

ac-alt-load-test-parallel.title: Load Test and Parallel Operation of Alternators: Conditions, Circulating Current and Load Sharing
ac-alt-load-test-parallel.body:
◆ Why this matters

Two questions decide whether an alternator can be trusted in service. The first is what its terminal voltage really does when the load is applied and removed. The earlier lessons predict that from open-circuit and short-circuit data; the load test measures it. The second is how the machine behaves once it is connected to other machines. A power station does not run one large alternator; it runs several in parallel on a common bus. That lets one unit be taken out for maintenance without a blackout, lets units be added as demand grows, and lets the operator run only as many machines as the load needs, each near its best efficiency. This lesson covers the direct load test, the conditions that must hold at the instant a machine is connected to a bus, what goes wrong when one of them does not, and how the load divides between the machines afterwards. How the operator checks that the conditions hold (lamps and the synchroscope) is the next row of the syllabus, and a separate lesson.

Prerequisites: voltage regulation and its EMF and MMF predictions (the definition the load test measures), the phasor diagram of an alternator (E_f, V, I and δ), and synchronising power and torque (why a machine that is slightly out of step is pulled back).

◆ The load test: measuring regulation directly

Regulation is defined by what the machine does: the rise in terminal voltage when the rated load is thrown off, with the speed and the field current unchanged. The EMF, MMF, Potier, ASA and slip-test lessons all estimate it from other tests. The load test performs the definition itself.

  • Set up. Drive the alternator at rated speed and connect a load bank: resistors for unity power factor, resistors with reactors for lagging, capacitors for leading. Read the line voltage, the line current, the three-phase power with two wattmeters, and the field current.
  • Load it. Adjust the load bank and the field rheostat until the machine delivers rated current at rated terminal voltage V and the specified power factor. For a balanced load the power factor is cos φ = (W₁ + W₂)/(√3 V I), so the wattmeters confirm that it is right. Note the field current.
  • Throw the load off. Open the load switch without touching the field rheostat or the speed. The voltage that appears is E₀, the open-circuit emf at that same field current.
% regulation = (E₀ − V)/V × 100    (E₀ = terminal voltage after the load is thrown off; V = rated terminal voltage on load; speed and field current unchanged between the two readings)

Because the machine is used exactly as it is, saturation and armature reaction are included as they really are: nothing is assumed about X_s, and no Potier triangle is needed. That is the strength of the test. Its weakness is that it needs a load bank and a prime mover that can supply the full rating, so it suits small and laboratory machines; large alternators are assessed from open-circuit, short-circuit and related tests instead.

Direct load testEMF, MMF, Potier, ASA
Data usedThe machine actually loadedOpen-circuit and short-circuit tests (and a zero-power-factor test for Potier and ASA)
Full-rating load bank and prime moverNeededNot needed
What it assumesNothing about X_s or the saturation curveA model of saturation and armature reaction; the EMF method over-states regulation, the MMF method under-states it, and Potier and ASA come closer
Where it is usedSmall and laboratory machinesMachines too large to load fully

◆ Efficiency by direct loading, and why large machines do not use it

The same test gives efficiency: the output comes from the wattmeters and the input from a calibrated drive (torque × speed), so η = output/input. On a small machine that is fine. On a large one it fails for a numerical reason rather than a practical one. Efficiency is high, so the loss is a small difference between two large readings. Take 10 MW of output at 98 % efficiency: the input is 10.204 MW and the loss is 0.204 MW. An input reading that is only 1 % high is an error of 0.102 MW, which changes the loss by 50 %. Large alternators are therefore assessed from separately measured losses, which this lesson does not develop.

◆ Worked example (verified) — a direct load test

A 3-phase, star-connected, 5 kVA, 415 V, 50 Hz alternator is driven at 1500 rpm. At rated load the ammeter reads 6.96 A at 0.8 power factor lagging with the terminal voltage held at 415 V, and the mechanical input to the alternator is 5.10 kW. The load is then thrown off with the speed and field current unchanged, and the line voltage rises to 468 V. Find the regulation, the output, the efficiency and the loss, and see what a 1 % error in the input reading does.

Step 1: regulation. (E₀ − V)/V = (468 − 415)/415 = 53/415 = 12.77 %. Line values give the same ratio as phase values.

Step 2: output. P = √3 V I cos φ = √3 × 415 × 6.96 × 0.8 = 4002.3 W = 4.002 kW, which agrees with the rated 5 kVA × 0.8 = 4.000 kW to within 0.06 %.

Step 3: efficiency and loss. η = 4002.3/5100 = 78.48 %; the loss is 5100 − 4002.3 = 1097.7 W.

Step 4: a 1 % error in the input. If the input reads 5151 W instead of 5100 W, then η = 4002.3/5151 = 77.70 % and the loss becomes 5151 − 4002.3 = 1148.7 W. The efficiency moves by 0.78 percentage points, but the loss is out by 4.6 %. On this machine (efficiency near 78 %) the effect is modest; on the 98 % machine above it was 50 %.

◆ Why machines are paralleled, and the conditions for it

Connecting an alternator to a live bus is not like closing a switch on a passive load. Both sides are sources, so whatever difference exists between them at the instant of closing drives current straight through the two armatures. Four conditions make that difference zero for a three-phase machine (a single-phase machine needs the first, second and fourth).

ConditionMeaning, and how it is setIf it is violated
1. VoltageThe rms terminal voltage of the incoming machine equals the bus voltage. Set with the field current.A circulating current I_c = ΔE/(Z_s1 + Z_s2) flows. It is almost purely reactive, so little power moves but the armatures heat.
2. FrequencyThe incoming machine's frequency equals the bus frequency. Set with the prime-mover speed. The number of poles need not match: N = 120f/p.The phase angle between the two emfs keeps drifting at the difference frequency. The difference voltage swells and fades at that beat, and so do the current and the torque. Closing at the wrong point in the beat is a shock to both machines.
3. Phase sequenceThe three phases reach their peaks in the same order (a-b-c) on both sides. Checked at installation, and again after any re-wiring; corrected by interchanging two leads.No adjustment of speed or field can fix it. At best one pair of corresponding phases matches, and the other two pairs see √3 E across the switch: 10,999 V for the machines in the examples below. This is close to a short circuit.
4. Phase angleCorresponding emfs are in phase at the instant of closing, so the voltage across the switch is zero. Chosen by the moment of closing.A current 2E sin(δ/2)/(Z_s1 + Z_s2) flows and real power passes between the machines, jerking the rotors until they lock into step.

Two things are not conditions. The machines need not have the same kVA rating, and they need not run at the same speed, only at the frequencies that match. Some textbooks also ask for similar waveforms, because a large difference in harmonic content causes harmonic circulating currents; the operator cannot adjust that at the moment of closing.

◆ What a mismatch does: the circulating current

Close the switch when the emfs differ by ΔE = E₁ − E₂ (phasors, per phase). That difference is applied around a loop containing both armatures, so the two synchronous impedances are in series:

I_c = (E₁ − E₂)/(Z_s1 + Z_s2)    (per phase; Z_s = R_a + jX_s; I_c lags ΔE by tan⁻¹(X/R), nearly 90°)

Voltage mismatch. With the emfs in phase, ΔE is simply the difference of magnitudes. Because X_s is much larger than R_a, the current lags ΔE by nearly 90°, so it is almost reactive: the machine with the higher emf delivers lagging reactive current and the other absorbs it. Little real power moves, but the extra current heats both armatures and uses up rated capacity.

Phase-angle mismatch. With equal magnitudes E and an angle δ between them, the difference has magnitude 2E sin(δ/2), so

|I_c| = 2E sin(δ/2) / |Z_s1 + Z_s2|    (equal emf magnitudes E; δ = phase angle between the emfs)

Now the difference emf lies about 90° ahead of the midpoint of the two emfs, and the current lags it by nearly 90°, so the current is almost in phase with the emfs. That means real power: the leading machine delivers it and the lagging machine receives it, which retards the first and accelerates the second. This is the synchronising action of the previous lesson, and it is what pulls a machine that was closed slightly out of phase into step.

◆ Worked example (verified) — how large the currents are

Two identical 3-phase, star-connected alternators are rated 15 MVA, 11 kV (rated current 787 A). Each has Z_s = 0.2 + j8 Ω per phase. They are paralleled on open circuit, and the nominal emf of each is 6350 V per phase (about 11 kV line). Find the circulating current for (a) a 2 % voltage mismatch and (b) a 10° phase-angle mismatch with equal magnitudes.

Common step. The loop impedance is Z_s1 + Z_s2 = 0.4 + j16 Ω, so |Z| = 16.005 Ω, at an angle of tan⁻¹(16/0.4) = 88.57°.

(a) Voltage mismatch. Let one emf be 1 % above 6350 V and the other 1 % below, so ΔE = 2 % of 6350 = 127 V. Then |I_c| = 127/16.005 = 7.94 A, lagging ΔE by 88.57°. That is only 1.0 % of rated current, and it is almost entirely reactive.

(b) Phase-angle mismatch. ΔE = 2 × 6350 × sin 5° = 1106.9 V, so |I_c| = 1106.9/16.005 = 69.16 A, which is 8.8 % of rated current and 8.7 times the current of case (a). The current lags the leading machine's emf by only 3.57°, so it is nearly all real current: the leading machine sends 1.315 MW into the lagging one, which receives 1.309 MW. The difference, 5.74 kW, is the I²R loss in the two armatures (3 × 69.16² × 0.4).

Lesson from the numbers. A voltage error of 2 % is hardly noticed; a phase error of 10° pushes over a megawatt of real power through the pair, so it is the phase angle and the frequency, not the voltage, that make the closing instant critical.

◆ Sharing the load once the machines are connected

Real power and the governor. Once in parallel, the machines rotate in step at one frequency. A speed governor lets the frequency fall a little as the load on the machine rises, so each machine has a straight droop line

f = fnl − k P    k = (fnl − ffl)/Prated (Hz per kW)    Pi = (fnl,i − f)/ki

With a common frequency f and a total load Pload = ΣPi, the frequency and the shares follow:

f = (Σ fnl,i/ki − Pload) / Σ(1/ki)    (a load change ΔP divides in proportion to 1/ki, and moves f by ΔP/Σ(1/ki))

Reactive power and the field. The frequency droop says nothing about reactive power. That is set by the excitation: raising one machine's field current makes it supply more lagging reactive current and the other machines less, while the real-power shares stay essentially unchanged.

To changeAdjustOn an infinite busOn a small isolated system
Real power of one machineIts governor (steam, water or fuel input)P changes, the load angle changes; f and V do notP of that machine rises, the other's share falls, and f rises
Reactive power of one machineIts field currentQ changes; P does notQ shares change; the bus voltage moves a little; P shares stay about the same

◆ Worked example (verified) — sharing by droop

Machine 1 is rated 1000 kW and its governor runs from 51.0 Hz at no load to 49.5 Hz at full load. Machine 2 is rated 800 kW and runs from 51.5 Hz to 49.5 Hz. Together they supply 1200 kW. Find the common frequency and each output. Then find the governor settings that would give exactly 50.00 Hz with 700 kW and 500 kW, and the effect of a further 100 kW of load.

Step 1: droops. k₁ = (51.0 − 49.5)/1000 = 0.0015 Hz/kW; k₂ = (51.5 − 49.5)/800 = 0.0025 Hz/kW.

Step 2: common frequency. Σ f_nl/k = 51.0/0.0015 + 51.5/0.0025 = 34,000 + 20,600 = 54,600; Σ(1/k) = 666.67 + 400.00 = 1066.67 kW/Hz. So f = (54,600 − 1200)/1066.67 = 50.0625 Hz.

Step 3: outputs. P₁ = (51.0 − 50.0625)/0.0015 = 625 kW (62.5 % of its rating); P₂ = (51.5 − 50.0625)/0.0025 = 575 kW (71.9 % of its rating). They add to 1200 kW. The smaller machine, with the steeper droop line, is the more heavily loaded of the two per unit.

Step 4: resetting the governors. For 50.00 Hz with P₁ = 700 kW and P₂ = 500 kW the no-load settings must be fnl,1 = 50.00 + 0.0015 × 700 = 51.05 Hz and fnl,2 = 50.00 + 0.0025 × 500 = 51.25 Hz. Machine 1's set-point goes up by 0.05 Hz and machine 2's goes down by 0.25 Hz: the same droop lines, moved up or down.

Step 5: a further 100 kW. It divides in proportion to 1/k: machine 1 takes 100 × 666.67/1066.67 = 62.5 kW and machine 2 takes 37.5 kW. The frequency falls by 100/1066.67 = 0.09375 Hz, which is also k₁ × 62.5 = 0.09375 Hz for machine 1 alone.

Drawn to scale from the two droop lines (machine 1: f = 51.0 − 0.0015 P₁; machine 2: f = 51.5 − 0.0025 P₂, drawn mirrored so that the horizontal axis is the total load of 1200 kW). The solid lines cross at 50.0625 Hz where P₁ = 625 kW and P₂ = 575 kW. The dashed lines are the same droops after the governor resets of step 4, and cross at 50.00 Hz where P₁ = 700 kW and P₂ = 500 kW.

◆ What this lesson does not cover

This lesson covers the direct load test, the conditions for paralleling and what happens when each is violated, the circulating current, and how real and reactive power are shared. It does not cover the methods used to check the conditions and to choose the closing instant (the dark-lamp, bright-lamp and three-lamp methods and the synchroscope): those are the next row of the syllabus and have their own lesson, Methods of Synchronisation. It does not cover hunting, and it does not develop efficiency by separately measured losses.

Common mistake: using one machine's synchronous impedance for the circulating current. The difference emf drives current around a loop through both armatures, so the impedances add: 200 V across two 5 Ω reactances is 20 A, not 40 A. Two other slips: mixing line and phase voltages (every value here is per phase), and treating a voltage-mismatch circulating current as real power when it is almost entirely reactive.
Placement trap: "An alternator on the infinite bus should deliver more power, so increase its field current." It does not. On an infinite bus the frequency and the voltage are fixed, so more steam or water (the governor) increases the real power by advancing the rotor, and more field current increases the lagging reactive current. Field current is the reactive-power (Mvar) control and the governor is the real-power (MW) control. Keeping the two controls apart is what a question like this tests.

◆ Quick revision

  • Load test: rated current at rated V and the specified pf, note I_f, throw the load off at the same speed and I_f, read E₀; regulation = (E₀ − V)/V × 100. It needs a full-rating load, so it is used on small machines.
  • Loss by direct loading is a small difference of two large readings, so large machines use separately measured losses
  • Four conditions for paralleling: voltage, frequency, phase sequence, phase angle at closing. Rating and speed (as opposed to frequency) are not conditions
  • I_c = (E₁ − E₂)/(Z_s1 + Z_s2), impedances in series; a voltage mismatch gives mostly reactive current, a phase-angle mismatch (2E sin(δ/2)/|Z|) gives mostly real current and real power exchange
  • Droop: f = f_nl − kP; a common f fixes the shares; a load change divides in proportion to 1/k; governor set-points move the lines
  • Governor = real power (MW); field current = reactive power (Mvar)

ac-alt-methods-synchronisation.title: Methods of Synchronisation: Dark Lamps, Two Bright One Dark and the Synchroscope
ac-alt-methods-synchronisation.body:
◆ Why this matters

The previous lesson listed four conditions that must hold at the instant an alternator is connected to a bus: equal voltage, equal frequency, the same phase sequence, and emfs in phase. It also showed what a mismatch costs: a 10° phase error between two 15 MVA machines drives 69 A of mostly real current through their armatures. This lesson is about how the operator sees those conditions. Voltage is easy: two voltmeters and the field rheostat. Frequency is a frequency meter and the governor. What no ordinary meter shows is the phase angle between two voltages that are turning at almost the same speed, and the phase sequence. Lamps and the synchroscope exist to show exactly those two things, and they all work from one fact: the phase angle between the incoming machine and the bus slides at the difference frequency.

Prerequisites: the four conditions and the circulating current (why closing at the wrong instant hurts), synchronising power and torque (why a machine that closes near the correct phase is pulled into step), and the idea of an emf as a phasor with a magnitude and a phase angle.

◆ What the operator has to see

ConditionHow it is setHow it is seen
VoltageField currentTwo voltmeters (or a double voltmeter), one on the bus and one on the incoming machine
FrequencyPrime-mover speed (the governor)Two frequency meters, and the rate of the lamp pattern or of the synchroscope pointer
Phase sequenceInterchange two leads of the incoming machineThe lamp pattern (each lamp connection gives a different signature, below); not the synchroscope
Phase angleThe instant at which the switch is closedLamps dark (or one dark and two equally bright), or the synchroscope pointer at the top of its dial

◆ The beat between the machines

Let the bus run at fb and the incoming machine at fi = pN/120, where p is the number of poles and N the speed in rpm. The phase angle θ of the incoming machine's emf ahead of the bus voltage then grows by 360 degrees every 1/Δf seconds, where Δf = fi − fb. If the incoming machine is fast, Δf is positive and θ grows; if it is slow, θ falls. Each time θ passes through a full 360° the pattern repeats, so the repeat time is 1/|Δf|, called the beat period.

Δf = fi − fb = pN/120 − fb    dθ/dt = 360 Δf degrees per second    Tbeat = 1/|Δf|    (Δf > 0: incoming machine fast, θ grows; Δf < 0: slow, θ falls)

For example, Δf = 0.2 Hz slides the angle at 72° per second and repeats every 5 s. The angle stays within ±5° of coincidence for only 10/72 = 0.139 s of each beat, well under a quarter of a second: this is why the slip is made as small as the operator can manage.

◆ Method 1: three lamps wired straight (the dark-lamp method)

Connection. One lamp is connected across each pole of the open paralleling switch, that is, between corresponding phases of the two sides: a to a′, b to b′, c to c′ (unprimed letters on the bus side, primed on the incoming machine). Each lamp sees the difference of two emfs of equal magnitude E that differ in phase by θ, so

|Vlamp| = 2E |sin(θ/2)|    (all three lamps, correct phase sequence; zero at θ = 0, 2E at θ = 180°)

The lamps are therefore dark when the emfs coincide, and a lamp must stand up to twice the phase voltage. At high voltage they are fed through potential transformers, or two lamps are put in series.

What is seenWhat it means
All three lamps brighten and fade together, once per beat periodPhase sequence correct; the frequencies differ by 1/(beat period). These lamps do not say whether the incoming machine is fast or slow.
All three lamps steady at one brightnessSequence correct, frequencies equal, phase angle fixed: dark if the emfs are in phase
The lamps brighten and fade in turn (a rotating pattern)Phase sequence reversed. The three lamps can never all be dark together, however the speed is adjusted.

The closing instant. Close the switch in the middle of the dark period, with the flicker slow. A filament shows no glow until its voltage is a fair fraction of its rating, so the lamps look dark over a range of angle on either side of zero; the true zero is the middle of that range, which is why the operator judges the centre of the dark period and not its start.

◆ Method 2: one lamp straight, two crossed (two bright, one dark)

Connection. Lamp L1 is wired straight across a–a′. Lamps L2 and L3 are crossed: L2 between b and c′, L3 between c and b′. At correct phase, b and c′ are 240° (equivalently 120°) apart, so each crossed lamp sees √3 E while L1 sees zero: one dark, two bright. For a correct phase sequence and an angle θ between the machines, the three lamp voltages are

L1 = 2E |sin(θ/2)|    L2 = 2E |sin(120° + θ/2)|    L3 = 2E |sin(120° − θ/2)|    (correct sequence; at θ = 0: L1 = 0, L2 = L3 = √3 E = 1.732 E)
θStraight connection (each lamp), in units of ECrossed: L1L2L3
0°001.7321.732
60°1.0001.0001.0002.000
120°1.7321.73201.732
180°2.0002.0001.0001.000
240°1.7321.7321.7320
300°1.0001.0002.0001.000

As θ grows, the dark lamp moves from L1 (at 0°) to L2 (at 120°) to L3 (at 240°) and back to L1: each lamp is dark once per beat, at θ = 0°, 120° and 240° respectively, so the dark position steps round every one third of a beat period. If the incoming machine is fast the dark position moves L1 → L2 → L3; if it is slow it moves L1 → L3 → L2. With the reverse phase sequence the three lamps brighten and fade all together instead. This connection therefore reads the sequence and the direction of the frequency error at once, and its closing cue is sharper: L1 dark and L2 and L3 equally bright (about 1.73 E each). The usual reason given is that the eye judges two bright lamps equal more accurately than it judges the middle of a dark period.

Drawn to scale from L1 = 2|sin(θ/2)|, L2 = 2|sin(120° + θ/2)| and L3 = 2|sin(120° − θ/2)| in units of E (correct sequence, crossed connection). The circles mark the dark lamps at 0°, 120° and 240° and the two crossed lamps at 1.732 E at θ = 0, the closing instant.

Lamp connectionCorrect sequence, Δf ≠ 0Reversed sequence
Three straight (dark-lamp)All flicker togetherBrighten in turn (rotating); never all dark
One straight, two crossedDark lamp rotates: fast L1 → L2 → L3, slow L1 → L3 → L2All flicker together

Note that the two signatures are opposite. The textbooks name these lamp connections in different ways, so this lesson describes them by how the lamps are wired, which is what decides the pattern.

◆ Method 3: the synchroscope

A synchroscope is a dial instrument with a pointer that takes up the phase angle between the incoming machine and the bus. The pointer at the top of the dial (12 o'clock) means θ = 0, the bottom means 180°. If the two frequencies differ, the pointer turns continuously at the beat rate, one revolution per beat period. On the usual dial the clockwise sense is marked fast (the incoming machine is faster than the bus) and the anticlockwise sense slow, so, unlike the straight lamps, it shows the direction of the error as well as its size. The classical instrument is a small electrodynamic or moving-iron device; modern ones compute the angle electronically. The details of the mechanism are not needed here, only what the dial tells you and what it does not.

What it does not show. A synchroscope compares one pair of voltages. It cannot show a reversed phase sequence (which is why the sequence is verified separately, once, at installation and after any re-wiring), and it says nothing about voltage magnitude (that is the voltmeters' job). A pointer that is stationary at 12 o'clock proves that the frequencies and phase agree on the one phase compared, and no more.

Automatic synchronisers. Modern plant uses an automatic synchroniser or a synchronism-check relay (ANSI device number 25). It measures the voltage difference, the frequency difference and the angle, trims the governor and closes the breaker with an allowance for the breaker's own closing time. The internal workings are not covered here.

◆ Closing on the fast side, and allowing for the switch

  • Slightly fast, not slightly slow. After closing, a machine that was slightly fast leads the bus by a small angle, so it delivers a little real power (generator action). A machine that was slightly slow lags the bus and takes real power: it is motored by the bus, and a prime mover such as a steam turbine can be damaged when driven, so a reverse-power relay is fitted to trip it. The operator therefore aims for a slow drift on the fast side.
  • The switch has a closing time. A breaker takes a definite time tc from the close command to the contacts touching. In that time the angle changes by 360 Δf tc degrees, so the command is given that many degrees before coincidence (with the incoming machine behind the bus if it is fast). Given at exact coincidence, the contacts close at 360 Δf tc degrees of error.
  • A smaller slip gives more tolerance. The same timing error produces a smaller angle error at a smaller Δf.
θlead = 360 Δf tc    θerr = 360 Δf terr    |Ic| = 2E sin(θerr/2)/|Zs1 + Zs2|    (tc = closing time of the switch, terr = error in timing the close command)

◆ The order of operations

  1. Bring the incoming machine to about rated speed and set its voltage with the field until it matches the bus voltage.
  2. Check the phase sequence (once on installation or after any re-wiring; the lamp pattern shows it every time). If it is reversed, interchange any two leads of the incoming machine, never the bus.
  3. Trim the governor until the frequency is very slightly above the bus frequency, so that the pattern turns slowly.
  4. Give the close command with the lead for the switch's closing time, as the angle approaches coincidence.
  5. The machine now floats on the bus at nearly zero output. Raise its governor to take real power and adjust its field for reactive power, as in the previous lesson.
MethodShowsDoes not show
Three straight lampsPhase angle (dark), beat rate, sequence (together = right)Whether the machine is fast or slow
One straight, two crossedPhase angle (one dark, two equal), beat rate, direction (fast or slow), sequence (rotating = right)Voltage magnitude
SynchroscopePhase angle continuously, beat rate, directionPhase sequence; voltage magnitude

◆ Worked example (verified) — beat, closing lead and timing tolerance

Two identical 3-phase, star-connected alternators (the 15 MVA, 11 kV machines of the previous lesson) are to be paralleled: each has Zs = 0.2 + j8 Ω per phase and an emf of 6350 V per phase, so the loop impedance is |Zs1 + Zs2| = 16.005 Ω and the rated current is 787.3 A. The bus is at 50 Hz and the 4-pole incoming machine runs at 1506 rpm. The switch closes 0.25 s after the command.

Step 1: the beat. fi = 4 × 1506/120 = 50.2 Hz, so Δf = +0.2 Hz (fast). The beat period is 1/0.2 = 5.0 s and the angle slides 360 × 0.2 = 72° per second. With three straight lamps they brighten and fade together every 5 s; with the crossed connection the dark lamp moves L1 → L2 → L3, one step every 5/3 = 1.667 s.

Step 2: the lead. θlead = 72 × 0.25 = 18.0°. The command is given when the incoming emf is 18.0° behind the bus, so that it is at zero when the contacts touch.

Step 3: what a timing error costs. A timing error of 0.05 s, 0.1 s or 0.5 s gives an angle error of 3.6°, 7.2° or 36°, and |Ic| = 2E sin(θerr/2)/|Z|:

Timing errorAngle error2E sin(θerr/2)Circulating currentPercent of rated
0.05 s3.6°398.9 V24.9 A3.2 %
0.1 s7.2°797.4 V49.8 A6.3 %
0.5 s36°3924.5 V245.2 A31.1 %

Step 4: a smaller slip. With the slip cut to 0.05 Hz, the same 0.1 s timing error is only 360 × 0.05 × 0.1 = 1.8°, and |Ic| = 2 × 6350 × sin 0.9°/16.005 = 199.5/16.005 = 12.46 A (1.6 % of rated), four times smaller than at 0.2 Hz.

◆ Worked example (verified) — reading the lamps

The bus is at 50 Hz and the incoming machine has 4 poles. Decide what each observation means.

  • Straight lamps, all three brighten and fade together every 8 s. Phase sequence correct; |Δf| = 1/8 = 0.125 Hz. These lamps do not say fast or slow.
  • Crossed connection, the dark lamp moves L1 → L2 → L3 and completes a round in 4 s. Sequence correct; |Δf| = 1/4 = 0.25 Hz; the direction L1 → L2 → L3 means fast, so fi = 50.25 Hz and N = 120 × 50.25/4 = 1507.5 rpm.
  • Crossed connection, all three lamps brighten and fade together. Phase sequence reversed. Interchange any two leads of the incoming machine.
  • Straight lamps that brighten in turn. Also a reversed sequence, seen through the other connection.

◆ What this lesson does not cover

This lesson covers the lamp connections, the synchroscope and the closing instant. It does not cover how the rotor oscillates after closing (hunting) or the damper winding that reduces it, the internal construction of the synchroscope beyond what its dial shows, the internal working of automatic synchronisers, or single-phase machines. The four conditions themselves, the circulating current and the sharing of load are in the previous lesson, "Load Test and Parallel Operation of Alternators".

Common mistake: reading the lamp pattern of one connection with the rule of the other. With three straight lamps, flickering together means the phase sequence is right and rotating means it is wrong; with one straight and two crossed lamps it is exactly the other way round. Other slips: closing at the moment the lamps first go dark instead of the middle of the dark period, and issuing the command at exact coincidence when the switch needs 360 Δf tc degrees of lead.
Placement trap: "The synchroscope pointer is stationary at 12 o'clock, so the machine is ready to close." Not necessarily. The synchroscope compares one phase pair, so it cannot detect a reversed phase sequence, and it says nothing about the voltage magnitude. The sequence must have been verified separately, and the two voltmeters read before closing. Also, a pointer that is exactly stationary is not the aim: a slow drift on the fast side is what leaves the machine taking a little load rather than being motored.

◆ Quick revision

  • Beat: Δf = pN/120 − fb; the angle slides at 360Δf degrees per second; one beat (1/|Δf|) is one lamp flicker or one turn of the synchroscope pointer
  • Straight lamps: |V| = 2E|sin(θ/2)|, all equal; dark at coincidence, close in the middle of the dark period; flicker together = sequence right, rotating = sequence wrong; direction not shown
  • One straight and two crossed lamps: L1 dark with L2 = L3 = √3E at coincidence; the dark lamp rotates L1 → L2 → L3 if fast and L1 → L3 → L2 if slow; all three flickering together = sequence wrong
  • Synchroscope: pointer angle = θ, clockwise = fast, 12 o'clock = in phase; it does not check the sequence or the voltage magnitude
  • Close slightly fast (a slow machine is motored and can trip the reverse-power relay) and give the command 360 Δf tc degrees before coincidence; a smaller slip gives more tolerance
  • After closing, the governor sets the real power and the field sets the reactive power

ac-sync-motor-principle-phasor.title: Synchronous Motor: Principle of Operation and Phasor Diagrams
ac-sync-motor-principle-phasor.body:
◆ Why this matters

A synchronous motor runs at one unyielding speed — synchronous speed Ns = 120f/p — from zero load right up to its pull-out limit. While induction motors always consume lagging reactive power to magnetise their air gaps, a synchronous motor's power factor is completely controllable through its DC field excitation: it can operate at lagging, unity, or leading power factor. In heavy industrial installations (cement mills, mine hoists, rubber mixers, large reciprocating compressors) synchronous motors provide constant high-torque drive while simultaneously acting as on-site power factor correctors for the entire industrial facility.

Authoritative syllabus topic: Principle of operation of synchronous motor-Phasor diagram (Course ID: 23EEP504, Module III, Row 1).

◆ Principle of Operation and Why It Is Not Self-Starting

The stator of a 3-phase synchronous motor carries a balanced 3-phase distributed winding. When connected to a 3-phase supply of frequency f, it produces a constant-magnitude rotating magnetic field (RMF) spinning synchronously at:

Synchronous Speed:
Ns = 120 · f / p   [rpm]  |  ωs = 2π Ns / 60 = 4π f / p   [rad/s]

The rotor carries field poles (salient or cylindrical) excited with direct current (DC) from an external exciter or brushless rectifier, establishing fixed magnetic poles (alternating North and South).

For continuous unidirectional electromagnetic torque, magnetic locking must take place: stator North must attract rotor South, and stator South must attract rotor North, dragging the rotor around at synchronous speed. However, at standstill (N = 0):

  • At time t = 0, suppose a stator North pole aligns near a rotor South pole. An attractive tangential torque pulls the rotor clockwise.
  • Half a cycle later (after 10 ms on a 50 Hz supply), the stator RMF has advanced by 180° electrical. The stator pole opposite the rotor South pole is now a North pole turned South, producing a repulsive counter-clockwise torque.
  • Because of the high rotational inertia of the rotor mass, the rotor cannot accelerate from rest to synchronous speed (e.g. 1500 rpm) in 10 ms.

Consequently, the average torque over one electrical cycle is identically zero. A pure synchronous motor has zero starting torque and cannot start on its own.

◆ Methods of Starting Synchronous Motors

Starting MethodMechanismPractical Application
Damper (Amortisseur) WindingsHeavy copper bars embedded in rotor pole faces shorted by end rings. Operates as a squirrel-cage induction motor until ~95% Ns; DC field is then applied and magnetic locking occurs.Most widely used standard industrial method.
Pony MotorA small auxiliary induction motor (with one pair of poles fewer) or DC motor accelerates the unloaded rotor up to synchronous speed before mains connection.Used where damper winding starting current is unacceptable to the grid.
Variable Frequency Drive (VFD)Inverter frequency is ramped smoothly from 0 Hz upwards. Synchronism is maintained from standstill without high starting inrush current.Modern large pump/compressor variable-speed drives.

◆ Phasor Diagrams and Terminal Voltage Equations

In a synchronous motor, electrical energy is absorbed from the AC bus and converted into mechanical torque. The applied terminal phase voltage V must overcome the generated back-EMF Eb (counter-EMF) and the armature impedance drop:

Motor Voltage Equation (per phase):
V = Eb + Ia · Zs = Eb + Ia(Ra + j Xs)
Er = V − Eb = Ia · Zs
Ia = (V − Eb) / Zs = Er / Zs

where:

  • V: Applied terminal phase voltage (reference phasor V ∠0°).
  • Eb: Excitation back-EMF per phase, lagging V by the load angle (or torque angle) δ, i.e., Eb ∠−δ.
  • Er: Resultant EMF across the synchronous impedance Zs.
  • Ia: Armature phase current, lagging Er by internal impedance angle θ = tan−1(Xs/Ra).
  • ϕ: Power factor angle between terminal voltage V and armature current Ia.

◆ The Three Excitation Regimes

Excitation StateBack-EMF ConditionPower FactorArmature CurrentGrid Reactive Power
Under-excitedEb cos δ < VLagging (cos ϕ < 1)High (large lagging reactive component)Absorbs lagging VARs (acts like an inductor)
Normal excitationEb cos δ = VUnity (cos ϕ = 1.0)Minimum Ia for a given mechanical loadZero net reactive power exchange
Over-excitedEb cos δ > VLeading (cos ϕ < 1)High (large leading reactive component)Delivers lagging VARs (acts like a capacitor bank)
Common mistake: Applying the alternator voltage equation Ef = V + IaZs to a synchronous motor. In a generator, internal EMF delivers power into the line. In a motor, terminal voltage V pushes current against counter-EMF Eb, so V = Eb + IaZs ⇒ Eb = V − IaZs. Consequently, in a motor, Eb lags V by the load angle δ, whereas in a generator Ef leads V by δ.
Placement trap: "If you increase the DC excitation of a running synchronous motor, does it speed up?"
Answer: Absolutely not. The steady-state speed is rigidly pinned to the grid frequency: Ns = 120f/p. Increasing field excitation increases the internal back-EMF Eb, which swings the armature current Ia from lagging to leading, supplying reactive power to the grid. The speed remains strictly constant up to the pull-out torque.

◆ Quick revision

  • Synchronous speed: Ns = 120f/p. Speed regulation of a synchronous motor is strictly 0% under all steady-state loads.
  • Zero starting torque: Net average starting torque at standstill is zero because the high-speed stator RMF reverses relative polarity every 10 ms before rotor inertia can accelerate.
  • Starting: Achieved by damper windings (acting as an induction motor rotor up to ~95% Ns), pony motor, or VFD.
  • Phasor equation: V = Eb + IaZs; Eb lags V by torque angle δ.
  • Excitation control: Under-excited = lagging pf (absorbs VARs); Normal = unity pf (minimum Ia); Over-excited = leading pf (generates VARs).

ac-sync-motor-power-torque-losses.title: Synchronous Motor: Power and Torque Equations, Losses, and Efficiency
ac-sync-motor-power-torque-losses.body:
◆ Why this matters

The electromagnetic power developed in a synchronous motor determines its mechanical drive capability, overload capacity, and stability boundary. Unlike induction motors, where torque is driven by slip, a synchronous motor develops torque entirely at synchronous speed via the angular displacement (load angle δ) between the rotor magnetic axis and the stator rotating field axis. Understanding the power-angle relationship, pull-out torque, and internal losses is critical for industrial drive sizing and power system transient stability.

Authoritative syllabus topic: Power and Torque Equations- Losses and Efficiency (Course ID: 23EEP504, Module III, Row 2).

◆ Power Flow in a Synchronous Motor

The energy conversion process from electrical input terminals to the rotating shaft proceeds through distinct stages:

  1. Electrical Power Input (Pin): Total 3-phase power absorbed from the mains:
    Pin = √3 · VL · IL · cos φ = 3 · V · Ia · cos φ
  2. Stator Copper Losses (Pcu): Ohmic dissipation in armature resistance:
    Pcu = 3 · Ia2 · Ra
  3. Gross Mechanical Power Developed (Pdev): Electromagnetic power converted at the air gap:
    Pdev = Pin − Pcu = 3 · Eb · Ia · cos(δ + φ)
  4. Rotational and Core Losses (Prot): Stator core hysteresis & eddy current losses, plus rotor mechanical friction and windage losses:
    Prot = Pcore + Pfriction+windage
  5. Net Shaft Output (Pout): Useful mechanical power delivered to the coupled mechanical load:
    Pout = Pdev − Prot = ωs · Tshaft

◆ Derivation of the Mechanical Power Equation

Taking terminal voltage V as reference phasor (V ∠0°), the back-EMF is Eb ∠−δ. Synchronous impedance is Zs ∠θ = Ra + j Xs, where θ = tan−1(Xs / Ra). The per-phase armature current is:

Armature Current Phasor:
Ia = (V − Eb) / Zs = (V ∠0° − Eb ∠−δ) / (Zs ∠θ)
Ia = (V / Zs) ∠−θ − (Eb / Zs) ∠(−δ − θ)

The gross mechanical power developed per phase is Pdev,ph = Re[Eb · Ia*]:

General Power Equation per phase (with Ra ≠ 0):
Pdev,ph = [V · Eb / Zs] · cos(θ − δ) − [Eb2 / Zs] · cos θ
Since cos θ = Ra / Zs:
Pdev,ph = [V · Eb / Zs] · cos(θ − δ) − [Eb2 · Ra / Zs2]

Total developed 3-phase power is Pdev = 3 · Pdev,ph.

◆ Condition for Maximum Developed Power (Pull-Out Limit)

Differentiating Pdev,ph with respect to load angle δ and setting dPdev / dδ = 0:

  • d/dδ [cos(θ − δ)] = sin(θ − δ) = 0 ⇒ δ = θ = tan−1(Xs / Ra).
  • Maximum developed power per phase:
    Pdev,max = [V · Eb / Zs] − [Eb2 · Ra / Zs2]

In practical large synchronous machines, the armature resistance is negligible compared to synchronous reactance (Ra ≪ Xs, Zs ≈ Xs, and θ ≈ 90°). The power equation simplifies to the classic power-angle formula:

Ideal Power-Angle Formula (Ra ≈ 0):
Pdev = 3 · [V · Eb / Xs] · sin δ  |  Pmax = 3 · [V · Eb / Xs]
Td = Pdev / ωs = [3 / ωs] · [V · Eb / Xs] · sin δ  |  Tpull-out = [3 / ωs] · [V · Eb / Xs]
Common mistake: Assuming the maximum developed power occurs at δ = 90° under all conditions. It occurs at exactly 90° only when armature resistance is zero (Ra = 0). When Ra is considered, maximum power occurs at δ = θ = tan−1(Xs / Ra) < 90°. For typical synchronous motors with Xs/Ra ≈ 8, θ ≈ 82.8°.
Placement trap: "What happens if the mechanical shaft load exceeds the pull-out torque Tpull-out?"
Answer: Unlike an induction motor which slips and slows down steadily to a lower stable speed, a synchronous motor pulls out of step. The electromagnetic synchronising torque fails (dP/dδ < 0), the rotor abruptly drops out of synchronism, severe hunting and violent current surges occur, and the motor stalls unless tripped immediately by overload/out-of-step protection relays.

◆ Quick revision

  • Gross mechanical power developed: Pdev = 3 · Eb · Ia · cos(δ + φ) = Pin − 3 Ia2 Ra.
  • Power-angle equation: Pdev,ph = [V Eb / Zs] cos(θ − δ) − [Eb2 Ra / Zs2].
  • Negligible resistance (Ra ≈ 0): Pdev = 3 · [V Eb / Xs] sin δ, peaking at δ = 90°.
  • Pull-out torque: Tmax = Pdev,max / ωs.
  • Stability: Stable operation requires positive synchronising power coefficient: dPdev / dδ > 0 (i.e. 0 ≤ δ < θ).
  • Efficiency: η = Pout / Pin = (Pdev − Prot) / Pin.

ac-sync-motor-v-inverted-curves.title: Synchronous Motor: V-Curves and Inverted V-Curves (Synchronous Condenser)
ac-sync-motor-v-inverted-curves.body:
◆ Why this matters

The defining capability of a synchronous motor is that its armature current and power factor can be continuously manipulated simply by adjusting its DC field excitation current (If), without altering its shaft speed or real power delivery. Plotting armature current Ia against field current If yields the iconic V-Curves, while plotting power factor cos φ against If yields the Inverted V-Curves. These curves form the operational bible for synchronous motor drive engineers and substation operators deploying synchronous condensers for transmission voltage support.

Authoritative syllabus topic: V and Inverted V curves (Course ID: 23EEP504, Module III, Row 3).

◆ Physical Mechanism: Constant Power with Variable Excitation

Consider a synchronous motor driving a constant mechanical shaft load. The real electrical power developed per phase is constant:

Constant Real Power Constraints:
P = 3 · V · Ia · cos φ = constant  ⇒  Ia · cos φ = constant
P ≈ 3 · [V · Eb / Xs] · sin δ = constant  ⇒  Eb · sin δ = constant

This reveals two geometric rules on the phasor plane:

  1. The active component of armature current (Ia cos φ) is pinned constant. The tip of the Ia phasor must lie on a vertical line perpendicular to terminal voltage V.
  2. The vertical projection of back-EMF (Eb sin δ) is pinned constant. As field current If changes (which changes Eb ∝ If), the tip of the Eb phasor must trace a horizontal locus parallel to V.

◆ Under-Excited vs Normal vs Over-Excited Operation

Excitation LevelArmature Current (Ia)Power Factor (cos φ)Reactive Power (Q)Operating Function
Under-excited (If < If,normal)Higher than minimum; lags VLagging (inductive)Absorbs VARs from gridHeavy drive with poor pf
Normal excitation (If = If,normal)Minimum possible (Ia = P / 3V)Unity (1.0)Zero net reactive powerMost efficient motor operation
Over-excited (If > If,normal)Higher than minimum; leads VLeading (capacitive)Delivers VARs to gridPower factor correction

◆ Synchronous Condensers (Syncons)

A synchronous condenser is a synchronous motor operated at no mechanical load (no shaft connection, purely idling) with its field heavily over-excited. Because mechanical shaft output is zero, it draws only a tiny active current to supply internal friction and core losses, while drawing a huge leading reactive current (nearly 90° ahead of terminal voltage):

Reactive Power Supplied by Synchronous Condenser:
QC = √3 · VL · Ia · sin φ ≈ 3 · V · Ia   [kvar or Mvar]
Rating required to improve plant pf from cos φ1 to cos φ2:
QC = P · [tan φ1 − tan φ2]

Unlike static capacitor banks whose reactive power output drops quadratically during voltage dips (Qcap ∝ V2), a synchronous condenser inherently provides dynamic reactive current boost during grid faults and provides rotating physical inertia to stabilize grid frequency.

Common mistake: Believing that over-exciting a synchronous motor raises the terminal voltage V of the machine when tied to an infinite bus. The infinite bus voltage is rigidly fixed by the grid. Over-excitation raises the internal generated back-EMF Eb, making Eb cos δ > V, which drives a leading reactive current into the bus.
Placement trap: "Can a synchronous motor operate at zero power factor?"
Answer: Yes! When running at zero mechanical load (no-load) and over-excited, the active power is virtually zero (only small loss components), so the current leads terminal voltage by almost 90°. The power factor is cos 90° = 0 leading. This is the precise operating mode of a synchronous condenser.

◆ Quick revision

  • V-Curves: Plot of Ia vs If for various constant loads. Shape is a 'V' because Ia is high when under-excited (lagging), minimum at normal excitation (unity pf), and high when over-excited (leading).
  • Inverted V-Curves: Plot of cos φ vs If, reaching a peak of 1.0 at normal excitation and drooping on both sides.
  • Compounding curve: The locus of minimum armature current points across load curves, leaning slightly to the right as load increases.
  • Synchronous Condenser: An over-excited synchronous motor running at no load to supply leading reactive power for power factor correction and grid voltage support.
  • Dynamic advantage: Provides physical inertia and voltage support during grid faults, unlike static shunt capacitor banks.

ac-ind-motor-construction-principle.title: Three-Phase Induction Motor: Constructional Features and Principle of Operation
ac-ind-motor-construction-principle.body:
◆ Why this matters

The three-phase induction motor is the uncontested workhorse of modern global industry, accounting for over 70% of all industrial electric motor energy consumption. Invented by Nikola Tesla, its brilliance lies in brushless, self-starting operation: no external DC excitation, no commutators, no slip rings (in cage motors), and rugged, low-maintenance mechanical construction. It converts electrical energy into mechanical power entirely via electromagnetic induction across an air gap.

Authoritative syllabus topic: Three Phase Induction Motors-Constructional features- Principle of Operation (Course ID: 23EEP504, Module III, Row 4).

◆ Constructional Features: Stator and Rotor

A 3-phase induction motor consists of two primary electromagnetic structures separated by a small, uniform air gap (typically 0.4 mm to 2.5 mm depending on frame size):

  • Stator: Built from thin (0.35 mm to 0.5 mm) high-grade silicon steel laminations insulated by varnish to minimize core hysteresis and eddy-current losses. The inner periphery is slotted to house a balanced, distributed 3-phase winding (star or delta connected) displaced by 120° electrical in space.
  • Rotor: Also laminated and keyed onto the drive shaft. Depending on rotor construction, motors are classified into two distinct classes:
    1. Squirrel-Cage Rotor: Heavy copper or aluminum conductor bars embedded in semi-closed or closed rotor slots, permanently short-circuited at both ends by heavy conducting end rings. It possesses no external terminals. To eliminate magnetic locking (cogging), reduce harmonic crawling torques, and quiet operational hum, the rotor slots are purposefully skewed at an angle along the axial length.
    2. Wound Rotor (Slip-Ring Motor): Carries a full 3-phase distributed winding wound for the exact same number of magnetic poles as the stator. The three phase terminals are brought out through three insulated bronze/brass slip rings mounted on the shaft with stationary carbon brushes. This permits connection of external balanced resistances during starting to produce immense starting torque with low starting current.

◆ Production of Rotating Magnetic Field (RMF)

When balanced 3-phase currents flow through the spatial 120° distributed stator windings:

Three-Phase Stator Currents:
iR = Im sin(ωt)
iY = Im sin(ωt − 120°)
iB = Im sin(ωt − 240°)

The total resultant magnetic flux in the air gap is constant in magnitude at every instant:

Resultant Air-Gap Flux:
Φresultant = 1.5 · Φm = constant
Speed of rotation: Ns = 120f / p   [rpm]

◆ Principle of Operation and Slip

The working sequence occurs through classical electromagnetic principles:

  1. The stator RMF rotates at speed Ns and cuts the stationary rotor bars.
  2. By Faraday's law of induction, an alternating EMF is induced in each rotor bar: e = B · l · vrel.
  3. Because the rotor circuit is completely closed (via end rings or external resistors), heavy circulating currents flow through the rotor conductors.
  4. By Lenz's law, the induced currents must flow in such a direction as to oppose the cause producing them — which is the relative motion between the rotating stator field and the slower rotor conductors.
  5. To oppose this relative motion, the rotor experiences an electromagnetic force (F = B · I · l) that drags the rotor in the same direction as the RMF.
Fundamental Slip and Frequency Equations:
Fractional Slip: s = (Ns − N) / Ns  |  Percentage Slip: %s = [(Ns − N) / Ns] × 100
Rotor Running Speed: N = Ns · (1 − s)
Rotor Induced EMF frequency: fr = s · f
Rotor Induced EMF at slip s: E2 = s · E20  |  Rotor Reactance at slip s: X2 = s · X20
Common mistake: Believing that the rotor can ever reach synchronous speed (N = Ns) in motoring mode. If N = Ns, relative velocity (Ns − N) = 0. Therefore, rate of flux cutting is zero, induced rotor EMF drops to zero, rotor current drops to zero, and electromagnetic torque collapses to zero. Frictional drag immediately slows the rotor down. Hence, an induction motor must always operate at a speed strictly less than Ns (i.e., s > 0).
Placement trap: "What is the frequency of the rotor current in a 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor running at 1440 rpm?"
Solution:
Ns = 120 × 50 / 4 = 1500 rpm.
Slip s = (1500 − 1440) / 1500 = 60 / 1500 = 0.04 (4%).
Rotor frequency fr = s × f = 0.04 × 50 = 2 Hz!
Candidate trap: Many candidates say 50 Hz. Under running conditions, rotor frequency is merely 1 to 3 Hz!

◆ Quick revision

  • RMF magnitude: 3-phase distributed winding establishes an RMF of constant amplitude 1.5 Φm rotating at Ns = 120f/p.
  • Self-starting: Induction motors are inherently self-starting because at standstill s = 1.0, relative speed is maximum, producing large initial induced currents and torque.
  • Skewed slots: Rotor slots are skewed to prevent magnetic cogging (locking with stator teeth), eliminate 7th/11th harmonic crawling, and silence magnetic hum.
  • Slip ring vs Cage: Squirrel-cage motors are virtually indestructible and maintenance-free; wound-rotor motors allow external rotor resistance to deliver maximum starting torque at reduced starting current.
  • Operating slip: Typically 1% to 5% at full load; rotor electrical frequency is fr = s · f.

ac-ind-motor-power-torque-slip.title: Three-Phase Induction Motor: Power Flow, Torque Equation, and Torque-Slip Characteristics
ac-ind-motor-power-torque-slip.body:
◆ Why this matters

The torque-slip relationship governs every facet of induction motor operation: starting acceleration, full-load stability, overload withstand, and braking. Furthermore, the elegant power division across the air gap — linking electrical input, rotor ohmic losses, and converted mechanical shaft power — provides electrical engineers with the famous golden ratio 1 : s : (1 − s), which unlocks motor diagnostics and thermal rating analysis.

Authoritative syllabus topic: Power and Torque Equations-Torque Slip Characteristics (Course ID: 23EEP504, Module III, Row 5).

◆ The Air-Gap Power Division: The 1 : s : (1−s) Golden Rule

Electrical power enters the stator, experiences stator copper loss (3 I12 R1) and stator core loss, and crosses the air gap as magnetic power. This electromagnetic power transferred across the air gap is termed Air-Gap Power (Pgap).

The Fundamental Power Division:
Air-Gap Power: Pgap = 3 · I2'2 · (R2' / s) = ωs · Td
Rotor Copper Loss: Pcu2 = 3 · I2'2 · R2' = s · Pgap
Gross Mechanical Power Developed: Pmech = Pgap − Pcu2 = (1 − s) · Pgap = ω · Td

Pgap : Pcu2 : Pmech = 1 : s : (1 − s)

Rotor electrical efficiency is simply Pmech / Pgap = (1 − s) = N / Ns. High operating efficiency demands small steady-state slip!

◆ Derivation of the Electromagnetic Torque Equation

Electromagnetic torque developed by the rotor is given by air-gap power divided by synchronous angular speed (ωs = 2π Ns / 60):

Electromagnetic Torque Equation:
Td = Pgap / ωs = [3 / ωs] · [V12 · (R2' / s)] / [ (R1 + R2' / s)2 + (X1 + X2')2 ]

Setting standstill slip s = 1 gives the Starting Torque:

Starting Torque (s = 1):
Tstart = [3 / ωs] · [V12 · R2'] / [ (R1 + R2')2 + (X1 + X2')2 ]

◆ Maximum (Breakdown / Pull-Out) Torque

By applying the maximum power transfer theorem to the equivalent circuit, maximum torque occurs when the load resistance R2'/s equals the magnitude of the standstill source impedance:

Condition for Maximum Torque:
R2' / smT = √[ R12 + (X1 + X2')2 ]  ⇒  smT ≈ R2' / (X1 + X2')

Maximum Torque Formula:
Tmax = [3 / (2 ωs)] · [V12] / [ R1 + √[ R12 + (X1 + X2')2 ] ] ≈ [3 V12] / [ 2 ωs (X1 + X2') ]

◆ Critical Properties of Maximum Torque

PropertyBehavior / DependencyPhysical Engineering Consequence
Magnitude of TmaxProportional to V12; Completely independent of R2'Adding rotor resistance in slip-ring motors does not change the maximum torque capability!
Slip at Tmax (smT)Directly proportional to R2' (smT ∝ R2')Inserting external resistance shifts the peak torque point towards standstill (s = 1).
Starting Torque ConditionTstart = Tmax when R2' = X1 + X2' (i.e. smT = 1.0)Enables wound-rotor motors to launch high-inertia crushers with maximum breakdown torque.
Common mistake: Assuming that adding external resistance to a wound rotor increases the maximum breakdown torque. It does not! The peak torque value Tmax remains completely unchanged. External resistance simply increases starting torque and shifts the slip at which Tmax occurs closer to standstill (s = 1.0).
Placement trap: "If the line voltage supplied to a 3-phase induction motor drops by 10%, by what percentage does the developed torque drop?"
Solution: Developed torque is strictly proportional to voltage squared: T ∝ V2.
Tnew / Told = (0.90 V)2 / V2 = 0.81.
The torque drops by 19% (not 10%)! A 10% under-voltage reduces torque capability by almost one-fifth, which can cause stalling under heavy loads.

◆ Quick revision

  • Golden Power Ratio: Pgap : Pcu2 : Pmech = 1 : s : (1 − s).
  • Rotor copper loss: Pcu2 = s · Pgap.
  • Torque equation: T = [3 / ωs] · [V2 (R2/s)] / [(R1 + R2/s)2 + X2].
  • Breakdown torque: Tmax is proportional to V2, inversely proportional to total leakage reactance, and independent of rotor resistance R2.
  • Slip at breakdown: smT ≈ R2' / (X1 + X2'); directly proportional to rotor resistance.

ac-ind-motor-phasor-equivalent-circuit.title: Three-Phase Induction Motor: Phasor Diagram and Equivalent Circuit
ac-ind-motor-phasor-equivalent-circuit.body:
◆ Why this matters

An induction motor can be accurately conceptualized and analysed as a generalized rotating transformer whose secondary winding is short-circuited and rotates at slip speed. By mapping the electromagnetic interactions across the air gap into an equivalent electrical network, engineers can calculate input currents, power factor, electromagnetic torque, copper and iron losses, and operating efficiency at any slip without performing complex coupled magnetic field calculations.

Authoritative syllabus topic: Phasor diagram-Equivalent circuit (Course ID: 23EEP504, Module III, Row 6).

◆ The Transformer Analogy and Equivalent Circuit Development

At standstill (s = 1.0), the induction motor is identical to a conventional static 3-phase transformer with a short-circuited secondary. Under running conditions at slip s, the rotor induced EMF and leakage reactance operate at slip frequency (fr = s · f):

Rotor Loop Equation at Slip s:
E2s = s · E20  |  X2s = s · X20
I2 = E2s / √[ R22 + (s X20)2 ] = (s · E20) / √[ R22 + (s X20)2 ]

Dividing numerator and denominator by slip s yields the crucial transformation to stator supply frequency f:

Equivalent Stationary Rotor Circuit (Frequency f):
I2 = E20 / √[ (R2 / s)2 + X202 ]

The equivalent rotor resistance R2 / s is now decomposed into two physically distinct components:

Separation of Rotor Resistance:
R2 / s = R2 + R2 · [(1 − s) / s]

• R2: The actual physical rotor winding ohmic resistance, dissipating I22 R2 as rotor copper heat.
• R2[(1 − s) / s]: The fictitious electrical resistance representing the mechanical load on the motor shaft!

◆ Phasor Diagram of the Induction Motor

The phasor diagram links the terminal applied voltage V1 to the air gap flux Φm and rotor currents:

  • Mutual Flux (Φm): Set as the horizontal reference phasor along the positive axis.
  • Induced Counter-EMF (E1 = E2'): Lags Φm by exactly 90° (due to Faraday's law e = −N dΦ/dt).
  • Rotor Current (I2'): Lags induced EMF E2' by rotor power factor angle φ2 = tan−1(s X20 / R2).
  • No-Load Stator Current (I0): Vector sum of core-loss current Ic (in phase with −E1) and magnetizing current Im (in phase with Φm):
    I0 = Ic + Im.
  • Total Stator Input Current (I1): Vector sum of no-load current and referred rotor load current:
    I1 = I0 + I2'.
  • Applied Terminal Voltage (V1): Overcomes back-EMF and stator leakage impedance:
    V1 = −E1 + I1(R1 + j X1).
Common mistake: Confusing the rotor power factor angle φ2 with the stator input power factor angle φ1. The stator current I1 includes the large magnetizing component I0 (which lags terminal voltage by nearly 80°–85° due to the physical air gap). Consequently, the overall motor power factor at no load is terribly low (0.1 to 0.2 lagging), only climbing to 0.82–0.88 lagging at full load.
Placement trap: "Why does an induction motor draw 30% to 40% of its rated current at no-load, while a power transformer draws only 2% to 5%?"
Answer: The air gap! A transformer has an unbroken, continuous closed ferromagnetic core with very low reluctance, requiring only a tiny magnetizing current. In an induction motor, the air gap (despite being under 1 mm) represents enormous magnetic reluctance, requiring a massive magnetizing MMF (and thus 30%–40% rated current) to establish the working flux Φm.

◆ Quick revision

  • Transformer analogy: An induction motor is a generalized transformer with a rotating secondary. Standstill = shorted transformer.
  • Load representation: Mechanical shaft load is represented by equivalent electrical resistance RL' = R2' · (1 − s) / s.
  • Air-gap power: Total power entering the rotor is Pgap = 3 · I2'2 · (R2' / s).
  • No-load current: I0 is 30% to 40% of rated current, at a low power factor (0.1 to 0.2 lag), primarily to overcome air-gap reluctance.
