  • Stator equation: V1 = −E1 + I1(R1 + j X1).

ac-ind-motor-tests-numerical.title: Three-Phase Induction Motor: No-Load and Blocked-Rotor Tests (Parameter Determination)
ac-ind-motor-tests-numerical.body:
◆ Why this matters

Testing large induction motors by applying direct mechanical brake loads is impractical, unsafe, and extremely wasteful of electrical power. Just as open-circuit and short-circuit tests determine transformer parameters, the No-Load Test (running uncoupled at rated voltage) and the Blocked-Rotor Test (rotor locked stationary at reduced voltage) extract all per-phase equivalent circuit parameters (R1, R2', X1, X2', Xm, Rc), constant rotational losses, and blocked-rotor impedances with minimal power consumption.

Authoritative syllabus topic: No load and Blocked rotor tests-Numerical problems (Course ID: 23EEP504, Module III, Row 7).

◆ The No-Load Test (Open-Circuit Analogue)

The motor is uncoupled from its mechanical load and run freely at rated line voltage and rated frequency. Because the motor runs at virtually synchronous speed (s ≈ 0), the fictitious load resistance R2'[(1 − s)/s] → ∞ acts like an open circuit. Rotor current is negligible, and all drawn power goes into stator copper loss, core loss, and friction/windage loss:

No-Load Test Calculations (Star-Connected Stator assumed):
Applied Phase Voltage: V0 = Vline,0 / √3
Phase No-Load Current: I0 = Iline,0
Total 3-Phase No-Load Power: W0 = √3 · Vline,0 · Iline,0 · cos φ0
No-Load Power Factor: cos φ0 = W0 / (√3 · Vline,0 · Iline,0)
Constant Rotational Loss: Prot = W0 − 3 · I02 · R1 = Pcore + Pfriction+windage
Magnetizing Current: Im = I0 · sin φ0  |  Core Current: Ic = I0 · cos φ0
Magnetizing Reactance: Xm = V0 / Im  |  Core Resistance: Rc = V0 / Ic

◆ The Blocked-Rotor Test (Short-Circuit Analogue)

The rotor shaft is mechanically clamped so it cannot turn (N = 0, s = 1.0). The load resistance R2'[(1 − s)/s] = 0, representing a short circuit. A low 3-phase voltage (typically 10% to 20% of rated voltage) is applied through an autotransformer until rated full-load current circulates through the stator windings:

Blocked-Rotor Calculations (per phase):
Phase Blocked Voltage: Vsc = Vline,sc / √3
Phase Blocked Current: Isc = Iline,sc
Total 3-Phase Short-Circuit Power: Wsc = 3 · Isc2 · R01
Total Equivalent Resistance referred to Stator: R01 = Wsc / (3 · Isc2)
Total Equivalent Impedance: Z01 = Vsc / Isc
Total Equivalent Reactance: X01 = √[ Z012 − R012 ]

◆ Separation of Stator and Rotor Resistances and Leakage Reactances

The blocked rotor test yields total combined equivalent parameters: R01 = R1 + R2' and X01 = X1 + X2'. To separate them:

  1. Stator Resistance (R1): Measured directly across stator winding terminals using DC resistance measurement (Ohm's law or Kelvin double bridge), corrected by a factor of 1.2 to 1.25 for skin effect at 50 Hz AC:
    R1,ac ≈ 1.2 · R1,dc
  2. Rotor Resistance (R2'): Derived by subtraction:
    R2' = R01 − R1
  3. Leakage Reactance Splitting (IEEE / NEMA Standard):
    • Class A / Wound-Rotor Motors: X1 = 0.50 · X01  |  X2' = 0.50 · X01
    • Class B (Normal start torque, low start current): X1 = 0.40 · X01  |  X2' = 0.60 · X01
    • Class C (High start torque, double cage): X1 = 0.30 · X01  |  X2' = 0.70 · X01
Common mistake: Neglecting the √3 conversion factor when taking test readings from line instruments. A wattmeter measurement on 3-phase gives total 3-phase power (W0 = W1 + W2), whereas the ammeter and voltmeter give line current and line voltage. In per-phase star calculations, failure to divide line voltage by √3 introduces a catastrophic factor-of-3 error into equivalent impedances and reactances!
Placement trap: "Why is core loss neglected during the blocked rotor test even though full-load rated current is flowing?"
Answer: Core loss (hysteresis + eddy current) is proportional to flux density squared, which depends on applied voltage: Pcore ∝ V2. In the blocked-rotor test, the applied voltage is only 10% to 15% of rated voltage. Consequently, core loss during the blocked rotor test is only (0.12)2 ≈ 1.4% of rated core loss, which is completely negligible compared to the full-load copper loss 3 Isc2 R01!

◆ Quick revision

  • No-load test: Conducted at rated voltage, rated frequency, with uncoupled shaft. Yields magnetizing parameters (Xm, Rc) and rotational losses (Pcore + Pfriction+windage).
  • Blocked-rotor test: Conducted with shaft locked, at reduced voltage to circulate rated current. Yields total equivalent impedance Z01, resistance R01, and leakage reactance X01.
  • Core loss omission: Core loss is negligible in blocked-rotor test because applied voltage is very low (~12% rated).
  • Parameter splitting: R1 is obtained from DC bridge test (+20% skin effect); R2' = R01 − R1; X1 ≈ X2' ≈ 0.5 X01 for standard machines.

ac-ind-motor-circle-diagram.title: Circle Diagram of Induction Motors: Graphical Construction, Power Lines, and Performance Determination
ac-ind-motor-circle-diagram.body:
The circle diagram of a three-phase induction motor is a graphical representation of its approximate equivalent circuit that yields complete operating performance—input current, power factor, electromagnetic torque, mechanical output, rotor and stator copper losses, slip, and maximum overload capabilities—across all operating slips from standstill to synchronism without solving transcendental algebraic equations.

1. Theoretical Foundation: Circle Locus of Stator Current

Consider the approximate equivalent circuit of an induction motor referred to the stator, where the shunt magnetizing branch (R_0, X_0) is connected across the primary supply terminals. The stator input current phasor is:

\[ \vec{I}_1 = \vec{I}_0 + \vec{I}_2' \] \[ \vec{I}_2' = \frac{V_{1,ph}}{\left(R_1 + \frac{R_2'}{s}\right) + j(X_1 + X_2')} = \frac{V_{1,ph}}{R_{01} + \frac{R_2'}{s} + j X_{01}} \]

As the slip \(s\) varies from \(s = 0\) (synchronous speed, open rotor) to \(s = 1\) (standstill, short-circuit rotor) and beyond into braking (\(s > 1\)), the variable resistance \(R_{eff} = R_1 + R_2'/s\) varies while the total leakage reactance \(X_{01} = X_1 + X_2'\) remains constant. In circuit theory, the current locus of a series circuit with constant reactance and variable resistance fed from a constant voltage source is a circle whose diameter is:

\[ D = \frac{V_{1,ph}}{X_{01}} = \frac{V_{1,ph}}{X_1 + X_2'} \]

2. Essential Test Data and Coordinate Scaling

Construction requires two experimental tests conducted at rated frequency:

Test Measured Quantities Derived Parameters at Rated Voltage
No-Load Test Rated line voltage \(V_0\), no-load line current \(I_0\), no-load input power \(W_0\) Phase angle \(\phi_0 = \arccos\left(\frac{W_0}{\sqrt{3} V_0 I_0}\right)\), constant iron and friction losses \(P_{core+fw} = W_0\)
Blocked-Rotor Test Reduced line voltage \(V_{sc}\), short-circuit line current \(I_{sc,test}\), input power \(W_{sc,test}\) Scaled current \(I_{sc} = I_{sc,test} \frac{V_1}{V_{sc}}\), scaled power \(W_{sc} = W_{sc,test} \left(\frac{V_1}{V_{sc}}\right)^2\), \(\phi_{sc} = \arccos\left(\frac{W_{sc}}{\sqrt{3} V_1 I_{sc}}\right)\)

3. Step-by-Step Graphical Construction

  1. Reference Axes: Draw the applied phase voltage \(V_{1,ph}\) along the vertical axis (+Y). The horizontal axis (+X) represents active in-phase current.
  2. No-Load Vector: From the origin \(O\), draw no-load current vector \(OA = I_0\) at angle \(\phi_0\) lagging \(V_1\). Point \(A\) is the zero-output operating point.
  3. Short-Circuit Vector: From origin \(O\), draw blocked-rotor current vector \(OF' = I_{sc}\) at angle \(\phi_{sc}\) lagging \(V_1\). Join points \(A\) and \(F'\). The line \(AF'\) is the Output Line.
  4. Horizontal Reference Line and Circle Center: Through \(A\), draw a horizontal line parallel to the X-axis. The center of the circle \(C_0\) lies on this line. Construct the perpendicular bisector of chord \(AF'\); its intersection with the horizontal line fixes center \(C_0\). With radius \(C_0 A\), describe the circular arc through \(A\) and \(F'\).
  5. Loss Division and Torque Line: Drop a vertical line from \(F'\) perpendicular to the horizontal axis through \(A\), meeting it at point \(D\). The vertical height \(F'D\) represents total standstill copper losses \(W_{sc} - W_0\). Divide segment \(F'D\) at point \(E\) such that: \[ \frac{F'E}{ED} = \frac{\text{Rotor } I^2 R \text{ loss at standstill}}{\text{Stator } I^2 R \text{ loss at standstill}} = \frac{R_2'}{R_1} \] Join \(A\) to \(E\). The line \(AE\) is the Torque Line.
Figure 1: Complete circle diagram of a three-phase induction motor showing no-load vector OA, blocked-rotor point F', output line AF', torque line AE, operating point P, and maximum power/torque tangents.

4. Operating Point Performance Evaluation

For any specified stator load current \(I_1\), describe an arc of radius \(I_1\) from origin \(O\) intersecting the circle locus at operating point \(P\). Drop a vertical line from \(P\) intersecting the output line at \(Q\), the torque line at \(R\), the horizontal line through \(A\) at \(M\), and the horizontal X-axis at \(S\):

  • Input Power: \(P_{in} = \sqrt{3} V_L \times PS \times \text{Power scale}\)
  • Net Mechanical Power Output: \(P_{out} = \sqrt{3} V_L \times PQ \times \text{Power scale}\)
  • Rotor Copper Loss: \(P_{cu,rotor} = \sqrt{3} V_L \times QR \times \text{Power scale}\)
  • Stator Copper Loss: \(P_{cu,stator} = \sqrt{3} V_L \times RM \times \text{Power scale}\)
  • Core & Friction Losses: \(P_{fixed} = \sqrt{3} V_L \times MS \times \text{Power scale}\)
  • Electromagnetic Air-Gap Power (Torque): \(P_{ag} = \sqrt{3} V_L \times PR \times \text{Power scale}\), hence torque \(T = P_{ag} / \omega_s\)
  • Rotor Operational Slip: \(s = \frac{QR}{PR} = \frac{\text{Rotor Copper Loss}}{\text{Rotor Input Power}}\)
  • Efficiency: \(\eta = \frac{PQ}{PS} \times 100%\)
  • Power Factor: \(\cos\phi_1 = \frac{PS}{OP}\)

5. Maximum Power Output and Breakdown Torque

\[ P_{max} = 3 V_{1,ph} R_{circle} (1 - \sin\theta_{out}) \] \[ T_{max} = \frac{3 V_{1,ph} R_{circle} (1 - \sin\theta_{trq})}{\omega_s} \]

Maximum power output occurs at the tangent to the circle parallel to the Output Line \(AF'\). Maximum electromagnetic torque occurs at the tangent parallel to the Torque Line \(AE\). Because the torque line has a smaller slope than the output line (\(\theta_{trq} < \theta_{out}\)), maximum torque exceeds maximum power and occurs at a higher operating slip.

Common Mistake

Unscaled Blocked-Rotor Values: A frequent laboratory error is plotting the raw current and power measured at reduced voltage \(V_{sc}\) directly onto the circle diagram. Because the circle is referenced to rated voltage \(V_1\), the current must be scaled linearly by \((V_1 / V_{sc})\), and the power must be scaled quadratically by \((V_1 / V_{sc})^2\). Plotting unscaled values collapses the circle radius and yields completely invalid predictions.

Exam & Placement Trap

Rotor vs Stator Copper Loss Intercept Order: In competitive exams, questions frequently reverse the vertical loss segments from point \(P\). Remember the top-to-bottom hierarchy from the circle arc: First is Net Output (PQ) down to the output line; second is Rotor Copper Loss (QR) between the output line and torque line; third is Stator Copper Loss (RM) between the torque line and the horizontal reference line through A; and fourth is Fixed Iron/Mechanical Loss (MS) below point A down to the voltage axis origin. Confusing QR and RM inverts the slip calculation \(s = QR / PR\).

Scope boundary: This lesson covers standard circular locus construction from no-load and blocked-rotor test data for cylindrical-rotor induction machines. Exact equivalent circuit circular modifications (Heyland and Behrend circles) and deep-bar frequency-dependent parameter shifts are reserved for specialized machine design electives.

◆ Quick revision

  • Circle locus diameter equals \(V_{1,ph} / X_{01}\), derived from constant reactance and variable rotor resistance.
  • Point \(A\) represents no-load operation (\(s \approx 0\)); point \(F'\) represents standstill short-circuit operation (\(s = 1\)).
  • Line \(AF'\) is the Output Line; line \(AE\) is the Torque Line.
  • Vertical segment \(F'D\) is divided at \(E\) in the ratio of rotor resistance to stator resistance (\(R_2' / R_1\)).
  • Slip at any load point \(P\) is given by \(s = QR / PR\); efficiency is \(\eta = PQ / PS\).
  • Maximum power output occurs at the tangent parallel to \(AF'\); maximum torque occurs at the tangent parallel to \(AE\).

ac-ind-motor-cogging-crawling.title: Cogging and Crawling in Cage Motors: Space Harmonics, Parasitic Torques, and Mitigation
ac-ind-motor-cogging-crawling.body:
In practical three-phase squirrel-cage induction motors, the air-gap flux density waveform is not purely sinusoidal but contains spatial harmonics caused by discrete winding distribution and slotting. These space harmonics produce parasitic torques that give rise to two critical operational anomalies: crawling (stable rotation at sub-synchronous speed) and cogging (standstill magnetic locking).

1. Spatial MMF Harmonics in 3-Phase Stator Windings

A symmetrical three-phase winding carrying balanced sinusoidal currents produces a stepped, trapezoidal MMF distribution. By Fourier analysis, the total stator MMF contains fundamental and space harmonics of order:

\[ n = 6k \pm 1 \quad (k = 1, 2, 3, dots) implies n = 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, dots \]

Triplen harmonics (\(n = 3, 9, 15, dots\)) are absent because the phase displacement of \(120^\circ\) causes them to cancel in a balanced three-phase system. Each spatial harmonic has \(n \times P\) magnetic poles and rotates at a harmonic synchronous speed:

\[ N_{sn} = \frac{N_{s1}}{n} = \frac{120 f}{n P} \]
Harmonic Order \(n\) Order Formula Direction of Rotation Synchronous Speed (4-Pole, 50 Hz) Nature of Developed Torque
Fundamental (\(n=1\)) Fundamental Forward (\(+N_{s1}\)) 1500 rpm Main motoring torque accelerating rotor to rated speed
5th Harmonic (\(n=5\)) \(6(1) - 1\) Backward / Reverse (\(-N_{s1}/5\)) -300 rpm Braking / generating torque in forward motoring quadrant
7th Harmonic (\(n=7\)) \(6(1) + 1\) Forward (\(+N_{s1}/7\)) +214.3 rpm Motoring torque below \(N_{s1}/7\), generator braking above it
11th Harmonic (\(n=11\)) \(6(2) - 1\) Backward (\(-N_{s1}/11\)) -136.4 rpm High-frequency ripple and vibration

2. The Crawling Phenomenon

Crawling is the phenomenon where a squirrel-cage induction motor fails to accelerate up to its rated operating speed and instead runs stably at approximately one-seventh of synchronous speed (\(N \approx N_{s1}/7\)).

The mechanism is governed by the superposition of the fundamental and harmonic torque-speed curves:

  • The 7th harmonic field rotates forward at \(N_{s7} = N_{s1}/7\). It develops positive motoring torque for speeds \(N < N_{s7}\), reaches a peak positive torque just below \(N_{s7}\), and crosses zero to become negative (regenerative braking) for \(N > N_{s7}\).
  • When this 7th harmonic torque is superposed onto the fundamental torque-speed curve, it creates a pronounced saddle dip in the resultant torque curve just below \(N_{s1}/7\).
  • If the load torque curve \(T_{load}\) intersects this saddle region at a point where \(dT_{motor}/dN < dT_{load}/dN\), a stable operating point (Point C) is created. The motor settles at this low crawl speed and cannot accelerate further.
Figure 2: Torque-speed characteristics demonstrating the crawling phenomenon caused by the forward 7th space harmonic field, saddle dip creation, and design remedies.

3. The Cogging Phenomenon (Magnetic Locking)

Cogging, also known as tooth locking or magnetic locking, is the refusal of a squirrel-cage induction motor to start from rest when energized at rated voltage. The rotor remains locked at standstill, drawing heavy starting current and humming loudly.

Physical Mechanism: When the number of stator slots \(S_s\) is equal to or an integral multiple of the number of rotor slots \(S_r\) (\(S_s = m \cdot S_r\)), every stator tooth is simultaneously aligned directly opposite a rotor tooth at specific angular intervals. In this aligned position:

  • Air-gap permeance reaches a pronounced periodic maximum, creating a deep minimum in magnetic reluctance.
  • Strong reluctance alignment forces develop between opposing teeth that act like magnetic detents.
  • If this harmonic reluctance torque exceeds the fundamental starting torque developed by the windings, the rotor becomes mechanically locked at standstill.

4. Engineering Remedies and Design Rules

Mitigation Technique Operating Principle Primary Target
Rotor Bar Skewing Rotor slots are twisted axially by one stator slot pitch (\(\tau_{ss}\)). The slot harmonic EMF induced along the conductor integrates to zero over its axial length: \[ K_{skew} = \frac{\sin(\theta_{sk}/2)}{\theta_{sk}/2} \] Eliminates cogging, suppresses crawling dips, and reduces acoustic magnetic noise.
Fractional-Pitch Windings (Chording) Selecting a coil pitch \(W/\tau = 5/6\) introduces a pitch factor \(k_{pn} = \cos(n \alpha / 2)\) that virtually eliminates the 5th and 7th spatial harmonics from the stator MMF. Suppresses crawling saddle dips and harmonic losses.
Judicious Slot Number Selection Designers enforce strict slot combination inequalities: \[ S_s e S_r, \quad S_s - S_r e \pm 1, \pm 2, \pm P, \pm 2P \] Prevents cogging, sub-synchronous crawling, and unbalanced magnetic pull (UMP).
Slip-Ring (Wound Rotor) Motors Wound-rotor induction motors do not suffer from cogging because external rotor resistance boosts fundamental starting torque well above any reluctance detent. Inherently immune to cogging lock.

Common Mistake

Confusing Space Harmonics with Time Harmonics: Space harmonics are spatial distortions in air-gap flux density caused by winding layout and tooth slotting under pure sinusoidal AC voltage. Time harmonics, by contrast, are electrical voltage/current harmonics generated by non-linear power electronic converters (VFD inverters). Space harmonics rotate at fractions of synchronous speed (\(N_s/n\)), whereas time harmonics create fields that rotate at multiples of synchronous speed (\(n \times N_s\)).

Exam & Placement Trap

Harmonic Rotation Direction and Order: Competitive exams frequently ask why the 5th harmonic does not cause crawling. The reason is direction: the 5th harmonic rotates backward (order \(6k-1 = 5\) for \(k=1\)), producing a braking torque in the forward motoring direction. Only forward space harmonics (order \(6k+1 = 7, 13, dots\)) produce forward motoring torque capable of forming a stable crawling intersection.

Scope boundary: This lesson covers spatial MMF harmonic parasitic torques in cage motors. Dynamic torque ripple induced by inverter PWM switching harmonics and sub-synchronous resonance (SSR) in transmission systems are covered under Power Electronics and Power System Dynamics.

◆ Quick revision

  • Three-phase spatial MMF harmonics follow \(n = 6k \pm 1\); triplen harmonics cancel completely in balanced 3-phase windings.
  • The 5th harmonic rotates backward at \(N_s/5\) (braking); the 7th harmonic rotates forward at \(N_s/7\) (motoring crawl).
  • Crawling occurs when the 7th harmonic forward torque dip creates a stable operating intersection with the load torque at \(N \approx N_s/7\).
  • Cogging (magnetic locking at standstill) occurs when stator and rotor slot numbers are identical or integral multiples (\(S_s = m S_r\)).
  • Skewing rotor slots by one stator slot pitch makes the net harmonic EMF along the bar integrate to zero, eliminating cogging.
  • Chording the stator winding with pitch ratio \(5/6\) suppresses both 5th and 7th spatial harmonics.

ac-ind-motor-starters.title: Induction Motor Starters: DOL, Star-Delta, Autotransformer, and Rotor Resistance
ac-ind-motor-starters.body:
At standstill (\(s = 1\)), a three-phase induction motor behaves as a short-circuited transformer, drawing an inrush current 5 to 8 times its rated full-load value. Starters are protective power apparatus engineered to limit starting current to safe values, protect line voltage regulation, and manage developed starting torque to safely accelerate mechanical loads.

1. The Fundamental Starting Torque Equation

From the equivalent circuit of an induction motor, torque developed is proportional to rotor input power: \(T propto I_2^2 \frac{R_2'}{s}\). At any operating slip \(s\):

\[ \frac{T_{st}}{T_{fl}} = \left(\frac{I_{st}}{I_{fl}}\right)^2 \times s_{fl} \]

where \(I_{st}\) is the actual motor starting current per phase, \(I_{fl}\) is the full-load operating current per phase, and \(s_{fl}\) is the rated full-load slip (typically 2% to 5%). This quadratic current relationship dictates that reducing starting voltage to curtail current will quadratically reduce developed starting torque.

2. Detailed Examination of Starting Methods

A. Direct-On-Line (DOL) Starting

The motor is connected directly across rated supply mains via a contactor with thermal overload relays:

  • Motor Voltage: Full rated voltage \(V_1\).
  • Starting Current: Full short-circuit current \(I_{st} = I_{sc} \approx (5 - 8) I_{fl}\).
  • Starting Torque: \(\frac{T_{st}}{T_{fl}} = \left(\frac{I_{sc}}{I_{fl}}\right)^2 s_{fl}\). Typically 1.2 to 2.0 times rated torque.
  • Applications: Limited to small motors (typically \(le 5\text{ kW}\)) or large industrial installations with dedicated, stiff supply transformers.

B. Star-Delta (\(Y-\Delta\)) Starter

Applicable only to motors designed to run in Delta with all 6 stator winding terminals (\(U_1, U_2, V_1, V_2, W_1, W_2\)) brought out to the terminal box:

  • Starting Phase: Windings connected in Star. Phase voltage is reduced to \(V_{ph} = V_L / \sqrt{3}\).
  • Starting Current: Phase current is \(I_{ph,Y} = I_{ph,\Delta} / \sqrt{3}\). Because line current in star equals phase current, whereas line current in delta is \(\sqrt{3} I_{ph,\Delta}\):
    \[ I_{st,Y} = \frac{1}{3} I_{st,\Delta} \]
    Starting line current drawn from supply is reduced to exactly one-third (33.3%) of DOL line current.
  • Starting Torque: Torque is proportional to \(V_{ph}^2\):
    \[ T_{st,Y} = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 T_{st,\Delta} = \frac{1}{3} T_{st,\Delta} \]
  • Transition: Once speed reaches \(\approx 80%\) of rated speed, a timer switches the connection from Star to Delta.

C. Autotransformer Starter

A three-phase tapped autotransformer steps down the voltage applied to the stator terminals during starting to \(x \cdot V_1\) (where tapping \(x\) is typically 0.50, 0.65, or 0.80):

  • Motor Terminal Voltage: \(V_{motor} = x V_1\).
  • Motor Current: \(I_{st,motor} = x I_{sc}\).
  • Supply Mains Line Current: By transformer action, \(I_{line} = x \times I_{st,motor} = x^2 I_{sc}\).
  • Starting Torque:
    \[ \frac{T_{st}}{T_{fl}} = x^2 \left(\frac{I_{sc}}{I_{fl}}\right)^2 s_{fl} \]
  • Advantage: Produces the highest starting torque per ampere drawn from the supply line compared to any other cage motor starter.

D. Rotor Resistance Starter (Slip-Ring Motors Only)

Applicable exclusively to wound-rotor (slip-ring) induction motors. External variable resistor banks are inserted into the three rotor phases via slip rings and carbon brushes:

  • Current Suppression: Adding external resistance \(R_{ext}\) increases total rotor impedance \(Z_2 = \sqrt{(R_2 + R_{ext})^2 + X_2^2}\), dramatically reducing starting current.
  • Torque Enhancement: Maximum torque occurs at slip \(s_{mT} = \frac{R_2 + R_{ext}}{X_2}\). By selecting \(R_{ext}\) such that \(R_2 + R_{ext} = X_2\), maximum breakdown torque is achieved right at standstill (\(s = 1\)):
    \[ T_{st} = T_{max} = \frac{3 V_{1,ph}^2}{2 \omega_s X_{01}} \]
  • Unique Feature: It is the only starter that simultaneously decreases starting current while increasing starting torque (up to 250% rated torque with only 1.5 to 2.5 times rated current).
Figure 3: Comprehensive comparative analysis of induction motor starters showing voltage, current, torque, and machine compatibility.

3. Comparison Matrix of Starting Methods

Parameter Direct-On-Line (DOL) Star-Delta (\(Y-\Delta\)) Autotransformer (\(x\)) Rotor Resistance
Motor Voltage at Start \(V_L\) (100%) \(V_L / \sqrt{3}\) (57.7%) \(x V_L\) (e.g. 65%) \(V_L\) (100%)
Supply Line Current \(I_{sc}\) (100%) \(\frac{1}{3} I_{sc}\) (33.3%) \(x^2 I_{sc}\) (e.g. 42.3%) Reduced (1.5 - 2.5 \(I_{fl}\))
Starting Torque \(T_{st,DOL}\) (100%) \(\frac{1}{3} T_{st,DOL}\) (33.3%) \(x^2 T_{st,DOL}\) (e.g. 42.3%) Maximum (up to \(T_{max}\))
Applicable Machine Squirrel cage / Slip-ring Squirrel cage (\(\Delta\) run) Squirrel cage Slip-ring only
Equipment Cost Lowest Low Medium - High High (Slip-ring + resistors)

Common Mistake

Autotransformer Current Confusion: Students frequently mix up the current drawn by the motor with the current drawn from the supply mains during autotransformer starting. The motor draws current \(I_{st,motor} = x I_{sc}\) (linear with tapping), but the primary of the autotransformer draws \(I_{line} = x^2 I_{sc}\) from the supply bus (quadratic with tapping). Always specify whether supply line current or motor terminal current is required.

Exam & Placement Trap

Star-Delta Line Current Reduction Factor: A classic interview trap asks: "If star voltage is \(1/\sqrt{3}\) of line voltage, why does line current reduce by \(1/3\) instead of \(1/\sqrt{3}\)?" The answer involves two steps: in star, phase voltage drops by \(1/\sqrt{3}\), which reduces phase current to \(I_{ph} / \sqrt{3}\). In delta, line current is \(\sqrt{3} I_{ph}\), but in star, line current equals phase current \(I_{ph}\). Thus, \(I_{line,Y} / I_{line,\Delta} = (I_{ph,\Delta} / \sqrt{3}) / (\sqrt{3} I_{ph,\Delta}) = 1/3\). Both the current and torque drop by 1/3, not \(1/\sqrt{3}\)!

Scope boundary: This lesson covers electromechanical and electromagnetic starters for constant-frequency AC induction motors. Solid-state soft starters (thyristor phase control) and Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) are covered in dedicated Power Electronics coursework.

◆ Quick revision

  • General torque equation: \(T_{st} / T_{fl} = (I_{st} / I_{fl})^2 \times s_{fl}\).
  • DOL starting draws \(5 - 8 \times I_{fl}\) and delivers 100% full-voltage torque; restricted to small motors (\(le 5\text{ kW}\)).
  • Star-Delta reduces starting line voltage by \(1/\sqrt{3}\), starting line current by \(1/3\), and starting torque by \(1/3\).
  • Autotransformer with tapping \(x\) reduces motor current to \(x I_{sc}\), mains line current to \(x^2 I_{sc}\), and torque to \(x^2 T_{st,DOL}\).
  • Rotor resistance starting (wound rotor only) reduces starting current while increasing starting torque up to \(T_{max}\) at \(s = 1\).

ac-ind-motor-braking.title: Braking of Induction Motors: Plugging, DC Dynamic Braking, and Regenerative Braking
ac-ind-motor-braking.body:
Electrical braking of induction motors involves operating the machine so that it develops electromagnetic torque opposing the direction of shaft rotation. Compared to mechanical friction brakes, electrical braking provides rapid deceleration, precise stopping control, reduced mechanical wear, and the ability to regenerate kinetic energy back to the supply mains.

1. Three Operational Quadrants of the Induction Machine

The operational state of an induction machine is uniquely defined by its rotor slip \(s\):

\[ s = \frac{N_s - N}{N_s} \]
Operating Mode Rotor Speed \(N\) Slip Range \(s\) Torque Direction Energy Flow
Motoring \(0 < N < N_s\) \(0 < s < 1\) Positive (with rotation) Electrical input from grid converted to mechanical output
Regenerative Braking \(N > N_s\) \(s < 0\) (Negative) Negative (opposes rotation) Mechanical shaft power converted to electrical power returned to grid
Plugging (Reverse Current) \(-N_s < N < 0\) (relative) \(1 < s le 2\) Negative (opposes rotation) Both electrical input and mechanical energy dissipated as heat
Figure 4: Operating torque-speed characteristics of three-phase induction machine across motoring, regenerative braking, plugging, and DC injection dynamic braking modes.

2. Detailed Analysis of Braking Methods

A. Plugging (Reverse Current Braking)

Plugging is initiated by interchanging any two stator supply leads while the motor is running at rated forward speed. This reverses the phase sequence of stator currents, causing the stator rotating magnetic field to reverse direction from \(+N_s\) to \(-N_s\).

  • Operating Slip at Instant of Plugging:
    \[ s_{plug} = \frac{-N_s - N}{-N_s} = \frac{N_s + N}{N_s} = 1 + \frac{N}{N_s} = 2 - s_{fl} \]
    If full-load slip \(s_{fl} = 0.04\), the initial plugging slip is \(s_{plug} = 2 - 0.04 = 1.96\).
  • Torque and Severe Heat Dissipation: The machine develops strong opposing torque that rapidly decelerates the rotor. However, total power dissipated in the rotor circuit is: \[ P_{rotor} = 3 I_2^2 \frac{R_2'}{s_{plug}} + \text{Kinetic energy loss} \] The motor absorbs both mechanical kinetic energy from the load AND electrical energy from the AC supply mains, dissipating both entirely as heat within stator and rotor windings.
  • Zero-Speed Switch (Anti-Plugging Relay): If the reversed supply remains connected when the rotor passes through zero speed, the motor will immediately accelerate in the reverse direction. A centrifugal zero-speed switch mounted on the shaft automatically de-energizes the reversing contactor the moment speed drops to zero.

B. DC Dynamic Braking (DC Injection)

The stator is disconnected from the 3-phase AC supply and immediately connected across a DC voltage source across two or three stator terminals:

  • Stationary Magnetic Field: The DC stator current produces a stationary spatial magnetic field with alternating magnetic poles along the stator circumference.
  • Generator Action: As the rotor spins through this stationary magnetic field, voltages and currents are induced in the rotor bars at frequency \(f_r = (N / N_s) f\). By Lenz's law, the interaction between induced rotor currents and the stationary field produces a braking torque opposing rotation.
  • Kinetic Energy Dissipation: All mechanical kinetic energy of the rotating mass is converted into electrical energy and dissipated as \(I_2^2 R_2\) heat in the rotor circuit. No electrical energy is drawn from the mains to be wasted.
  • Standstill Limitation: Because induced rotor EMF is proportional to speed (\(E_2 propto N \Phi\)), the braking torque diminishes as rotor speed decreases and drops to zero at standstill. DC injection cannot hold an overhauling load stationary without a mechanical holding brake.

C. Regenerative Braking

Regenerative braking occurs naturally whenever the rotor speed exceeds the synchronous speed of the stator rotating field (\(N > N_s\), \(s < 0\)):

  • Operating Condition: Common in electric trains descending mountain grades, cranes and hoists lowering heavy overhauling loads, or when a VFD decelerates a motor by ramping down the stator supply frequency faster than the rotor can coast down.
  • Power Flow: With negative slip, the rotor induced EMF and current reverse phase relative to the air-gap flux. Active power reverses direction and flows from the rotor across the air gap back into the AC supply mains.
  • Reactive Power Requirement: The induction machine cannot generate its own magnetizing reactive power. It must remain connected to an energized AC grid that supplies lagging reactive volt-amperes (VARs), or be connected to a switched capacitor bank for self-excitation.
  • Limitation: Regenerative braking is impossible below synchronous speed on a fixed-frequency grid.

3. Comprehensive Comparison of Induction Motor Braking

Feature Plugging DC Dynamic Braking Regenerative Braking
Initial Slip Range \(1 < s le 2\) (starts \(\approx 1.95\)) Stationary field (\(0 < \nu le 1\)) \(s < 0\) (super-synchronous)
Energy Efficiency Extremely wasteful (consumes grid power to brake) Efficient (dissipates only kinetic energy) Highest (recovers energy back to grid)
Deceleration Rate Fastest / violent Smooth and controllable Effective only for \(N > N_s\)
Torque at Standstill High (reverses if not disconnected) Zero (cannot hold load) Zero (stops braking at \(N = N_s\))
Mandatory Auxiliary Component Centrifugal zero-speed anti-plugging switch DC power supply and switching contactor Energized AC grid or reactive capacitor bank

Common Mistake

Assuming DC Dynamic Braking Can Hold a Suspended Load: Engineers sometimes assume DC injection braking can serve as an elevator holding brake. In DC injection, induced rotor current depends strictly on the speed at which rotor conductors cut the stationary stator magnetic flux (\(E_2 propto N\)). At zero speed, induced EMF and torque are identically zero. An overhauling hoist load will slip and accelerate downward unless an electro-mechanical friction brake engages at zero speed.

Exam & Placement Trap

Energy Dissipation During Plugging vs Coasting: A favorite university exam derivation asks for the total energy dissipated in the rotor during plugging from rated speed to rest. While bringing a motor to rest by pure mechanical friction dissipates its kinetic energy \(W_k = \frac{1}{2} J \omega^2\), plugging dissipates three times the stored kinetic energy (\(3 W_k\)) in the rotor circuit! This is because the grid continuously feeds electrical power into the machine during the entire deceleration period.

Scope boundary: This lesson covers electrical braking methods for fixed-frequency and line-connected three-phase induction motors. Four-quadrant active front-end (AFE) regenerative converters and dynamic braking chopper resistor networks are treated in Advanced Power Electronics and Electric Drives.

◆ Quick revision

  • Plugging reverses two stator phases, causing stator field to rotate at \(-N_s\); slip starts at \(s_{plug} = 2 - s_{fl} \approx 1.95 - 1.98\).
  • Plugging dissipates three times the machine kinetic energy as heat; a zero-speed switch is mandatory to prevent reverse acceleration.
  • DC dynamic braking injects DC into stator to create a stationary field; kinetic energy is dissipated in the rotor resistance.
  • DC braking torque falls to zero at standstill and cannot hold an overhauling load.
  • Regenerative braking occurs when \(N > N_s\) (\(s < 0\)); active power is returned to the grid, but external lagging VARs are required for excitation.

ac-spim-double-revolving.title: Single-Phase Induction Motors: Principle of Operation and Double-Field Revolving Theory
ac-spim-double-revolving.body:
◆ Why this matters

Three-phase induction motors dominate industrial factories because a balanced three-phase stator current naturally establishes a rotating magnetic field of constant magnitude that exerts starting torque on the rotor. However, domestic homes, retail stores, commercial offices, and light workshops are almost universally supplied with single-phase alternating current. A single stator winding supplied with single-phase current produces a pulsating, stationary magnetic field—one that alternates back and forth along a single physical axis without rotating. Consequently, a single-phase induction motor has zero starting torque and cannot start on its own. Yet, if given a manual or auxiliary spin in either clockwise or counter-clockwise direction, it immediately picks up speed and accelerates to its normal running condition. Ferraris' Double-Field Revolving Theory provides the classical physical and mathematical explanation for why single-phase motors cannot self-start and how they sustain rotation once set into motion.

Prerequisites: Three-Phase Induction Motors: Constructional Features and Principle of Operation (rotating magnetic fields, induction of rotor EMF, and torque production) and Power and Torque Equations, Torque-Slip Characteristics.

◆ The Pulsating Stator Field and its Mathematical Decomposition

Consider a single-phase stator winding distributed in slots around the stator bore. When connected to a single-phase sinusoidal supply of angular frequency ω = 2πf, the stator current is i(t) = I_m cos(ωt). At any spatial angle θ along the airgap periphery measured from the magnetic axis of the stator winding, the spatial magnetomotive force (MMF) is distributed sinusoidally:

F(θ, t) = F_m cos(θ) cos(ωt)

Using the fundamental trigonometric identity 2 cos A cos B = cos(A − B) + cos(A + B), this pulsating stationary field splits cleanly into two equal parts:

F(θ, t) = ½ F_m cos(θ − ωt) + ½ F_m cos(θ + ωt) = F_f(θ, t) + F_b(θ, t)
Field ComponentMathematical ExpressionAmplitudeDirection of RotationSynchronous Speed
Forward Rotating Field (F_f)½ F_m cos(θ − ωt)Half peak (F_m / 2)Forward (+θ direction)+N_s = +120f / P
Backward Rotating Field (F_b)½ F_m cos(θ + ωt)Half peak (F_m / 2)Backward (−θ direction)−N_s = −120f / P

Thus, a single alternating pulsating magnetic field is physically and mathematically equivalent to two identical revolving fields, each having half the peak amplitude, spinning in opposite directions at synchronous speed N_s.

◆ Forward and Backward Slip Relations

Let the rotor turn at rotational speed N rpm in the forward direction. The slips of the rotor with respect to each of the two revolving fields are fundamentally different:

  • Forward slip (s_f): The relative speed between the forward field (+N_s) and the rotor (+N) is (N_s − N). Thus:
    s_f = (N_s − N) / N_s = s
  • Backward slip (s_b): The backward field rotates at −N_s. The relative speed between the backward field and the forward-spinning rotor (+N) is (−N_s − N). Taking the forward reference:
    s_b = (−N_s − N) / (−N_s) = (N_s + N) / N_s = (2N_s − (N_s − N)) / N_s = 2 − s

The relationship s_b = 2 − s is universal. The frequencies of the currents induced in the rotor by the two fields are:

f_f = s_f · f = s · f      f_b = s_b · f = (2 − s) · f

Under normal running conditions (for example, s = 0.05 on a 50 Hz supply):

  • Forward rotor current frequency: f_f = 0.05 × 50 = 2.5 Hz (very low, near DC).
  • Backward rotor current frequency: f_b = (2 − 0.05) × 50 = 1.95 × 50 = 97.5 Hz (almost double line frequency).

Figure 1: Torque-slip curves of a single-phase induction motor based on Double-Field Revolving Theory. At standstill (s = 1), forward torque T_f exactly balances backward torque T_b, making net starting torque zero.

◆ Why the Motor Sustains Rotation Once Started

At standstill (N = 0, s = 1), forward slip s_f = 1 and backward slip s_b = 2 − 1 = 1. Both fields induce identical currents in the rotor cage and generate equal, opposing torques. Net torque is zero. The motor merely hums and draws heavy locked-rotor current without turning.

Now suppose the rotor is spun forward by an external impulse (so N > 0 and s < 1):

  1. Forward field interaction: The forward slip s becomes small (e.g. 0.04). The effective rotor resistance to the forward field is R_2'/s, which is large (e.g. 25 × R_2'). The forward rotor current is in near-phase with the forward induced EMF, producing a high forward driving torque T_f.
  2. Backward field interaction: The backward slip s_b = 2 − s becomes large (e.g. 1.96). The effective rotor resistance to the backward field is R_2'/(2−s) ≈ R_2'/2, which is very small. The rotor presents a predominantly inductive impedance to the high-frequency backward field. High inductive currents flow in the rotor bars, setting up a strong counter-MMF that almost completely expels and damps out the backward flux in the airgap. Consequently, the backward braking torque T_b becomes very small.
  3. Net acceleration: Because T_f >> T_b, the net torque T_net = T_f − T_b is positive and large. The motor accelerates rapidly in the forward direction until electromagnetic driving torque balances mechanical load torque and rotational losses.

If the rotor had initially been spun in the reverse direction, the same phenomenon would occur in reverse, accelerating the motor in the backward direction. Single-phase induction motors have no preferred direction of rotation until started.

Common mistake: Assuming that the backward revolving field disappears once the motor reaches full speed. The backward field does not vanish; it remains present throughout operation. Because the rotor runs past the backward field at slip s_b ≈ 2, it induces double-frequency currents (96–98 Hz) that cause continuous backward rotor copper loss and create a persistent 100 Hz pulsating torque vibration (humming) characteristic of all single-phase motors.
Placement trap: "If a single-phase induction motor is running normally at full load and its auxiliary winding switch is opened, will the motor stop?" No, it continues running! The auxiliary winding is required ONLY to establish an initial phase-displaced field for starting torque. Once running, the single main winding produces the pulsating flux, and the rotor's own rotation sustains the dominant forward revolving field.

◆ Quick revision

  • A single-phase stator winding produces a pulsating stationary magnetic field of form F_m cos(θ) cos(ωt).
  • By Double-Field Revolving Theory, this field decomposes into two counter-rotating fields of amplitude F_m / 2 at speeds +N_s and −N_s.
  • Forward slip is s_f = s; backward slip is s_b = 2 − s.
  • At standstill (s = 1), s_f = s_b = 1; forward torque equals backward torque (T_f = T_b), so net starting torque is zero.
  • When rotated forward (s < 1), forward torque dominates (T_f >> T_b) because the backward field is heavily damped by high-frequency inductive rotor currents.
  • Single-phase motors require an auxiliary starting mechanism (split-phase, capacitor, or shading ring) to initiate rotation.

ac-spim-equiv-circuit.title: Single-Phase Induction Motor Equivalent Circuit and Parameter Determination
ac-spim-equiv-circuit.body:
◆ Why this matters

To predict the running performance, stator line current, power factor, electromagnetic torque, copper losses, and efficiency of a single-phase induction motor, electrical engineers translate the double-field revolving theory into a lumped-parameter equivalent electrical circuit. In a three-phase motor, a single per-phase equivalent circuit suffices because the airgap flux rotates uniformly. In a single-phase motor, the stator carries only one winding current I_1, which must simultaneously establish both the forward and backward rotating magnetic flux waves. As a result, the stator equivalent impedance connects in series with two separate rotor equivalent networks—one corresponding to the forward field (operating at slip s) and the other corresponding to the backward field (operating at slip 2 − s). Determining these parameters from experimental no-load and blocked-rotor tests is an essential industry and laboratory competency.

Prerequisites: Single-Phase Induction Motors: Principle of Operation and Double-Field Revolving Theory (forward and backward slips s and 2 − s) and Three-Phase Induction Motor: Phasor Diagram and Equivalent Circuit.

◆ Development of the Equivalent Circuit

Let the single-phase stator winding have resistance R_1 and leakage reactance X_1. The stator input current I_1 flows through the stator impedance Z_1 = R_1 + jX_1.

Because the pulsating magnetising flux decomposes into two equal rotating fields of half magnitude, the total magnetising reactance X_m is divided into two equal series reactances: 0.5 X_m for the forward branch and 0.5 X_m for the backward branch.

Similarly, the rotor parameters referred to the stator winding (resistance R_2' and standstill leakage reactance X_2') are divided between the two rotating systems:

  • Forward rotor impedance (Z_f): In the forward branch, the rotor operates at forward slip s. The rotor branch consists of 0.5 jX_m in parallel with (0.5 R_2'/s + 0.5 jX_2'):
    Z_f = R_f + jX_f = ½ · [ jX_m · (R_2'/s + jX_2') ] / [ R_2'/s + j(X_m + X_2') ]
  • Backward rotor impedance (Z_b): In the backward branch, the rotor operates at backward slip (2 − s). The rotor branch consists of 0.5 jX_m in parallel with (0.5 R_2'/(2−s) + 0.5 jX_2'):
    Z_b = R_b + jX_b = ½ · [ jX_m · (R_2'/(2−s) + jX_2') ] / [ R_2'/(2−s) + j(X_m + X_2') ]

The total input impedance seen by the single-phase supply voltage V is the direct series sum of the stator impedance, the forward rotor impedance, and the backward rotor impedance:

Z_in = Z_1 + Z_f + Z_b = (R_1 + R_f + R_b) + j(X_1 + X_f + X_b)

The stator current drawn from the supply is:

I_1 = V / Z_in      cos φ = (R_1 + R_f + R_b) / |Z_in|

Figure 2: Complete equivalent circuit of a single-phase induction motor based on double-field revolving theory. Forward branch Z_f and backward branch Z_b are in series with stator impedance Z_1.

◆ Power Flow and Torque Equations

The total airgap power transferred across the airgap divides between forward and backward systems:

  • Forward airgap power: P_gf = I_1^2 · R_f (W)
  • Backward airgap power: P_gb = I_1^2 · R_b (W)
  • Net airgap power: P_g = P_gf − P_gb = I_1^2 · (R_f − R_b) (W)

Rotor copper losses are proportional to the respective slips:

P_cur,f = s_f · P_gf = s · I_1^2 · R_f      P_cur,b = s_b · P_gb = (2 − s) · I_1^2 · R_b
P_cur,total = s · P_gf + (2 − s) · P_gb

The total mechanical power developed by the rotor is:

P_m = P_gf(1 − s) − P_gb[1 − (2 − s)] = (1 − s)(P_gf − P_gb)

The net electromagnetic torque developed at synchronous angular speed ω_s = 2πN_s / 60 rad/s is:

T_net = P_g / ω_s = [ I_1^2 (R_f − R_b) ] / ω_s  (N·m)

◆ Experimental Determination of Circuit Parameters

Two tests are performed in the laboratory:

TestOperating ConditionApproximation UsedParameters Extracted
Blocked-Rotor TestRotor locked stationary (s = 1), reduced voltage applied to circulate rated currents_f = s_b = 1; magnetising branch drawing negligible current: Z_f = Z_b = ½ (R_2' + jX_2')R_sc = R_1 + R_2' ⇒ R_2' = R_sc − R_1
X_sc = X_1 + X_2' ⇒ X_1 = X_2' = ½ X_sc
No-Load TestMotor uncoupled, running light at rated voltage and frequency (s ≈ 0)s ≈ 0 ⇒ R_2'/s → ∞, so Z_f ≈ ½ jX_m
s_b ≈ 2 ⇒ Z_b ≈ ½ (R_2'/2 + jX_2')		X_nl ≈ X_1 + ½ X_m + ½ X_2'
⇒ X_m = 2(X_nl − X_1 − ½ X_2')
Rotational loss P_rot = P_nl − I_nl^2(R_1 + R_f,nl + R_b,nl)
Common mistake: Neglecting the backward branch resistance R_b when computing net developed torque. In a three-phase motor, T = I_2'^2 (R_2'/s) / ω_s. In a single-phase motor, you must always subtract R_b: T = I_1^2(R_f − R_b) / ω_s. Omitting R_b overestimates net torque and developed power.
Placement trap: "Why does the backward rotor copper loss remain significant even when the backward airgap power P_gb is small?" Because rotor copper loss is P_cur,b = s_b · P_gb = (2 − s) · P_gb. At normal running slip s = 0.05, the slip multiplier is (2 − 0.05) = 1.95! Even if P_gb is only 10% of forward power, multiplying it by 1.95 makes the backward rotor heating substantial.

◆ Quick revision

  • Single-phase equivalent circuit connects stator impedance Z_1 in series with forward impedance Z_f and backward impedance Z_b.
  • Forward branch components are scaled by slip s; backward branch components are scaled by slip 2 − s.
  • Net developed airgap power is P_g = I_1^2 (R_f − R_b); net torque is T = P_g / ω_s.
  • Total rotor copper loss is P_cur = s · P_gf + (2 − s) · P_gb.
  • Blocked-rotor test (s = 1) yields R_2' and total leakage reactance X_1 + X_2'.
  • No-load test (s ≈ 0) isolates the magnetising reactance X_m and rotational losses.

ac-spim-types-split-cap.title: Types of Single-Phase Induction Motors: Split-Phase and Capacitor-Start Motors
ac-spim-types-split-cap.body:
◆ Why this matters

Because a pure single-phase stator winding produces zero starting torque, every practical single-phase induction motor must be equipped with an auxiliary starting mechanism that creates a temporary two-phase system during startup. By placing an auxiliary (starting) winding in space-quadrature (90° electrical) with the main (running) winding on the stator core and introducing a phase displacement angle α between their currents, a revolving magnetic field is synthesized. The magnitude of the resulting starting torque is governed by the relation T_st ∝ I_m · I_a · sin α. The two most common workhorses utilizing this principle in residential appliances and light industrial machinery are the resistance split-phase motor and the capacitor-start induction motor.

Prerequisites: Single-Phase Induction Motors: Principle of Operation and Double-Field Revolving Theory (zero standstill torque and double-field analysis).

◆ The General Principle of Phase Splitting

To produce a rotating magnetic field at standstill, the stator is provided with two independent windings:

  • Main Winding (M): Occupies roughly two-thirds of the stator slots. Designed to carry rated continuous running current.
  • Auxiliary Winding (A): Placed in the remaining one-third of the slots, physically centered 90° electrical away from the main winding axis.

When connected in parallel across the single-phase supply voltage V, the main current I_m lags V by angle φ_m, and the auxiliary current I_a lags V by angle φ_a. The phase angle displacement between the two currents is α = φ_m − φ_a. The starting torque developed at standstill is:

T_st = k · I_m · I_a · sin α    (where k is a design constant and α is the phase split angle)

To maximize starting torque per ampere of starting current, the phase angle α should ideally approach 90° (time-quadrature), where sin α = 1.0.

◆ Split-Phase (Resistance-Start) Induction Motors

In a resistance split-phase motor, no external components are added; the phase difference is achieved purely through winding geometry and wire sizing:

  • Main Winding: Wound with heavy, thick copper magnet wire and placed deep in the stator slots. This gives it low resistance and high inductive reactance (high L/R ratio). The current I_m lags the terminal voltage by φ_m ≈ 70° to 80°.
  • Auxiliary Winding: Wound with much thinner wire with fewer turns and placed near the slot openings. This gives it high resistance and low inductive reactance (low L/R ratio). The current I_a lags the terminal voltage by only φ_a ≈ 30° to 40°.
  • Phase Split: The resulting phase displacement is α = φ_m − φ_a ≈ 30° to 40°. Because sin(35°) ≈ 0.57, a moderate revolving field is established.
  • Centrifugal Switch: Connected in series with the auxiliary winding. As the rotor accelerates and reaches roughly 75% to 80% of synchronous speed, centrifugal weights overcome spring tension and open the switch contacts, isolating the auxiliary winding. The motor then continues running on the main winding alone.
CharacteristicResistance Split-Phase MotorCapacitor-Start Motor
Starting Torque150% to 200% of Full-Load Torque (FLT)300% to 450% of FLT
Starting CurrentHigh (6 to 8 times Full-Load Current)Moderate (4 to 5 times Full-Load Current)
Phase Angle Split (α)30° to 40° (sin α ≈ 0.55)75° to 90° (sin α ≈ 0.98–1.0)
Auxiliary Circuit ComponentThin copper wire (high internal resistance)Intermittent-duty AC electrolytic capacitor
Centrifugal SwitchRequired (opens at 75%–80% speed)Required (opens at 75%–80% speed)
Typical ApplicationsWashing machines, small centrifugal pumps, oil burners, blowers, bench grindersDomestic refrigerators, air compressors, reciprocating water pumps, heavy conveyor feeds

Figure 3: Phasor comparison of starting currents. In the capacitor-start motor, the series capacitor causes auxiliary current I_a to lead voltage V, establishing perfect 90° time quadrature (sin α = 1.0) and maximum starting torque.

◆ Capacitor-Start Induction Motors

A capacitor-start motor introduces an alternating-current electrolytic capacitor in series with the auxiliary winding and centrifugal switch. The capacitive reactance X_c is chosen larger than the inductive reactance X_a of the auxiliary winding:

X_net = X_c − X_a  (capacitive)   ⇒   tan φ_a = (X_c − X_a) / R_a  (leading)

As illustrated in the phasor diagram, I_a leads the supply voltage V by φ_a ≈ 15° to 20°, while I_m lags V by φ_m ≈ 70° to 75°. The total angle between them is:

α = φ_m + φ_a ≈ 70° + 20° = 90°

Because sin 90° = 1.0, the starting torque reaches 300% to 450% of full-load torque. Once the motor reaches 75% to 80% speed, the centrifugal switch disconnects both the capacitor and the auxiliary winding.

◆ Condition for Maximum Starting Torque per Ampere

To find the optimum capacitor value that maximizes starting torque per ampere of total starting current, the quadrature condition α = 90° is enforced. Since φ_a = 90° − φ_m:

tan φ_a = (X_c − X_a) / R_a = cot φ_m = R_m / X_m
X_c = X_a + R_a · (R_m / X_m)   ⇒   C = 1 / (2π f X_c)
Common mistake: Choosing the starting capacitor to achieve series resonance with the auxiliary winding reactance (X_c = X_a). Resonance makes the auxiliary branch purely resistive (φ_a = 0°), so I_a is in phase with V. The phase split would then be only α = φ_m ≈ 70°, which does NOT yield 90° quadrature and fails to deliver maximum starting torque.
Placement trap: "Can you reverse the direction of rotation of a split-phase or capacitor-start motor by reversing the two supply power leads?" No! Reversing the AC supply line leads reverses the polarity of BOTH the main and auxiliary windings simultaneously, leaving the spatial rotation of the resulting magnetic field completely unchanged. To reverse rotation, you must interchange the terminal connections of EITHER the main winding OR the auxiliary winding, but not both.

◆ Quick revision

  • Starting torque is governed by T_st = k · I_m · I_a · sin α. Maximum torque occurs at α = 90°.
  • Split-phase motors use thick wire on the main winding (high X) and thin wire on the auxiliary winding (high R) to get α ≈ 30°–40°.
  • Capacitor-start motors use an electrolytic capacitor in series with the auxiliary winding to make I_a lead V, achieving α ≈ 90° and 300%–450% FLT starting torque.
  • A centrifugal switch disconnects the auxiliary circuit at 75%–80% of synchronous speed in both motor types.
  • To reverse rotation, reverse connections to EITHER the main winding OR the auxiliary winding, never both.

ac-spim-types-permcap-shaded.title: Permanent-Split Capacitor, Two-Value Capacitor, and Shaded-Pole Induction Motors
ac-spim-types-permcap-shaded.body:
◆ Why this matters

While split-phase and capacitor-start motors provide effective starting torque, they rely on mechanical centrifugal switches that can stick, pit, arc, or fail over time. Moreover, once the switch opens, the motor runs as a pure single-phase machine with high backward field losses, low power factor (0.6 to 0.7), and noticeable acoustic hum. To achieve silent continuous operation, superior power factor, or maintenance-free simplicity, alternative single-phase motor configurations were developed: the Permanent-Split Capacitor (PSC) motor (which eliminates the centrifugal switch entirely), the Two-Value Capacitor (Capacitor-Start Capacitor-Run) motor (which optimizes both starting and running conditions), and the Shaded-Pole motor (the simplest and most rugged electric motor ever devised).

Prerequisites: Types of Single-Phase Induction Motors: Split-Phase and Capacitor-Start Motors (phase splitting and auxiliary winding design).

◆ 1. Permanent-Split Capacitor (PSC) Motor

The Permanent-Split Capacitor (PSC) motor—also known as the single-value capacitor-run motor—has both main and auxiliary windings permanently connected across the AC supply. A continuous-duty oil-filled or metallized polypropylene capacitor (typically 2 to 10 μF, rated 400–450 V AC) remains in series with the auxiliary winding at all times:

  • No Centrifugal Switch: Eliminates mechanical failure, contact oxidation, and switch clicking noises. Highly reliable.
  • Near-Circular Field at Full Load: The capacitor is sized to produce exact 90° time quadrature between main and auxiliary currents at rated running load. This eliminates the backward revolving field, dramatically reducing rotor copper losses and acoustic hum.
  • Starting Torque: Because the capacitor is sized small for running efficiency, the starting current in the auxiliary winding is modest. The starting torque is low to moderate (50% to 100% of full-load torque).
  • Running Performance: Excellent full-load efficiency (65% to 75%) and very high power factor (0.85 to 0.95).
  • Easy Reversibility: By designing both windings with identical wire size and turns, rotation can be reversed with a single-pole double-throw (SPDT) switch that connects the capacitor in series with either winding.
  • Applications: Ceiling fans, table fans, office ventilation blowers, oil burners, furnace draft inducers, and air conditioning fan coils.

◆ 2. Two-Value Capacitor (Capacitor-Start Capacitor-Run) Motor

The two-value capacitor motor combines the massive starting torque of a capacitor-start motor with the high efficiency and quiet running of a PSC motor by using two separate capacitors:

  1. Starting Capacitor (C_s): A high-capacitance AC electrolytic unit (150 to 300 μF) designed for short-time intermittent duty.
  2. Running Capacitor (C_r): A lower-capacitance oil-filled or polypropylene unit (10 to 30 μF) designed for continuous duty.

During starting, both capacitors are connected in parallel (C_total = C_s + C_r), drawing large leading auxiliary current that produces 90° quadrature and 300% to 400% full-load starting torque. At 75% to 80% speed, the centrifugal switch disconnects the starting capacitor C_s, while C_r remains permanently in circuit to maintain a circular field, high power factor, and high efficiency under load.

Applications: Heavy commercial refrigeration compressors, reciprocating air compressors, industrial conveyor belts, and deep-well water pumps.

Figure 4: Operating principle of a shaded-pole motor. Induced current in the short-circuited copper shading ring delays flux changes in the shaded portion, sweeping the magnetic axis continuously from unshaded to shaded region.

◆ 3. Shaded-Pole Induction Motor

The shaded-pole motor has salient (projecting) poles on its stator. A narrow slot cuts across roughly one-third of each pole face, and a heavy, short-circuited copper band called a shading coil or shading ring is fitted around the smaller portion:

  • Time Interval 1 (Flux Rising, dΦ/dt > 0): As alternating current in the main stator coil increases from zero toward its positive peak, the rising flux induces a circulating current in the copper shading ring. By Lenz's Law, this induced current creates a counter-MMF opposing the flux rise. Consequently, the magnetic flux is crowded into the unshaded portion of the pole.
  • Time Interval 2 (Flux Near Peak, dΦ/dt ≈ 0): When the stator current reaches its maximum, the rate of flux change is zero. No current is induced in the shading ring. Flux distributes uniformly across both the unshaded and shaded sections.
  • Time Interval 3 (Flux Falling, dΦ/dt < 0): As the stator current falls toward zero, the collapsing flux induces a circulating current in the shading ring that opposes the decrease. Thus, flux is sustained in the shaded portion even after it has largely collapsed in the unshaded section.
  • Resultant Motion: The center of magnetic flux sweeps progressively across the pole face from the unshaded section toward the shaded section. This produces a weak, elliptical rotating magnetic field capable of dragging the rotor into rotation.
FeaturePSC MotorTwo-Value Capacitor MotorShaded-Pole Motor
Starting Torque50% to 100% FLT300% to 400% FLTVery Low (30% to 50% FLT)
Efficiency65% to 75%65% to 75%Extremely Low (15% to 35%)
Power Factor0.85 to 0.95 (High)0.80 to 0.90 (High)0.50 to 0.60 (Poor)
Centrifugal SwitchNoneRequired (opens start cap)None
ReversibilityEasily reversible (SPDT switch)Reversible by terminal swapNon-reversible (mechanically fixed)
Cost & RuggednessModerate cost, high reliabilityHighest cost (2 caps + switch)Lowest cost, exceptionally rugged
Typical UsesCeiling fans, furnace blowersAir compressors, water pumpsSmall cooling fans, hair dryers, microwave turntables
Common mistake: Believing that reversing the stator supply leads can reverse a shaded-pole motor. Reversing the AC supply does not alter the physical sequence of flux delay established by the shading ring. The motor will ALWAYS rotate from unshaded to shaded portion. Reversing requires physically turning the rotor/stator assembly around or providing dual shading coils.
Placement trap: "Why is the efficiency of a shaded-pole motor so low (under 35%) compared to other induction motors?" Two major technical reasons: (1) The short-circuited copper shading ring carries continuous, heavy circulating currents throughout normal running, causing high, unavoidable I^2R loss. (2) The rotating magnetic field is highly elliptical, containing a strong backward-revolving flux component that produces continuous counter-torque and severe rotor harmonic heating.

◆ Quick revision

  • PSC motors keep a continuous-duty capacitor in series with the auxiliary winding at all times; no centrifugal switch.
  • PSC motors deliver smooth, silent running, high power factor (0.9), and moderate starting torque (50%–100% FLT).
  • Two-value capacitor motors use a large electrolytic capacitor for starting and a small oil-filled capacitor for running; highest starting torque (350% FLT).
  • Shaded-pole motors use a short-circuited copper ring around 1/3 of the pole face to delay flux, sweeping the field from unshaded to shaded section.
  • Shaded-pole motors have low starting torque (40% FLT), poor efficiency (15%–35%), fixed rotation direction, and lowest cost.

ac-ig-grid-connected.title: Grid-Connected Induction Generator: Operating Principle, Power Flow, and Applications
ac-ig-grid-connected.body:
◆ Why this matters

Synchronous alternators supply over 90% of bulk electrical utility power, but they require precise DC field excitation systems, automatic voltage regulators, and strict synchronisation procedures (voltage, frequency, phase angle, and phase sequence). In renewable energy generation—specifically wind turbine farms and micro-hydro stations—the prime mover speed fluctuates continuously with changing wind and water flow. If a synchronous alternator were coupled directly to a wind turbine, wind gusts would induce massive mechanical stress, torque oscillations, and frequent pole-slipping. A grid-connected squirrel-cage induction generator (SCIG) solves this elegantly: it synchronises automatically upon connection to the grid, handles variable mechanical inputs smoothly through speed slip, requires no DC excitation, and cannot suffer loss of synchronism.

Prerequisites: Power and Torque Equations, Torque-Slip Characteristics (motoring slip region 0 < s < 1) and Load Test and Parallel Operation of Alternators.

◆ Principle of Operation at Super-Synchronous Speed

Consider a standard three-phase squirrel-cage induction machine whose stator is connected to a stiff AC grid of line voltage V_1 and frequency f. The grid sets up a rotating magnetic field in the airgap turning at synchronous speed N_s = 120f / P.

If an external prime mover (such as a wind turbine or hydro turbine) couples to the rotor shaft and drives it faster than synchronous speed in the direction of the rotating field:

N_r > N_s   ⇒   s = (N_s − N_r) / N_s < 0  (negative slip)

What happens inside the machine when slip goes negative?

  1. Reversal of Relative Motion: In motoring mode (N_r < N_s), the rotating airgap field cuts rotor conductors in the forward direction. When N_r > N_s, the rotor conductors overtake the airgap flux wave. The relative motion between the rotor conductors and the airgap field reverses by 180°.
  2. Reversal of Induced Rotor EMF and Current: By Faraday's Law, the polarity of induced rotor EMF reverses. The active component of rotor current referred to stator, I_2' = V_1 / (R_2'/s + jX_2'), reverses its sign because the effective resistance term R_2'/s is negative.
  3. Electromagnetic Torque Reversal: The electromagnetic torque equation is:
    T_e = (3 / ω_s) · [ V_1^2 · (R_2'/s) ] / [ (R_1 + R_2'/s)^2 + (X_1 + X_2')^2 ]
    Because s is negative, R_2'/s is negative, which makes T_e negative. A negative electromagnetic torque opposes the mechanical driving torque of the prime mover. The machine acts as a mechanical brake on the turbine, absorbing mechanical shaft power and converting it into electrical power delivered to the stator terminals.

Figure 5: Phasor and power flow diagram of a grid-connected induction generator. Real current reverses to export active power P to the grid, while magnetising current I_m is drawn from the grid (absorbing lagging reactive power Q).

◆ The Crucial Reactive Power Constraint

The single most critical operational limitation of an induction generator is its total inability to supply its own magnetising current. It has no DC excitation system or rotor slip rings.

  • To establish its airgap magnetic field, the machine must draw lagging reactive power (Q_in > 0) from the grid.
  • Magnetising current I_m is large (typically 30% to 50% of rated stator current).
  • Consequently, viewed from the grid, an induction generator delivers active power (MW) but simultaneously acts as a large inductive consumer of reactive power (MVAR).
  • In generator sign convention, delivering real power while absorbing lagging reactive power corresponds to operating at a leading power factor.
  • To prevent pulling down local utility grid voltage, wind power installations provide switched shunt capacitor banks or static VAR compensators (STATCOMs) at the generator terminals to supply the required magnetising MVARs locally.

◆ Advantages and Limitations in Wind Power Systems

FeatureSquirrel-Cage Induction Generator (SCIG)Synchronous Alternator
Excitation SystemNone required; draws VARs from grid or capacitor bankRequires DC exciter, brushes/brushless exciter, and AVR
SynchronisationAutomatic on grid switch closure (no hunting, no synchronising lamps)Requires strict voltage, frequency, and phase angle matching
Response to Wind GustsInherently compliant; speed slips slightly, absorbing wind gusts as kinetic energyStiff; gusts induce heavy mechanical shaft stresses and torque swings
Short-Circuit BehaviorOn grid fault, terminal voltage drops, excitation vanishes, and fault current decays rapidly to zeroField current sustains heavy fault current feeding into grid faults
Standalone CapabilityCannot operate without external capacitor bankOperates standalone with full voltage and frequency control
Common mistake: Believing that an induction generator exports reactive power into the grid. It cannot! An induction generator always absorbs lagging reactive power from the grid to sustain its magnetising field.
Placement trap: "What happens if a grid-connected wind turbine induction generator is suddenly disconnected from the grid during strong winds?" Because excitation is supplied by the grid, terminal voltage instantly drops to zero. Electromagnetic braking torque vanishes, and the wind turbine will experience dangerous mechanical runaway unless emergency aerodynamic stall control or mechanical disc brakes are deployed within seconds.

◆ Quick revision

  • An induction machine operates as a generator when driven above synchronous speed (N_r > N_s), giving negative slip (s < 0).
  • Negative slip reverses the active rotor current and electromagnetic torque, converting mechanical turbine power into electrical output.
  • The grid clamps the generator's terminal voltage and frequency.
  • An induction generator cannot self-excite on its own; it always absorbs lagging reactive power from the grid (operating at leading power factor as a generator).
  • Shunt capacitor banks or STATCOMs are standardly installed to supply magnetising VARs locally.

ac-ig-self-excited.title: Self-Excited Induction Generator (SEIG): Standalone Operation and Voltage Buildup
ac-ig-self-excited.body:
◆ Why this matters

A grid-connected induction generator relies on the electrical utility to supply its magnetising current and establish its terminal voltage and frequency. However, in remote rural communities, mountainous terrain, island microgrids, and off-grid telecommunications stations, no utility grid exists. To generate clean electrical power from local micro-hydro streams or small wind turbines without the prohibitive capital cost, delicate electronics, and high maintenance of synchronous alternators, engineers employ the Self-Excited Induction Generator (SEIG). By connecting a balanced three-phase capacitor bank across the terminals of a standard, off-the-shelf squirrel-cage induction motor, the machine can boot up, build up stable terminal voltage from residual magnetism, and supply isolated electrical loads reliably.

Prerequisites: Grid-Connected Induction Generator: Operating Principle, Power Flow, and Applications (induction generation principle and reactive power needs) and Voltage Regulation of Alternators: EMF and MMF Methods (open-circuit magnetization curves).

◆ Mechanism of Voltage Buildup

The voltage buildup in an isolated SEIG is directly analogous to the buildup of voltage in a self-excited DC shunt generator, but occurs with alternating three-phase quantities:

  1. Residual Magnetism: When the prime mover spins the unexcited rotor at speed N, the small residual magnetic flux trapped in the rotor core iron cuts the stator turns, inducing a tiny residual alternating EMF E_res (typically 2% to 6% of rated voltage).
  2. Capacitive Current Excitation: This small EMF appears across the terminal capacitor bank, driving a small leading capacitive current I_c = E_res / X_c. Because the current leads the voltage by 90°, it supplies the exact lagging reactive power needed to magnetise the stator core.
  3. Flux Amplification: The leading current produces an armature reaction flux that reinforces and strengthens the residual rotor flux. The enhanced flux induces a larger terminal EMF.
  4. Saturation and Equilibrium: The voltage and capacitive current grow exponentially until the linear volt-ampere characteristic of the capacitor bank (V = I_c · X_c) intersects the non-linear magnetic saturation curve of the iron core at stable operating point P_0.

Figure 6: Voltage buildup in a Self-Excited Induction Generator (SEIG). Self-excitation stabilizes at point P_0 where the capacitor load line intersects the magnetic saturation curve. If C < C_crit, no intersection occurs and voltage fails to build up.

◆ Conditions for Self-Excitation

For an isolated induction generator to successfully build up voltage, four critical conditions must be satisfied:

  1. Residual Magnetism: The rotor core must retain sufficient residual flux. If the machine has been dismantled, dropped, or unpowered for years, the rotor core may become demagnetized. It must then be "flashed" by applying a momentary DC voltage (such as from a 12 V automotive battery) across any two stator leads.
  2. Critical Capacitance (C > C_crit): The capacitive reactance X_c = 1/(2πfC) must be less than the unsaturated magnetising reactance X_m,unsat (the slope of the linear airgap line). The critical capacitance is:
    C_crit = 1 / (2π f X_m,unsat)
    If C < C_crit, the capacitor line is steeper than the airgap line and lies entirely above the saturation curve; voltage cannot build up.
  3. Critical Speed (N > N_crit): Because the generated EMF E_0 is proportional to rotor speed, running at reduced speed lowers the entire saturation curve. For a given connected capacitance, there exists a minimum critical speed below which excitation collapses.
  4. Correct Capacitor Connection: The capacitor bank must be connected with balanced three-phase symmetry.

◆ Delta versus Star Connected Capacitor Banks

To supply a total three-phase magnetising reactive power Q_c at line-to-line voltage V_L and frequency f:

  • Star (Y) Connection: Each capacitor experiences phase voltage V_ph = V_L / √3:
    C_Y = Q_c / (3 · 2π f · V_ph^2) = Q_c / (2π f · V_L^2)
  • Delta (Δ) Connection: Each capacitor experiences the full line-to-line voltage V_L:
    C_Δ = (Q_c / 3) / (2π f · V_L^2) = Q_c / (3 · 2π f · V_L^2) = C_Y / 3

Connecting the capacitor bank in Delta requires exactly one-third the capacitance (C_Δ = C_Y / 3) compared to Star for the same reactive MVAR rating. Delta connection is universally preferred in commercial practice because it slashes capacitor volume, physical footprint, and component costs by 66.7%.

◆ Load Characteristics and Voltage Collapse

Under isolated operation, an SEIG has poor inherent voltage regulation:

  • Resistive Loads: Adding resistance draws active current, which increases stator and rotor internal drops, causing terminal voltage to decrease moderately.
  • Inductive Loads (Lagging PF): Highly detrimental. An inductive load demands lagging reactive power, directly robbing the stator of the capacitive VARs needed to maintain core excitation. As reactive current drops, flux decreases, generated EMF drops, and the generator can enter sudden, catastrophic voltage collapse where terminal voltage drops to zero.
  • Remedy (Series Compensation): Installing series capacitors in the line feeders (short-shunt or long-shunt connections) boosts terminal voltage automatically as load current increases, achieving near-flat voltage regulation.
Common mistake: Applying an inductive motor load directly to an uncompensated standalone SEIG. When an induction motor starts, it draws 6 times rated current at 0.2 power factor lagging. This massive lagging VAR surge completely collapses the SEIG's excitation in fractions of a second.
Placement trap: "If you increase the capacitance across an SEIG beyond C_crit, does the voltage keep rising indefinitely?" No! The terminal voltage is strictly clamped by magnetic saturation of the iron core. Once saturated, enormous increases in capacitance produce only minor increases in terminal voltage, while driving excessive stator core losses and stator overheating.

◆ Quick revision

  • An SEIG operates standalone by connecting a 3-phase capacitor bank across its stator terminals.
  • Voltage buildup initiates from residual rotor magnetism, and stabilizes at the intersection of the capacitor load line V = I_c X_c with the core saturation curve.
  • Voltage buildup requires: (1) residual magnetism, (2) C > C_crit = 1/(2πf X_m,unsat), (3) speed N > N_crit.
  • Delta connection requires only one-third the capacitance of star: C_Δ = C_Y / 3.
  • Lagging inductive loads steal magnetising VARs, causing severe voltage drops or complete voltage collapse.

ac-ig-torque-slip-circle.title: Complete Torque-Slip Characteristics and Circle Diagram of Induction Generator
ac-ig-torque-slip-circle.body:
◆ Why this matters

An induction machine is a truly versatile electromechanical energy conversion device that operates seamlessly across three distinct quadrants depending on its rotor speed: Motoring (0 < s < 1), Generating (s < 0), and Braking / Plugging (s > 1). When designing wind turbine drive trains and hydro-electric governor controls, engineers must evaluate the generator's peak breakdown torque to prevent turbine runaway during severe wind gusts. Analytically and geometrically, the complete behavior of an induction machine in generating mode is captured by extending the classical Heyland-Behrend Circle Diagram into the lower half-plane (Quadrant IV). This provides a comprehensive graphical determination of electrical power output, mechanical input, stator and rotor copper losses, operating power factor, and generator efficiency without solving tedious non-linear complex phasor networks.

Prerequisites: Construction of Circle Diagram and Numerical Problems (three-phase induction motor circle diagram construction) and Grid-Connected Induction Generator: Operating Principle, Power Flow, and Applications.

◆ Complete Three-Quadrant Torque-Slip Characteristic

From the approximate equivalent circuit of an induction machine connected to stator phase voltage V_1 at synchronous speed ω_s, the electromagnetic torque across all operating regimes is:

T_e = (3 / ω_s) · [ V_1^2 · (R_2'/s) ] / [ (R_1 + R_2'/s)^2 + X_sc^2 ]    (where X_sc = X_1 + X_2')
Operating ModeRotor Speed (N_r)Slip (s)Effective Rotor Resistance (R_2'/s)Electromagnetic Torque (T_e)Power Conversion
Generating RegionN_r > N_s (Super-synchronous)s < 0 (e.g. −0.05)NegativeNegative (opposes motion)Mechanical input from turbine converted to Electrical output exported to grid
Motoring Region0 < N_r < N_s (Sub-synchronous)0 < s < 1PositivePositive (assists rotation)Electrical input from grid converted to Mechanical shaft output
Braking / PluggingN_r < 0 (Reverse rotation)s > 1 (e.g. 1.8)Positive and smallPositive (opposes reverse rotation)Both Mechanical and Electrical inputs converted into massive rotor heat

◆ Mathematical Derivation: Maximum Generating Torque vs Maximum Motoring Torque

To find the maximum (breakdown) torque, we differentiate T_e with respect to the variable parameter (R_2'/s) and set the derivative to zero:

d T_e / d(R_2'/s) = 0   ⇒   (R_2'/s)^2 = R_1^2 + X_sc^2 = Z_sc^2   ⇒   R_2'/s = ± √(R_1^2 + X_sc^2) = ± Z_sc

This yields two distinct breakdown operating points:

  • Motoring Breakdown (s > 0): Occurs at slip s_max,m = + R_2' / Z_sc. Substituting R_2'/s = + Z_sc into the torque equation gives:
    T_max,m = 3 V_1^2 / [ 2 ω_s · ( √(R_1^2 + X_sc^2) + R_1 ) ] = 3 V_1^2 / [ 2 ω_s · (Z_sc + R_1) ]
  • Generating Breakdown (s < 0): Occurs at slip s_max,g = − R_2' / Z_sc. Substituting R_2'/s = − Z_sc into the torque equation gives:
    T_max,g = 3 V_1^2 / [ 2 ω_s · ( √(R_1^2 + X_sc^2) − R_1 ) ] = 3 V_1^2 / [ 2 ω_s · (Z_sc − R_1) ]

Critical Insight: Because stator resistance R_1 is positive and non-zero, the denominator of T_max,g contains (Z_sc − R_1), whereas the denominator of T_max,m contains (Z_sc + R_1). Therefore:

T_max,g > T_max,m      Ratio: T_max,g / T_max,m = (Z_sc + R_1) / (Z_sc − R_1) > 1.0

The maximum generating torque of an induction machine is always strictly greater than its maximum motoring torque. In typical industrial machines where R_1 / X_sc ≈ 0.15 to 0.25, the maximum generating torque is 30% to 60% larger than the peak motoring torque!

Figure 7: Complete Circle Diagram of an induction machine. The circle continues into the lower half-plane (s < 0) where active current reverses. Vertical segments dropped from operating point P measure electrical output, mechanical input, and copper losses.

◆ Reading Generator Performance from the Circle Diagram

When operating in generating mode at point P on the lower semicircle, drop a vertical line intersecting the diameter line at M, the output line at D, and the torque line at E:

  • Electrical Active Output Power: Represented by the vertical distance from P to the horizontal diameter axis:
    P_out(elec) = Length(PM) × Power Scale (kW)
  • Mechanical Active Input Power: Represented by the vertical distance from P to the torque line:
    P_in(mech) = Length(PE) × Power Scale (kW)
  • Rotor Copper Loss: Represented by the vertical intercept between the torque line and the output line:
    P_cur = Length(ED) × Power Scale (kW)
  • Stator Copper and Core Loss: Represented by the vertical intercept between the output line and the diameter axis:
    P_st = Length(DM) × Power Scale (kW)
  • Generator Efficiency:
    η_gen = P_out(elec) / P_in(mech) = Length(PM) / Length(PE)
Common mistake: Using the motoring efficiency formula η = Length(output) / Length(input) with the same segments. In motoring mode, electrical power is input (vertical to axis) and mechanical power is output (vertical to output line). In generating mode, mechanical power is the input (from P to torque line) and electrical power delivered is the output (from P to diameter axis).
