Placement trap: "Why is the breakdown generating torque greater than the breakdown motoring torque, whereas for a synchronous machine both are equal?" In a synchronous machine, prime mover power is P = (E_f V / X_s) sin δ, which is completely symmetric between +δ (generator) and −δ (motor). In an induction machine, stator winding resistance R_1 causes internal voltage drop that reduces the effective airgap voltage in motoring mode, but boosts the effective internal voltage in generating mode. Mathematically, the denominator contains (Z_sc − R_1) for generating vs (Z_sc + R_1) for motoring, making T_max,g strictly greater.

◆ Quick revision

  • The induction machine operates in three quadrants: Motoring (0 < s < 1), Generating (s < 0), and Plugging (s > 1).
  • Breakdown generating torque is T_max,g = 3 V_1^2 / [2 ω_s (Z_sc − R_1)].
  • Breakdown motoring torque is T_max,m = 3 V_1^2 / [2 ω_s (Z_sc + R_1)].
  • Because R_1 > 0, maximum generating torque is always greater than maximum motoring torque (T_max,g > T_max,m).
  • On the circle diagram, the generating locus occupies the lower semicircle below the horizontal diameter.
  • Vertical distance from point P to the diameter represents electrical power exported; distance to torque line represents mechanical input from prime mover.

es-8085-architecture-pins.title: 8085 Microprocessor Architecture & Pin Diagram
es-8085-architecture-pins.body:
The Intel 8085 is an 8-bit classic microprocessor fabricated with N-channel Silicon Gate (NMOS) technology, operating with an on-chip clock generator powered by a single +5 V DC supply. Packaged in a standard 40-pin Dual In-line Package (DIP), it features a 16-bit address bus capable of addressing 64 KB of memory, a multiplexed 8-bit address/data bus, 5 hardware interrupt pins, and built-in serial I/O communication ports.

1. Internal Architecture of the 8085

The internal architecture of the 8085 comprises several functional units interconnected via an internal 8-bit bidirectional data bus:

  • Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU): Performs 8-bit arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, increment, decrement) and logical operations (AND, OR, XOR, compare, rotate, complement). Results are typically routed into the Accumulator.
  • Accumulator (Register A): An 8-bit register that serves as one of the primary operands for almost all ALU operations and receives the result of ALU computations.
  • Temporary Register: An internal 8-bit register invisible to the programmer, used by the ALU to store the second operand during two-operand operations.
  • Flag Register: An 8-bit register containing 5 hardware status flip-flops updated by ALU arithmetic and logical operations:
    • Sign Flag (S): Set to 1 if bit D7 of the result is 1 (negative in two's complement); 0 otherwise.
    • Zero Flag (Z): Set to 1 if the entire 8-bit result is exactly 00H; cleared to 0 if non-zero.
    • Auxiliary Carry Flag (AC): Set to 1 if a carry is generated from bit D3 to bit D4 during addition (used exclusively for BCD arithmetic by DAA).
    • Parity Flag (P): Set to 1 if the result contains an even number of 1s (even parity); cleared to 0 for odd parity.
    • Carry Flag (CY): Set to 1 if an arithmetic operation generates an overflow carry out of bit D7 or a borrow during subtraction.
  • General-Purpose Register Array: Six 8-bit registers: B, C, D, E, H, L. They can be used independently as 8-bit registers or paired as 16-bit register pairs (BC, DE, HL) to perform 16-bit arithmetic or hold 16-bit memory addresses. The HL pair serves as the default data pointer (Memory register M).
  • Special-Purpose 16-Bit Registers:
    • Program Counter (PC): Holds the 16-bit memory address of the next instruction byte to be fetched and executed. Automatically increments after each fetch.
    • Stack Pointer (SP): Holds the 16-bit memory address of the current top of the stack located in R/W RAM. Decrements before a push and increments after a pop.
  • Instruction Register & Decoder: During the opcode fetch cycle, the fetched 8-bit opcode is loaded into the Instruction Register (IR). The Instruction Decoder translates the bit pattern into micro-operations that configure internal timing signals.
  • Timing and Control Unit: The heartbeat of the CPU. It synchronizes all internal registers and external buses using clock cycles (T-states), generating control signals (RD#, WR#, ALE, IO/M#).

2. Pin Diagram and Signal Functional Groups

The 40 pins of the 8085 DIP IC are logically classified into six functional groups:

Signal Group Pin Numbers Direction Functional Description
Address Bus A15 - A8 (Pins 21-28) Output Higher-order 8 bits of memory address or duplicated I/O port address. Tri-stated during Hold and Halt.
Multiplexed Bus AD7 - AD0 (Pins 12-19) Bidirectional Multiplexed bus carrying lower 8 bits of address during T1, and bidirectional data during T2-T3.
Control & Status ALE (30), RD# (32), WR# (31), IO/M# (34), S1 (33), S0 (29) Output ALE: Address Latch Enable.
RD#: Active-low read strobe.
WR#: Active-low write strobe.
IO/M#, S1, S0: Machine cycle identification.
Power & Clock Vcc (40), Vss (20), X1, X2 (1, 2), CLK OUT (37) Power / IO +5 V supply, Ground, crystal pins (f_XTAL = 2 * f_CLK), and clock output.
Interrupts TRAP (6), RST 7.5 (7), RST 6.5 (8), RST 5.5 (9), INTR (10), INTA# (11) Input (INTA# Out) Hardware interrupts in descending priority: TRAP down to INTR.
DMA & Reset HOLD (39), HLDA (38), READY (35), RESET IN# (36), RESET OUT (3) Inputs / Outputs DMA bus request/acknowledge, slow memory wait states, and CPU reset.

3. Bus Multiplexing & Demultiplexing with ALE

To reduce the pin count of the 8085 to 40 pins, the low-order address bus lines (A7-A0) and data bus lines (D7-D0) are time-multiplexed onto lines AD7-AD0.

  • During state T1 of every machine cycle, the 8085 puts the lower-order address bits onto AD7-AD0 and asserts Address Latch Enable (ALE) HIGH.
  • At the trailing (falling) edge of ALE, an external transparent octal latch (such as the 74LS373) latches the address present on AD7-AD0.
  • During states T2, T3, and T4, lines AD7-AD0 are freed to transfer data in either direction, while the external latch outputs maintain the static address lines A7-A0 for memory or I/O chips.

Clock Frequency & State Duration Formulas

Operating Clock Frequency: \(f_{CLK} = \frac{f_{XTAL}}{2}\)

Duration of One Clock State (T-state): \(T_{state} = \frac{1}{f_{CLK}}\)

Example: For a 6.144 MHz crystal connected across pins X1-X2, the internal CPU clock runs at \(f_{CLK} = 3.072\text{ MHz}\), yielding \(T_{state} = \frac{1}{3.072 \times 10^6} \approx 325.52\text{ ns}\).

Exam Pitfall Alert: Never confuse the crystal frequency \(f_{XTAL}\) with the processor operating clock frequency \(f_{CLK}\). The 8085 contains an internal divide-by-two flip-flop; hence a 6 MHz crystal yields an internal system operating speed of 3 MHz. Always divide by 2 when computing machine cycle and instruction execution times!

es-8085-addressing-instruction-bytes.title: 8085 Addressing Modes & Byte-Level Instruction Classification
es-8085-addressing-instruction-bytes.body:
The 8085 microprocessor features an instruction set of 74 distinct operation codes (opcodes) comprising 246 total instruction permutations. Every instruction specifies an operation to be performed and the operand(s) on which the CPU operates. The method by which the CPU locates or specifies these operands is designated as the Addressing Mode.

1. The Five Addressing Modes of 8085

The 8085 microprocessor supports five fundamental addressing modes:

Addressing Mode Example Operational Description
Immediate MVI A, 32H
LXI H, 2050H		 Operand data is specified directly within instruction bytes following the opcode.
Register MOV B, C
ADD D		 Both source and destination operands reside within CPU internal registers.
Direct LDA 4000H
STA 5050H		 The exact 16-bit memory address is given in bytes 2 and 3 of the instruction.
Register Indirect MOV A, M
ADD M		 The 16-bit memory address is held in a register pair (such as HL pair M).
Implicit / Implied CMA
STC, HLT		 Operand is inherent in opcode itself; no explicit operand is needed.

2. Instruction Classification Based on Byte Length

Depending on the size in memory required to store the instruction, 8085 instructions fall into three categories:

1-Byte Instructions

An instruction consisting solely of an 8-bit opcode. The operand is either a register or implied in the opcode: 

MOV A, B    ; Opcode 78H (1 byte)
ADD C       ; Opcode 81H (1 byte)
CMA         ; Opcode 2FH (1 byte)
HLT         ; Opcode 76H (1 byte)

2-Byte Instructions

The first byte contains the opcode, and the second byte contains 8 bits of immediate data or an 8-bit I/O port address: 

MVI A, 45H  ; Byte 1: Opcode, Byte 2: Data
ADI 08H     ; Byte 1: Opcode, Byte 2: Data
IN  80H     ; Byte 1: Opcode, Byte 2: Port

3-Byte Instructions

The first byte contains the opcode, the second byte stores the lower-order 8 bits of a 16-bit address or data, and the third byte stores the higher-order 8 bits: 

LXI H, 2050H ; B1: Opcode, B2: 50H, B3: 20H
STA 4000H   ; B1: Opcode, B2: 00H, B3: 40H
JMP 3000H   ; B1: Opcode, B2: 00H, B3: 30H

Memory Storage of Multi-Byte Instructions (Little-Endian Rule)

The 8085 stores 16-bit addresses and constants in memory in Little-Endian format (Least Significant Byte first):

If instruction LXI B, 1234H is stored starting at memory location 2000H:

  • 2000H: 01H (Opcode for LXI B)
  • 2001H: 34H (Low-order byte of data)
  • 2002H: 12H (High-order byte of data)
Common Pitfall in Assembly Memory Footprints: Never write the high-order address byte first in machine code! When hand-assembling STA 8050H, students frequently place 80H before 50H. In 8085, the low byte 50H always occupies the lower memory address (PC+1), followed by high byte 80H at (PC+2).

es-8085-instruction-cycles-timing.title: Instruction Cycles & Timing Diagrams of the 8085
es-8085-instruction-cycles-timing.body:
Execution of any program by the 8085 is governed by a precise sequence of cyclic operations synchronized to clock transitions. Understanding the hierarchy of Instruction Cycles, Machine Cycles, and T-states is essential for designing deterministic interfaces and evaluating microprocessor performance.

1. The Timing Hierarchy: Instruction Cycle, Machine Cycle, & T-State

  • T-State: The fundamental unit of CPU time, defined as one complete period of the internal clock frequency \(T_{state} = 1/f_{CLK}\).
  • Machine Cycle (MC): The time required by the microprocessor to perform one complete bus access to external memory or an I/O device. Typical machine cycles take 3 to 6 T-states.
  • Instruction Cycle (IC): The total time required by the CPU to fetch, decode, and execute a complete assembly instruction. An instruction cycle consists of 1 to 5 machine cycles (1 to 18 T-states).

2. Machine Cycle Status Signals

The 8085 outputs three status signals—IO/M#, S1, and S0—at the beginning of every machine cycle to identify the nature of the upcoming bus operation:

Machine Cycle IO/M# S1 S0 Active Strobe T-States
Opcode Fetch (OF) 0 1 1 RD# = 0 4 T (or 6 T)
Memory Read (MR) 0 1 0 RD# = 0 3 T
Memory Write (MW) 0 0 1 WR# = 0 3 T
I/O Read (IOR) 1 1 0 RD# = 0 3 T
I/O Write (IOW) 1 0 1 WR# = 0 3 T
Interrupt Ack (INA) 1 1 1 INTA# = 0 6 T or 12 T

3. Detailed Timing of Opcode Fetch Machine Cycle (4 T-States)

The Opcode Fetch cycle is the first machine cycle (M1) of every instruction. It requires 4 T-states:

  1. State T1:
    • CPU places high-order Program Counter (PCH) onto A15-A8 and low-order Program Counter (PCL) onto AD7-AD0.
    • Status signals are asserted: IO/M# = 0, S1 = 1, S0 = 1.
    • ALE pulses HIGH during the first half of T1 and goes LOW, enabling external latches to capture the lower address.
  2. State T2:
    • AD7-AD0 lines enter high impedance.
    • The CPU asserts RD# LOW. External memory chip drives the opcode byte onto lines AD7-AD0.
    • The Program Counter is incremented by 1 (PC = PC + 1).
  3. State T3:
    • The CPU reads the opcode byte from AD7-AD0 into the internal Instruction Register (IR).
    • RD# rises to HIGH, terminating the read operation.
  4. State T4:
    • The external buses (AD7-AD0) remain idle.
    • The internal Instruction Decoder decodes the opcode and determines which subsequent machine cycles (if any) are required.

Timing Calculation for Multi-Cycle Instructions

For an instruction taking \(M\) machine cycles and \(T_{total}\) states:

\[T_{exec} = T_{total} \times T_{state} = \frac{T_{total}}{f_{CLK}}\]

Common Instruction Profiles:

  • MOV r1, r2: 1 MC (Opcode Fetch 4T) = 4 T-states
  • MOV r, M: 2 MC (Opcode Fetch 4T + Memory Read 3T) = 7 T-states
  • LXI H, 2050H: 3 MC (OF 4T + MR 3T + MR 3T) = 10 T-states
  • STA 2050H: 4 MC (OF 4T + MR 3T + MR 3T + MW 3T) = 13 T-states
  • JNZ addr: If condition TRUE → 3 MC (10 T); If condition FALSE → 2 MC (7 T).
Wait State Insertion Trap: When the 8085 communicates with slow memory devices, it samples the READY pin during state T2. If READY is LOW, the processor enters an idle state called a Wait State (\(T_w\)) between T2 and T3. The processor does not proceed to T3 until READY returns HIGH.

es-8085-basic-alps-delay-programs.title: 8085 Assembly Language Programming & Precise Software Delays
es-8085-basic-alps-delay-programs.body:
Assembly Language Programming (ALP) directly controls the microprocessor hardware at register level. This lesson covers fundamental arithmetic/logical algorithms (8-bit addition, subtraction, data block transfer, multi-byte addition) and rigorous mathematical formulation of software time delays using single and nested register loops.

1. Fundamental 8085 Assembly Programs

Program 1: 8-Bit Addition with Carry Storage

Add two 8-bit numbers stored at memory locations 2050H and 2051H. Store the sum at 2052H and carry at 2053H: 

; Point HL to 1st operand
LXI H, 2050H
MOV A, M
INX H
; Add second operand
ADD M
MOV L, A
; Initialize carry reg
MVI C, 00H
JNC SKIP
INR C
SKIP:
STA 2052H
MOV A, C
STA 2053H
HLT

Program 2: Block Data Transfer

Transfer a block of 10 data bytes from source address starting at 3000H to destination address starting at 4000H: 

; Source & Dest pointers
LXI H, 3000H
LXI D, 4000H
; Byte counter (10 bytes)
MVI C, 0AH
LOOP:
MOV A, M
STAX D
INX H
INX D
DCR C
JNZ LOOP
HLT

2. Software Delay Calculations

Because microprocessors execute instructions at exact, deterministic clock speeds, subroutines containing decrementing loops are commonly used to create precise real-time time delays.

8-Bit Register Delay Formula

Consider the standard single-register delay loop: 

DELAY:  MVI C, N        ; 7 T
LOOP:   DCR C           ; 4 T
        JNZ LOOP        ; 10 T / 7 T
        RET             ; 10 T

For an 8-bit count \(N\):

  • MVI C, N executes once: \(7\text{ T}\)
  • DCR C executes \(N\) times: \(4 \times N\text{ T}\)
  • JNZ is taken \((N - 1)\) times: \(10 \times (N - 1)\text{ T}\)
  • JNZ falls through on the last iteration: \(7 \times 1\text{ T}\)
  • RET executes once: \(10\text{ T}\)

Summing these T-states: \[T_{total} = 7 + 4N + 10(N - 1) + 7 + 10 = 14N + 14\text{ T-states}\]

16-Bit Register Pair Delay Formula

To achieve delays greater than a few milliseconds without cascading multiple loops, a 16-bit register pair is used: 

DELAY16: LXI B, COUNT   ; 10 T
LOOP16:  DCX B          ; 6 T
         MOV A, C       ; 4 T
         ORA B          ; 4 T
         JNZ LOOP16     ; 10 T / 7 T
         RET            ; 10 T

Because DCX B does NOT affect the Zero flag, MOV A, C followed by ORA B is essential to logically test if both registers \(B\) and \(C\) have reached zero.

Total T-states: \[T_{total} = 10 + (\text{COUNT} - 1) \times 24 + 21 + 10 = 24 \times \text{COUNT} + 17\text{ T-states}\] Operating at \(3.072\text{ MHz}\), setting \(\text{COUNT} = 0000H\) (65,536 iterations) produces a maximum single-call delay of: \[T_{delay} = \frac{24 \times 65536 + 17}{3.072 \times 10^6} \approx 0.512\text{ s} \quad (512\text{ ms})\]

Key Delay Equations Reference

8-Bit Single Loop: \(T_{delay} = (14N + 14) \times T_{state}\)

16-Bit Pair Loop: \(T_{delay} = (24 \times \text{COUNT} + 17) \times T_{state}\)

Clock Period: \(T_{state} = \frac{1}{f_{CLK}} = \frac{2}{f_{XTAL}}\)

Critical Assembly Gotcha: Notice why ORA B is necessary in the 16-bit delay loop! Many beginners write only DCX B followed directly by JNZ LOOP16. However, in the 8085 architecture, DCX and INX modify zero status flags! Without MOV A, C and ORA B, the CPU condition flags remain whatever they were prior to entering the loop, causing either an infinite loop or premature loop termination.

es-8255-ppi-architecture-modes.title: 8255 Programmable Peripheral Interface — Architecture & Modes
es-8255-ppi-architecture-modes.body:
The Intel 8255 Programmable Peripheral Interface (PPI) is a general-purpose programmable I/O device designed to interface parallel peripherals to microprocessor buses. It provides 24 I/O pins grouped into three 8-bit ports (A, B, and C) configurable through internal control registers in different functional modes.

1. Functional Block Diagram and Architecture

2. Pin Description and Addressing

PinCountFunction
D7–D08Bidirectional data bus — connects directly to CPU data bus
PA7–PA08Port A — 8-bit data I/O lines (Modes 0, 1, 2)
PB7–PB08Port B — 8-bit data I/O lines (Modes 0, 1)
PC7–PC08Port C — split into upper (PC7–PC4) and lower (PC3–PC0); data or handshaking
CS#1Chip Select (active low)
RD#, WR#2Read and Write control strobes (active low)
A1, A02Port selection: 00=Port A, 01=Port B, 10=Port C, 11=Control Register
RESET1Active high reset; clears control register; all ports default to input mode

3. Operating Modes of 8255

ModeNameFeatures
Mode 0Basic Input/OutputSimple I/O without handshaking; outputs latched, inputs buffered; Ports A, B, CU, CL independently set
Mode 1Strobed Input/OutputHandshake data transfer; Port A uses Port C upper lines, Port B uses Port C lower lines for handshaking (STB#, IBF, INTR for input; OBF#, ACK#, INTR for output)
Mode 2Strobed Bidirectional BusGroup A only; Port A becomes bidirectional 8-bit bus using 5 handshake lines from Port C (PC7–PC3)
BSR ModeBit Set/Reset ModeD7=0; allows setting or resetting any individual bit of Port C without affecting port modes

4. Control Word Formats

I/O Mode Control Word (D7 = 1):
D7 = 1 | D6 D5 (Group A Mode: 00=Mode 0, 01=Mode 1, 1x=Mode 2) | D4 (Port A: 1=In, 0=Out) | D3 (Port C Upper: 1=In, 0=Out) | D2 (Group B Mode: 0=Mode 0, 1=Mode 1) | D1 (Port B: 1=In, 0=Out) | D0 (Port C Lower: 1=In, 0=Out)

BSR Control Word (D7 = 0):
D7 = 0 | D6 D5 D4 = 000 (don't care) | D3 D2 D1 = Bit Select (000=PC0 to 111=PC7) | D0 = 1 (Set) or 0 (Reset)
Placement Trap — BSR Mode vs I/O Mode: In campus interviews and GATE exams, a common question asks what happens when a byte with MSB=0 (e.g. 0BH or 06H) is written to the control register. It does NOT configure the ports into an invalid mode; rather, D7=0 selects Bit Set/Reset (BSR) mode, modifying solely the selected bit in Port C while leaving all other port configurations completely unaffected.

es-io-seven-segment-adc-dac.title: Interfacing I/O Devices — Seven-Segment LED, ADC and DAC
es-io-seven-segment-adc-dac.body:
Interfacing bridges the digital microprocessor system with human operators and the physical analog domain. Three fundamental peripheral interfaces are studied: seven-segment displays for human-readable numeric readout, Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADC) for sensory telemetry acquisition, and Digital-to-Analog Converters (DAC) for actuator command synthesis.

1. Seven-Segment Display Interfacing

A seven-segment display consists of 7 individual LEDs arranged in a figure-8 pattern (segments a through g) plus an optional decimal point (dp).

ConfigurationCommon Pin Tied ToSegment Active LevelHex Code for '0'Hex Code for '8'
Common Cathode (CC)Ground (0 V)Active HIGH (Logic 1)3FH7FH
Common Anode (CA)+5 V (VCC)Active LOW (Logic 0)C0H80H

2. ADC Interfacing (e.g. ADC 0808 / 0809)

ADC Step Size and Conversion Equations:
Resolution Step Size: ΔV = Vref / (2n − 1)
Digital Output Code: D = round( Vin / ΔV ) = round( Vin × (2n − 1) / Vref )
Handshake Sequence: Assert Start of Conversion (SOC) pulse → Monitor End of Conversion (EOC) signal (goes low then returns high when ready) → Enable Output Enable (OE) to place converted byte on CPU data bus.

3. DAC Interfacing (e.g. DAC 0808)

DAC Transfer Characteristics:
Analog Output Voltage: Vout = Vref × (D / 2n)
Full-Scale Voltage: VFS = Vref × ((2n − 1) / 2n) = Vref − 1 LSB
DAC Step Size: ΔV = Vref / 2n
Placement Trap — ADC vs DAC Resolution Formula: An ADC step size divides by (2n − 1) because code 0 corresponds to 0V and code (2n − 1) corresponds to Vref. A DAC step size divides by 2n because code (2n − 1) produces Vref − 1 LSB (it never reaches full Vref exactly). Confusing these denominators leads to precision errors in placement test calculations.

es-intro-architecture-applications.title: Introduction to Embedded System, Architecture of Embedded system, Applications
es-intro-architecture-applications.body:
An embedded system is a microprocessor- or microcontroller-based computing system designed to perform dedicated functions within a larger mechanical or electrical engineering installation, often operating under stringent real-time, environmental, and resource constraints.

1. Embedded System vs General Purpose Computing

FeatureGeneral-Purpose ComputerEmbedded System
Primary ObjectiveMultipurpose computational flexibility (word processing, gaming, web)Dedicated single-purpose mission (engine control, MPPT inverter)
Hardware PlatformHigh-frequency CPU (GHz), expandable RAM/SSD, active coolingMicrocontroller / DSP / SoC with on-chip flash & RAM, fanless
Operating SystemFull desktop/server OS (Windows, Linux, macOS) with virtual memoryRTOS (FreeRTOS, Zephyr) or Bare-metal firmware superloop
Power & CostHigh power consumption (15W–500W); high unit costUltra-low power (µW–few Watts); strict BOM cost constraints
DeterminismSoft timing; latency jitter acceptable to human operatorsHard deterministic deadlines; late responses constitute failure

2. Embedded System Architectural Topology

3. Electrical Engineering Embedded Applications

DomainSystem DescriptionCore Embedded Function
Renewable EnergySolar Inverter MPPT TrackerSamples PV array voltage and current via ADC; runs Perturb & Observe or Incremental Conductance algorithm; adjusts PWM duty cycle on DC-DC boost converter at 20 kHz
Electric MobilityEV Battery Management System (BMS)Monitors cell voltages, pack current, and temperatures; computes State of Charge (SoC) and State of Health (SoH); commands passive/active balancing circuits
Industrial DrivesVector-Controlled VFDImplements Clarke and Park transformations; calculates space vector PWM (SVPWM) switching times for 3-phase inverter IGBT bridge
Power GridDigital Protection RelaySamples CT/PT waveforms at 64 samples/cycle; performs Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT); issues circuit breaker trip pulse within 20 ms of fault detection
Placement Trap — Microprocessor vs Microcontroller in Embedded Systems: Microprocessors (like 8085) contain CPU ALU and registers only, requiring external chips for RAM, ROM, and I/O. Microcontrollers (like 8051 or ARM Cortex-M) integrate CPU, RAM, ROM/Flash, timers, interrupts, and I/O ports onto a single monolithic die. Embedded systems predominantly use microcontrollers to minimise PCB footprint, component count, power consumption, and manufacturing cost.

es-system-constraints-realtime.title: Embedded System Constraints, Hard and Soft Real Time Systems
es-system-constraints-realtime.body:
Unlike desktop software that optimizes for average throughput, embedded design is dictated by strict physical and temporal constraints. The most critical operational property is real-time determinism, where computation correctness depends unconditionally on when results are produced.

1. Embedded System Design Constraints

Constraint DimensionPhysical LimitationDesign Trade-Off & Mitigation
Temporal (Deadlines)Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) must never exceed physical deadlinesDeterministic RTOS scheduling, interrupt priorities, cache-bypass architectures
Memory (Footprint)Extremely tight on-chip SRAM (e.g. 128 bytes to 64 KB)Static memory allocation only; strictly banning malloc()/free() to eliminate heap fragmentation
Power & EnergyBattery-powered operation (e.g. coin cell lasting 5+ years)Aggressive sleep/standby modes, clock gating, dynamic voltage frequency scaling (DVFS)
Cost & BOMHigh-volume production runs (millions of units)Selecting lowest pin-count, lowest memory MCU capable of satisfying WCET bounds
Reliability & SafetyZero tolerance for unplanned reboot or memory leak crashesHardware Watchdog Timers (WDT), MISRA-C compliance, ECC memory

2. Hard vs Soft Real-Time Systems

CharacteristicHard Real-Time SystemSoft Real-Time System
Deadline ConsequenceMissing a deadline is a catastrophic system failureMissing a deadline degrades Quality of Service (QoS)
Utility FunctionDrops abruptly to zero (or negative / disastrous) at deadlineDecays smoothly after deadline expires
Timing ValidationRigorous static Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) analysisStatistical average execution time and queuing models
EEE Domain ExamplesAutomotive Airbag, ABS Controller, Nuclear Protection RelaySmart Energy Meter LCD display update, Video streaming, IoT weather logger

3. Real-Time Scheduling and Latency Budget

Real-Time Response Time Formulation:
Total Response Time: Tresp = Tlat + TWCET + Tout ≤ Deadline
Where:
• Tlat = Interrupt latency (hardware vector fetch + context save)
• TWCET = Worst-case instruction execution time of the ISR / task
• Tout = Actuator delay / output stage settling time
Placement Trap — Real-Time Speed Fallacy: A system is not "real-time" simply because it runs on a high-speed clock (e.g. 3.0 GHz quad-core CPU). If that CPU runs an operating system with non-deterministic thread preemption, garbage collection pauses, or dynamic page faults, it CANNOT be used for hard real-time control. Determinism (guaranteed latency bounds), not raw clock speed, defines real-time capability.

es-8051-architecture-memory-sfr.title: 8051 Microcontroller: Architecture, Pin Diagram, Memory Organization and SFRs
es-8051-architecture-memory-sfr.body:
The Intel 8051 (MCS-51 architecture) is the canonical 8-bit microcontroller designed specifically for embedded control applications. It implements a Harvard memory architecture with separate physical program and data address spaces, 128 bytes of on-chip RAM, 4 KB of on-chip ROM, four 8-bit I/O ports, two 16-bit timers, and a comprehensive Special Function Register (SFR) array.

1. 8051 Internal Hardware Architecture

2. Pin Configuration (40-Pin DIP)

Pin GroupPin NumbersFunction Description
Port 0 (P0.0–P0.7)Pins 39–32Dual-purpose: 8-bit bidirectional open-drain I/O port, OR multiplexed low-order address/data bus (AD0–AD7) during external memory accesses.
Port 1 (P1.0–P1.7)Pins 1–88-bit quasi-bidirectional I/O port with internal pull-up resistors. Dedicated exclusively to general I/O in the standard 8051.
Port 2 (P2.0–P2.7)Pins 21–28Dual-purpose: 8-bit quasi-bidirectional I/O port with internal pull-ups, OR higher-order address bus (A8–A15) for external memory addressing.
Port 3 (P3.0–P3.7)Pins 10–178-bit quasi-bidirectional I/O with internal pull-ups. Every pin serves a specialized alternate hardware function (RXD, TXD, INT0#, INT1#, T0, T1, WR#, RD#).
ALE / PROG#Pin 30Address Latch Enable output pulse (frequency fosc/6) used to demultiplex AD0–AD7 on Port 0 into external address latch (74LS373).
PSEN#Pin 29Program Store Enable read strobe (active low); asserted only when fetching instructions from external Program ROM.
EA# / VPPPin 31External Access input: When held HIGH, 8051 executes from on-chip ROM (0000H–0FFFH) and then external ROM (1000H–FFFFH). When held LOW, on-chip ROM is disabled and ALL fetches execute from external ROM.
RSTPin 9Active HIGH reset input; holding high for at least 2 machine cycles reinitializes PC to 0000H, SP to 07H, and all ports to FFH.

3. Internal RAM Structure (00H–7FH) and SFR Space (80H–FFH)

Memory BlockAddress RangeInternal Organization & Features
Register Banks (0–3)00H–1FH32 bytes organized as four banks of 8 registers (R0–R7). Bank selection configured via RS1 and RS0 bits in PSW (Bank 0 default on reset).
Bit-Addressable RAM20H–2FH16 bytes (128 bits total) individually accessible via bit instructions (SETB, CLR, JB, JNB). Bit addresses range from 00H to 7FH.
General-Purpose Scratchpad30H–7FH80 bytes of scratchpad RAM for runtime variable storage, buffers, and the hardware stack (stack grows upward toward 7FH).
Special Function Registers (SFR)80H–FFHDirectly controls on-chip peripherals. Registers whose hexadecimal addresses end in 0H or 8H are bit-addressable (ACC, B, PSW, P0–P3, TCON, SCON, IE, IP).

4. Crucial SFR Mappings and Machine Timing

Classic 8051 Timing Relationships:
1 Machine Cycle = 12 Oscillator Clock Periods = 6 State Periods (S1–S6)
Machine Cycle Period: Tcyc = 12 / fosc
Example: For standard fosc = 11.0592 MHz, Tcyc = 12 / 11.0592 × 106 ≈ 1.085 µs.
For fosc = 12.0 MHz, Tcyc = 12 / 12.0 × 106 = 1.000 µs exactly.
Placement Trap — SP Initial State and Bank 1 Collision: On hardware reset, the 8051 Stack Pointer (SP) initializes to 07H. The first PUSH or LCALL instruction increments SP to 08H before writing. But address 08H is the exact location of Register R0 of Register Bank 1! If your application switches to Register Bank 1 without re-initializing SP (e.g. MOV SP, #2FH), subroutine calls or stack pushes will silently corrupt Bank 1 register contents.

es-8051-io-port-addressing.title: Structure of IO port, Addressing modes
es-8051-io-port-addressing.body:
Operating and programming the 8051 requires understanding the physical silicon driver circuitry of its four parallel ports and the complete spectrum of addressing modes that the CPU core provides to locate operands.

1. Silicon Internal Circuitry of 8051 I/O Ports

PortOutput Driver StageInput Configuration RequirementSpecial Hardware Notes
Port 0True Open-Drain (no internal pull-up). When used as general I/O, external pull-up resistors (typically 10 kΩ) are mandatory.Must write '1' to latch bit to turn off lower N-FET, putting pin in high-Z input state.Acts as push-pull AD0–AD7 data bus only during external memory access (switched by internal control multiplexer).
Port 1Quasi-Bidirectional with internal weak pull-up FET (~20–40 kΩ).Must write '1' to latch bit before reading external logic levels.Dedicated purely to general digital I/O in standard 8051.
Port 2Quasi-Bidirectional with internal weak pull-up FET.Must write '1' to latch bit before reading external logic levels.Emits higher address byte A8–A15 during MOVX @DPTR or external program fetches.
Port 3Quasi-Bidirectional with internal weak pull-up FET.Must write '1' to latch bit before reading external logic levels.Contains specialized input buffers and open-drain/alternate drivers for RXD, TXD, INT0#, INT1#, T0, T1, WR#, RD#.

2. Read-Modify-Write (RMW) vs Port-Pin Reading

The 8051 has two distinct instructions for accessing ports:

  • Read-Pin Instructions: Instructions that read the port as an input operand (e.g. MOV A, P1) read the electrical voltage directly from the external physical pin.
  • Read-Modify-Write Instructions: Instructions that read, modify, and rewrite port bits (e.g. ANL P1, #0F0H, CPL P1.2, DJNZ P1, Loop) read the internal latch register, NOT the physical pin. This prevents reading a false '0' if an external capacitive or transistor load momentarily pulls a high pin down.

3. The Seven 8051 Addressing Modes

Addressing ModeOperand SpecificationAssembly ExampleTarget Memory Space
1. ImmediateConstant numeric data embedded directly in instruction bytes preceded by '#'MOV A, #55H
MOV DPTR, #2000H		Program Code bytes
2. RegisterAccesses registers R0–R7 of active bank, Accumulator (A), or B registerMOV A, R4
ADD A, R2		Internal Working Registers
3. Direct8-bit memory address given directly in instruction (00H–7FH for RAM, 80H–FFH for SFRs)MOV A, 30H
MOV 80H, #0FFH		Internal RAM & Special Function Registers
4. Register IndirectRegister pointer (@R0, @R1 for internal RAM, @DPTR for external RAM)MOV A, @R0
MOVX A, @DPTR		Internal 128B RAM or External 64KB Data RAM
5. IndexedBase register (DPTR or PC) added to offset in Accumulator (A)MOVC A, @A+DPTR
MOVC A, @A+PC		Program ROM lookup tables
6. RelativeSigned 8-bit offset (−128 to +127 bytes) added to current PC after fetchSJMP TargetLabel
DJNZ R1, Loop		Program memory branch bounds
7. Bit-DirectDirectly addresses individual bits in 20H–2FH RAM and bit-addressable SFRsSETB P1.0
CLR C
JB 20H.3, Label		128 Bit-RAM flags and SFR control bits
Placement Trap — SFR Access vs Indirect Addressing: In the classic 8051, Special Function Registers (80H–FFH) can ONLY be accessed via DIRECT addressing (e.g. MOV A, 80H). If you load R0 with 80H and execute MOV A, @R0, it will NOT read Port 0! In the classic 8051, indirect addressing of 80H–FFH is invalid; in the 8052, it accesses the upper 128 bytes of scratchpad RAM, completely bypassing the SFR registers.

🔌 GPIO Push-Pull vs Open-Drain Output Architectures

ArchitectureInternal StructureActive Drive High?Typical Use Cases
Push-PullPMOS to $V_{DD}$ + NMOS to GNDYes (Actively sources & sinks current)High-speed digital outputs, SPI, PWM
Open-DrainNMOS to GND only (No PMOS)No (Requires external pull-up resistor)I2C bus, level shifting, wired-AND logic

es-8051-inst-data-arith-logic-bool.title: Instruction set- Data transfer, Arithmetic, Logical, Boolean
es-8051-inst-data-arith-logic-bool.body:
The 8051 microcontroller employs a powerful 8-bit CISC instruction set consisting of 111 distinct instructions (49 single-byte, 45 two-byte, and 17 three-byte opcodes). Operating on an internal two-phase clock architecture where one machine cycle equals 12 oscillator periods (12 clock states S1P1–S6P2), instructions execute in 1, 2, or 4 machine cycles. Understanding the hardware data paths, Program Status Word (PSW) flag dependencies, and native Boolean processor operations is foundational for writing robust bare-metal firmware and debugging high-reliability embedded control systems.

1. Data Transfer Group: Internal, External, and Program Memory

Because the 8051 features a true Harvard architecture with distinct address spaces, data movement requires separate instructions depending on the physical storage medium:

  • Internal RAM & SFR Movement (MOV <dest>, <src>): Operates entirely on the on-chip 128/256-byte data memory and 8-bit SFRs. Supports immediate, direct, register, and register-indirect addressing (e.g. MOV A, #55H, MOV 30H, A, MOV A, @R0). Executes in 1 or 2 machine cycles without asserting external control strobes.
  • External Data Memory (MOVX <dest>, <src>): Accesses off-chip SRAM or memory-mapped peripherals in the 64 KB XDATA space. Always employs the Accumulator as either source or destination. Uses the 16-bit Data Pointer (MOVX A, @DPTR, MOVX @DPTR, A; 2 machine cycles, asserting RD# or WR#) or 8-bit register-indirect addressing (MOVX A, @R0; asserts P2 as high address latch).
  • Program Flash/ROM Lookup (MOVC A, @A+<base>): Reads constant mathematical tables, character fonts, or calibration coefficients from non-volatile code memory. Generates the Program Store Enable (PSEN#) strobe. Operates exclusively via indexed addressing:
    • MOVC A, @A+DPTR: Effective Address = DPTR + A (2 bytes, 2 machine cycles). Ideal for tables positioned anywhere in 64 KB program ROM.
    • MOVC A, @A+PC: Effective Address = (PC + 1) + A (1 byte, 2 machine cycles). Ideal for position-independent relative lookup tables placed immediately following the calling code.
  • Stack Operations (PUSH <direct> / POP <direct>): The 8051 Stack Pointer (SP) is an 8-bit register in internal RAM that initialises to 07H on reset. Stack operations use pre-increment for push (SP ← SP + 1, then Store) and post-decrement for pop (Retrieve, then SP ← SP - 1). Stack instructions only accept direct internal RAM addresses (e.g. PUSH 0E0H pushes ACC, not PUSH A).
  • Data Exchange (XCH A, <byte> / XCHD A, @Ri): XCH swaps full 8-bit contents between Accumulator and a register/memory byte. XCHD A, @Ri swaps only the lower 4-bit nibbles (bits 3–0), leaving upper nibbles intact—a crucial instruction for packed BCD manipulation.

2. Arithmetic Operations and Flag Dynamics

The 8051 arithmetic logic unit performs 8-bit addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, increments, and decimal adjustment. The status of operations is reflected in the Program Status Word (PSW, SFR D0H):

MnemonicBytesCyclesFlags AffectedFunctional Operation
ADD A, <src>1–21CY, AC, OV, PA ← A + src. CY set if carry out of bit 7; AC set if carry out of bit 3.
ADDC A, <src>1–21CY, AC, OV, PA ← A + src + CY. Used for chained multi-byte addition routines.
SUBB A, <src>1–21CY, AC, OV, PA ← A - src - CY. Subtract with borrow. CY set if borrow required.
INC <byte>1–21–2None (P if A)Increments operand. Crucially, does not alter CY or AC flags!
DEC <byte>1–21–2None (P if A)Decrements operand. 00H rolls under to 0FFH without asserting CY.
MUL AB14CY=0, OVMultiplies unsigned A × B. Low byte → A, high byte → B. OV=1 if product > 255.
DIV AB14CY=0, OVDivides A by B. Quotient → A, Remainder → B. OV=1 if division by zero (B=0).
DA A11CYDecimal Adjust Accumulator. Converts binary sum of two packed BCD operands into valid BCD.
8051 Machine Cycle Timing & Instruction Duration

The time required for an instruction to execute on a classic 8051 microcontroller is given by:

$$T_{mc} = \frac{12}{f_{osc}}, \quad t_{inst} = MC \times T_{mc}$$

Where \(f_{osc}\) is the crystal frequency and \(MC\) is the instruction machine cycle count (1, 2, or 4). At \(f_{osc} = 11.0592\text{ MHz}\), \(T_{mc} \approx 1.0851\,\mu\text{s}\). At \(12.0\text{ MHz}\), \(T_{mc} = 1.0000\,\mu\text{s}\).

3. Logical and Bit-Level (Boolean) Processor

The 8051 contains a complete, autonomous single-bit Boolean processor integrated into the ALU. It features its own single-bit accumulator (the Carry flag CY), bit-addressable RAM (128 individual addressable bits from address 00H to 7FH mapped across RAM bytes 20H–2FH), and bit-addressable SFR registers (where address byte ends in 0 or 8):

  • Byte-Level Logic: ANL, ORL, XRL perform bitwise logic between Accumulator and registers/constants. CLR A sets all bits to 0. CPL A inverts all bits (1's complement). RL A and RR A rotate bits without Carry; RLC A and RRC A rotate 9 bits including Carry. SWAP A exchanges the high and low nibbles (bits 7–4 and bits 3–0).
  • Boolean Bit Operations: SETB bit sets target bit to 1; CLR bit clears target bit to 0; CPL bit inverts target bit.
  • Single-Cycle Bit Logic: The Carry bit can directly execute Boolean equations:
    • ANL C, bit \( o CY = CY \land \text{bit}\)
    • ANL C, /bit \( o CY = CY \land \overline{\text{bit}}\) (AND with inverted bit without modifying the bit itself!)
    • ORL C, bit \( o CY = CY \lor \text{bit}\)
    • ORL C, /bit \( o CY = CY \lor \overline{\text{bit}}\)
    • MOV C, bit / MOV bit, C transfers bits between memory/SFRs and the Carry flag.
Placement Trap — SUBB Carry Contamination & MUL AB Flag Quirks: 1. The 8051 has no plain SUB instruction. If you execute SUBB A, R2 without first executing CLR C, any residual borrow from a prior operation will subtract an extra 1 from the result! Always clear carry before the first subtraction byte.
2. MUL AB always forces the Carry flag (CY) to 0, regardless of the result. Do not attempt to test JC after multiplication! Instead, test the Overflow flag (OV): OV = 1 indicates that the product exceeded 8 bits and register B contains a non-zero high byte.

Key Takeaways & Interview Checklist

  • Data transfer: MOV for internal RAM (1–2 MC), MOVX for external RAM via DPTR (2 MC), MOVC for program ROM tables (2 MC).
  • Stack mechanics: SP initialises to 07H on reset; PUSH pre-increments SP, POP post-decrements SP. Only direct addressing allowed (e.g. PUSH 0E0H).
  • Arithmetic: SUBB always subtracts Carry; INC and DEC do NOT affect any status flags except Parity.
  • Boolean processor: Carry flag acts as a 1-bit accumulator. Bit addressing covers RAM 20H–2FH (bits 00H–7FH) and SFRs ending in 0H or 8H.

es-8051-branching-sjmp-ajmp-ljmp.title: Instruction set- Branching – SJMP, AJMP, LJMP
es-8051-branching-sjmp-ajmp-ljmp.body:
Program control transfer instructions govern sequential code flow through conditional jumps, unconditional branches, subroutine calls, and returns. In the 8051 architecture, branch instructions are categorized by their memory targeting range: Short (SJMP), Absolute (AJMP), and Long (LJMP). Mastering their opcode encoding, relative displacement arithmetic, and 2 KB page boundary constraints is essential for code size optimization and avoiding catastrophic runtime execution faults.

1. Unconditional Branch Hierarchy: SJMP, AJMP, and LJMP

The 8051 provides three distinct unconditional jump instructions to optimize instruction footprint and execution speed:

  • SJMP (Short Jump — 2 Bytes, 2 Machine Cycles): Opcode 80H <rel>. Employs an 8-bit signed 2's complement relative displacement. The jump range is strictly from -128 bytes backward to +127 bytes forward relative to the address of the next instruction (\(\text{PC}_{\text{next}} = \text{PC}_{\text{current}} + 2\)). Because it is relocatable (independent of absolute memory addresses), it is universally used for local loops and short branches.
  • AJMP (Absolute Jump — 2 Bytes, 2 Machine Cycles): Opcode [a10 a9 a8 0 0 0 0 1] [a7 ... a0]. Provides an 11-bit target address (000H–7FFH) that allows branching anywhere within the current 2 KB code page. The CPU constructs the 16-bit target by keeping the upper 5 bits of \(\text{PC}_{\text{next}}\) unchanged and substituting bits 10–0 with the opcode's 11-bit field: $$\text{Target Address} = (\text{PC}_{\text{next}} \,\&\,\text{F800H}) \mid \text{addr11}$$
  • LJMP (Long Jump — 3 Bytes, 2 Machine Cycles): Opcode 02H <addr16_high> <addr16_low>. Loads a full 16-bit destination address into the Program Counter, enabling unconditional branching anywhere across the entire 64 KB code space (0000H–FFFFH).
  • JMP @A+DPTR (Indirect Jump — 1 Byte, 2 Machine Cycles): Opcode 73H. Computes destination address as \(\text{DPTR} + \text{A}\) and loads it into PC. Enables ultra-fast O(1) multi-way branch tables (state machines and switch-case statements).

2. Subroutine Linkage: ACALL, LCALL, RET, and RETI

Modular firmware relies on subroutines and interrupt service handlers. The stack mechanism preserves return addresses:

  • ACALL <addr11> (2 Bytes, 2 Machine Cycles): Pushes the 16-bit address of the next instruction onto the stack (low-order byte first, then high-order byte; SP increments by 2). Branches within the current 2 KB page.
  • LCALL <addr16> (3 Bytes, 2 Machine Cycles): Pushes \(\text{PC}_{\text{next}}\) onto the stack and branches anywhere in 64 KB code memory.
  • RET (Return from Subroutine — 1 Byte, 2 Machine Cycles): Pops the 2-byte return address from the stack (high byte first, then low byte; SP decrements by 2) and loads it into the Program Counter to resume execution.
  • RETI (Return from Interrupt — 1 Byte, 2 Machine Cycles): Performs the identical stack-pop sequence as RET, but additionally clears the internal interrupt-in-service flip-flop. This re-enables lower- or equal-priority interrupts that were blocked while servicing the ISR.
Relative Offset Calculation Equation (SJMP / DJNZ / CJNE)

The 8-bit signed relative displacement byte is calculated as:

$$\text{Offset} = \text{Target Address} - (\text{Instruction Address} + \text{Instruction Length})$$

If \(\text{Offset} < 0\), convert to 8-bit two's complement: \(\text{Hex Byte} = 100\text{H} - |\text{Offset}|\). Legal range: \(-128 \le \text{Offset} \le +127\).

3. Conditional Branching and Decision Structures

Unlike processors with individual condition code flags for every branch, the 8051 provides powerful compound comparison instructions:

MnemonicBytesCyclesCondition Evaluated & Branch Decision
JZ rel / JNZ rel22Branches if Accumulator A is zero (JZ) or non-zero (JNZ). Directly tests A register contents; no Zero flag exists in PSW!
JC rel / JNC rel22Branches if Carry flag CY = 1 (JC) or CY = 0 (JNC).
JB bit, rel / JNB bit, rel32Branches if specified direct bit is 1 (JB) or 0 (JNB). Samples pin inputs or RAM flags without altering Accumulator.
JBC bit, rel32Jump if Bit is Set and Clear Bit. If target bit = 1, branches and atomically resets the bit to 0. Perfect for interrupt status polling.
CJNE dest, src, rel32Compares destination and source. If \(dest \ne src\), branch taken. If \(dest < src\) (unsigned), sets Carry flag CY = 1; otherwise clears CY = 0!
DJNZ <byte>, rel2–32Decrements target register or direct byte. If the decremented value is non-zero, branch taken. Foundation of hardware delay loops.
Placement Trap — The 2 KB Page Rollover & RET vs RETI Lockout: 1. AJMP Boundary Hazard: If an AJMP instruction sits at address 07FEH, fetching its 2 bytes increments PC to 0800H. The CPU calculates the target using the new page (0800H–0FFFH), jumping to an unintended address in Page 1 instead of Page 0! High-quality assemblers detect this and flag an error.
2. RET in ISR Fatal Trap: If an Interrupt Service Routine exits with RET instead of RETI, the CPU returns to the main code, but its internal interrupt priority latch remains asserted. The MCU will never service another interrupt of that priority level or lower until power is cycled!

Key Takeaways & Interview Checklist

  • Branch ranges: SJMP (-128 to +127 bytes, relocatable), AJMP (within same 2 KB page, 11-bit address), LJMP (anywhere in 64 KB, 16-bit address).
  • Subroutine return: RET for functions; RETI for ISRs (clears interrupt-active flip-flop).
  • CJNE sets Carry flag if \(dest < src\), enabling instantaneous magnitude comparison in a single 3-byte instruction.
  • Zero testing: JZ and JNZ test Accumulator bits directly via internal NOR gating—there is no Z flag in the 8051 PSW!

es-8051-basic-assembly-programs.title: Basic ALPs in Topics 3.1 -3.2
es-8051-basic-assembly-programs.body:
Assembly Language Programming (ALP) directly translates theoretical instruction sets into deterministic, cycle-accurate firmware algorithms. In industrial electrical and electronics engineering, ALPs perform time-critical sensor acquisition, multi-byte mathematical modeling, data block transfers, code conversion, and table lookups. This lesson develops production-standard assembly subroutines demonstrating 16-bit arithmetic, lookup table synthesis, and array sorting on the classic 8051 core.

1. Block Data Movement and Memory Replication

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Basic ALPs in Topics 3.1 -3.2

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Basic ALPs in Topics 3.1 -3.2.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

Data movement algorithms transfer sensor telemetry blocks between fast internal scratchpad RAM (00H–7FH) and external non-volatile SRAM/FRAM (0000H–FFFFH) accessed through the 16-bit DPTR. 

; ==============================================================
; BLOCK TRANSFER: Copy N bytes from Internal RAM (30H) to Ext RAM (2000H)
; ==============================================================
            MOV   R0, #30H          ; Source pointer in internal RAM (1 MC)
            MOV   DPTR, #2000H      ; Destination pointer in external RAM (2 MC)
            MOV   R7, #64           ; Byte counter N = 64 (1 MC)
COPY_LOOP:  MOV   A, @R0            ; Fetch byte from internal RAM (1 MC)
            MOVX  @DPTR, A          ; Write byte to external RAM via WR# (2 MC)
            INC   R0                ; Advance source pointer (1 MC)
            INC   DPTR              ; Advance destination pointer (2 MC)
            DJNZ  R7, COPY_LOOP     ; Decrement counter and loop if != 0 (2 MC)
            RET                     ; Return to caller (2 MC)

Each loop iteration requires exactly 8 machine cycles (\(1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 8\text{ MC}\)). At 12 MHz (\(1.0\,\mu\text{s}/\text{MC}\)), copying 64 bytes consumes \(4\text{ (setup)} + (64 \times 8) + 2\text{ (ret)} = 518\,\mu\text{s}\).

2. Multi-Byte 16-Bit Arithmetic with Carry Propagation

Because the 8051 ALU is strictly 8-bit, 16-bit and 32-bit mathematical operations require multi-precision chaining where the Carry flag links sequential word operations: 

; ==============================================================
; 16-BIT ADDITION: (R3:R2) + (R5:R4) -> Result in (R3:R2)
; ==============================================================
ADD_16BIT:  MOV   A, R2             ; Load lower byte of operand 1 (1 MC)
            ADD   A, R4             ; Add lower byte of operand 2, sets CY (1 MC)
            MOV   R2, A             ; Store lower byte of sum (1 MC)
            MOV   A, R3             ; Load upper byte of operand 1 (1 MC)
            ADDC  A, R5             ; Add upper byte + Carry from lower sum (1 MC)
            MOV   R3, A             ; Store upper byte of sum (1 MC)
            RET

; ==============================================================
; 16-BIT SUBTRACTION: (R3:R2) - (R5:R4) -> Result in (R3:R2)
; ==============================================================
SUB_16BIT:  CLR   C                 ; MANDATORY: Clear carry before subtraction!
            MOV   A, R2             ; Load lower byte of minuend
            SUBB  A, R4             ; Subtract lower byte of subtrahend
            MOV   R2, A             ; Store lower byte of difference
            MOV   A, R3             ; Load upper byte of minuend
            SUBB  A, R5             ; Subtract upper byte with borrow from low byte
            MOV   R3, A             ; Store upper byte of difference
            RET
Block Transfer Loop Overhead & Execution Cycles

The total execution cycles for an \(N\)-byte memory transfer loop is given by:

$$\text{Total Cycles} = \text{Setup Cycles} + N \times \left( \text{Read}_{MC} + \text{Write}_{MC} + \text{Inc}_{MC} + \text{DJNZ}_{MC} \right) + \text{RET}_{MC}$$

For internal-to-external RAM: \(\text{Setup} = 4\), \(\text{Loop} = 8\text{ MC/byte}\), \(\text{RET} = 2\). Transfer throughput: \(\text{Throughput} = \frac{N}{\text{Total Time}}\,\text{B/s}\).

3. Program ROM Lookup Tables for Fast Font/Math Conversion

The MOVC A, @A+DPTR instruction is the cornerstone of embedded lookup tables. The following routine converts a 4-bit hexadecimal nibble (0–F in Accumulator A) into its equivalent 7-segment display cathode code in a single lookup: 

; ==============================================================
; HEX TO 7-SEGMENT CONVERSION ROUTINE (Common Cathode)
; ==============================================================
HEX_TO_7SEG:
            ANL   A, #0FH           ; Mask upper nibble, ensuring 0 <= A <= 15
            MOV   DPTR, #SEG_TABLE  ; Load base address of lookup table in ROM
            MOVC  A, @A+DPTR        ; Fetch 7-segment pattern into Accumulator
            RET

; Segment table stored in Flash/ROM (a-b-c-d-e-f-g-dp active HIGH):
SEG_TABLE:  DB    3FH, 06H, 5BH, 4FH, 66H, 6DH, 7DH, 07H
            DB    7FH, 6FH, 77H, 7CH, 39H, 5EH, 79H, 71H

4. Array Sorting: Bubble Sort Implementation

Sorting an array of \(N\) numbers stored in internal RAM addresses (starting at 50H) using the Bubble Sort algorithm. The outer loop executes \(N-1\) passes, while the inner loop compares adjacent elements using CJNE and exchanges them if out of order: 

; ==============================================================
; BUBBLE SORT: Sort N bytes in ascending order at RAM 50H
; ==============================================================
            MOV   R7, #09H          ; Outer loop count (N - 1 passes, for N=10)
OUTER_PASS: MOV   R0, #50H          ; Pointer to start of array
            MOV   A, R7
            MOV   R6, A             ; Inner loop count = remaining passes
INNER_PASS: MOV   A, @R0            ; Fetch element [i]
            MOV   R2, A             ; Preserve element [i] in R2
            INC   R0                ; Advance pointer to element [i+1]
            MOV   A, @R0            ; Fetch element [i+1]
            CLR   C
            SUBB  A, R2             ; Compare: Element[i+1] - Element[i]
            JNC   NO_SWAP           ; If Element[i+1] >= Element[i], order is correct
            ; Swap elements if Element[i] > Element[i+1]
            MOV   A, @R0            ; Load Element[i+1]
            XCH   A, R2             ; Swap with Element[i] in R2
            MOV   @R0, A            ; Put Element[i] into address [i+1]
            DEC   R0                ; Back up pointer to address [i]
            MOV   @R0, AR2          ; Put Element[i+1] into address [i]
            INC   R0                ; Restore pointer to address [i+1]
NO_SWAP:    DJNZ  R6, INNER_PASS    ; Decrement inner pass counter
            DJNZ  R7, OUTER_PASS    ; Decrement outer pass counter
            RET
Placement Trap — The Missing DEC DPTR & Accumulator Destruction: 1. Standard 8051 hardware provides INC DPTR but omits DEC DPTR! If you need to scan an external array backward, you cannot write DEC DPTR. You must either manipulate DPL directly (handling the underflow to DPH manually) or add 0FFFFH in two's complement.
2. In lookup tables, MOVC A, @A+DPTR overwrites the index in Accumulator A with the retrieved table data. If you need the original index for subsequent logic, you must preserve it in another register before executing MOVC.

Key Takeaways & Interview Checklist

  • Block transfer: Loop overhead is 8 machine cycles per byte using MOVX and INC DPTR.
  • 16-bit arithmetic: Always ADD the lower byte first, then ADDC the upper byte; for subtraction, issue CLR C before the lower byte SUBB.
  • Lookup tables: MOVC A, @A+DPTR executes in 2 machine cycles and consumes zero RAM; maximum direct single-index table size is 256 bytes.
  • Bubble sort: Uses SUBB or CJNE for comparison, and XCH for in-place RAM swapping.

es-8051-embedded-c-programming.title: Embedded C Programming – Declaring variables, Delay generation and port programming in Embedded C
es-8051-embedded-c-programming.body:
While assembly language provides cycle-by-cycle hardware control, modern industrial microcontroller development overwhelmingly relies on Embedded C (notably the Keil C51 cross-compiler). Embedded C delivers rapid development, modular abstraction, maintainability, and portable driver architectures. However, efficient 8051 C programming requires deep comprehension of the underlying 8-bit hardware architecture—specifically memory space extensions (data, bdata, xdata, code), register-mapped bit types (sbit, sfr), memory models (Small vs Large), and volatile loop optimization dynamics.

1. Keil C51 Hardware Data Types and Memory Space Qualifiers

Standard ANSI C has no concept of separate memory spaces or single-bit registers. Keil C51 introduces hardware-specific extensions to map C variables directly to 8051 physical structures:

KeywordSize / BitsMemory Space / Physical Address RangeDescription & Hardware Usage
bit1 bit20H–2FH in internal RAM (128 bits total)Independent single-bit software flags; 0 or 1. Packed into 16 bytes of bit RAM.
sbit1 bitBit-addressable SFRs (P0, P1, P2, P3, TCON, PSW)Declares an alias to a specific bit in a Special Function Register (e.g. sbit LED = P1^0;).
sfr8 bits80H–FFH in on-chip SFR spaceDefines an 8-bit Special Function Register byte address (e.g. sfr P1 = 0x90;).
sfr1616 bitsContiguous 16-bit SFR pairs (low byte at addr, high at addr+1)Defines 16-bit SFRs such as sfr16 DPTR = 0x82; (DPL at 82H, DPH at 83H).
data8 bits00H–7FH (Direct On-chip RAM)Fastest variable storage; 1 machine cycle direct addressing (MOV A, direct). Limited to 128 bytes.
bdata8 bits20H–2FH (Bit-addressable RAM)Byte variables whose individual bits can be manipulated directly with sbit aliases.
idata8 bits00H–FFH (Indirect On-chip RAM)Accesses full 256 bytes in 8052 cores using @R0/@R1 indirect addressing.
xdata8 bits0000H–FFFFH (External RAM)64 KB external SRAM. Access requires 16-bit DPTR (MOVX @DPTR; 2–4 machine cycles).
code8 bits0000H–FFFFH (Program Flash/ROM)Read-only constants and lookup tables placed in non-volatile ROM (MOVC). Conserves RAM.

2. Keil C51 Compiler Memory Models

The memory model selected in compiler build options sets the default storage class for all unadorned variables:

  • Small Model (Default & Recommended): All unadorned variables default to data (internal RAM 00H–7FH). Yields optimal speed and smallest code size. Heavy RAM usage requires manual placement of large arrays into xdata.
  • Compact Model: Variables default to pdata (paged external RAM; 256 bytes via @R0/@R1).
  • Large Model: Variables default to xdata (external 64 KB RAM). Every single variable read/write emits MOV DPTR, #addr followed by MOVX A, @DPTR, multiplying code size and cutting execution speed by 50–75%.

3. Calibrated Software Delay Generation in Embedded C

Software delay loops in C depend on compiler optimization levels and variable types. Because an 8-bit MCU performs 16-bit arithmetic using multi-instruction sequences, using unsigned int counters generates more cycles per loop than unsigned char: 

#include <reg51.h>

// Calibrated 1 ms delay function for 8051 running at 11.0592 MHz
void delay_ms(unsigned int ms) {
    unsigned int i;
    unsigned char j;
    for(i = 0; i < ms; i++) {
        // Inner loop calibrated for exactly 1 millisecond
        for(j = 0; j < 120; j++) {
            // volatile qualifier ensures compiler does not optimize empty loop away
        }
    }
}
Embedded C Software Delay Loop Estimation

The time delay produced by nested C for loops is approximately:

$$T_{delay} \approx N_{outer} \times \left( k_{inner} \times N_{inner} + C_{overhead} \right) \times \frac{12}{f_{osc}}$$

Where \(k_{inner}\) is the assembly machine cycle count generated per inner loop iteration (typically 4 to 8 cycles in Keil C51), and \(C_{overhead}\) is the outer loop loop-reloading overhead.

4. I/O Port Programming and Bit Manipulation in C

The 8051 ports (P0–P3) are memory-mapped to SFR addresses 80H, 90H, A0H, and B0H. In C51, reg51.h provides direct byte access to P1 and bit access via sbit: 

#include <reg51.h>

// Declare individual port bit pins
sbit LED_PIN   = P1^0;      // Output: LED connected to P1.0
sbit PUSH_BTN  = P1^7;      // Input: Push button connected to P1.7

void main(void) {
    // STEP 1: Initialize port pins
    LED_PIN = 0;            // Turn LED OFF (active high)
    PUSH_BTN = 1;           // MANDATORY: Write 1 to configure P1.7 as INPUT!

    while(1) {
        // Read input pin
        if(PUSH_BTN == 0) {  // Active LOW button pressed
            delay_ms(20);   // Software switch debouncing delay (20 ms)
            if(PUSH_BTN == 0) {
                LED_PIN = ~LED_PIN; // Toggle LED state
                while(PUSH_BTN == 0); // Wait for button release
            }
        }
    }
}
Placement Trap — Dead Loop Elimination & Large Model Penalty: 1. Dead Loop Elimination: If you compile an empty delay loop (for(i=0; i<1000; i++);) with Keil optimization level 8 without the volatile qualifier, the compiler deletes the entire loop because it has no side effects! Always declare delay counters as volatile.
2. Reading Quasi-Bidirectional Ports: You CANNOT read an external switch input from a port pin if the port latch currently holds a 0! Writing 0 turns ON the internal NMOS pulldown transistor, forcing the physical pin to ground regardless of external switch voltage. Always write 1 to the pin beforehand (e.g. P1 |= 0xF0;) to float the line before reading.

Key Takeaways & Interview Checklist

  • Keil keywords: sbit maps to SFR bits; sfr maps to 8-bit SFR bytes; bit maps to 128 bits in RAM 20H–2FH.
  • Memory spaces: data (fastest direct RAM, 128 B), xdata (external RAM, 64 KB via DPTR), code (read-only program ROM).
  • Port inputs: Must write logic 1 to the port pin before reading to turn off the lower NMOS transistor.
  • Compiler models: Always default to the Small model; avoid Large model unless external RAM is mandatory.

es-8051-alp-delay-port-programming.title: ALP: Time delay and I/O port programming
es-8051-alp-delay-port-programming.body:
Precise time delay generation and robust GPIO handling are the dual cornerstones of assembly-level embedded control. In safety-critical industrial applications—such as thyristor firing pulse generation, inverter gate driver timing, and stepper motor commutation—software execution must achieve microsecond accuracy. This lesson provides rigorous mathematical cycle derivation for single, nested, and triple register delay loops, alongside an in-depth analysis of the 8051 quasi-bidirectional port structure and Read-Modify-Write (RMW) hardware circuitry.

1. Mathematical Derivation of Cycle-Accurate Assembly Delays

Unlike high-level compilers whose machine code varies with optimization settings, assembly delay subroutines are deterministic. Every instruction consumes an exact integer number of machine cycles:

  • Single Register Delay Loop: 
    DELAY_1REG: MOV   R2, #N            ; 1 machine cycle
AGAIN:      DJNZ  R2, AGAIN         ; 2 machine cycles (executed N times)
            RET                     ; 2 machine cycles
    The total machine cycles executed is: $$\text{Cycles} = 1 + (2 \times N) + 2 = 2N + 3\,\text{machine cycles}$$ For \(N = 250\) at 12 MHz (\(T_{mc} = 1.0\,\mu\text{s}\)), total delay = \(2(250) + 3 = 503\,\mu\text{s}\).
  • Two-Register Nested Delay Loop: 
    DELAY_2REG: MOV   R3, #M            ; 1 machine cycle
OUTER_LOOP: MOV   R2, #N            ; 1 machine cycle
INNER_LOOP: DJNZ  R2, INNER_LOOP    ; 2 machine cycles (N iterations)
            DJNZ  R3, OUTER_LOOP    ; 2 machine cycles (M iterations)
            RET                     ; 2 machine cycles
    In each pass of the outer loop, the inner loop executes: $$\text{Inner Loop Cycles} = 1\,\text{(MOV)} + 2N\,\text{(DJNZ)} + 2\,\text{(DJNZ R3)} = 2N + 3\,\text{cycles}$$ This sequence repeats \(M\) times. Adding initial setup and return overhead yields: $$\text{Total Cycles} = 1 + M \times (2N + 3) + 2 = 3 + M(2N + 3)$$ For \(M = 100, N = 200\) at 12 MHz: \(\text{Total Cycles} = 3 + 100(400 + 3) = 40,303\,\mu\text{s} \approx 40.3\,\text{ms}\).
Cycle-Accurate Nested Delay & Square Wave Frequency Equations

For a 2-register nested 8051 assembly delay loop:

$$t_{delay} = \left[ 3 + M(2N + 3) \right] \times \frac{12}{f_{osc}}$$

When toggling a GPIO pin symmetrically to produce a square wave with half-period \(t_{half}\):

$$f_{square} = \frac{1}{2 \times t_{half}} = \frac{1}{2 \times \text{Cycles}_{half} \times T_{mc}}$$

2. The Quasi-Bidirectional Port Architecture

The 8051's Ports 1, 2, and 3 are termed quasi-bidirectional because they can function as inputs or outputs without a dedicated Data Direction Register (such as TRIS on PIC or DDR on AVR):

  • Internal Pull-Up Circuitry: Each pin incorporates a weak internal pull-up FET (effective resistance \(\approx 50–100\,\text{k}\Omega\)). When the internal latch holds a logic 1, the lower NMOS pulldown transistor is turned OFF, and the weak internal pull-up pulls the pin HIGH. External circuitry can easily pull this pin LOW without damaging the MCU.
  • Input Mode Configuration: To use a port pin as an input, the CPU must write a 1 to the latch flip-flop (e.g. SETB P1.0). This turns the lower NMOS transistor OFF, allowing the external signal to drive the line. If a 0 were left in the latch, the lower NMOS would remain turned ON, clamping the pin hard to ground (0 V) and preventing any external device from asserting a HIGH.
  • Port 0 Difference: Port 0 lacks internal pull-up resistors! It has a pure open-drain pulldown NMOS in GPIO mode. To use Port 0 as output or input GPIO, external \(10\,\text{k}\Omega\) pull-up resistors to \(V_{CC}\) are strictly mandatory.

3. Read-Modify-Write (RMW) Instructions vs Standard Reads

The 8051 hardware features two distinct internal read paths: Read Pin and Read Latch:

CategoryInstructionsInternal Read PathEngineering Purpose
Standard Pin ReadMOV A, P1, MOV 30H, P2Samples the physical voltage pad via the Read Pin bufferReads real external digital inputs (switches, sensors). Requires latch Q=1 beforehand.
Read-Modify-Write (RMW)ANL P1, #mask, ORL P1, #mask, XRL P1, #mask, CPL P1.0, CLR P1.0, SETB P1.0, DJNZ P1, rel, JBC P1.0, relReads the internal output D-latch flip-flop directlyModifies specific bit(s) without risk of reading false zeros caused by heavy external analog loads on other pins.

4. Production Industrial ALP: Stepper Motor 4-Step Commutation

Driving a 4-phase unipolar stepper motor connected to Port 1 (P1.3–P1.0) through a ULN2003 Darlington driver. The routine outputs the 4-step sequence (09H \( o\) 0CH \( o\) 06H \( o\) 03H) with calibrated 10 ms inter-step delay: 

; ==============================================================
; STEPPER MOTOR 4-STEP DRIVE ROUTINE (Port 1, Pins P1.0-P1.3)
; ==============================================================
STEPPER_RUN:
            MOV   P1, #09H          ; Step 1: Coils A and D active (1001b)
            ACALL DELAY_10MS        ; Hold for 10 ms
            MOV   P1, #0CH          ; Step 2: Coils A and B active (1100b)
            ACALL DELAY_10MS        ; Hold for 10 ms
            MOV   P1, #06H          ; Step 3: Coils B and C active (0110b)
            ACALL DELAY_10MS        ; Hold for 10 ms
            MOV   P1, #03H          ; Step 4: Coils C and D active (0011b)
            ACALL DELAY_10MS        ; Hold for 10 ms
            SJMP  STEPPER_RUN       ; Continuous rotation

; 10 ms Delay Subroutine at 12 MHz (10,000 Machine Cycles)
DELAY_10MS: MOV   R3, #25           ; Outer loop count M = 25
STEP_OUTER: MOV   R2, #198          ; Inner loop count N = 198
STEP_INNER: DJNZ  R2, STEP_INNER    ; Inner: 198 * 2 = 396 cycles
            DJNZ  R3, STEP_OUTER    ; Outer pass: 1 + 396 + 2 = 399 cycles
            RET                     ; Total = 3 + 25 * 399 = 9,978 cycles ~ 10 ms
Placement Trap — Port Latch Contention & DJNZ Loop Boundary 00H: 1. The Loaded Transistor Trap: If P1.0 drives the base of a heavily saturated NPN BJT, the pin pad is clamped to 0.7 V. If you execute a non-RMW read like MOV A, P1, the CPU reads bit 0 as a 0. If you then write back MOV P1, A, you will accidentally turn OFF the transistor! RMW instructions prevent this by reading the latch flip-flop.
2. DJNZ 00H Roll-Over: In DJNZ Rn, label, the register is decremented before testing for zero. If Rn contains 00H upon entering the loop, decrementing produces 0FFH (255 decimal)—causing the loop to execute 256 times rather than zero times!

Key Takeaways & Interview Checklist

  • Nested delay math: Exact cycles = \(3 + M(2N + 3)\). Never omit the outer loop DJNZ or inner reload instruction overhead.
  • Quasi-bidirectional I/O: Ports 1–3 have internal weak pull-ups; Port 0 is true open-drain requiring external 10 k\(\Omega\) pull-ups.
  • Input setup: Writing 1 to a port pin turns OFF the lower NMOS driver, permitting external input sampling.
  • RMW mechanics: Instructions like CPL P1.0 read the internal latch flip-flop, not the physical pad, preserving correct state under analog loading.

es-8051-timers-tcon-tmod.title: 8051 Timers/Counters: TCON, TMOD, Modes 0–3, and Delay Generation
es-8051-timers-tcon-tmod.body:
The classic Intel 8051 microcontroller incorporates two independent 16-bit timer/counter peripherals: Timer 0 and Timer 1. Operating directly on silicon hardware, these timers free the central processing unit from executing wasteful, blocking software delay loops. Whether generating deterministic millisecond tick delays for an embedded operating system, producing precision baud rate clocks for asynchronous serial communication, or tallying high-speed external events on industrial sensors, mastering the control registers (TMOD and TCON) and timer operating modes (0 through 3) is a core competency for embedded systems engineers.

1. Timer vs. Counter Principles & Hardware Operation

Although designated as "Timer/Counter", both units use identical 16-bit counting hardware (accessible as byte registers TH0/TL0 and TH1/TL1). The fundamental distinction lies entirely in the clock source selected by the \(C/\overline{\text{T}}\) bit in the Timer Mode (TMOD) register:

  • Timer Mode (\(C/\overline{\text{T}} = 0\)): The register increments once every machine cycle. In classic 8051 architecture, one machine cycle equals 12 oscillator periods (\(T_{mc} = 12 / f_{osc}\)). At \(f_{osc} = 11.0592\text{ MHz}\), the timer ticks every \(1.0851\,\mu\text{s}\); at \(12.0\text{ MHz}\), it ticks every \(1.0000\,\mu\text{s}\). Because the clock is derived from a crystal oscillator, the timer provides deterministic real-time delays.
  • Counter Mode (\(C/\overline{\text{T}} = 1\)): The register increments on every 1-to-0 negative transition detected on external pin T0 (P3.4) or T1 (P3.5). The CPU samples external pin states during phase 2 of state 5 (S5P2) of every machine cycle. Detecting a high-to-low transition requires at least two machine cycles (one cycle high, one cycle low). Consequently, the maximum external input pulse frequency is strictly limited to \(f_{osc} / 24\) (e.g. 500 kHz at 12 MHz).
FeatureTimer Mode (\(C/\overline{\text{T}} = 0\))Counter Mode (\(C/\overline{\text{T}} = 1\))
Clock Input SourceInternal prescaled clock (\(f_{osc} / 12\))External falling-edge pulses on P3.4 (T0) / P3.5 (T1)
Clock PeriodFixed: \(T_{mc} = 12 / f_{osc}\)Aperiodic / External event rate
Maximum Frequency\(f_{osc} / 12\) (1.0 MHz at 12 MHz crystal)\(f_{osc} / 24\) (500 kHz at 12 MHz crystal)
Primary ApplicationPrecise delays, periodic task scheduling, UART baud ratesPulse counting, tachometers, flow meters, event frequency

2. The TMOD Register & Operating Modes 0 to 3

The Timer Mode register (TMOD, SFR 89H) is an 8-bit register that configures the operational mode of both timers. The upper nibble controls Timer 1, while the lower nibble controls Timer 0. Crucially, TMOD is NOT bit-addressable; any modification must write the entire 8-bit byte (e.g. MOV TMOD, #01H).

  • GATE (Bit 7 / Bit 3): Gating control. When GATE = 0, the timer runs whenever software sets the run bit (TRx = 1). When GATE = 1, the timer runs only when TRx = 1 AND the external interrupt pin INTx# (P3.2 for T0, P3.3 for T1) is held HIGH. This hardware gating enables microsecond pulse-width measurement without CPU polling overhead.
  • C/T# (Bit 6 / Bit 2): Clock selector (0 = Internal Timer, 1 = External Counter).
  • M1, M0 (Bits 5-4 / Bits 1-0): Mode selection bits establishing four distinct timer configurations:
    • Mode 0 (M1=0, M0=0) — 13-bit Timer: Employs 8 bits of THx and the lower 5 bits of TLx (bits 4–0) as a 13-bit counter (range 0 to 8,191 counts). Preserved strictly for backward compatibility with the legacy Intel 8048. Rarely used in modern firmware.
    • Mode 1 (M1=0, M0=1) — 16-bit Timer: Chains all 8 bits of TLx and THx to form a full 16-bit up-counter (range 0 to 65,535 counts). Upon rolling over from FFFFH to 0000H, the overflow flag TFx is asserted. Ideal for general-purpose millisecond delays. Requires manual software reloading of both THx and TLx registers after each overflow.
    • Mode 2 (M1=1, M0=0) — 8-bit Auto-Reload: TLx functions as an 8-bit counter (0 to 255 counts). The reload byte is loaded into THx. When TLx overflows from FFH to 00H, the hardware automatically re-copies the contents of THx into TLx in a single clock cycle while setting TFx. This eliminates software reload jitter and is the standard generator for UART baud rates.
    • Mode 3 (M1=1, M0=1) — Split Timer: Timer 0 splits into two independent 8-bit timers: TL0 (uses Timer 0 control bits TR0 and TF0) and TH0 (usurps Timer 1 control bits TR1 and TF1). Timer 1 is left with no run bit or interrupt flag, but can still run as an un-gated baud rate clock in Mode 0, 1, or 2.

3. The TCON Register & Timer Control Flags

The Timer Control register (TCON, SFR 88H) is bit-addressable. Its upper nibble contains timer run control bits and overflow status flags:

  • TF1 (TCON.7) & TF0 (TCON.5): Timer 1 and Timer 0 overflow flags. Set by hardware whenever the respective timer rolls over from all 1s to all 0s. In polling mode, firmware must explicitly clear this flag using CLR TFx. When vectoring to a timer Interrupt Service Routine, the 8051 hardware automatically clears TFx.
  • TR1 (TCON.6) & TR0 (TCON.4): Timer 1 and Timer 0 run control bits. Setting SETB TRx turns the timer on; clearing CLR TRx halts the timer.
  • IE1, IT1, IE0, IT0 (TCON.3–0): External interrupt flags and edge/level trigger selectors.
Timer Delay & Initial Count Formulations

For a classic 8051 running on crystal frequency \(f_{osc}\), the machine cycle period \(T_{mc}\) and initial load count \(N\) are given by:

$$T_{mc} = \frac{12}{f_{osc}}, \quad N_{counts} = \frac{\text{Delay}}{T_{mc}}, \quad N_{initial} = 65536 - N_{counts} \quad (\text{Mode 1})$$

For Mode 2 auto-reload with reload byte \(\text{THx}\):

$$f_{overflow} = \frac{f_{osc}}{12 \times (256 - \text{THx})}, \quad f_{sq} = \frac{f_{overflow}}{2}$$

4. Assembly Language Programming (ALP) for Timer Delay

The standard sequence for generating a time delay using polling is: (1) configure TMOD; (2) load initial count into THx:TLx; (3) start timer with SETB TRx; (4) monitor overflow with JNB TFx, $; (5) stop timer with CLR TRx; (6) reset flag with CLR TFx. 

; ==============================================================
; 8051 ALP: 10 ms Delay Routine using Timer 0 Mode 1 (f_osc = 12 MHz)
; Initial Count = 65536 - 10000 = 55536 = D8F0H (TH0=D8H, TL0=F0H)
; ==============================================================
DELAY_10MS:
            MOV   TMOD, #01H        ; Timer 0 in 16-bit Mode 1 (1 MC)
            MOV   TH0, #0D8H        ; Load high byte (2 MC)
            MOV   TL0, #0F0H        ; Load low byte (2 MC)
            SETB  TR0               ; Start Timer 0 (1 MC)
WAIT_TF0:   JNB   TF0, WAIT_TF0     ; Poll TF0 until roll-over sets it (2 MC)
            CLR   TR0               ; Stop Timer 0 (1 MC)
            CLR   TF0               ; Clear TF0 flag (CRITICAL in polling!) (1 MC)
            RET                     ; Return to caller (2 MC)
Placement Trap — TMOD Bit-Addressability & TFx Polling Clearance: 1. Writing SETB TMOD.0 or CLR TMOD.3 produces an assembly failure or corrupts lower RAM bits. TMOD is strictly byte-accessible. Always use MOV TMOD, #imm or logical instructions (ANL TMOD, #mask, ORL TMOD, #mask).
2. In polling mode, hardware never auto-clears TFx! If you omit CLR TF0, subsequent calls will see TF0 = 1 instantly, causing the polling loop to fall through with zero delay!

Key Takeaways & Interview Checklist

  • Timer clock = \(f_{osc} / 12\); Counter clock = falling edge on external pin (max frequency = \(f_{osc} / 24\)).
  • TMOD (89H): byte-only. Mode 1 is 16-bit manual reload; Mode 2 is 8-bit auto-reload (hardware copies THx to TLx).
  • TCON (88H): bit-addressable. TRx turns timer on/off; TFx asserts on roll-over.
  • Hardware auto-clears TFx only when vectoring to an interrupt; polling firmware must execute CLR TFx explicitly.

🎛️ 8051 Microcontroller TMOD Register Bit-Field Map

The TMOD register (8-bit, non-bit-addressable) configures Timer 1 (bits 7-4) and Timer 0 (bits 3-0):

BitNameFunction
7 / 3GATEGating control (1 = Timer runs only when INTx pin is HIGH; 0 = Software TRx control)
6 / 2C/TCounter/Timer Select (0 = Internal clock oscillator/12; 1 = External pin falling edge counter)
5,4 / 1,0M1, M0Mode selection (00: 13-bit, 01: 16-bit Timer, 10: 8-bit Auto-reload, 11: Split Timer)

es-8051-serial-scon-smod-sbuf.title: 8051 Serial Port: SCON, SMOD, SBUF, Modes, Baud Rates, and ALP
es-8051-serial-scon-smod-sbuf.body:
Serial data transmission transmits information bit-by-bit over a single conductive wire, drastically slashing pin count, board complexity, and cabling costs compared to wide parallel buses. The 8051 microcontroller incorporates a full-duplex Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter (UART) peripheral capable of simultaneous transmission and reception over external pins TXD (P3.1) and RXD (P3.0). Understanding the dual-register architecture of SBUF, the control bits of SCON, the baud-doubling role of SMOD in PCON, and the mathematics of Timer 1 auto-reload baud generation is fundamental for embedded IoT communication.

1. Full-Duplex Architecture & The SBUF Mystery

The 8051 serial subsystem interfaces with firmware through the Serial Data Buffer (SBUF, SFR address 99H). In silicon, address 99H maps to two physically separate internal registers:

  • Transmit Buffer (Write-Only): Executing MOV SBUF, A writes data into the transmit buffer and triggers the internal parallel-to-serial shift register. The byte is framed with start and stop bits and clocked out serially via TXD (P3.1).
  • Receive Buffer (Read-Only): Executing MOV A, SBUF reads the contents of the independent receive buffer. When serial data arrives on RXD (P3.0), the serial-to-parallel shift register clocks in the bits and latches the completed byte into the receive buffer, asserting the receive flag RI.

Because these two registers share the same address, reading SBUF immediately after writing does not read back what was just written; it reads the last character received on RXD.

2. The SCON Register & Serial Operating Modes

The Serial Control register (SCON, SFR 98H) is bit-addressable and configures framing, receiver enable, and communication flags:

BitSymbolFunction
SCON.7SM0Serial Port Mode specifier bit 0
SCON.6SM1Serial Port Mode specifier bit 1
SCON.5SM2Multiprocessor communication enable bit (Modes 2 & 3)
SCON.4RENReceiver Enable bit (1 = Enable reception; 0 = Disable)
SCON.3TB8Transmitted 9th data bit in Modes 2 and 3 (parity or address bit)
SCON.2RB8Received 9th data bit in Modes 2 and 3 (or stop bit in Mode 1)
SCON.1TITransmit Interrupt flag. Set by hardware at start of stop bit. Must be cleared by software!
SCON.0RIReceive Interrupt flag. Set by hardware halfway through stop bit. Must be cleared by software!

The combinations of SM0 and SM1 establish four serial communication modes:

  • Mode 0 (SM0=0, SM1=0) — Synchronous Shift Register: 8 data bits are transmitted/received synchronously via RXD while TXD outputs the shift clock pulses. Baud rate is fixed at \(f_{osc} / 12\). Used for expanding I/O using external serial shift registers (e.g. 74HC595).
  • Mode 1 (SM0=0, SM1=1) — 8-bit UART with Variable Baud Rate: Standard asynchronous framing: 1 start bit (low), 8 data bits (LSB first), and 1 stop bit (high) — total 10 bits per character.
