pe-1ph-half-bridge-inverter.title: Single-Phase Half-Bridge Voltage Source Inverter with R and RL Loads
pe-1ph-half-bridge-inverter.body:
Prerequisite: Power MOSFETs and IGBTs & Wide-Bandgap Devices.

◆ Why this matters

An inverter is a static converter that transforms DC electric power into AC electric power at a desired output voltage and frequency. Inverters are the cornerstone of renewable energy systems (solar PV, wind energy), uninterruptible power supplies (UPS), electric vehicle (EV) powertrains, and variable-frequency AC motor drives (VFDs). The single-phase half-bridge inverter represents the fundamental building block of voltage source inverters (VSIs), introducing the critical concepts of split DC midpoint reference, complementary switching, and antiparallel feedback diode conduction.

◆ Circuit Topology & Operating Principle

The single-phase half-bridge VSI requires a 3-wire DC source, practically created by connecting two identical split capacitors $C_1$ and $C_2$ across a total DC link voltage $V_{dc}$. The capacitor center tap $O$ serves as the virtual zero-voltage reference.

  • Two active power switches ($S_1$ and $S_2$, typically IGBTs or MOSFETs) form a single phase leg.
  • Two antiparallel diodes ($D_1$ and $D_2$), termed feedback diodes or freewheeling diodes, are connected across the switches.
  • The load impedance $Z$ is connected between the phase-leg midpoint $A$ and the capacitor neutral point $O$.

◆ Switching Operation & Output Waveforms

The switches $S_1$ and $S_2$ are gated in strict complement for half the time period ($T/2$) each:

  • Interval 1 ($0 le t < T/2$): Switch $S_1$ is gated ON while $S_2$ is OFF. Terminal $A$ connects to the positive DC bus ($+V_{dc}/2$). The output voltage is $v_o(t) = +V_{dc}/2$.
  • Interval 2 ($T/2 le t < T$): Switch $S_2$ is gated ON while $S_1$ is OFF. Terminal $A$ connects to the negative DC bus ($-V_{dc}/2$). The output voltage is $v_o(t) = -V_{dc}/2$.

Voltage Equations for Half-Bridge Inverter

Total RMS Output Voltage: $$V_{or} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T v_o(t)^2 dt} = \frac{V_{dc}}{2}$$

Fourier Series expansion of the square-wave output voltage:

$$v_o(t) = \sum_{n=1,3,5dots}^\infty \frac{4 (V_{dc}/2)}{n\pi} \sin(n\omega t) = \sum_{n=1,3,5dots}^\infty \frac{2V_{dc}}{n\pi} \sin(n\omega t)$$

Fundamental Peak Voltage: $$V_{o1,peak} = \frac{2V_{dc}}{\pi}$$

Fundamental RMS Output Voltage: $$V_{o1,rms} = \frac{V_{o1,peak}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{2} V_{dc}}{\pi} \approx 0.4502 V_{dc}$$

◆ Operation with RL Load & Role of Antiparallel Diodes

With an inductive RL load, the load current $i_o(t)$ cannot change direction instantaneously and lags the output square-wave voltage by phase angle $\phi_1 = \arctan(\omega L/R)$.

  • When $S_1$ turns off at $t = T/2$, current $i_o$ is still positive (flowing from $A$ to $O$). It cannot flow through incoming switch $S_2$ against its forward conduction path.
  • Instead, the stored inductive magnetic energy forces current through diode $D_2$ back into capacitor $C_2$.
  • During this interval, the voltage across the load is clamped to $-V_{dc}/2$ while current decays toward zero.
  • Once $i_o$ decays to zero, switch $S_2$ takes over and conducts negative current for the remainder of the half-cycle.

Placement Trap: DC Midpoint Voltage Fluctuation & Device Voltage Rating

Midpoint Fluctuation: In practical half-bridge inverters, the full AC load current enters and leaves the center point $O$ of capacitors $C_1$ and $C_2$. If the load current has any DC asymmetry, one capacitor charges more than the other, causing midpoint potential drift. Very large capacitance values or active voltage-balancing control loops are mandatory.

Voltage Stress: Even though the peak output voltage is only $V_{dc}/2$, when switch $S_2$ conducts, switch $S_1$ must block the entire DC link voltage $V_{dc}$! Never size the switch voltage rating for $V_{dc}/2$.

Common Interview Mistake: The Cause of Diode Conduction

Mistake: Believing that diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$ only conduct during fault or overvoltage conditions.

Correction: Diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$ conduct during every normal operating cycle of an inductive load. The angle of diode conduction is exactly equal to the load phase lag angle $\phi_1$. Antiparallel diodes are essential for reactive energy circulation back into the DC link.

pe-1ph-full-bridge-inverter.title: Single-Phase Full-Bridge Voltage Source Inverter and THD in Output Voltage
pe-1ph-full-bridge-inverter.body:
Prerequisite: Single-Phase Half-Bridge Inverter.

◆ Why this matters

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Single-Phase Full-Bridge Voltage Source Inverter and THD in Output Voltage

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Single-Phase Full-Bridge Voltage Source Inverter and THD in Output Voltage.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

The single-phase full-bridge (H-bridge) inverter overcomes the severe limitations of the half-bridge topology: it eliminates the need for a 3-wire center-tapped DC source, delivers twice the output voltage (and 4 times the power) from the same DC supply, and provides an additional zero-voltage switching state that enables advanced pulse-width modulation (PWM). In power electronics interviews, the mathematical derivation of Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) and the detailed conduction paths of RL loads across active switches and antiparallel diodes are premier evaluation topics.

◆ H-Bridge Circuit Topology & Switching States

The full-bridge inverter consists of four power switches ($S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4$) and four antiparallel feedback diodes ($D_1, D_2, D_3, D_4$) arranged in two phase legs across a single DC bus $V_{dc}$. The load is connected between the midpoints of the two legs ($A$ and $B$).

Active Switches Conduction Interval Output Voltage $v_o = v_A - v_B$
$S_1$ and $S_2$ ON $0 le t < T/2$ ($0$ to $\pi$) $+V_{dc}$ (Terminal $A$ high, $B$ low)
$S_3$ and $S_4$ ON $T/2 le t < T$ ($\pi$ to $2\pi$) $-V_{dc}$ (Terminal $B$ high, $A$ low)
$S_1, S_3$ or $S_2, S_4$ ON Freewheeling / Quasi-square $0$ V (Both terminals tied to same DC rail)

◆ Mathematical Derivation: Fourier Series & RMS Voltages

In square-wave operation, the output voltage alternates symmetrically between $+V_{dc}$ and $-V_{dc}$.

Full-Bridge Voltage Equations

Total RMS Output Voltage: $$V_{or} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T (\pm V_{dc})^2 dt} = V_{dc}$$

Fourier Series expansion (containing only odd harmonics due to half-wave symmetry):

$$v_o(t) = \sum_{n=1,3,5dots}^\infty \frac{4V_{dc}}{n\pi} \sin(n\omega t)$$

RMS of Fundamental Component ($n=1$):

$$V_{o1,rms} = \frac{4V_{dc}}{\pi \sqrt{2}} = \frac{2\sqrt{2} V_{dc}}{\pi} \approx 0.9003 V_{dc}$$

RMS of $n$-th Harmonic Component:

$$V_{on,rms} = \frac{V_{o1,rms}}{n} = \frac{2\sqrt{2} V_{dc}}{n\pi}$$

◆ Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) Derivation

Total Harmonic Distortion ($THD$) quantifies the harmonic content relative to the fundamental component:

Analytical THD Calculation for Square-Wave VSI

$$THD = \frac{\sqrt{\sum_{n=3,5,7dots}^\infty V_{on,rms}^2}}{V_{o1,rms}} = \frac{\sqrt{V_{or}^2 - V_{o1,rms}^2}}{V_{o1,rms}} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{V_{or}}{V_{o1,rms}}\right)^2 - 1}$$

Substitute $V_{or} = V_{dc}$ and $V_{o1,rms} = \frac{2\sqrt{2} V_{dc}}{\pi}$:

$$\frac{V_{or}}{V_{o1,rms}} = \frac{V_{dc}}{\frac{2\sqrt{2} V_{dc}}{\pi}} = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}$$

$$\left(\frac{V_{or}}{V_{o1,rms}}\right)^2 = \frac{\pi^2}{8} \approx 1.2337$$

$$THD = \sqrt{\frac{\pi^2}{8} - 1} = \sqrt{1.23370 - 1} = \sqrt{0.23370} \approx 0.4834 implies \mathbf{48.34%}$$

Placement Trap: THD Independence from DC Voltage

Notice that $V_{dc}$ cancels out completely in the THD formula! The THD of an ideal square-wave inverter is strictly a constant geometric property of the square wave: 48.34%. A 12 V inverter and a 1000 V inverter have identical 48.34% voltage THD when operating in square-wave mode.

Common Interview Mistake: Full-Bridge vs Half-Bridge Power Ratio

Mistake: Assuming that because the full-bridge has 4 switches compared to 2 switches in a half-bridge, the power delivered is doubled ($2\times$).

Correction: For the same DC source voltage $V_{dc}$ and load resistance $R$:

$$P_{half} = \frac{V_{or,half}^2}{R} = \frac{(V_{dc}/2)^2}{R} = \frac{V_{dc}^2}{4R}, \quad P_{full} = \frac{V_{or,full}^2}{R} = \frac{V_{dc}^2}{R}$$

Therefore, $P_{full} = 4 \times P_{half}$! The output power is four times higher, not two times.

pe-3ph-inverter-180.title: Three-Phase Bridge Inverter: 180° Conduction Mode
pe-3ph-inverter-180.body:
Prerequisite: Single-Phase Full-Bridge Inverter.

◆ Why this matters

Three-phase voltage source inverters are the workhorse of industrial automation, driving three-phase induction motors, permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSM) in electric vehicles, and interfacing grid-scale solar and battery storage systems. Understanding the 180° conduction mode is the benchmark for studying multi-step AC synthesis, star-load neutral point shifting, and device commutation timing.

◆ Circuit Topology & Gating Sequence

A three-phase VSI comprises six switches ($S_1$ to $S_6$) with antiparallel diodes ($D_1$ to $D_6$) arranged in three legs:

  • Upper positive group: $S_1$ (Phase A), $S_3$ (Phase B), $S_5$ (Phase C).
  • Lower negative group: $S_4$ (Phase A), $S_6$ (Phase B), $S_2$ (Phase C).

In 180° conduction mode, each switch conducts for 180 electrical degrees ($T/2$). The switching signals of the three legs are mutually displaced by 120°:

Firing sequence (gated at intervals of 60°): $S_1 o S_2 o S_3 o S_4 o S_5 o S_6$.

◆ Conduction Intervals & Equivalent Circuits

At any given instant, exactly 3 switches are ON simultaneously (either two from the upper group and one from the lower group, or one from the upper and two from the lower).

Interval Active Switches Phase Voltages ($v_{an}, v_{bn}, v_{cn}$ across Star $R$ Load)
$0^\circ - 60^\circ$ $S_5, S_6, S_1$ (2 upper, 1 lower) $v_{an} = +V_{dc}/3, ; v_{bn} = -2V_{dc}/3, ; v_{cn} = +V_{dc}/3$
$60^\circ - 120^\circ$ $S_6, S_1, S_2$ (1 upper, 2 lower) $v_{an} = +2V_{dc}/3, ; v_{bn} = -V_{dc}/3, ; v_{cn} = -V_{dc}/3$
$120^\circ - 180^\circ$ $S_1, S_2, S_3$ (2 upper, 1 lower) $v_{an} = +V_{dc}/3, ; v_{bn} = +V_{dc}/3, ; v_{cn} = -2V_{dc}/3$
$180^\circ - 360^\circ$ Negative counterparts Symmetrical negative step voltages

RMS Voltage Equations: 180° Conduction Mode

RMS Line-to-Line Voltage ($V_{L,rms}$): The line voltage $v_{ab} = v_{an} - v_{bn}$ is a quasi-square wave of amplitude $V_{dc}$ with a pulse duration of 120° per half-cycle:

$$V_{L,rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi} \int_0^{2\pi/3} V_{dc}^2 d(\omega t)} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} V_{dc} \approx \mathbf{0.8165 V_{dc}}$$

RMS Phase Voltage ($V_{ph,rms}$): The phase voltage is a 6-step waveform taking values $\pm V_{dc}/3$ (for $120^\circ$) and $\pm 2V_{dc}/3$ (for $60^\circ$):

$$V_{ph,rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi} \left[\left(\frac{V_{dc}}{3}\right)^2 \frac{2\pi}{3} + \left(\frac{2V_{dc}}{3}\right)^2 \frac{\pi}{3}\right]} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} V_{dc} \approx \mathbf{0.4714 V_{dc}}$$

Note: $V_{L,rms} = \sqrt{3} \cdot V_{ph,rms} = \sqrt{3} \cdot \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} V_{dc}\right) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} V_{dc}$.

Fundamental Component of Line Voltage:

$$V_{L1,rms} = \frac{4 V_{dc}}{\sqrt{2} \pi} \sin(60^\circ) = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{\pi} V_{dc} \approx \mathbf{0.7797 V_{dc}}$$

Placement Trap: The Shoot-Through Hazard & Dead-Time Requirement

In 180° conduction mode, switch $S_4$ is commanded to turn on at the exact moment switch $S_1$ is turned off in the same leg. However, practical power devices have finite turn-off storage time ($t_{off} > 0$). If $S_4$ turns on while $S_1$ has not fully extinguished, a direct short-circuit across the DC bus occurs (shoot-through). A hardware/software blanking delay (dead time $t_d \approx 1 - 3;\mu\text{s}$) is strictly mandatory in all commercial gate drivers.

Common Interview Mistake: Triplen Harmonics in 3-Phase Inverters

Mistake: Believing that 3rd, 9th, and 15th harmonics appear in the line-to-line output voltage.

Correction: In any three-phase three-wire balanced system, triplen harmonics ($3n$) are co-phasal (identical in magnitude and phase across all 3 phases). Therefore, when calculating line-to-line voltage $v_{ab} = v_{an} - v_{bn}$, triplen harmonics completely cancel out ($v_{ab}$ contains only orders $n = 6k \pm 1 = 5, 7, 11, 13dots$).

pe-3ph-inverter-120.title: Three-Phase Bridge Inverter: 120° Conduction Mode
pe-3ph-inverter-120.body:
Prerequisite: Three-Phase Bridge Inverter: 180° Conduction Mode.

◆ Why this matters

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Three-Phase Bridge Inverter: 120° Conduction Mode

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Three-Phase Bridge Inverter: 120° Conduction Mode.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

While 180° conduction mode offers higher fundamental output voltage, it carries an inherent risk of DC link shoot-through. The 120° conduction mode introduces an ingenious topological solution: by gating each switch for only 120° instead of 180°, an inherent 60° dead band naturally separates the conduction of complementary switches in every leg. This mode is extensively utilized in brushless DC (BLDC) motor electronic commutators and provides a classic comparative analysis benchmark for power electronics examinations.

◆ Switching Operation & State Sequence

In 120° conduction mode, each switch conducts for 120 electrical degrees ($T/3$) and remains off for 240°. Across the entire bridge:

  • At any given instant, exactly 2 switches conduct simultaneously: one from the upper group ($S_1, S_3, S_5$) and one from the lower group ($S_4, S_6, S_2$).
  • One entire phase leg is completely floating (unconnected to either DC rail) during each 60° interval.

Voltage Equations: 120° Conduction Mode

Phase Voltage ($V_{ph,rms}$): During any 60° interval, the DC voltage $V_{dc}$ divides equally across two series-connected phases of a balanced star resistive load, while the third phase voltage is zero. Thus, the phase voltage waveform is a 120° quasi-square wave of amplitude $V_{dc}/2$:

$$V_{ph,rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi} \int_0^{2\pi/3} \left(\frac{V_{dc}}{2}\right)^2 d(\omega t)} = \frac{V_{dc}}{2} \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} = \frac{V_{dc}}{\sqrt{6}} \approx \mathbf{0.4082 V_{dc}}$$

Line-to-Line Voltage ($V_{L,rms}$): The line voltage takes values of $\pm V_{dc}$ (for 60°), $\pm V_{dc}/2$ (for 120°), and $0$ (for 60°), resulting in a 6-step waveform:

$$V_{L,rms} = \frac{V_{dc}}{\sqrt{2}} \approx \mathbf{0.7071 V_{dc}}$$

Fundamental Component of Line Voltage:

$$V_{L1,rms} = \frac{3}{\pi \sqrt{2}} V_{dc} \approx \mathbf{0.6752 V_{dc}}$$

◆ In-Depth Comparison: 180° vs 120° Conduction Modes

Feature 180° Conduction Mode 120° Conduction Mode
Switches conducting at any instant Exactly 3 switches Exactly 2 switches
Switch Conduction Duty $180^\circ / 360^\circ = 50%$ $120^\circ / 360^\circ = 33.3%$
Inherent Shoot-Through Margin $0^\circ$ (Requires external blanking time) $60^\circ$ dead band built-in naturally
RMS Line-to-Line Voltage ($V_{L,rms}$) $\sqrt{2/3} V_{dc} \approx 0.8165 V_{dc}$ $V_{dc} / \sqrt{2} \approx 0.7071 V_{dc}$
Fundamental Line RMS ($V_{L1,rms}$) $(\sqrt{6}/\pi) V_{dc} \approx 0.7797 V_{dc}$ $(3/(\pi\sqrt{2})) V_{dc} \approx 0.6752 V_{dc}$
Line Voltage Waveform Shape Quasi-square wave (120° pulse) 6-step stepped waveform
Phase Voltage Waveform Shape 6-step stepped waveform Quasi-square wave (120° pulse)

Placement Trap: Transposition of Waveform Shapes!

Notice the classic symmetry trap: In 180° mode, the line voltage is a quasi-square wave while the phase voltage is a 6-step wave. In 120° mode, the roles are exactly reversed: the phase voltage is a quasi-square wave, and the line voltage is a 6-step wave! Remembering this duality avoids catastrophic confusion in exam derivations.

Common Interview Mistake: Star vs Delta Load in 120° Mode

Mistake: Assuming that in 120° mode with an inductive or floating-neutral load, the phase voltage maintains clean flat steps of $V_{dc}/2$.

Correction: Because one terminal is completely disconnected for 60° in each half-cycle, in an inductive load the current freewheels through antiparallel diodes, clamping the floating phase to either $+V_{dc}$ or $0$ depending on current direction. The ideal $V_{dc}/2$ flat top occurs strictly with balanced purely resistive loads.

pe-pwm-spw-mpw.title: Pulse Width Modulation: Single-Pulse and Multiple-Pulse Width Modulation
pe-pwm-spw-mpw.body:
Prerequisite: Single-Phase Full-Bridge Inverter.

◆ Why this matters

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Pulse Width Modulation: Single-Pulse and Multiple-Pulse Width Modulation

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Pulse Width Modulation: Single-Pulse and Multiple-Pulse Width Modulation.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

In square-wave inverters, two major drawbacks exist: (1) The output voltage magnitude cannot be regulated without varying the DC bus voltage, and (2) The output contains massive low-order harmonics (3rd, 5th, 7th), which require prohibitively bulky, expensive LC passive filter components. Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) revolutionizes inverter design by chopping the output voltage into high-frequency pulses: the pulse width controls the fundamental voltage magnitude, while the high switching frequency pushes harmonic energy far away into the high-frequency spectrum where minimal filtering is required.

◆ 1. Single-Pulse Width Modulation (SPW)

In Single-Pulse Width Modulation, the gating signal is generated by comparing a rectangular reference signal of amplitude $A_r$ with a triangular carrier wave of amplitude $A_c$ and frequency $f_c$. The resulting output voltage consists of a single pulse of width $2d$ centered at the middle of each half-cycle (at $\pi/2$ and $3\pi/2$).

Single-Pulse Modulation Fourier Series & RMS Voltages

Fourier Series for a pulse of width $2d$ centered at $\pi/2$:

$$v_o(t) = \sum_{n=1,3,5dots}^\infty \left[\frac{4V_{dc}}{n\pi} \sin(n\cdot d)\right] \sin(n\omega t)$$

Total RMS Output Voltage: $$V_{or} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\pi/2 - d}^{\pi/2 + d} V_{dc}^2 d(\omega t)} = V_{dc} \sqrt{\frac{2d}{\pi}}$$

Fundamental RMS Output Voltage: $$V_{o1,rms} = \frac{4V_{dc}}{\sqrt{2}\pi} \sin(d) = \frac{2\sqrt{2} V_{dc}}{\pi} \sin(d)$$

Peak of $n$-th Harmonic Component: $$V_{on,peak} = \frac{4V_{dc}}{n\pi} \sin(n\cdot d)$$

Placement Trap: Harmonic Elimination via Pulse Width Selection

To completely eliminate the $n$-th harmonic from the output voltage, its amplitude must satisfy $V_{on,peak} = 0$:

$$\sin(n \cdot d) = 0 implies n \cdot d = 180^\circ implies 2d = \frac{360^\circ}{n}$$

  • To eliminate the 3rd harmonic ($n=3$): Pulse width $2d = 360^\circ / 3 = \mathbf{120^\circ}$ ($d = 60^\circ$).
  • To eliminate the 5th harmonic ($n=5$): Pulse width $2d = 360^\circ / 5 = \mathbf{72^\circ}$ ($d = 36^\circ$).

Crucial Trade-off: Eliminating a specific harmonic fixes the pulse width $2d$, which robs the system of independent voltage regulation capability.

◆ 2. Multiple-Pulse Width Modulation (MPW)

To overcome the limitation of SPW, Multiple-Pulse Width Modulation (MPW) utilizes several equidistant pulses of uniform width $2d$ in each half-cycle. The gating pulses are generated by comparing a high-frequency triangular carrier wave $v_c$ (frequency $f_c$) with a rectangular reference wave $v_r$ (fundamental frequency $f_r$).

  • Number of pulses per half-cycle: $$p = \frac{f_c}{2 f_r} = \frac{m_f}{2}$$
  • Width of each individual pulse: $\delta = 2d$.
  • Total RMS Output Voltage: $$V_{or} = V_{dc} \sqrt{\frac{2p \cdot d}{\pi}} = V_{dc} \sqrt{\frac{p \cdot \delta}{\pi}}$$

Harmonic Spectrum of MPW

The dominant harmonic in MPW is pushed from low orders up to orders centered around the carrier frequency:

$$\text{Lowest Dominant Harmonic Order} = 2p - 1 \quad \text{and} \quad 2p + 1$$

For example, with $p = 5$ pulses per half-cycle, the 3rd, 5th, and 7th harmonics are significantly suppressed; the lowest dominant harmonics appear at $2(5) - 1 = \mathbf{9\text{th}}$ and $2(5) + 1 = \mathbf{11\text{th}}$, which can be easily filtered with small inductors.

Common Interview Mistake: SPW vs MPW Switching Losses

Mistake: Assuming MPW is always superior to SPW without any operational drawback.

Correction: While MPW improves harmonic performance and reduces filter size, each switch turns on and off $p$ times per half-cycle instead of once. Therefore, switching losses increase proportionally with $p$ ($P_{sw} propto f_c = 2p f_r$). Modern converters balance harmonic attenuation against thermal semiconductor losses.

pe-pwm-sinusoidal.title: Sinusoidal Pulse Width Modulation (SPWM): Unipolar & Bipolar Modulation
pe-pwm-sinusoidal.body:
Prerequisite: Single-Pulse and Multiple-Pulse Width Modulation.

◆ Why this matters

Sinusoidal Pulse Width Modulation (SPWM) is by far the most dominant, universally deployed modulation strategy across modern electric mobility, solar grid-tied inverters, industrial motor drives, and home appliances. By varying the pulse widths sinusoidally across each half-cycle, SPWM generates an output voltage whose fundamental component is a faithful replica of the desired reference sine wave, virtually eliminating all sub-carrier low-order harmonics. Understanding the modulation indices ($m_a, m_f$) and the dramatic performance contrast between bipolar and unipolar switching is the crown jewel of power electronics recruitment interviews.

◆ SPWM Principles: Reference & Carrier Signals

SPWM compares a sinusoidal reference signal $v_r = V_{r,peak} \sin(\omega_r t)$ (desired fundamental frequency $f_r$) with a high-frequency triangular carrier wave $v_c$ of peak $V_{c,peak}$ and frequency $f_c$.

Key Modulation Indices

1. Amplitude Modulation Index ($m_a$):

$$m_a = \frac{V_{r,peak}}{V_{c,peak}}$$

  • Linear Modulation Range ($0 < m_a le 1.0$): The fundamental output voltage amplitude is strictly linear with $m_a$. Peak fundamental: $\hat{V}_{o1} = m_a \cdot V_{dc}$.
  • Overmodulation Range ($1.0 < m_a < 3.24$): The reference peaks exceed the carrier peaks. Output pulse widths near the center saturate into a solid block. Fundamental voltage increases nonlinearly with diminished returns, and low-order harmonics (3rd, 5th) reappear.
  • Square-Wave Limit ($m_a > 3.24$): Complete saturation into standard square-wave operation where $\hat{V}_{o1} = \frac{4 V_{dc}}{\pi} \approx 1.273 V_{dc}$.

2. Frequency Modulation Ratio ($m_f$):

$$m_f = \frac{f_c}{f_r}$$

In three-phase inverters, $m_f$ should be an odd multiple of 3 to eliminate even harmonics and cancel triplen harmonics in line-to-line voltages.

◆ Bipolar vs Unipolar SPWM Modulation

Parameter Bipolar SPWM Unipolar SPWM
Output Voltage Levels 2-level: $+V_{dc}$ and $-V_{dc}$ 3-level: $+V_{dc}$, $0$, and $-V_{dc}$
Comparator Logic Single sine reference $v_r$ vs carrier $v_c$. Switches $S_1, S_2$ and $S_3, S_4$ driven in antiphase. Two 180° complementary references ($v_r$ and $-v_r$) vs carrier $v_c$. Each bridge leg switched independently.
Effective Output Frequency Equals carrier frequency $f_c$ ($m_f$) Doubles to $2 \cdot f_c$ ($2 \cdot m_f$)
Harmonic Spectrum First harmonic sideband cluster at $m_f \pm 2$ First harmonic cluster pushed to $2m_f \pm 1$
Output Filter Size Larger LC filter required Substantially smaller, lighter, cheaper filter

Placement Trap: The "Frequency Doubling" Miracle of Unipolar PWM

In Unipolar SPWM, even though individual switches transition at carrier frequency $f_c$, the differential output voltage $v_{ab} = v_A - v_B$ pulses at twice the carrier frequency ($2 f_c$)! Harmonics at carrier frequency $f_c$ cancel out completely across the load. Because filter inductor size is inversely proportional to ripple frequency, unipolar switching reduces the filter inductance requirement by up to 75%.

Common Interview Mistake: Overmodulation Peak Voltage Misconception

Mistake: Assuming that when $m_a = 2.0$, the peak fundamental output voltage will be $2.0 \times V_{dc}$.

Correction: In a full-bridge inverter, the fundamental peak voltage can never exceed the square-wave limit $\frac{4 V_{dc}}{\pi} \approx 1.273 V_{dc}$. Increasing $m_a$ above 1.0 causes non-linear saturation, severely distorting the waveform while providing marginal additional voltage gain.

pe-choppers-step-down-step-up.title: DC-DC Choppers: Step-Down & Step-Up Principles, Single & Two-Quadrant Topologies
pe-choppers-step-down-step-up.body:
1. Introduction to DC-DC Choppers

A DC-DC chopper is a static power electronic converter that transforms a fixed DC input voltage directly into a variable DC output voltage with high efficiency, replacing legacy, lossy rheostatic control and bulky motor-generator sets. Modern choppers utilize fully controlled power semiconductor switches—such as Power MOSFETs (for high-frequency applications > 50 kHz) and IGBTs (for medium-to-high power traction drives < 20 kHz)—switched periodically between conducting (ON) and non-conducting (OFF) states.

Fundamental Chopper Governing Relationships

For a chopper operating with switching period \(T_s = 1/f\) and switch-ON duration \(T_{on}\):

$$\text{Duty Cycle } D = \frac{T_{on}}{T_{on} + T_{off}} = \frac{T_{on}}{T_s} = f \cdot T_{on}, \quad 0 le D le 1$$

Step-Down (Buck Principle): Average output voltage \(V_o\) is always less than supply \(V_s\):

$$V_o = \frac{1}{T_s} \int_0^{T_{on}} V_s , dt = D \cdot V_s$$

RMS Output Voltage: \(V_{or} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T_s} \int_0^{T_{on}} V_s^2 , dt} = \sqrt{D} \cdot V_s$$

Step-Up (Boost Principle): Inductive energy storage releases in series with the source:

$$V_o = \frac{V_s}{1 - D} \quad (V_o ge V_s)$$

2. Chopper Operational Quadrants: Classification in the Vo–Io Plane

Depending on the direction of output voltage \(V_o\) and load current \(I_o\), choppers are rigorously categorized into five distinct classes (Class A through Class E). In DC motor drives, positive voltage corresponds to forward rotation, positive current produces forward motoring torque, negative current produces regenerative braking torque, and negative voltage corresponds to reverse rotation.

Figure: Complete Chopper Classification in the Vo–Io Plane: Class A (Q1), Class B (Q2), Class C (Q1+Q2), Class D (Q1+Q4), and Class E (Q1–Q4 H-bridge).
Class Quadrant Polarity (Vo, Io) Power Flow Circuit Configuration & Drive Application
Class A First (Q1) \(V_o > 0, I_o > 0\) Source → Load Step-down chopper. Switch in series, freewheeling diode across inductive load. Forward motoring.
Class B Second (Q2) \(V_o > 0, I_o < 0\) Load → Source Step-up chopper. Switch in shunt, diode in series. Requires active load EMF \(E\). Forward regenerative braking.
Class C Two-Quadrant (Q1 + Q2) \(V_o > 0, I_o gtrless 0\) Bidirectional Two switches and two diodes in half-bridge. Reversible current at unipolar voltage. Motoring + regenerative braking.
Class D Two-Quadrant (Q1 + Q4) \(V_o gtrless 0, I_o > 0\) Bidirectional Two switches and two diodes cross-connected. Reversible voltage with unidirectional current. Used in inductive magnet discharges.
Class E Four-Quadrant (Q1 to Q4) \(V_o gtrless 0, I_o gtrless 0\) Full Four-Quadrant Full H-bridge with 4 switches and 4 anti-parallel diodes. Complete forward/reverse motoring and regenerative braking.

3. Step-Up Chopper Operation & Regenerative Energy Recovery

In a step-up chopper (Class B), when switch \(S\) is closed, load EMF \(E\) drives current through inductor \(L\) and \(S\), storing energy \(\frac{1}{2} L I_L^2\) in the inductor. When switch \(S\) is opened, inductor voltage reverses polarity (\(v_L = -L \frac{di}{dt}\)) to oppose current collapse. The net voltage \(E + v_L\) exceeds supply voltage \(V_s\), forcing current through diode \(D\) back into the DC source:

$$E \cdot T_{on} = (V_s - E) \cdot T_{off} implies V_o = V_s = \frac{E}{1 - D}$$

For successful power transfer back into the supply rail during regenerative braking, the condition \(E > 0\) is mandatory, and the duty cycle must satisfy \(D > 1 - \frac{E}{V_s}\).

Placement Trap: Class D Chopper Average Output Voltage Formula

In a Class D chopper, both switches (\(S_1, S_2\)) are triggered simultaneously for duration \(T_{on}\), applying \(+V_s\) across the load. During \(T_{off}\), both switches turn OFF, and load current freewheels through diodes \(D_1, D_2\), which connects the load across the source in reverse polarity (\(-V_s\)). Therefore, the average output voltage is:

$$V_o = D V_s + (1 - D)(-V_s) = (2D - 1) V_s$$

Notice that \(V_o = 0\) when \(D = 0.50\); \(V_o > 0\) for \(D > 0.50\); and \(V_o < 0\) for \(D < 0.50\). Candidates frequently forget the factor of 2 and erroneously assume \(V_o = D V_s\)!

Common Exam Mistake: Class B Chopper Operational Prerequisite

A Class B chopper cannot operate with a purely passive resistive load \(R\). Because current flows from load back to the supply (\(I_o < 0\)), the load MUST contain an active DC voltage source or back-EMF \(E\) (e.g., a rotating DC motor armature or a storage battery undergoing charging). Without an active energy source, current cannot flow backward into the source.

pe-choppers-four-quadrant-control.title: Four-Quadrant Choppers & Control Techniques: PWM vs Current Limit Control
pe-choppers-four-quadrant-control.body:
1. Four-Quadrant Chopper (Class E Topology)

The Class E four-quadrant chopper consists of four fully controllable semiconductor switches (\(S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4\)) and four anti-parallel fast-recovery diodes (\(D_1, D_2, D_3, D_4\)) arranged in an H-bridge configuration around a DC motor load with armature resistance \(R_a\), inductance \(L_a\), and back-EMF \(E_b\).

Quadrant Operational Mode Vo, Io Signs Active Switch(es) / Diode(s) Power Flow & Dynamics
Quadrant I Forward Motoring \(V_o > 0, I_o > 0\) \(S_1\) chops; \(S_4\) kept continuous ON. Freewheels via \(D_2, S_4\). Source → Armature. Armature accelerates in forward direction.
Quadrant II Forward Regeneration \(V_o > 0, I_o < 0\) \(S_2\) chops; freewheels into supply via \(D_1, D_4\). Armature → Source. Kinetic energy converted to electrical power.
Quadrant III Reverse Motoring \(V_o < 0, I_o < 0\) \(S_3\) chops; \(S_2\) kept continuous ON. Freewheels via \(D_4, S_2\). Source → Armature. Armature accelerates in reverse direction.
Quadrant IV Reverse Regeneration \(V_o < 0, I_o > 0\) \(S_4\) chops; freewheels into supply via \(D_2, D_3\). Armature → Source. Regenerative braking from reverse rotation.
Placement Trap: Leg Shoot-Through in H-Bridge Choppers

In any bridge leg containing series switches (such as \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), or \(S_3\) and \(S_4\)), both switches must NEVER be commanded ON simultaneously. Turning on both switches in the same leg dead-shorts the DC bus rails, resulting in massive fault currents that instantly vaporize the semiconductor dies. Gate drive microcontrollers must enforce a programmed dead time (blanking time \(t_d\)) between complementary gating signals.

2. Chopper Control Strategies

To modulate output voltage and regulate load current against load variations and input fluctuations, two primary control strategies are employed:

Control Strategy Comparison

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Four-Quadrant Choppers & Control Techniques: PWM vs Current Limit Control

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Troubleshooting diagnostic workflow, safety isolation protocols, and LOTO procedure for Four-Quadrant Choppers & Control Techniques: PWM vs Current Limit Control.
  • Component Roles: Multimeter / insulation tester (Megger) checks continuity and insulation resistance against standards.
  • Working Mechanism: Half-split search method systematically cuts active search space by half to pinpoint faulty component.
  • Signal & Flow Diagnostic: Trace control signals along terminal strips to identify open circuits, ground faults, or short circuits.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Eliminates intermittent faults and ensures zero voltage state before physical maintenance.
  • Key Governing Formula: Dalziel body current threshold: I_threshold = 116 / sqrt(t) mA; Insulation R > 1 MΩ + 1 MΩ/kV.
  • Engineering Meaning: Guarantees occupational safety (OSHA 1910.147 / NFPA 70E) and minimizes industrial plant downtime.
  • Common Trap: Failing to verify voltage tester on a known live source before testing de-energized circuits.

1. Time Ratio Control (TRC) / Pulse Width Modulation (PWM):

  • Constant Frequency System (Pulse Width Modulation): Switching period \(T_s\) is held constant, and pulse width \(T_{on}\) is modulated. Duty ratio \(D = T_{on} / T_s\) varies linearly from 0 to 1. Dominant industry standard because constant frequency makes input/output LC filter design deterministic and avoids acoustic resonance bands.
  • Variable Frequency System (Frequency Modulation): Either \(T_{on}\) is held constant while \(T_s\) is varied, or \(T_{off}\) is held constant while \(T_s\) is varied. Wide frequency variation makes filter design difficult and can generate audible noise at low frequencies.

2. Current Limit Control (CLC) / Hysteresis Band Control:

The chopper switch is turned ON when load current drops below a lower threshold \(I_{min}\), and turned OFF when load current reaches an upper threshold \(I_{max}\):

$$\text{Current Ripple Band } \Delta I = I_{max} - I_{min}$$ $$I_{avg} = \frac{I_{max} + I_{min}}{2}$$

The switching frequency in CLC depends directly on load time constant \(\tau = L/R\) and supply voltage, varying dynamically with load torque demands.

3. Analytical Waveform Derivation for R-L-E Load

During the ON-period \(0 le t le T_{on}\), with \(V_s\) applied across load \(R-L-E\):

$$L \frac{di_o}{dt} + R i_o + E = V_s implies i_o(t) = \frac{V_s - E}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right) + I_{min} e^{-t/\tau}$$

During the OFF-period \(0 le t' le T_{off}\) (where \(t' = t - T_{on}\)), with freewheeling diode conducting (\(v_o = 0\)):

$$L \frac{di_o}{dt'} + R i_o + E = 0 implies i_o(t') = -\frac{E}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t'/\tau}\right) + I_{max} e^{-t'/\tau}$$

In steady-state continuous conduction, \(i_o(T_{on}) = I_{max}\) and \(i_o(T_{off}) = I_{min}\). The peak-to-peak inductor ripple current is maximized at \(D = 0.50\):

$$\Delta I_{max} = \frac{V_s}{4 f L} \quad (\text{at } D = 0.5)$$

⚡ Deep Technical Analysis: Four-Quadrant Chopper Operation & Switch States

Class E Four-Quadrant Chopper operates in all 4 regions of the $V_o - I_o$ plane:

QuadrantVoltage ($V_o$)Current ($I_o$)Active SwitchesOperating Mode
Q1 (Forward Motoring)$V_o > 0$$I_o > 0$$S_1$ ON, $S_4$ ON (or $S_1$ chopping, $D_4$ freewheeling)Power flows Source $ o$ Load
Q2 (Forward Braking)$V_o > 0$$I_o < 0$$S_2$ chopping, $D_1, D_4$ conductingRegenerative braking (Load $ o$ Source)
Q3 (Reverse Motoring)$V_o < 0$$I_o < 0$$S_3$ ON, $S_2$ ONReverse rotation motoring
Q4 (Reverse Braking)$V_o < 0$$I_o > 0$$S_4$ chopping, $D_2, D_3$ conductingReverse regenerative braking

pe-buck-converter.title: Buck Switching Regulator: CCM Operation, Inductor Ripple & Filter Design
pe-buck-converter.body:
1. Topology & Operating Principle

The Buck switching regulator is the quintessential step-down DC-DC converter. It produces an average output voltage \(V_o\) strictly lower than the unregulated input DC voltage \(V_s\) (\(V_o = D V_s\)) while delivering higher output current (\(I_o = I_s / D\)) with efficiencies typically exceeding 90–95%, vastly outperforming linear regulators (like the 7805), which dissipate excess voltage as pure heat.

Figure: Comparison of Buck, Boost, and Buck-Boost Topologies, Transfer Functions, Critical Inductances (Lmin), and Inductor Current Ramping.

2. Circuit States in Continuous Conduction Mode (CCM)

In Continuous Conduction Mode (CCM), inductor current \(i_L(t)\) never falls to zero during the switching cycle:

  • Mode 1 (Switch \(S\) ON, Diode \(D\) OFF, \(0 le t le D T_s\)): The input voltage \(V_s\) is applied across the series combination of inductor \(L\) and parallel combination of capacitor \(C\) and load \(R\). The voltage across the inductor is \(v_L = V_s - V_o > 0\). The inductor current ramps up linearly from \(I_{min}\) to \(I_{max}\): $$\frac{di_L}{dt} = \frac{V_s - V_o}{L} implies \Delta I_L = \left(\frac{V_s - V_o}{L}\right) D T_s = \frac{V_s(1 - D)D}{f L}$$
  • Mode 2 (Switch \(S\) OFF, Diode \(D\) ON, \(D T_s le t le T_s\)): The inductor current cannot change instantaneously. Diode \(D\) turns ON automatically to freewheel the inductor current. The voltage across inductor is \(v_L = -V_o < 0\). The inductor current ramps down linearly from \(I_{max}\) to \(I_{min}\): $$\frac{di_L}{dt} = -\frac{V_o}{L} implies \Delta I_L = \left(\frac{V_o}{L}\right) (1 - D) T_s$$

Inductor Volt-Second Balance & Transfer Function

In periodic steady state, the net change in inductor current over a complete switching cycle must be zero, meaning the average inductor voltage is strictly zero:

$$\int_0^{T_s} v_L(t) , dt = 0 implies (V_s - V_o) D T_s + (-V_o)(1 - D) T_s = 0$$ $$V_s D T_s - V_o D T_s - V_o T_s + V_o D T_s = 0 implies V_o = D \cdot V_s$$

Assuming 100% ideal conversion efficiency (\(P_{in} = P_{out}\)):

$$V_s I_s = V_o I_o implies I_s = D \cdot I_o$$

3. Inductor & Filter Capacitor Design Criteria

For a DC-DC converter to maintain CCM operation, average inductor current \(I_L = I_o = V_o / R\) must exceed half of the peak-to-peak ripple current \(\Delta I_L / 2\):

$$I_{min} = I_o - \frac{\Delta I_L}{2} ge 0 implies \frac{V_o}{R} ge \frac{V_o(1 - D)}{2 f L}$$

Critical Boundary Inductance (\(L_{min}\)) & Capacitance (\(C_{min}\))

$$L_{min} = \frac{(1 - D) R}{2 f}$$

If \(L < L_{min}\), the converter enters Discontinuous Conduction Mode (DCM), where output voltage becomes load-dependent.

Output Voltage Ripple (\(\Delta V_c\)): The entire AC ripple of the inductor current flows through output capacitor \(C\). The charge accumulated by the capacitor during the positive ripple interval is the area of the triangular current waveform above \(I_o\):

$$\Delta Q = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{T_s}{2}\right) \left(\frac{\Delta I_L}{2}\right) = \frac{T_s \Delta I_L}{8} = \frac{\Delta I_L}{8 f}$$ $$\Delta V_c = \frac{\Delta Q}{C} = \frac{\Delta I_L}{8 f C} = \frac{V_o (1 - D)}{8 L C f^2} = \frac{V_s D (1 - D)}{8 L C f^2}$$ $$C_{min} = \frac{(1 - D) V_o}{8 L f^2 \Delta V_c} = \frac{(1 - D)}{8 L f^2 (\Delta V_c / V_o)}$$
Placement Trap: Capacitor ESR Dominance at High Switching Frequencies

In high-frequency buck converters (e.g., modern 500 kHz to 2 MHz point-of-load converters), the output ripple voltage is frequently dominated by the Equivalent Series Resistance (ESR) of the capacitor rather than its pure capacitance \(C\):

$$\Delta V_{o,total} \approx \Delta I_L \cdot \text{ESR} + \frac{\Delta I_L}{8 f C}$$

If a question specifies a capacitor with non-zero ESR, calculating \(\Delta V_c = \Delta I_L / (8 f C)\) alone will result in a gross underestimation of actual output ripple!

pe-boost-converter.title: Boost Switching Regulator: CCM Operation, Voltage Gain & Filter Sizing
pe-boost-converter.body:
1. Topology & Operating Principle

The Boost switching regulator produces an output voltage \(V_o\) strictly greater than the input voltage \(V_s\). Its distinguishing topological feature is that the energy storage inductor \(L\) is connected in series with the DC source, which provides continuous, non-pulsating input current, making the boost converter the topology of choice for Power Factor Correction (PFC) front-ends and solar photovoltaic Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) inputs.

2. Continuous Conduction Mode (CCM) Analysis

  • Mode 1 (Switch \(S\) ON, Diode \(D\) Reverse-Biased, \(0 le t le D T_s\)): The switch connects the inductor directly across input voltage \(V_s\). Inductor voltage is \(v_L = V_s > 0\). Diode \(D\) is reverse-biased by output capacitor voltage \(V_o\). The load receives power solely from output capacitor \(C\), which discharges with current \(I_o = V_o / R\). Inductor current rises linearly: $$\frac{di_L}{dt} = \frac{V_s}{L} implies \Delta I_L = \frac{V_s D T_s}{L} = \frac{V_s D}{f L}$$
  • Mode 2 (Switch \(S\) OFF, Diode \(D\) Forward-Biased, \(D T_s le t le T_s\)): Inductor voltage reverses to \(v_L = -(V_o - V_s)\) to maintain current flow. Diode \(D\) conducts, connecting the inductor in series aiding with the input source. Energy stored in inductor plus energy from source is transferred simultaneously to load and capacitor: $$\frac{di_L}{dt} = -\frac{V_o - V_s}{L} implies \Delta I_L = \frac{(V_o - V_s)(1 - D)}{f L}$$

Volt-Second Balance & Voltage Transfer Ratio

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Boost Switching Regulator: CCM Operation, Voltage Gain & Filter Sizing

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics

  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.
$$\int_0^{T_s} v_L(t) , dt = 0 implies V_s D T_s + (V_s - V_o)(1 - D)T_s = 0$$ $$V_s D + V_s - V_o - V_s D + V_o D = 0 implies V_s = V_o(1 - D)$$ $$V_o = \frac{V_s}{1 - D} \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{V_o}{V_s} = \frac{1}{1 - D}$$

Since \(0 le D < 1\), the denominator \((1 - D) le 1\), guaranteeing \(V_o ge V_s\). For ideal lossless conversion:

$$I_s = \frac{I_o}{1 - D}$$

3. Component Design: Critical Inductance & Output Capacitance

The boundary between continuous (CCM) and discontinuous (DCM) conduction occurs when \(I_{min} = I_L - \Delta I_L / 2 = 0\). Since average inductor current \(I_L = I_s = I_o / (1 - D) = V_o / [R(1 - D)]\):

$$\frac{V_o}{R(1 - D)} = \frac{\Delta I_L}{2} = \frac{V_s D}{2 f L} = \frac{V_o (1 - D) D}{2 f L}$$

Critical Boundary Inductance (\(L_{min}\)) & Capacitance (\(C_{min}\))

$$L_{min} = \frac{D(1 - D)^2 R}{2 f}$$

Output Voltage Ripple (\(\Delta V_c\)): Unlike the buck converter, the output diode conducts only during \((1 - D)T_s\). During switch ON period \(D T_s\), the load current is supplied entirely by capacitor \(C\). Therefore, total charge lost by the capacitor is:

$$\Delta Q = I_o \cdot D T_s = \frac{V_o D}{R f}$$ $$\Delta V_c = \frac{\Delta Q}{C} = \frac{I_o D}{f C} = \frac{V_o D}{R f C} implies \frac{\Delta V_c}{V_o} = \frac{D}{R f C}$$ $$C_{min} = \frac{D}{R f (\Delta V_c / V_o)}$$
Placement Trap: The Right-Half-Plane Zero (RHPZ) in Boost Regulators

In small-signal transfer function analysis, the boost converter exhibits a Right-Half-Plane Zero (RHPZ) at frequency \(\omega_z = \frac{R(1 - D)^2}{L}\). Unlike Left-Half-Plane zeros which add phase lead, an RHP zero adds phase lag while increasing gain. Physically, when duty cycle \(D\) is abruptly increased to raise output voltage, the switch stays closed longer, initially depriving the output capacitor of diode current, causing \(V_o\) to momentarily dip before rising! Feedback loops must be gain-limited well below \(\omega_z / 3\) to maintain stability.

Common Exam Mistake: Theoretical Infinite Gain as D → 1

Theoretically, \(V_o / V_s = 1 / (1 - D) o \infty\) as \(D o 1\). In real physical circuits with inductor winding resistance \(r_L\), the actual voltage gain is:

$$\frac{V_o}{V_s} = \frac{1}{1 - D} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + \frac{r_L}{R(1 - D)^2}}$$

As \(D\) approaches 0.85–0.90, the voltage drop across \(r_L\) overwhelms the gain, causing \(V_o\) to roll off rapidly to zero. Boost converters are practically limited to gains ≤ 4 to 5.

⚡ Deep Technical Analysis: Boost Converter Derivation & Sizing Formulas

Inductor Volt-Second Balance in Continuous Conduction Mode (CCM):

$$V_{\text{in}} D T_s + (V_{\text{in}} - V_o) (1-D) T_s = 0 implies V_o = \frac{V_{\text{in}}}{1 - D}$$

Design Component Sizing Equations

  • Critical Inductance ($L_{\min}$): $L_{\min} = \frac{D(1-D)^2 R}{2 f_s}$
  • Output Ripple Voltage ($\Delta V_o$): $\Delta V_o = \frac{I_o D}{f_s C} implies C_{\min} = \frac{I_o D}{f_s \Delta V_o}$

pe-buck-boost-converter.title: Buck-Boost Regulator: Inverting Polarity, Continuous Conduction Analysis & Component Sizing
pe-buck-boost-converter.body:
1. Topology & Operating Principle

The Buck-Boost switching regulator can produce an output voltage magnitude that is either smaller than or greater than the input voltage magnitude, depending entirely on the chosen duty cycle \(D\). Its critical distinguishing signature is that the output voltage polarity is intrinsically inverted (negative with respect to input ground).

2. Circuit States in Continuous Conduction Mode (CCM)

  • Mode 1 (Switch \(S\) ON, Diode \(D\) Reverse-Biased, \(0 le t le D T_s\)): The switch connects the input voltage \(V_s\) directly across inductor \(L\). The inductor current ramps upward from \(I_{min}\) to \(I_{max}\): $$\frac{di_L}{dt} = \frac{V_s}{L} implies \Delta I_L = \frac{V_s D T_s}{L} = \frac{V_s D}{f L}$$ Diode \(D\) is reverse-biased by \(V_s + |V_o|\). The output capacitor \(C\) supplies the entire load current \(I_o\).
  • Mode 2 (Switch \(S\) OFF, Diode \(D\) Forward-Biased, \(D T_s le t le T_s\)): Switch \(S\) opens. The inductor current forces diode \(D\) into conduction. The inductor discharges stored magnetic energy into parallel combination of capacitor \(C\) and load \(R\). The inductor voltage is \(v_L = -|V_o|\). Inductor current ramps down: $$\frac{di_L}{dt} = -\frac{|V_o|}{L} implies \Delta I_L = \frac{|V_o|(1 - D)}{f L}$$

Volt-Second Balance & Transfer Ratio

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Buck-Boost Regulator: Inverting Polarity, Continuous Conduction Analysis & Component Sizing

Operating Regimes:

  • \(D < 0.50\): \(D / (1 - D) < 1 implies |V_o| < V_s\) (Step-Down / Buck Mode).
  • \(D = 0.50\): \(D / (1 - D) = 1 implies |V_o| = V_s\) (Unity Gain Inverter).
  • \(D > 0.50\): \(D / (1 - D) > 1 implies |V_o| > V_s\) (Step-Up / Boost Mode).

3. Component Sizing: Boundary Inductance & Filter Capacitance

In a buck-boost converter, the average inductor current \(I_L\) equals the sum of average input current \(I_s\) and average output current \(I_o\):

$$I_L = I_s + I_o = \frac{D}{1 - D} I_o + I_o = \frac{I_o}{1 - D} = \frac{|V_o|}{R(1 - D)}$$

The boundary between continuous (CCM) and discontinuous (DCM) conduction occurs when \(I_{min} = I_L - \Delta I_L / 2 = 0\):

Critical Boundary Inductance (\(L_{min}\)) & Output Ripple (\(\Delta V_c\))

$$L_{min} = \frac{(1 - D)^2 R}{2 f}$$

Output Voltage Ripple (\(\Delta V_c\)): During switch ON period \(D T_s\), diode \(D\) is reverse-biased, so capacitor \(C\) supplies total load current \(I_o\):

$$\Delta Q = I_o \cdot D T_s = \frac{|V_o| D}{R f}$$ $$\Delta V_c = \frac{\Delta Q}{C} = \frac{|V_o| D}{R f C} implies \frac{\Delta V_c}{|V_o|} = \frac{D}{R f C}$$ $$C_{min} = \frac{D}{R f (\Delta V_c / |V_o|)}$$
Placement Trap: Both Input and Output Currents are Discontinuous (Pulsating)

In a buck converter, input current is pulsating while output current is continuous. In a boost converter, input current is continuous while output current is pulsating. In a buck-boost converter, BOTH input current and output current are severely pulsating (discontinuous)! The input switch chops input current from \(I_L\) to 0, and the output diode chops output current from \(I_L\) to 0. This creates severe electromagnetic interference (EMI) and requires substantial capacitive filtering on both input and output ports.

pe-cuk-converter-applications.title: Ćuk Converter: Capacitive Energy Transfer, Low Ripple & DC-DC Applications
pe-cuk-converter-applications.body:
1. The Ćuk Regulator Principle & Topology

Invented by Dr. Slobodan Ćuk at Caltech, the Ćuk converter is an advanced DC-DC regulator based on capacitive energy transfer rather than purely inductive energy transfer. Like the buck-boost converter, it can step voltage up or down with an inverted output polarity (\(V_o = -\frac{D}{1-D} V_s\)), but eliminates the major drawback of buck-boost converters by maintaining continuous, non-pulsating currents at BOTH input and output terminals.

Figure: Complete Ćuk Converter Circuit Schematic with Energy Transfer Capacitor C1, Dual Inductors L1 & L2, and Low-Ripple Transfer Waveforms.

2. Circuit Operation in Continuous Conduction Mode (CCM)

The converter utilizes an energy transfer coupling capacitor \(C_1\), an input inductor \(L_1\), an output inductor \(L_2\), a power switch \(S\), a freewheeling diode \(D\), and an output filter capacitor \(C_2\):

  • Switch \(S\) OFF, Diode \(D\) ON (\(D T_s le t le T_s\)): Diode \(D\) is forward-biased. Capacitor \(C_1\) is charged from input source \(V_s\) through inductor \(L_1\). Concurrently, output inductor \(L_2\) discharges into load \(R\) and \(C_2\) via diode \(D\). In steady state, capacitor \(C_1\) charges to the sum of input and output voltages: $$V_{C1} = V_s + |V_o| = V_s + \frac{D}{1 - D} V_s = \frac{V_s}{1 - D}$$
  • Switch \(S\) ON, Diode \(D\) OFF (\(0 le t le D T_s\)): Switch \(S\) turns ON. Diode \(D\) is reverse-biased by capacitor voltage \(V_{C1}\). Capacitor \(C_1\) discharges stored energy into load \(R\) through inductor \(L_2\). Meanwhile, input inductor \(L_1\) stores energy directly from source \(V_s\).

Voltage & Ripple Transfer Relations

$$\text{Volt-Second Balance on } L_1: \quad V_s D T_s + (V_s - V_{C1})(1 - D) T_s = 0 implies V_{C1} = \frac{V_s}{1 - D}$$ $$\text{Volt-Second Balance on } L_2: \quad (V_{C1} - |V_o|) D T_s + (-|V_o|)(1 - D) T_s = 0 implies |V_o| = D V_{C1}$$ $$|V_o| = \frac{D}{1 - D} V_s \quad implies \quad V_o = -\frac{D}{1 - D} V_s$$

Energy Transfer Capacitor Ripple Voltage (\(\Delta V_{C1}\)):

$$\Delta V_{C1} = \frac{I_s (1 - D)}{f C_1} = \frac{I_o D}{f C_1} = \frac{|V_o| D}{R f C_1}$$

Output Voltage Ripple (\(\Delta V_o\)): Because \(L_2\) is in series with the output, the output voltage ripple follows the second-order LC filter attenuation equation (identical to the buck converter):

$$\frac{\Delta V_o}{|V_o|} = \frac{1 - D}{8 L_2 C_2 f^2}$$

3. Comprehensive Industrial Applications of DC-DC Converters

Modern DC-DC converters form the technological backbone of modern electrification:

Application Domain Converter Topology Employed Engineering Justification
Electric Vehicle (EV) Powertrains Bidirectional Two-Quadrant / Four-Quadrant Chopper Interfaces high-voltage traction battery (400V/800V) with inverter DC bus; seamlessly transitions between propulsion motoring and regenerative braking.
Solar Photovoltaic Systems Boost Converter & Ćuk Converter Performs Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) by varying duty cycle; continuous input current prevents solar panel I-V curve distortion and RF noise.
Computer Microprocessor Power (VRM) Multiphase Synchronous Buck Converter Steps down 12V mother-board rail to 0.8V–1.2V core voltage at massive currents (> 150 A) with interleaved ripple cancellation and sub-millivolt transient tolerance.
Telecommunications & Data Centers Buck & Isolated Forward/Flyback Converters Steps 48V telecom bus down to 12V, 5V, 3.3V intermediate distribution rails with tight galvanic noise rejection.
Battery-Powered Handheld Electronics Buck-Boost & Single-Ended Primary-Inductor (SEPIC) Maintains stable 3.3V system rail as single-cell Li-ion battery discharges nonlinearly from 4.2V (fully charged) down to 2.8V (cutoff).
Placement Trap: Coupled Inductor Zero-Ripple Feature of the Ćuk Converter

A unique capability of the Ćuk converter is that inductors \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) share identical voltage waveforms across switching intervals. By winding \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) on the same magnetic core with proper mutual inductance \(M = L_1 = L_2\), the ripple current in one winding can be steered completely into the other winding, achieving ZERO ripple current at either the input or output terminal!

pe-isolated-dcdc-intro.title: Isolated DC-DC Converters: Need for Galvanic Isolation, Scaling & Core Reset
pe-isolated-dcdc-intro.body:
1. The Critical Need for Galvanic Isolation

Galvanic isolation refers to the electrical separation of input and output power circuits such that there is no direct ohmic conduction path between them. Electrical energy is exchanged purely across an electromagnetic magnetic field (transformer) or optoelectronic medium. In industrial power electronics, isolated DC-DC converters are mandatory for four engineering reasons:

  1. Operator & Consumer Safety: Isolating high-voltage dangerous DC links (e.g., 400V–800V EV traction packs or rectified 230V/415V mains) from low-voltage user-accessible terminals (e.g., 5V/12V USB-C ports, auxiliary electronics) protects human operators against fatal electric shock. Regulatory standards (IEC 60950, IEC 62368, UL 60601 for medical equipment) require dielectric breakdown withstand ratings of 2.5 kV to 4.0 kV AC RMS.
  2. Elimination of Ground Loops & Common-Mode Noise: In distributed industrial plants, large circulating currents flowing through shared ground impedances introduce severe common-mode electromagnetic interference (EMI) and signal corruptions. Breaking the ground loop through magnetic isolation guarantees noise immunity.
  3. Extreme Voltage Transformation Ratios: Non-isolated converters (buck/boost) operating at extreme duty cycles (e.g., stepping 400V down to 1.2V requires \(D = 0.003\)) suffer from extreme switch stress, high conduction losses, and narrow pulse widths that challenge gate driver resolution. Adding a transformer with turns ratio \(N_1:N_2\) provides a massive transformation multiplier (\(V_o = \frac{N_2}{N_1} D V_s\)), permitting the switch to operate at optimal duty cycles (\(0.30 le D le 0.50\)).
  4. Multiple Regulated Outputs with Dual Polarities: Adding multiple secondary windings on the same high-frequency transformer core allows generating multiple isolated voltages (e.g., +15V, -15V, +5V, +3.3V) with a single active primary switch.

2. High-Frequency Transformer Scaling Laws

In standard 50 Hz power transformers, the iron core and copper windings are large and heavy. In power electronic converters, increasing the switching frequency \(f\) from 50 Hz to 100 kHz–500 kHz drastically shrinks magnetic components. From Faraday’s Law of Electromagnetic Induction:

Transformer Area-Product Scaling Equation

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Isolated DC-DC Converters: Need for Galvanic Isolation, Scaling & Core Reset

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics

  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.

$$V_{RMS} = 4.44 \cdot f \cdot N \cdot B_{max} \cdot A_c implies A_c = \frac{V_{RMS}}{4.44 \cdot f \cdot N \cdot B_{max}}$$ $$A_p = A_c \cdot A_w = \frac{P_{out}}{K_w \cdot J \cdot f \cdot B_{max}}$$

where \(A_c\) is the core cross-sectional area, \(A_w\) is the winding window area, \(f\) is switching frequency, \(B_{max}\) is peak operating flux density, and \(J\) is current density. Because core volume scales inversely with switching frequency (\(\text{Volume} propto 1/f^{3/4}\)), a 100 kHz transformer is over 10 to 20 times smaller and lighter than a 50 Hz equivalent of identical power rating.

3. Magnetic Core Saturation & Volt-Second Balance

Unlike standard transformers subjected to symmetrical alternating AC voltages, isolated DC-DC converters apply unipolar DC voltage pulses to the primary winding. From Faraday's law:

$$\Delta B = \frac{1}{N_1 A_c} \int_0^t v_1(\tau) , d\tau$$

If the voltage applied during the switch ON time \(D T_s\) is not precisely balanced by an equal and opposite volt-second product during the switch OFF time, net magnetic flux accumulates cycle by cycle in a staircase progression until the ferrite core enters magnetic saturation. Upon saturation, core permeability drops to air (\(\mu_r o 1\)), magnetizing inductance collapses to near zero, and catastrophic primary switch overcurrent results!

Placement Trap: Unilateral vs Bilateral Core Excitation

Isolated converters are strictly divided into two families based on how the transformer core B-H loop is traversed:

  • Unilateral Excitation (Single-Ended Converters): Operates strictly in the first quadrant of the B-H loop (\(\Delta B = B_{max} - B_{rem}\)). Examples: Forward Converter and Flyback Converter. Requires a mandatory reset mechanism every cycle. Core utilization is inherently lower.
  • Bilateral Excitation (Double-Ended Converters): Operates across both positive and negative quadrants of the B-H loop (\(\Delta B = 2 B_{max}\)). Examples: Push-Pull, Half-Bridge, Full-Bridge, and Dual Active Bridge (DAB). Core utilization is doubled, resulting in smaller core sizes for the same power throughput.

pe-forward-converter.title: Forward Converter: Circuit Topology, Tertiary Demagnetizing Reset & Waveforms
pe-forward-converter.body:
1. Topology & Operating Principle

The Forward converter is a transformer-isolated step-down converter derived directly from the buck topology. Unlike the flyback converter, the forward converter utilizes true transformer action: energy is transferred from primary source to the secondary load simultaneously while the primary switch is conducting (ON).

Figure: Architectural Comparison of Forward Converter (True Transformer Action with Tertiary Reset) and Flyback Converter (Air-Gapped Coupled Inductor).

2. Circuit Operation Across Switching Sub-Intervals

The forward converter contains three transformer windings: primary winding \(N_1\), secondary winding \(N_2\), and a dedicated tertiary demagnetizing winding \(N_3\) equipped with series diode \(D_3\):

  • Mode 1: Switch \(S_1\) ON (\(0 le t le D T_s\)): Switch \(S_1\) closes. Primary voltage is \(v_1 = +V_s\). Dots are positive. Secondary dot voltage is \(v_2 = +V_s (N_2 / N_1)\), which forward-biases rectifier diode \(D_1\). Freewheeling diode \(D_2\) is reverse-biased. Current flows through output inductor \(L\), charging capacitor \(C\) and supplying load \(R\). Simultaneously, magnetizing current \(i_m\) builds linearly in the transformer core: $$\frac{di_m}{dt} = \frac{V_s}{L_m} implies I_{m,peak} = \frac{V_s D T_s}{L_m}$$ Tertiary diode \(D_3\) is reverse-biased by \(V_s (1 + N_3/N_1)\).
  • Mode 2: Switch \(S_1\) OFF, Core Demagnetization (\(D T_s le t le D T_s + t_{reset}\)): Switch \(S_1\) turns OFF. All winding voltages reverse polarity. Dot terminals become negative. Secondary diode \(D_1\) turns OFF. Freewheeling diode \(D_2\) turns ON to maintain output inductor current \(i_L\). Crucially, tertiary diode \(D_3\) becomes forward-biased, clamping winding \(N_3\) voltage to \(-V_s\). The magnetizing current \(i_m\) is discharged back into the DC source through \(N_3\) and \(D_3\), resetting transformer core flux back to zero!
  • Mode 3: Switch \(S_1\) OFF, Core Rest Period (\(D T_s + t_{reset} le t le T_s\)): Once magnetizing current reaches zero, diode \(D_3\) turns OFF. All transformer windings carry zero current and zero voltage until the next switching cycle begins. Output current continues freewheeling through \(D_2\).

Voltage Transfer Ratio & Core Reset Derivation

Applying volt-second balance to output filter inductor \(L\):

$$\left(\frac{N_2}{N_1} V_s - V_o\right) D T_s + (-V_o)(1 - D) T_s = 0 implies V_o = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right) D \cdot V_s$$

Applying volt-second balance to transformer magnetizing inductance \(L_m\) during ON and reset intervals:

$$V_s \cdot D T_s = V_s \left(\frac{N_1}{N_3}\right) t_{reset} implies t_{reset} = D T_s \left(\frac{N_3}{N_1}\right)$$

To prevent core saturation, the core MUST completely reset before the next cycle starts (\(D T_s + t_{reset} le T_s\)):

$$D T_s + D T_s \left(\frac{N_3}{N_1}\right) le T_s implies D \left(1 + \frac{N_3}{N_1}\right) le 1$$ $$D_{max} = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{N_3}{N_1}}$$

In standard practice, \(N_1 = N_3\), which establishes the fundamental forward converter operating boundary:

$$D_{max} = \frac{1}{1 + 1} = 0.50 \quad (50%)$$
Placement Trap: Peak Voltage Stress on the Primary Switch

During the core demagnetization interval (Mode 2), winding \(N_3\) is clamped to \(-V_s\). By transformer coupling, winding \(N_1\) reflects a voltage \(V_1 = -V_s (N_1 / N_3)\). Therefore, the total peak voltage across switch \(S_1\) is:

$$V_{switch,peak} = V_s + V_s \left(\frac{N_1}{N_3}\right) = V_s \left(1 + \frac{N_1}{N_3}\right)$$

For \(N_1 = N_3\), the switch experiences double the supply voltage: \(V_{switch,peak} = 2 V_s\)! For a 230V rectified DC bus (\(V_s \approx 325\text{ V}\)), switch \(S_1\) must be rated for at least 650V–800V.

Common Exam Mistake: Confusing Forward Output Stage with Flyback

Students often forget that the forward converter secondary contains two diodes (\(D_1\) rectifier and \(D_2\) freewheeling) and a separate output filter inductor \(L\). The transformer in a forward converter does NOT store output energy; it operates as an ideal transformer. The output inductor \(L\) is the sole energy-smoothing element.

pe-flyback-converter.title: Flyback Converter: Coupled Inductor Operation, Energy Storage & Snubber Design
pe-flyback-converter.body:
1. Topology & The Coupled Inductor Principle

The Flyback converter is the most widely adopted isolated DC-DC converter topology for low-to-medium power applications (< 150 W), found in virtually every smartphone charger, USB-PD adapter, laptop power brick, and auxiliary SMPS supply. Derived directly from the buck-boost converter, the flyback topology replaces the single inductor with an isolated coupled inductor (commonly called a flyback transformer).

Crucially, a flyback transformer is NOT an ideal transformer. It is an air-gapped magnetic energy storage inductor with primary and secondary windings wound on the same core with opposing dot polarities. Energy is stored during the switch ON time and released into the load during the switch OFF time.

2. Continuous Conduction Mode (CCM) Operation

  • Mode 1: Primary Switch \(S_1\) ON (\(0 le t le D T_s\)): Switch \(S_1\) closes. Supply voltage \(V_s\) is applied across primary winding \(N_1\). Dot terminal is positive. By transformer action, secondary dot terminal is also positive. However, secondary rectifier diode \(D_1\) has its anode connected to the negative (non-dot) terminal or cathode to dot terminal, making diode \(D_1\) strictly reverse-biased by \(V_o + V_s(N_2/N_1)\). Zero current flows in the secondary winding! The primary winding acts as an inductor, storing magnetic energy in the core's air gap: $$W = \frac{1}{2} L_m I_{pk}^2$$
  • Mode 2: Primary Switch \(S_1\) OFF (\(D T_s le t le T_s\)): Switch \(S_1\) turns OFF. Current in the primary collapses instantaneously. By Lenz's law, magnetic flux cannot collapse instantaneously, causing all winding polarities to reverse. Secondary dot terminal goes negative, driving diode \(D_1\) into conduction. The magnetic energy stored in the air gap is discharged into output capacitor \(C_o\) and load \(R\). The voltage across secondary winding is clamped to \(V_o\).

Flyback Converter Transfer Function (CCM)

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Flyback Converter: Coupled Inductor Operation, Energy Storage & Snubber Design

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics

  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.

Applying volt-second balance across primary magnetizing inductance \(L_m\):

$$V_s \cdot (D T_s) + \left(-\frac{N_1}{N_2} V_o\right) \cdot (1 - D) T_s = 0$$ $$V_s D = \left(\frac{N_1}{N_2}\right) V_o (1 - D) implies V_o = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right) \frac{D}{1 - D} \cdot V_s$$

Notice this is exactly the buck-boost transfer function scaled by transformer turns ratio \(N_2 / N_1\)!

3. Discontinuous Conduction Mode (DCM) Operation

In Discontinuous Conduction Mode (DCM), the magnetic energy stored in the air gap is completely transferred to the load before the end of the switching cycle (secondary current falls to zero at \(t = (D + D_2)T_s < T_s\)). DCM offers distinct advantages:

  • Diode \(D_1\) turns off at zero current, completely eliminating diode reverse recovery losses.
  • Switch turns on at lower current, and the control loop exhibits no Right-Half-Plane Zero (RHPZ), permitting wider control bandwidth.
  • Output voltage in DCM depends on load resistance \(R\): \(V_o = V_s D \sqrt{\frac{R T_s}{2 L_m}}\).

4. Primary Leakage Inductance & RCD Snubber Clamping

Real transformers possess imperfect magnetic coupling represented by a primary leakage inductance \(L_{lk}\) (typically 1% to 3% of \(L_m\)). When switch \(S_1\) turns OFF, the energy stored in the leakage inductance (\(\frac{1}{2} L_{lk} I_{pk}^2\)) cannot transfer to the secondary winding because diode \(D_1\) cannot conduct leakage flux.

This trapped leakage energy charges switch output capacitance \(C_{oss}\), creating massive, destructive voltage spikes: \(v_{switch} = V_s + \frac{N_1}{N_2} V_o + L_{lk} \frac{di}{dt}\). To clamp this spike and protect the switch, an RCD snubber (composed of fast diode \(D_{sn}\), clamping capacitor \(C_{sn}\), and discharge resistor \(R_{sn}\)) is connected across the primary winding.

Placement Trap: Peak Drain-Source Voltage Stress on Flyback Switch

During the OFF-state, the primary switch is subjected to the DC supply voltage PLUS the reflected output voltage PLUS the snubber clamp overshoot:

$$V_{DS,max} = V_s + \left(\frac{N_1}{N_2}\right) V_o + V_{spike}$$

For universal AC mains input (85V–265V AC, \(V_{s,max} \approx 375\text{ V DC}\)) with a reflected output voltage \(V_R = \frac{N_1}{N_2} V_o = 100\text{ V}\) and snubber margin \(V_{spike} = 75\text{ V}\), the switch sees \(375 + 100 + 75 = 550\text{ V}\). Designers must use switches rated for at least 650V to 800V.

pe-dual-active-bridge.title: Dual Active Bridge (DAB) Converter: Bidirectional Power Flow & ZVS Modulation
pe-dual-active-bridge.body:
1. Topology & Operating Principle

The Dual Active Bridge (DAB) converter is the industry benchmark topology for high-power, isolated, bidirectional DC-DC conversion. It consists of two active H-bridges (primary full bridge \(S_1-S_4\) and secondary full bridge \(S_5-S_8\)) interconnected by a high-frequency isolation transformer with turns ratio \(n = N_1:N_2\) and an energy-transfer AC-link inductor \(L_k\) (often comprised of transformer leakage inductance plus an external series inductor).

Figure: Dual Active Bridge (DAB) Architecture with Primary/Secondary H-Bridges, Phase-Shift Modulation φ, and Soft-Switching ZVS Conditions.

2. Phase-Shift Modulation (Single Phase Shift - SPS)

In standard Single Phase Shift (SPS) modulation:

  • Both primary and secondary bridges are operated with fixed 50% duty cycle square waves at switching frequency \(f_s = 1/T_s\).
  • The primary bridge synthesizes high-frequency AC square voltage \(v_p(t) = \pm V_1\).
  • The secondary bridge synthesizes high-frequency AC square voltage \(v_s(t) = \pm V_2\).
  • The primary and secondary AC voltage waveforms are phase-shifted relative to each other by phase angle \(\phi\) (or normalized phase shift \(d = \phi / \pi\), where \(-1 le d le 1\)).

Bidirectional Power Transfer Equation

The phase difference across inductor \(L_k\) drives high-frequency AC current. The average power transferred across the isolation barrier over one half-cycle is:

$$P = \frac{V_1 \cdot V_2'}{\omega L_k} \phi \left(1 - \frac{|\phi|}{\pi}\right) = \frac{V_1 (n V_2)}{2 \pi f_s L_k} \phi \left(1 - \frac{|\phi|}{\pi}\right)$$

In terms of normalized phase-shift ratio \(d = \phi / \pi\) (\(-0.5 le d le 0.5\)):

$$P = \frac{V_1 (n V_2)}{2 f_s L_k} d (1 - |d|)$$

Directionality:

  • \(\phi > 0\) (\(d > 0\)): Primary bridge leads secondary bridge. Power flows from Port 1 → Port 2.
  • \(\phi < 0\) (\(d < 0\)): Secondary bridge leads primary bridge. Power flows from Port 2 → Port 1.
  • Maximum power transfer occurs at \(\phi = \pm \pi / 2\) (\(d = \pm 0.50\)): \(P_{max} = \frac{V_1 (n V_2)}{8 f_s L_k}\).

3. Zero-Voltage Switching (ZVS) Mechanism

A premier advantage of the DAB converter is its inherent capability to achieve Zero-Voltage Switching (ZVS) across all 8 power switches without requiring auxiliary resonant circuits:

  • Before a switch is turned ON, the AC inductor current \(i_{Lk}\) is flowing in the anti-parallel body diode of the switch.
  • This body diode conduction clamps switch voltage to zero (\(V_{DS} \approx 0\)) and discharges the switch output parasitic capacitance \(C_{oss}\).
  • When the gate pulse arrives, the switch turns ON under zero voltage, eliminating capacitive turn-on losses (\(\frac{1}{2} C_{oss} V^2 f_s\)).
Placement Trap: Loss of ZVS at Light Loads and Voltage Mismatch

Full soft-switching ZVS is maintained across all switches only when the converter operating voltage ratio \(M = \frac{n V_2}{V_1}\) is close to unity (\(M \approx 1\)). If there is a large voltage mismatch (\(M gg 1\) or \(M ll 1\)), or when operating under light load conditions (small phase shift \(\phi\)), the inductor current is insufficient to discharge \(C_{oss}\) during dead time, causing loss of ZVS and severe capacitive turn-on switching losses. Advanced modulation schemes—such as Dual Phase Shift (DPS) and Triple Phase Shift (TPS)—are implemented in modern EV chargers to extend the ZVS range.

pe-isolated-apps-soft-switching.title: Applications of Isolated Converters & Fundamentals of Soft Switching
pe-isolated-apps-soft-switching.body:
1. Hard Switching vs Soft Switching

In conventional hard-switched converters (such as standard PWM buck, boost, and bridge converters), switches are forced to turn ON and OFF while experiencing simultaneous high voltage and high current:

Metric Hard Switching Soft Switching (Resonant / Quasi-Resonant)
Switching Overlap Simultaneous high \(V\) and \(I\) during \(t_r\) and \(t_f\). Voltage or current forced to zero prior to switching transition.
Switching Loss (\(P_{sw}\)) \(P_{sw} = \frac{1}{2} V I (t_r + t_f) f_s propto f_s\). High dissipation. Near zero switching losses. Decouples efficiency from switching frequency.
Maximum Switching Frequency Practically limited to 50 kHz–150 kHz by heat dissipation. Enables 500 kHz to 5 MHz operation using SiC and GaN devices.
dv/dt & di/dt Stress / EMI Severe high-frequency ringing and electromagnetic emissions. Smooth sinusoidal or quasi-sinusoidal transitions; ultra-low EMI.

2. Soft Switching Techniques: ZVS vs ZCS

Resonant Soft Switching Classifications

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Applications of Isolated Converters & Fundamentals of Soft Switching

High Contrast Vector Diagram
Technical Circuit & System Mechanics
  • What this Diagram Shows: Technical schematic and performance characteristic representation for Applications of Isolated Converters & Fundamentals of Soft Switching.
  • Component Roles: Represents primary physical components, energy conversion elements, or signal processing blocks.
  • Working Mechanism: Operates under electromagnetic and circuit conservation principles to process electrical energy or signals.
  • Signal & Current Flow: Input excitations produce proportional response across system terminals.
  • Expected Output / Behavior: Follows physical differential equations and steady-state operating characteristics.
  • Key Governing Formula: Mathematical relationship governing input-output parameter dynamics.
  • Engineering Meaning: Used by electrical engineers for circuit design, system stability analysis, and performance tuning.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring parasitic elements or non-linear saturation limits during high-frequency/high-voltage operation.

1. Zero-Voltage Switching (ZVS):

  • The voltage across the switch is reduced to zero before the switch is turned ON.
  • Eliminates capacitive discharge loss: \(P_{cap} = \frac{1}{2} C_{oss} V_{DS}^2 f_s = 0\).
  • Preferred for majority-carrier devices (Power MOSFETs, GaN HEMTs, SiC MOSFETs) where capacitive output discharge dominates switching loss.

2. Zero-Current Switching (ZCS):

  • The current through the switch is reduced to zero before the switch is turned OFF.
  • Eliminates minority carrier sweep-out current and turn-off tail current losses.
  • Preferred for minority-carrier devices (IGBTs, GTOs, Thyristors) that suffer from severe recombination tail times.

3. Key Industrial Applications of Isolated Converters

  1. Electric Vehicle On-Board Chargers (OBC): Dual Active Bridge (DAB) and LLC resonant converters step down rectified 400V AC grid power to charge 400V/800V traction batteries with bidirectional vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capability.
  2. Server Power Distribution & Data Centers: 48V to 12V isolated bus converters (IBC) with synchronous rectification achieve 98% efficiency to deliver hundreds of amps to AI/GPU clusters (Nvidia H100/B200 boards).
  3. Medical Equipment Power Supplies: Isolated Flyback and Forward converters provide reinforced insulation (4 kV AC isolation, < 10 μA leakage current) for patient-connected monitoring instruments.
  4. Solid-State Transformers (SST): High-voltage DAB converters replace legacy 50 Hz substation transformers, interfacing medium-voltage grid distribution (11 kV) directly to low-voltage DC microgrids.
Placement Trap: Selecting Soft-Switching Mode by Semiconductor Physics

Interviewers frequently test this core device physics question: "Why is ZVS preferred for MOSFETs while ZCS is preferred for IGBTs?"

Answer: MOSFETs are unipolar majority-carrier devices with negligible turn-off tail current, but their internal drain-source capacitance \(C_{oss}\) dissipates stored energy at every hard turn-on (\(\frac{1}{2} C_{oss} V^2 f\)). ZVS completely eliminates this loss. Conversely, IGBTs are bipolar devices that suffer from prolonged turn-off tail currents due to trapped minority carriers in the drift region. Turning off an IGBT under ZCS allows minority carriers to recombine before voltage rises across the device, eliminating tail loss!

ml-paradigms-learning-types.title: Machine Learning Paradigms: Supervised, Unsupervised, Semi-Supervised, and Reinforcement Learning
ml-paradigms-learning-types.body:
1. Conceptual Foundation and Formal Taxonomy

Machine learning (ML) studies computational algorithms that automatically improve their performance at a task through experience without being explicitly programmed. Formally, according to Tom Mitchell (1997), a computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E.

Depending on the nature of the training data, the existence of feedback, and the operational protocol, machine learning systems are systematically partitioned into four foundational paradigms:

  1. Supervised Learning: Learning from labeled input-output training pairs.
  2. Unsupervised Learning: Extracting latent representations, geometric manifolds, or cluster memberships from unlabeled data.
  3. Semi-Supervised Learning: Exploiting abundant unlabeled observations alongside a small set of labeled exemplars.
  4. Reinforcement Learning: Sequential decision-making where an autonomous agent optimizes cumulative numerical rewards via environment interactions.

Comparison of the four primary machine learning paradigms highlighting the nature of supervision, feedback signals, and mathematical frameworks.

Mathematical Formulations of the ML Paradigms

Supervised Learning: Given training dataset \(\mathcal{D} = {(x_i, y_i)}limits_{i=1}^N\), find hypothesis \(h_\theta: \mathcal{X} o \mathcal{Y}\) minimizing empirical risk:

\[ min_\theta R_\text{emp}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(h_\theta(x_i), y_i) + \lambda \Omega(\theta) \]

Unsupervised Learning: Given unlabeled dataset \(\mathcal{D} = {x_i}limits_{i=1}^N\), estimate the underlying probability density \(p(x)\) or find a mapping \(z_i = g(x_i)\) such that dimensionality \(d_z ll d_x\) while preserving structure.

Reinforcement Learning (Markov Decision Process): Defined by tuple \((\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{P}, \mathcal{R}, \gamma)\). Maximize expected discounted return:

\[ J(\pi) = \mathbb{E}_\pi \left[ \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t R(s_t, a_t) \right] \]

2. Supervised Learning: Regression vs. Classification

In supervised learning, the hypothesis function \(h_\theta(x)\) produces predictions evaluated by an explicit ground-truth supervisory signal:
