In alternating current distribution networks, inductive loads such as induction motors, air conditioning compressors, welding sets, and fluorescent magnetic ballasts draw both active power ($P$, kW) and reactive magnetizing power ($Q$, kVAr). Operating at low lagging power factor increases system line currents, escalating $I^2R$ distribution losses, worsening voltage regulation, consuming transformer/cable capacity, and incurring heavy financial penalties under industrial two-part maximum demand tariffs.

1. Principle of Reactive Power Compensation

Power factor is improved by connecting shunt capacitor banks across the inductive loads, providing leading reactive current that cancels out the lagging magnetizing current demanded by inductive coils:

$$Q_c = P (\tan \phi_1 - \tan \phi_2) = P \left( \tan(\arccos(\cos \phi_1)) - \tan(\arccos(\cos \phi_2)) \right)$$

Where:

  • $Q_c$ = Required capacitor bank rating in kVAr.
  • $P$ = Total active operating load in kW.
  • $\cos \phi_1$ = Initial uncompensated lagging power factor.
  • $\cos \phi_2$ = Target improved power factor (typically 0.98 to 0.99 lagging, or unity).

2. Microprocessor APFC Controller and C/k Ratio

The APFC relay samples the line voltage from a PT and line current from a CT installed on the main incomer upstream of all capacitor connections. It computes the instantaneous displacement power factor and steps capacitor stages in or out to match the dynamic reactive demand:

  • Target Power Factor & Deadband: A programmable target (e.g., $0.98\text{ lag}$) with a configurable deadband is configured to prevent perpetual hunting (rapid cyclic switching on and off).
  • The $C/k$ Ratio (Hunting Prevention): The threshold current required to trigger switching of the smallest capacitor step. It is calculated using the formula: $$C/k = \frac{Q_{\text{step}} \times 1000}{\sqrt{3} \times V_L \times I_{\text{CT1}}} \times \frac{1}{\text{CT Ratio}}$$ Where $Q_{{\text{step}}}$ is the smallest stage in kVAr, $V_L$ is line-to-line voltage, and $I_{{\text{CT1}}}$ is the CT primary rated current. Setting the sensitivity below $C/k$ causes destructive hunting and premature contactor welded contacts.
  • Stage Configurations: Binary banking ratios ($1:2:4:8$) provide high-resolution step increments with fewer capacitor stages, whereas equal staging ($1:1:1:1$) maximizes contactor longevity by rotating wear evenly across banks (FIFO algorithm).

3. Detuned Harmonic Filter Reactors (Series Reactors)

Modern electrical networks are heavily populated with non-linear loads (Variable Frequency Drives, UPS systems, LED drivers) generating harmonic currents ($5\text{th}, 7\text{th}, 11\text{th}$ harmonics):

  • Connecting pure shunt capacitors into a harmonically polluted network creates dangerous parallel resonance between the network leakage inductance ($L_{{sys}}$) and the capacitor capacitance ($C$), magnifying harmonic currents and voltages to levels that cause dielectric explosion of capacitor cans.
  • To prevent resonance, each capacitor bank is connected in series with a detuned iron-core reactor ($L$). The reactor is chosen such that the series resonant frequency ($f_r = 1 / (2\pi \sqrt{LC})$) lies well below the lowest dominant harmonic frequency (typically the 5th harmonic, 250 Hz in a 50 Hz system).
  • Common Detuning Factors ($p$):
    • $p = 7%$ ($X_L / X_C = 0.07$): Resonant frequency $f_r = 50 / \sqrt{0.07} \approx 189\text{ Hz}$. Protects against 5th and higher harmonics.
    • $p = 5.67%$: $f_r \approx 210\text{ Hz}$. Highly effective in low-order harmonic networks.
    • $p = 14%$: $f_r \approx 134\text{ Hz}$. Essential when 3rd harmonics (150 Hz) are present.

4. Contactor vs Thyristor Switching (Dynamic APFC)

Capacitor switching transients dictate the selection of switching hardware:

  • Specialized Capacitor Duty Contactors: Standard AC-3 contactors will weld instantly due to high inrush currents (up to 200 times rated current) during capacitor energization. Capacitor contactors feature leading auxiliary contacts with series damping resistors that pre-charge the capacitor and dissipate the peak current before the main contacts close. Minimum discharge rest time of 60 seconds is mandatory before re-energizing.
  • Thyristor Switched Capacitors (TSC / APFC-T): Uses anti-parallel SCRs with zero-voltage crossing switching circuits. Connects capacitors instantaneously (< 20 ms) with zero inrush current, making it mandatory for dynamic, rapidly fluctuating loads like spot welders, cranes, and injection molding presses.
Design & Standards Trap — Capacitor Voltage Rise with Detuned Reactors: Never use standard 415 V rated capacitors in series with a 7% detuned harmonic reactor on a 415 V system. The 7% series reactor elevates the terminal voltage across the capacitor cans by $1 / (1 - p) = 1 / 0.93 = 1.075\times$, causing continuous operating voltage to exceed 446 V. Installing 415 V capacitors will cause premature dielectric breakdown and catastrophic bulging. Always specify heavy-duty capacitors rated for 480 V or 525 V.

🔌 APFC Panel Detuned Series Reactor Tuning Frequency

Series detuned reactors (\(L\)) are connected with capacitor banks (\(C\)) to prevent harmonic resonance and absorb 5th / 7th harmonic currents:

$$\text{Tuning Factor: } p = \frac{X_L}{X_C} \times 100% \quad (p = 7% \text{ for 189 Hz, } p = 5.67% \text{ for 210 Hz})$$ $$\text{Series Tuning Frequency: } f_r = \frac{f_1}{\sqrt{p}} = \frac{50,\text{Hz}}{\sqrt{0.07}} = 189,\text{Hz}$$ $$\text{Elevated Capacitor Terminal Voltage: } V_{\text{cap}} = \frac{V_L}{\sqrt{3} \cdot (1 - p)}$$

esd-solar-pv-systems-efficiency.body:
Solar Photovoltaic Principles, Cell Technologies, and Topologies

📐 Technical Visual Analysis: Solar PV Systems: On-Grid, Off-Grid, and PV Cell Efficiencies

High Contrast Vector Diagram

Solar Photovoltaic (PV) power systems directly convert solar irradiance into direct-current (DC) electricity via the photovoltaic effect across semiconductor p-n junctions. Rooftop and utility-scale solar PV represents the primary decentralized renewable generation technology mandated under modern energy conservation building codes (ECBC) and green building rating systems.

1. Physics of the PV Cell and Operating Characteristics

A solar cell is essentially a large-area semiconductor p-n junction diode. Photons with energy greater than the semiconductor bandgap ($E_g = 1.12\text{ eV}$ for silicon) excite electron-hole pairs, which are separated by the internal electric field of the depletion region, generating a photocurrent ($I_{{ph}}$):

$$I = I_{{ph}} - I_0 \left[ exp\left(\frac{q(V + I R_s)}{n k T}\right) - 1 \right] - \frac{V + I R_s}{R_{{sh}}}$$

  • Key Operating Points:
    • Open-Circuit Voltage ($V_{{oc}}$): Maximum voltage across the terminals at zero current. Decreases with rising cell temperature by approximately $-0.30%/\text{°C}$ to $-0.35%/\text{°C}$.
    • Short-Circuit Current ($I_{{sc}}$): Maximum current when terminals are shorted. Increases slightly with temperature ($+0.04%/\text{°C}$) and is directly proportional to solar irradiance ($G$, W/m²).
    • Maximum Power Point ($P_{{mp}} = V_{{mp}} \times I_{{mp}}$): The unique operating coordinate where the product of voltage and current reaches its global peak on the P-V characteristic curve.
    • Fill Factor ($FF$): A primary metric of cell quality, defined as $FF = \frac{V_{{mp}} I_{{mp}}}{V_{{oc}} I_{{sc}}}$. Typical commercial silicon modules achieve $FF = 0.75 \text{ to } 0.82$.
  • Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT): Microprocessor-controlled DC-DC converter algorithms (Perturb and Observe P&O, Incremental Conductance) that dynamically adjust the inverter input impedance to extract maximum instantaneous power under varying irradiance and temperature.

2. Comparison of Solar Cell Technologies and Efficiencies

Commercial module efficiencies under Standard Test Conditions (STC: Irradiance = $1000\text{ W/m}^2$, Cell Temp = $25\text{°C}$, AM = 1.5 spectrum):

Technology Substrate & Structure Lab Efficiency Commercial Module $\eta$ Temp Coeff ($P_{max}$)
Polycrystalline (Poly-Si) Multi-crystalline ingot cast 22.3% 16% - 17.5% -0.40% / °C
Monocrystalline PERC Czochralski single crystal + rear passivation 24.5% 20.5% - 21.5% -0.35% / °C
TOPCon (n-type) Tunnel Oxide Passivated Contact 26.1% 22.0% - 23.0% -0.30% / °C
HJT (Heterojunction) Crystalline Si + amorphous Si thin layers 26.8% 22.5% - 24.0% -0.26% / °C

3. Grid-Tied (On-Grid) vs Off-Grid Configurations

  • On-Grid (Grid-Tied) System: Generates synchronized AC power directly fed to internal loads, with excess exported to the utility grid through a bi-directional Net Meter.
    • Anti-Islanding Protection (IEC 62116 / IEEE 1547): The grid inverter must detect loss of grid power and shut down completely within < 2.0 seconds. This is critical to prevent back-feeding the disconnected distribution line, which would endanger utility line workers performing repairs.
  • Off-Grid System: Fully independent of utility power, utilizing an MPPT charge controller, battery storage bank, and off-grid inverter. Essential for remote dwellings or regions with absent or highly unstable grid networks.
Design & Standards Trap — Temperature Derating of Open-Circuit Voltage: Never calculate maximum PV string length using standard test condition voltage ($V_{oc}$ at 25°C). Solar cell voltage increases significantly in sub-zero winter mornings ($V_{oc}$ temperature coefficient is negative, roughly -0.30% to -0.35%/°C). Designing strings to the inverter maximum voltage limit at 25°C will result in fatal overvoltage breakdown of inverter DC input stages during the first cold sunny morning.

esd-solar-pv-domestic-battery-design.title: Design of Domestic Solar PV Systems and Battery Sizing
esd-solar-pv-domestic-battery-design.body:
Residential Solar PV and Battery Energy Storage Design

Designing an off-grid or hybrid residential solar photovoltaic system requires systematic calculation of the daily energy consumption profile, seasonal solar insolation (Peak Sun Hours, PSH), PV generator array sizing, inverter power capacity, and battery storage Ah rating with appropriate Depth of Discharge (DoD) margins.

1. Daily Energy Demand Audit

The total connected load and daily operating hours are audited to calculate total watt-hours per day ($E_d$):

$$E_d = \sum (P_i \times t_i) \quad [\text{Wh/day}]$$

Accounting for system inefficiencies -- inverter efficiency ($\eta_{{inv}} \approx 90% \text{ to } 95%$), battery charge/discharge coulombic efficiency ($\eta_{{bat}} \approx 85% \text{ for lead-acid}, 95% \text{ for LiFePO4}$), and DC cable losses ($\eta_{{wire}} \approx 97%$):

$$E_{\text{req}} = \frac{E_d}{\eta_{\text{inv}} \times \eta_{\text{bat}} \times \eta_{\text{wire}}} \quad [\text{Wh/day}]$$

2. PV Array Capacity Sizing (kWp)

The required DC peak power capacity of the solar array ($P_{{array}}$) depends on the site's average equivalent Peak Sun Hours ($PSH$, typically 4.5 to 5.5 hours/day in tropical regions like India, where $1\text{ PSH} = 1\text{ kWh/m}^2/\text{day}$ at $1000\text{ W/m}^2$):

$$P_{\text{array}} (\text{Wp}) = \frac{E_{\text{req}}}{PSH \times DF}$$

Where $DF$ is the Derating Factor (typically 0.75 to 0.80) accounting for dust/soiling loss (3-5%), module temperature derating (8-12%), manufacturing tolerance, and mismatch loss.

The number of modules ($N_{{mod}}$) is:

$$N_{\text{mod}} = \leftlceil \frac{P_{\text{array}}}{P_{\text{mod_rated}}} \right ceil$$

3. Battery Bank Sizing for Off-Grid Systems

The battery energy storage system must provide electrical autonomy during cloudy or rainy days ($N_{{days}}$, typically 1 to 3 days) without sunlight:

$$\text{Battery Capacity (Ah)} = \frac{E_d \times N_{\text{days}}}{V_{\text{sys}} \times \text{DoD} \times \eta_{\text{bat}} \times k_T}$$

Where:

  • $V_{{sys}}$ = Nominal DC bus voltage (12 V for systems < 1 kW, 24 V for 1 to 3 kW, 48 V for > 3 kW).
  • $DoD$ = Maximum allowable Depth of Discharge:
    • Tubular Lead-Acid: $DoD = 0.50$ (50%). Discharging beyond 50% causes severe sulfation, grid corrosion, and slashes cycle life from 1500 to < 400 cycles.
    • Lithium Iron Phosphate ($\text{LiFePO}_4$): $DoD = 0.80 \text{ to } 0.90$ (80-90%). Delivers > 4000 to 6000 cycles with high thermal stability and zero maintenance.
  • $k_T$ = Temperature correction factor (battery capacity reduces in sub-ambient conditions, $k_T \approx 0.90$ at 15°C for lead-acid).

4. Inverter and Balance of System (BoS) Sizing

  • Inverter Sizing: Inverter continuous power ($P_{{inv}}$) must exceed the total connected running load with a 20-25% safety headroom. Inverter surge rating must handle motor starting inrush currents (typically 3 times continuous rating for 5 to 10 seconds).
  • Array String Configuration:
    • Number of modules in series ($N_s$): Configured such that total string maximum voltage at minimum ambient temperature does not exceed the MPPT inverter max input voltage ($N_s \times V_{{oc}}(\text{cold}) le V_{\text{mppt_max}}$), and string $V_{{mp}}$ at maximum cell temperature remains above the inverter lower MPPT voltage threshold ($N_s \times V_{{mp}}(\text{hot}) ge V_{\text{mppt_min}}$).
    • Number of strings in parallel ($N_p$): Sized to ensure total array short-circuit current does not exceed the inverter max input current ($N_p \times I_{{sc}} le I_{\text{inv_max}}$).
  • DC Protection: DC string fuses rated at $1.5 \times I_{{sc}}$, DC Isolator Switch rated at $1.25 \times V_{{oc}}$ and $1.25 \times I_{{sc}}$, and Type 2 DC Surge Protection Devices (SPD, 1000V DC) are mandatory on both positive and negative poles before entering the inverter.
Design & Standards Trap — Lead-Acid Depth of Discharge (DoD) vs LiFePO4: Never size lead-acid battery banks based on 80% or 100% nameplate capacity. Discharging tubular lead-acid batteries beyond 50% Depth of Discharge (DoD) initiates rapid plate sulfation, destroying active paste and slashing cycle life from 1500 cycles to under 400 cycles. Conversely, LiFePO4 batteries can safely cycle down to 85–90% DoD without degradation, requiring nearly 40% less physical battery storage capacity for the same daily usable kilowatt-hours.
